noticias.texto:
More than 150 Australian artists, including Hugh Jackman, Rebel Wilson and Jessica Mauboy, have backed a Greenpeace-led campaign against Woodside Energy’s proposal to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast.
Woodside, the country’s largest fossil fuel company, describes Browse as “Australia’s biggest undeveloped offshore gas resource”. The oil and gas giant is hoping to win federal government approval to drill more than 50 gas wells about 3km from the Scott Reef area, which is home to more than 1,500 species, including endangered pygmy blue whales.
Actors Jackman, Wilson, Richard Roxburgh and Mia Wasikowska are among prominent Australians who oppose the Browse development on the basis that the proposed gasfield could damage the unique reef ecosystem.
They join musicians Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly, Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker, Tina Arena, Jessica Mauboy, G Flip, Vance Joy, Missy Higgins and Baker Boy in signing an open letter calling on the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, not to approve the development.
The letter – which says the Browse project “would turn Scott Reef into an industrial gas zone with decades of deafening seismic blasting [and] carbon dumping beneath the ocean floor” – was also signed by authors JM Coetzee, Helen Garner, Anna Funder and Diana Reid.
“Drilling at Scott Reef could cause an oil spill up to 30 times bigger than the 2009 Montara disaster, polluting Scott Reef with oil condensate, impacting the Kimberley coastline and even reaching as far as Indonesia,” it continued.
The open letter comes after a supergroup of more than 20 Australian artists – including King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, Barnes, John Butler and Montaigne – last Monday released If Not Now, a musical call to arms about the reef.
The song, a reimagining of King Gizzard’s 2020 track, If Not Now, Then When?, is a collaboration between Greenpeace Australia Pacific, Green Music Australia and p(doom) Records.
Browse, first proposed by Woodside in 2018, would see gas piped about 900km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant, which is adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.
Last month, Guardian Australia revealed that WA’s independent environmental watchdog had sharply criticised the proposal, saying that plans to protect turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.
A draft letter from the Environmental Protection Authority, written in 2023, advised that it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level.
Greenpeace last month nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing, based on its ecological and scientific values.
Modelling by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis suggests that Browse would generate up to 6.8m tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions yearly at peak production, accounting for between 2.9% and 3.7% of Australia’s emissions in 2035.
“Browse gas is likely four times more expensive than existing domestic gas,” the institute found last year, adding that the project “is unlikely to be competitive either domestically or internationally, based on IEEFA cost estimates”.
Matt Roberts, executive director of the Conservation Council of Western Australia, earlier this month described Woodside’s proposal as “extremely concerning”.
“At the end of the day, we don’t need Browse gas. Western Australia has enough gas available to support us through the transition to a renewable future and regional demand for LNG is declining.
“The federal and state governments have enough evidence to reject this disastrous proposal and save Scott Reef, and we expect them to do just that.”
A spokesperson for the national EPA has told Guardian Australia the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.
A Woodside spokesperson said the proposed development “remains subject to a detailed, public and transparent assessment by state and Commonwealth regulators”.
Feedback had helped reduce “the infrastructure footprint around environmentally sensitive areas like Scott Reef – which will not be built on, drilled or mined”, they said.
“Browse is a natural gas and condensate development, not an oil development. References to a potential ‘oil spill’ from Browse are inaccurate.” The spokesperson added that the “longest credible duration of a potential well blowout, while still highly unlikely”, was around 12 hours.

noticias.titulo: ‘Heads should roll’: owner of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in skip bin demands investigation
noticias.resumen: Stuart Ramsey says it is a ‘bloody disgrace’ the gelding was left in waste container while awaiting burial Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast So You Are’s owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup runner’s body was found in a skip at a Sydney tip, insisting “heads have got to roll”. Stuart Ramsey says it is a “bloody disgrace” that the gelding was left in the skip bin while awaiting burial at Sydney’s Cleanaway Lucas Heights resource recovery centre. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
So You Are’s owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup runner’s body was found in a skip at a Sydney tip, insisting “heads have got to roll”.
Stuart Ramsey says it is a “bloody disgrace” that the gelding was left in the skip bin while awaiting burial at Sydney’s Cleanaway Lucas Heights resource recovery centre.
The grisly sight was uncovered by a Sydney man, with online footage outraging the racing industry and anti-horse racing activists alike.
The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, said on Wednesday that the matter “obviously needs to be investigated” but “we expect to get to the bottom of it”.
“We do need better ways of disposing of horses,” Minns said.
The trainer Bjorn Baker’s promising stayer took ill at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia’s most famous race on 3 November.
He was rushed to the REC Equine Specialists veterinary clinic at Horsley Park in Sydney’s west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning.
Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanised under anaesthesia.
Racing NSW said its ongoing investigations had found So You Are was being held temporarily awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.
It is common practice for vets to dispose of equine remains at landfill sites licensed to deal with horse carcasses, and is recommended by the NSW Department of Primary Industries in most cases.
For safe disposal, the carcass should be covered during transportation and buried under at least two metres of soil and a safe distance from water sources. Writing in the Conversation, veterinary sciences post-doc fellow at Charles Sturt university Cathrynne Henshall said the drugs used for euthanasia are slow to break down and poisonous to other animals, and can persist in the tissue of the dead animal for years and leach into the surrounding soil.
While the veterinary clinic has apologised, Ramsey, a renowned breeder who owns the boutique Hunter Valley farm Turangga Stud, wants answers and accountability over the disposal of the five-year-old, which earned $1.4m from eight career wins.
“There should be a full investigation,” he said. “Heads have got to roll – simple as that.
“He was more than just a racehorse. He brought our family together, and to think of the stress the family are under now because of this – it’s a bloody disgrace.
“We took 30-odd people down to Melbourne for the race. So You Are brought us all together, as only a horse can do. It’s very sad that it’s happened.”
REC’s managing partner, Jonathan Lumsden, said the centre had spoken to So You Are’s owners and trainers to apologise.
He said the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial but took “full responsibility” for choosing the service provider and arrangements.
“He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” Lumsden said.
Ramsey, who said he hadn’t been contacted by REC, was not satisfied with their explanation.
“So they should take responsibility,” he said. “It wasn’t the contractor’s fault; it was their fault. They were in charge of the horse.
“They didn’t even give us the option of burying him up at Turangga … they should all be out – gone.
“I don’t mean everyone, but the bosses and the people who’ve made the decisions.”
Ramsey said racehorses were among the best-looked-after animals in the world and spoke of his affinity for So You Are: “He meant so much to us.”
A review into a similar furore in New Zealand, when a horse’s body was dumped at a tip, led to the establishment of a dedicated equine crematorium run by a charitable trust, which opened in 2025.
The treatment of So You Are’s remains has sparked strong criticism from animal welfare groups.
“There is always the option to bury the horse or have the horse cremated,” said the Coalition for the Protection of Racehorses campaign director, Elio Celotto.
“However, it is more expedient to dump the horse at a local tip. This is business as usual for an industry where profit is always more important than sentiment.”
The Victorian Animal Justice party MP, Georgie Purcell, said the case should force the industry to confront serious questions about duty of care.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits from them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.
Racing NSW said “appropriate action” would be taken if any wrongdoing was discovered.
“Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process,” it said.
“That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.”
Baker said he was also left deeply distressed by the handling of the much-loved horse’s remains, adding that they deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.

noticias.titulo: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
noticias.resumen: CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips. A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.
A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit.
But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China.
Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility.
“Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire.
EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations.
He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains.
“Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said.
British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel.
“If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said.
Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts.
“There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said.
While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study.
“It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat.
But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty.
The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit.
Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away.

noticias.titulo: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot
noticias.resumen: Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said. Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
Suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.
Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.
He said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.
But the United States attorney general, Todd Blanche, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Donald Trump.
“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Blanche after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.
“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”
US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.
Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.

noticias.titulo: Israeli parliament elects new speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents
noticias.resumen: Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot , the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu . Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.
They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

noticias.titulo: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say
noticias.resumen: Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes. noticias.texto:
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.
Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.
Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.
Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.
Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”
The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.
The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.
“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”
There has been a sharp rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.
On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta. Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

noticias.titulo: ‘I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl buried in mud. I knew we had to do something’ – This is climate breakdown
noticias.resumen: When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development . The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan , a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan . Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense . Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
- Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan
- Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.
In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.
I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.
We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.
When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.
Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.
The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.
We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.
One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”
It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.
We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.
The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.
A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.
One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.
So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.
Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.
When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.
The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.
The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.
This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.
I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.
There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?
I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.
- This is climate breakdown was put together in collaboration with the Climate Disaster Project at the University of Victoria, Canada. Read more.

noticias.titulo: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody
noticias.resumen: Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said. Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating to espionage.
The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.
“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.
“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.
“Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”
The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.
He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.
US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.
He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.
As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.
Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.
“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.
“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution”.
He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.
“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

noticias.titulo: Shabana Mahmood to launch fast-track training to improve police leadership
noticias.resumen: After damning report into standards at the top of forces in England and Wales, 200 people a year with superintendent potential to be recruited Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say. Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say.
Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor.
“The conclusions of the Police Leadership Commission were candid and eye-opening. Police leadership is inconsistent and, at times, it is frankly inadequate,” Mahmood will say, according to extracts released by her aides.
“This is the consequence of an earlier failure to invest in the development of future leaders.
“This government will address it … through the launch of a new fast-stream programme which will place hundreds of talented recruits on a path towards superintendent.”
Between 2023 and 2025, the police inspectorate graded two forces as inadequate, 13 as requiring improving and no forces as outstanding for leadership.
Also moving the home secretary to act was that eight serving or former chief constables were under investigation for misconduct across the 43 forces in England and Wales.
Mahmood will also mention that Devon and Cornwall was at one stage paying for three chief constables, with two of them at one point suspended.
The new scheme to recruit future police leaders will be open to people from any job and includes those who are not working in law enforcement.
The aim is to put recruits on a five to 10-year path to the rank of superintendent and “build a deeper and broader pipeline” of future leaders, according to government sources.
New future leaders will not need a degree and Mahmood’s advisers believe the scheme brings a “new focus and scale” to reversing the lack of emerging high-calibre police leaders.
Nick Herbert, co-chair of the leadership commission and a former Tory policing minister, said: “The introduction of a leadership fast stream is a significant step towards putting those recommendations into practice, and it is hugely encouraging to see this progress.
Lord Herbert added: “Effective leadership is fundamental to improving police performance, cutting crime and keeping the public safe. The challenges facing policing demand ambitious reform, and we must build on this momentum to deliver lasting improvements to leadership at every level of the service.”
Former Labour home secretary David Blunkett, co-chair of the Police Leadership Commission, said more changes were needed: “It is important that the introduction of fast-stream progression is not presented in isolation from the commission’s wider recommendations for a comprehensive overhaul of leadership competencies and career progression.
“Fast-track must not be seen as an elite mechanism, but rather as an opportunity, much like in the civil service, for those with the ambition and ability to accelerate their progression through the leadership and management ranks.”
The Home Office said the 27 recommendations from the leadership commission are being considered. They include a new national academy of police leadership, and more money for leadership training, with a current spend of about £4m in a service costing £19bn a year.
The main question on chiefs’ minds is how many of the 43 police forces in England and Wales will be culled as part of the government’s planned radical changes.
Mahmood will not reveal how many big regional forces will be set up. The Guardian understands the still-unpublished review she ordered by Bernard Hogan-Howe recommended as few as nine.
But the home secretary’s speech will stress that local policing units will deal with everyday crimes if the changes go through, according to sources.
Police leaders have claimed a lack of money has put forces under strain.
Figures show that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding since March led to a 13% increase in arrests for breach of bail and an 8% increase in arrests so people can be returned to jail, compared with last year.
Police estimate this will cost forces £500m by March next year and fear the figure may rise.

noticias.titulo: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn
noticias.resumen: Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050 Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero. The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets. noticias.texto:
Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.
The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.
In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years.
Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade.
The electric vehicle rules are the single biggest contributor to those climate goals, meaning the government will have to find other major carbon emission reductions, unless it amends the budgets to allow more pollution.
Carmakers must sell a bigger proportion of electric cars each year under the rules, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle.
However, the industry has lobbied intensively for months to cut the headline targets from 80% electric by 2030 to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing that the mandate was putting them under too much financial pressure.
Electric cars were 26.6% of UK new car sales during the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target. However, carmakers are expected to comply with the mandate using a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”.
The committee’s chair, Nigel Topping, wrote to Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, to oppose any reduction of the targets.
Such cuts would, he said, “put the government’s commitment to tackling climate change at risk, miss an opportunity to reduce costs for a typical household by about £800 a year, increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels of oil a year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as our main export markets rapidly transition to electric vehicles”.
Some in government have become alarmed in recent months about the impact the government’s various changes could have on the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments.
The government has just cut funding for installing heat pumps, the second-biggest decarbonisation policy. Burnham has also alienated some Labour MPs by waving through gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield, and considering approval for the massive Rosebank oilfield.
MPs voted earlier this year to approve a new set of carbon reductions for the years 2038-42.
However, the Guardian has learned that one cabinet minister in the Keir Starmer government wanted the government to go back to parliament to scrap those planned reductions and enact a more conservative target instead.
The idea did not come to fruition though, with other cabinet ministers mostly opposed.
An industry source with knowledge of discussions in government said that serious consideration was still being given to changing the carbon budgets in the run-up to the UN’s Cop31 climate conference, subject to parliamentary approval.
The source said it was not clear if the proposal was still being discussed. A government source strongly denied that it was under consideration.
The changes to the mandate also mean the UK is unlikely to meet the carbon budget covering 2033 to 2037.
Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emissions reductions elsewhere, given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans. The policy could also face opposition from the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each of which have their own carbon budgets.
Burnham on Thursday told Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, that he was “proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification” and urged people to choose electric cars and heat pumps.
Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK, said: “The Burnham government cannot talk of climate leadership on the international stage while doing a U-turn on ZEV targets at home.”
Topping added: “Weakening the zero-emission vehicle mandate would miss an opportunity to reduce the cost of living for people, undermine Britain’s competitiveness and leave us more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices.
“People are buying electric vehicles in record numbers because they are cheaper to own than the alternative.
“The mandate gives those up and down the supply chain the certainty they need to invest, supports thousands of jobs, and keeps the UK on track to meet its climate commitments.
“British drivers deserve better than a backtrack on such critical policy.”
The car industry criticised the CCC’s analysis. Mike Hawes, chief executive of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said: “A successful EV transition needs a strong market and a competitive industry.
“The CCC, however, ignores the damaging cost of the targets it defends: billions in unsustainable discounts and millions more in government incentives.
“Contrary to the CCC’s claims, the mandate is deterring local investment, as however much manufacturers export, without a strong local market there is no business case to build here.”
A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phaseout of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets.
“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

noticias.titulo: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat
noticias.resumen: England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said. The head of Ofqual , Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.
The head of Ofqual, Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.
“If you are caught committing malpractice with an important, high-stakes qualification … in extreme cases you can lose the entire qualification which, as I am sure you can imagine, can be life-altering for somebody’s future,” Bauckham told the Press Association.
As coursework submission deadlines near, Ofqual is launching a publicity campaign to make it clear to students that using AI for assessments such as extended essays and failing to declare it will not be tolerated.
Bauckham is also writing to examination boards in England to tell them that exam hall invigilators and supervisors should be trained to spot the “emerging risk” posed by wearable devices during next summer’s exam season.
He said he was increasingly concerned about the potential use of wearable devices during exams, especially those able to access AI.
In a speech to an education conference in Birmingham on Wednesday, Bauckham will say: “It is completely unacceptable for any retailer, online or otherwise, to market items explicitly for the purpose of exam cheating. This has to be challenged.”
Ofqual recorded 2,225 cases of smart device and mobile phone cheating during GCSE, AS and A-levels in the summer 2025 exam season.
Bauckham also suggested that the use of extended essays was under threat because of students’ increased access to AI.
“We will need a radical rethink of the conditions under which it is done and the design of that coursework to make sure it is secure for the future and remains fit for purpose,” he said.
“Unsupervised extended essays, with no other forms of assessment associated with them … the time for that is likely to be quite short now.”
Academic subjects for GCSE and A-levels in England have had little or no coursework for the past decade, but A-level history and English are among those that still allow extended essays.
Bauckham said: “Where we do have extended writing being completed in unsupervised, uncontrolled conditions that is counting for coursework, counting for qualifications, I want … routes to malpractice, routes to cheating, to be closed down.”
Ofqual recorded 100 cases of plagiarism involving AI misuse in GCSE, AS and A-level entries last summer, an increase from 85 in 2024.
Bauckham said Ofqual was considering ways to guard against AI and plagiarism, including greater interrogation of the sources students use.
“It could mean linking the coursework in some formal way to the examination, whether that’s a written or a spoken examination, to make sure that we have a guarantee that students have genuinely done the work and genuinely understand it,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Hundreds protest against Nathan Cofnas talk on DEI at Oriel College in Oxford
noticias.resumen: Students oppose appearance of self-described ‘race realist’ who made plagiarism claims against Jason Arday Hundreds of protesters filled the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to voice their opposition to an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”. The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition from students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment. C
noticias.texto:
Hundreds of protesters filled the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to voice their opposition to an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”.
The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition from students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment.
Oriel, which allowed the Reform society to use a lecture theatre, declined to cancel the booking, saying it had a “statutory duty” to allow the blogger and academic to appear.
Earlier this year, Cofnas was the first to raise accusations of plagiarism against Prof Jason Arday.
Arday died weeks later, having resigned from his post as professor at the University of Cambridge, amid sustained media scrutiny which began with Cofnas’s claims.
The crowds outside sought to block the college’s main entrances, with hundreds chanting “Say his name – professor Jason Arday”, while several protesters held signs reading “Remember professor Jason Arday”.
One of the protesters, a first-year student studying English and German, who declined to give her name, said: “I think, given the situation at Cambridge with Jason Arday and given what happened, that we as an institution would be looking to not replicate that in any way or hinting that we could support that notion, [but] acting as an example in opposition.
“I think [Oxford and Cambridge], as two academic institutions, should be working together to banish this from ever happening again. And the fact that we can’t even act as the example, I think, makes me almost ashamed to be a part of this.”
Tommy, a second-year maths student at Oxford, said: “This is not the first of this kind of event. There was Tommy Robinson and the Oxford Union, and obviously there were protests for that as well. So I think it’s quite a nasty pattern that we’re seeing with these Oxford societies pandering to the far right, which is just really dangerous.”
Inside the lecture theatre, Cofnas was asked if he wanted to apologise to Arday’s family, but he declined. He said the implication behind the question was that “we shouldn’t criticise powerful figures”.
Cofnas added: “I would ask the people at Cambridge University who protected him for three years, who suppressed all criticism … I would ask them these questions,” earning a brief round of applause.
About 40 people made it into the venue, with less than a third of the space filled. Protests outside could be heard throughout Cofnas’s talk. At times some members of the audience appeared disengaged, looking at their phones.
Cofnas spent the majority of an hour talking about the history of what he called the “race equality thesis”, and his reasons for questioning it.
He has previously written that black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment” under a meritocratic system.
Anneliese Dodds, the MP for Oxford East, said she had contacted Oriel College after receiving complaints from constituents.
Dodds said: “Cofnas’ views are both repellent and contrary to the facts. Many of my student constituents have therefore contacted me to express their concerns about the student reform society choosing to provide him with publicity.
“I have written to Oriel College to ask what they are doing to act on students’ concerns about this meeting, including on safety grounds.”
While the protests were largely peaceful, a group of police appeared towards the end of the event to clear protesters from the entrances.
Hannah, a first-year law student, said that the size of the protest was proof that “even if Oxford won’t listen to us and won’t cancel the event, we’re still going to show up and we’re going to show that we won’t let that decision silence us. And we will still show that we don’t approve of this and we don’t want this type of behaviour here.”
Misan Harriman, the photographer and former chair of trustees of the Southbank Centre, said he attended the protest because he was concerned by the “damaging” rhetoric that Cofnas espoused.
“The university has failed all the students, not just the black students, by having them see this as something that could be remotely seen as part of the course of free speech,” Harriman said.
Additional reporting by Stanley Smith and Beatrix Arnold.

noticias.titulo: Tag team: dual waterspouts appear in San Francisco Bay amid stormy weather
noticias.resumen: Phenomenon is not a common occurrence in the Bay area and inclement weather is expected to continue for few days A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region. Two waterspouts – vortexes of air and water mist, essentially tornadoes – cut a sheer streak into the sky, as they spiraled above the bay, according to social media footage capturing the weather phenomenon. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region.
Two waterspouts – vortexes of air and water mist, essentially tornadoes – cut a sheer streak into the sky, as they spiraled above the bay, according to social media footage capturing the weather phenomenon.
While prevalent in the Great Lakes and the south-east Floridian coast, waterspout sightings are not common for the Bay area, according to federal storm data.
The National Weather Service (NWS) confirmed the waterspout occurrence in a special marine warning Monday. Some waterspouts, dubbed “fair weather”, are weak, while others, typically tornadic waterspouts can pose a risk to boaters and coastal areas if they travel on shore.
The inclement weather is set to continue for a few more days. According to an NWS forecast, the Bay area is predicted to be drenched in rain on Tuesday with potential thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday.
A high wind advisory is in place until early Wednesday morning and NWS has issued a coastal flood advisory from early Wednesday until Thursday morning. The two-day storm will bring 1.5in to 3in of rain to most of the Bay area with the northern counties getting up to 4in and the Santa Cruz mountains predicted at 5in.
Elevated tide levels raise the risk of coastal flooding through at least Thursday, according to the agency.
Powerful wind is also forecasted with East Bay Hills expected to see gusts reaching up to 70mph (112 km/h).
After Thursday evening, the showers may subside with some rain lingering over the Pacific and its adjacent inland communities.
The storm is expected to drop 4ft of snow over the Sierra Nevadas this week with NWS warning that mountain travel may become impossible on Wednesday and Thursday.
Owing to the Super El Niño, California is facing a wetter winter than typical, which is poised to bring storms and flooding across the state.

noticias.titulo: Shaken and stirred: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in picking new James Bond
noticias.resumen: Amazon’s executive chair and billionaire founder said he felt there was ‘something special’ about Robert Pattinson Amazon’s founder and billionaire chairman Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. Amazon paid more than $1bn for “creative control” of the Bond franchise last year, striking a deal with the longtime heirs and stewards of the films, shocking fans who worried that Bezos’ takeover would signal an end to the franchise as they knew it. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Amazon’s founder and billionaire chairman Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.
Amazon paid more than $1bn for “creative control” of the Bond franchise last year, striking a deal with the longtime heirs and stewards of the films, shocking fans who worried that Bezos’ takeover would signal an end to the franchise as they knew it.
Bezos said he felt there was “something special” about Pattinson, revealing during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he reviewed several rounds of auditions.
“There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists,” he said. “We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”
He added that he and the film’s director, Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, were initially biased against Pattinson, seeking an unknown talent. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” he said.
Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 and has gone on to star in films including The Twilight Saga, The Lost City of Z and Tenet.
Bezos’ Amazon acquired the MGM studio in an $8.5bn purchase in 2022. Bond fans and film critics have speculated over where Amazon will take the Bond franchise, with industry experts speculating the company may seek to expand the films into a Marvel-style universe of spinoffs.
Amazon has grown into a massive conglomerate in recent years, which includes not only an entertainment arm, but also computing and the company’s original business of online sales. Bezos also separately founded the space exploration company Blue Origin.
Amazon’s surveillance technology has come under criticism as a Guardian investigation this week unveiled that Israel was using its facial recognition tool to surveil Palestinians as part of a larger project to move its data on to Amazon servers.

noticias.texto:
The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official told the Guardian.
Donald Trump nominated Overton – a physician and prominent abortion opponent – in August. Overton has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the agency after a tumultous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the dangers of childhood vaccines.
Republican senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier on Tuesday that he remained undecided about her nomination ahead of a Senate health, labor and pensions committee vote scheduled for Wednesday.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines – including the measles, mumps and rubella shot – “almost disqualifying”. And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine critic.
A prominent reproductive rights group celebrated the White House’s decision to withdraw Overton’s nomination.
Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, formerly Naral Pro-Choice America, said: “Heidi Overton posed a serious threat to the future of medication abortion access. Voters rejected that anti-abortion agenda nationwide, and our members kept the pressure on to tank her confirmation. If Republicans try to rush through another nominee who threatens our healthcare, we’re ready to keep fighting.”
As the head of the FDA, Overton would have overseen the agency that regulates medication abortions. In a 2023 policy brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, Overton said Congress should strictly regulate the abortion pill mifeprestone “to protect women and children”, criticized federal policies that allow for the mailing of abortion pills and wrote that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate health, education, labor and pensions committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor.
Republicans are racing to try to confirm all of Trump’s current nominees before they hand over power to Senate Democrats in January.
Associated Press contributed reporting

noticias.titulo: Man armed with axe accused of destroying US military plane at Shannon airport in Ireland
noticias.resumen: Daithi O’Corrain charged with destruction of US government property, after allegedly smashing gauges and cutting hydraulic lines An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks.
O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan.
He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.
The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules, which had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said.
O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged with causing criminal damage and trespassing.
Manhattan US attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets – and thus our national security – will not be tolerated.”
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends said he disarmed the C-130 in protest against the US’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza.
O’Corrain plotted the attack on 11 April for months, US prosecutors said.
He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking on to the airport’s grounds, prosecutors allege.
O’Corrain subscribed to a phone app that provided live flight tracking and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors added.
He is also accused of trying to contact someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon airport, prosecutors said.
O’Corrain breached the airport’s perimeter at about 4.40 am and broke into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
The document added he used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed.
He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and put ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said: “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism.”

noticias.titulo: Nvidia beats Q3 expectations in first report post-Jensen Huang
noticias.resumen: The AI chipmaker said it doubled its third-quarter revenue and confirmed that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated as CEO after a Chinese spy scandal.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia beats Q3 expectations in first report post-Jensen Huang
November 18, 2026
US AI chip giant Nvidia doubled its third-quarter revenues to more than $115 billion (about €104.59 billion), the company said Tuesday.
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones also confirmed that the board of directors has no plans to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang resigned on Thursday after a string of extramarital affairs came to light, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
What did Nvidia say about the results and Huang?
In a statement on Tuesday, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" as the firm tries to move on from the Huang affair.
"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since she was appointed last week.
She did not address Huang's resignation or the uncertainty surrounding his successor as Nvidia's CEO.
During an earnings call with Nvidia investors on Tuesday, Chairman Jones said the board had "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Huang pitches return after 'outpouring' of support
The results, which exceeded expectations, were announced hours after Huang said he would be willing to return to the company if the board agreed.
After Huang's resignation, tech industry figures such as Elon Musk, as well as US President Donald Trump, called for Huang to be reinstated as part of a campaign called "Bring Jensen Back."
In a post on X — his first public statement since the scandal plunged the company and AI sector into crisis — Huang acknowledged that he had made "serious mistakes in his personal life" and had failed to "live up to the standards expected of everyone at" the company.
Huang also said he had received an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers" for him to return.
Who is Jensen Huang?
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips driving advanced AI models.
Under his leadership, Nvidia grew into one of the world's biggest — and most strategically important — companies.
Nvidia has been at the center of the AI boom that has pushed markets to record levels and spurred economic growth around the world.
Nvidia's chips are critical for training and operating advanced AI systems, making them crucial to governments, the military and the tech industry.

noticias.titulo: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
noticias.resumen: Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.
noticias.texto:
Kosovo: New Thaci conviction reignites debate about justice
November 17, 2026
A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.
Swift response from government
Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.
Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.
His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.
The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."
What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.
The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.
For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.
Government set up working group
After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.
The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."
Parliament considers amending law
In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.
The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.
How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?
"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.
"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.
"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.
'Room for criticism of both sides'
Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."
Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.
"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

noticias.titulo: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
noticias.resumen: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.
noticias.texto:
France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
November 16, 2026
French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.
UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.
Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.
Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.
Son of boxer, head of French football
Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.
He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.
Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."
"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.
If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.
Embattled Infantino
Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.
He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.
