Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.
FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.
Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.
The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.
The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

noticias.titulo: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
noticias.resumen: When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.
noticias.texto:
NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
November 16, 2026
Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.
NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.
But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).
When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.
Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.
It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.
How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?
In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.
On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.
In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.
Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.
That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.
Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.
Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment
The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.
"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.
"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.
Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1
No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.
The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.
We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.
But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

noticias.titulo: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
noticias.resumen: In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.
noticias.texto:
What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
November 16, 2026
After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."
Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. 
How it all started
The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.
Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.
In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."
Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.
In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.
A machismo problem
Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.
Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.
Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.
Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.
In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.
Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.
Questionable lifestyle choices
Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.
Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.
One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.
His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."
Why are all secretaries women?
In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.
Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.
Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.
In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.
In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."
Inappropriate casting
In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."
While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.
If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.
Pattinson as a modern 007?
Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.
Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.
Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."
Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.
This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

noticias.titulo: The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?
noticias.resumen: The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.
noticias.texto:
The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?
November 16, 2026
The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.
This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.
Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.
The normalization of right-wing extremism?
Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."
Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.
Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."
The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:
In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.
According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.
Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.
But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.
The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.
In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.
Controversial distancing efforts within the AfD
If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.
But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.
Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"
Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.
DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.
The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."
Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.
* Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
noticias.resumen: Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.
noticias.texto:
Iran's growing exodus of young talent
November 17, 2026
"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.
Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.
Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.
The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.
"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.
"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."
She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.
Turkey as a stopover
"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."
Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.
Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.
According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.
A US naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.
The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.
The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.
She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.
"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."
Young Iranians lose faith in the future
The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.
A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.
The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.
Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.
Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.
Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.
"That's my dream of a better future," he said.
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
noticias.resumen: The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.
noticias.texto:
COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
November 16, 2026
COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).
The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.
Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.
'Deep concern' over breaching 1.5C target
"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.
The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."
Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.
"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.
"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.
Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."
Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.
Climate finance central to talks
Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."
"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.
Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.
Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.
"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."
"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.
"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.
Draft shows 'seriousness' on major issues
At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.
"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."
But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.
"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."
David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.
"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."
Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.
Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

noticias.titulo: Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms
noticias.resumen: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.
noticias.texto:
Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms
November 16, 2026
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.
"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.
But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.
"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."
If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.
Asia backtracks despite Infantino scandals
That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.
It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.
Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.
Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.
Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.
Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.
Tashima and Vega, the early candidates
The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.
"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."
But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.
UEFA still searching for unity candidate
In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".
But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.
While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut
noticias.resumen: The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut
Published November 16, 2026last updated November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- Friedrich Merz and Markus Söder push for electricity tax cut after it failed to make it into budget last week
- Manuela Schwesig is voted in for another term as state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
- An AfD chocolate Saint Nicholas has put Christian leaders' noses out of joint as advent approaches
- NRW leaders head to ground-breaking ceremony as the A44 autobahn's 'bridge to nowhere' near Düsseldorf will finally be linked up to the network
- German national team gears up for evening Nations League match against neighbors and rivals Netherlands
Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.
Thank you for reading
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!
Wirtz and Co., demolish Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League quarterfinal match-up
Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.
It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.
Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.
Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."
Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.
Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.
By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.
Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.
"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."
READ — Germany to join other EU states in announcing Rwanda return hub
A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.
The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.
Tesla planning €3BN investment in German factory to produce Cybercabs
Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.
The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.
The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.
"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.
READ — Germany's Klopp wants Infantino out at FIFA
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.
Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.
Manuela Schwesig confirmed for another term in Meck-Pomm
Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.
The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.
The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.
She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).
Merz says he believes electricity tax cut will be agreed this week
While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.
"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.
Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."
He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."
Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.
Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."
After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."
He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."
Markus Söder: Cutting electricity tax key for 'credibility'
Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.
It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.
Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.
Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."
He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.
"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."
Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."
AfD chocolate Saint Nicholas in party's fan shop upsets religious leaders
A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.
Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.
The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.
"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."
Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.
Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.
The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.
He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."
"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.
All welcome at Bavarian politician Aiwanger's funeral, partner says
The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.
Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.
"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.
She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.
Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.
Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.
Germany's Nations League fate at stake against Netherlands
Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.
And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.
If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.
Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.
"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."
A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.
Work starting to link A44 'bridge to nowhere' to road network
The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.
Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.
A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.
State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.
A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.
The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.
The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.
Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.
Merz heads to Munich for CSU meeting
Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats(CDU).
No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.
The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.
It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.
Manuela Schwesig set for vote on new term as regional leader
The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.
The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.
The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.
But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.
Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.
The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.
Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.
Welcome
Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).
This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.
Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.
And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.
The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.
Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

noticias.titulo: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
noticias.resumen: In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?
noticias.texto:
A growing alliance wants to leave fossil fuels behind. Can it deliver?
November 16, 2026
This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.
But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.
They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).
What happened in Santa Marta?
Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.
The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.
Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.
What role will the 'coalition of the willing' play at COP?
A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.
Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.
It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.
"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.
She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.
One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."
She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.
The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.
This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.
Few countries have announced national TAFF plans
Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.
Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.
Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.
The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.
The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.
The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.
Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.
Focus on electrification
This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.
Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.
A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.
Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.
One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.
The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.
Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.
"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

noticias.titulo: US criticises Ukraine's 'deep strike' campaign against Russia
noticias.resumen: German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the US' warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine."
noticias.texto:
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the US' warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine."
A senior US defence official has criticised Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia, saying they had been ineffective in bringing the war to an end and arguing that, in some cases, they had likely "hardened the Russian public's resolve."
"Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line," Under Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby said while speaking from NATO's headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday.
"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," he continued.
He added that support for Kyiv moving forward should focus on "enabling and advancing Ukraine's ability to hold the line of battle and where possible make gains."
Ukraine has increasingly struck targets deep inside Russian territory as the war has gone on, using its burgeoning drone technology to carry out long-range attacks.
Ukrainian forces have particularly looked to target energy infrastructure such as oil refineries and terminals, as well as military sites like air bases, as they have sought to hamper the Russian economy and hit Vladimir Putin's war machine.
US President Donald Trump has previously demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were to blame for rising diesel fuel prices.
'Quite a stupid thing'
Colby's comments have drawn pushback from some European officials.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."
The comments came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy once again urged allies to speed up deliveries of interceptor missiles.
"Ukraine needs Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from the stocks you already have right now," he told the meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels via video link.
"And I ask the United States – please, do not delay these deliveries," Zelenskyy added. He also said Ukraine needed a further 40 F-16 fighter jets to help boost its air defences.
The pleas come as Ukraine gears up for what looks set to be another brutal winter under heavy bombardment from Russian forces.
Russia has repeatedly sought to ramp up attacks on Ukraine in wartime winter periods, targeting the country's energy sector as Moscow has attempted to break its resolve.

noticias.titulo: Five viral moments from Pope Leo XIV's South American tour
noticias.resumen: Pope Leo XIV's South American tour brought several memorable moments, from an unexpected encounter with a flying rosary bracelet to a helicopter journey into Peru's remote Andes.
noticias.texto:
Pope Leo XIV's South American tour was marked by a series of memorable moments.
In Peru, the pope travelled by military helicopter and jeep to reach the remote Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
During a visit to Lima, an enthusiastic devotee accidentally struck him in the face with a rosary bracelet thrown from the crowd. The pontiff rubbed his eye but continued greeting people before stopping to bless a baby.
In the Peruvian Amazon city of Pucallpa, Leo called for justice for Indigenous leaders killed while defending their territories. He also condemned deforestation and river pollution, warning against the irresponsible exploitation of natural resources.
During a youth vigil in Buenos Aires, Argentina, where 1.3 million people attended the event, the pope warned young people against lying, betraying or humiliating others to gain approval on social media.

noticias.titulo: GTA 6: What to know about the upcoming Grand Theft Auto game
noticias.resumen: Grand Theft Auto VI is generating huge excitement across Asia, despite restrictions on sales, censorship and the dominance of mobile gaming. While the game is not officially licensed in mainland China and faces content restrictions in Japan, fans are finding ways to access the franchise.
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto, better known as GTA, is one of the world's most successful and controversial video game franchises. Its sixth instalment is due to launch on 19 November, with excitement spreading across Asia despite censorship, restrictions and a gaming market dominated by mobile phones.
Created by Scottish studio Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games, GTA is an open-world action-adventure series. Players take on the role of criminals in fictional versions of American cities, where they can explore freely, steal cars, take part in high-speed chases and complete missions involving organised crime.
The games combine action and storytelling with satire of American society. Their depictions of violence, crime and sexual content have also made the franchise controversial.
The previous instalment, GTA V, was released in 2013 and became one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 230 million copies, according to its publisher.
Now, more than a decade later, anticipation is building for GTA VI. The new game returns players to Vice City, a fictional city inspired by Miami, Florida.

noticias.titulo: Dead Melbourne Cup racehorse found dumped in Sydney waste facility
noticias.resumen: REC Equine Specialists said So You Are had been euthanised before being collected by a "contracted provider" and taken to a "licensed landfill." The practice has apologised and said the horse should have been "promptly and respectfully buried."
noticias.texto:
REC Equine Specialists said So You Are had been euthanised before being collected by a "contracted provider" and taken to a "licensed landfill." The practice has apologised and said the horse should have been "promptly and respectfully buried."
A dead Australian racehorse has been found dumped in an industrial waste facility in Sydney, two weeks after finishing eighth in the prestigious Melbourne Cup.
The body of So You Are was found by a member of the public, who posted a video of the discovery on social media.
"That can't be normal. Does anyone know if that's legal?" Gregg Jowett said in the footage. "I'm disgusted by that."
Trainer Bjorn Baker announced on Monday that the thoroughbred had died following a "severe bout of colic."
"He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved."
Baker posted a later statement saying he was "deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains."
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death," he said, adding that he understood that the REC Equine Specialists veterinary practice had launched an investigation into the incident.
REC has apologised for the "distress" caused by the footage and said So You Are should have been "promptly and respectfully buried."
The practice said the horse had been euthanised under anaesthesia before being collected by a "contracted provider" and taken to a "licensed landfill."
"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry," it added.
The company said it had stopped using the provider "effective immediately."
Racing NSW, the regulating body in the state of New South Wales, said that under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, "a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process," per Australian media.
It added that a process was now underway to "determine what steps can be taken to ensure this cannot happen again."

noticias.titulo: US strikes targets in Qeshm Island after Iranian mines hit five ships in Hormuz
noticias.resumen: Iran says the US military carried out several attacks on Qeshm Island in southern Iran, while at least five ships were set on fire by mines in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the day.
noticias.texto:
Iran says the US military carried out several attacks on Qeshm Island in southern Iran, while at least five ships were set on fire by mines in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the day.
Iranian officials said the US military conducted airstrikes on Qeshm Island in southern Iran on Tuesday evening, with locals reporting at least five explosions.
Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan, told the official IRNA news agency that the US strikes did not caused damage to residential or commercial districts, adding that "the situation on Qeshm Island is under control and all relief, service and executive bodies are on full alert."
Iranian news agency IRNA reported that "the sound of five to six explosions was heard in the city of Qeshm," while the semi-official Fars news agency wrote quoting "residents of Qeshm Island" that the sound of several explosions were heard north-west of the city of Qeshm. with smoke billowing at the same time.
US officials confirmed late Tuesday that US fighter jets struck Iranian missile launch sites on the island, in the same pattern as over the previous days, in retaliation for Iran’s targeting of US personnel and assets.
The US airstrikes follow multiple incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, in which at least five ships hit naval mines while sailing through what Iran calls "unauthorised" routes in the waterway.
“Safe passage requires coordination with the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran, transit through designated safe zones, and having navigation systems switched on,” the Iranian army announced in a statement.
Iran claims downing of US military drone
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Tuesday that it shot down a US MQ-1 Predator reconnaissance and combat drone in the southern waters of Iran, near Qeshm Island. According to the Guard, this would be the eighteenth drone of this type that its forces have destroyed.
The IRGC said in a statement it used a "new advanced air defence system" which allegedly tracked and destroyed this drone at 13:45 local time.
Earlier on Tuesday, the IRGC claimed said it carried out a drone attack against a US radar system at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Airbase. Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, and US' Central Command (CENTCOM) said that they intercepted the drones, without any damage.
The IRGC said the attack was carried out in response to "repeated violations of Iran’s airspace by US military drones".
Since the start of the Iran war in February, Tehran has tried to restrict traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and has insisted that ships pass only along routes that the Islamic Republic has authorised.

noticias.titulo: Russia cannot have a say over NATO's military activities, Norwegian foreign minister warns
noticias.resumen: Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told Euronews that Moscow must not be allowed to dictate Europe's security arrangements while also warning against a return to spheres of influence.
noticias.texto:
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told Euronews that Moscow must not be allowed to dictate Europe's security arrangements while also warning against a return to spheres of influence.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide has warned that Russia cannot have any say over NATO's military activities within its own territory, pushing back against Moscow's demands to reshape Europe's security order as diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.
Speaking to Euronews, Barth Eide insisted that Europe's existing security architecture did not need to be renegotiated and that sovereign countries must remain free to choose their own alliances.
“We're not happy about this language about architecture,” he said. “We believe that we have a European security architecture. There was nothing wrong with it until Russia violated it.”
Barth Eide added that no deal should be imposed on Kyiv without Ukraine’s consent. “There should be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine."
He said discussions with Moscow following a ceasefire could address arms control, verification mechanisms and confidence-building measures, drawing on precedents established during the Cold War.
The minister also warned against any agreement between the world's major powers to carve up the globe into spheres of influence, invoking the legacy of the 1945 Yalta Conference.
“The last thing we want would be an agreement between great leaders to divide the world between them,” he said. “These kinds of spheres of interest should be a thing of the past.”

noticias.titulo: French foreign minister slams Lavrov accusations about 'direct participation' in Ukraine war
noticias.resumen: Russia said on Tuesday it was aware of French troops deployed to Ukraine, calling it "direct participation" in the war and saying a message had been issued to Paris. France has rejected the claim troops are directly involved in fighting as "absurd."
noticias.texto:
Russia said on Tuesday it was aware of French troops deployed to Ukraine, calling it "direct participation" in the war and saying a message had been issued to Paris. France has rejected the claim troops are directly involved in fighting as "absurd."
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot has denied allegations of direct participation in the war in Ukraine, in response to comments made by Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Tuesday.
He said that France was not involved in a military operation, but in "training and maintenance, carried out far from the front lines, with very limited scope and no involvement in warfare", in an interview with French talk show "C à Vous".
He added that the majority of training had taken place in Poland.
"We support the Ukrainian army and the Ukrainian resistance, and this is the least we can do, given that it is a people fighting for their independence and democracy, on the doorstep of Europe", he stated.
Barrot also accused the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party Jean-Luc Mélenchon of "relaying Russian propaganda", after the presidential hopeful shared an X stating "Alert. We must under no circumstances become a co-belligerent in Ukraine."
Barrot's comments come after Lavrov told reporters that "foreign military personnel" had been in Ukraine "for more than six months. And not just the French."
Lavrov declared that Russia had communicated concerns "through available channels", informing relevant countries that this amounted to "direct participation in the war, including target designation assistance, satellite data provision, and other forms of support."
His remarks follow revelations by French media, based on revelations from a source who disclosed that soldiers had been deployed on a secret training mission in Ukraine for several months to train personnel and help maintain equipment.
The source said the mission of a small contingent of French troops excludes any combat role. Speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity, they described the rotation of "French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine" as a reality.
"But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions", said the source.
Earlier on Tuesday, Deputy defence minister Alice Rufo told parliament that there was a "very limited" deployment of French troops in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance.
She added that was no "intention to fight, contrary to what the Russian foreign minister said this morning, which is absurd."
In November, the European Council adopted a decision extending the mandate of the European Union Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine(EUMAM Ukraine) for a further two years, with a budget allocation of nearly €300 million for this period.

noticias.titulo: EU climate chief Hoekstra: Electrification key for Europe to compete with China as COP pushes global target
noticias.resumen: Hoekstra tells On the Record that electrification is key to Europe's industrial competitiveness, as COP talks push for a global target of 35% by 2035.
noticias.texto:
Hoekstra tells On the Record that electrification is key to Europe's industrial competitiveness, as COP talks push for a global target of 35% by 2035.
The European Commission's proposed U-turn on its 2035 ban on new petrol and diesel cars does not give Brussels carte blanche to roll back its climate ambitions, Wopke Hoekstra has told Euronews.
In an exclusive interview with Euronews' On the Record, the EU's climate chief defended the Commission's decision to give the automotive industry greater flexibility as a way to protect European manufacturers while keeping the transition to electric vehicles on track.
His comments come as Europe's car industry struggles to remain competitive amid high energy costs and growing pressure from international rivals.
German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has announced plans to halt investments in Germany and is weighing plant closures, amid similar challenges facing Volkswagen, Stellantis, BMW and Volvo.
Hoekstra rejected calls for further concessions on the 2035 targets, including those backed by the European Parliament, arguing that additional flexibility risks undermining both the EU's climate ambitions and the competitiveness of European manufacturers as Chinese electric vehicle makers gain ground.
"Significantly loosening the targets of 2035 is exactly not what the Commission did," he said, defending the proposal as a compromise between climate action, industrial competitiveness and energy independence.
He also argued that further loosening the targets would do little to help European manufacturers, warning that the industry risks falling further behind if it slows its transition to electric vehicles while Chinese competitors continue to advance.
"I am not convinced that loosening the targets further (...) will be in the interest of European car makers," he said.
Electrification as a competitive edge
Hoekstra has also doubled down on efforts to electrify the European economy as he leads the bloc's negotiating team at this week's COP climate conference in Turkey.
The summit aims to establish a global target of 35% electrification by 2035, a goal backed by the EU. Brussels argues that accelerating electrification would also strengthen European competitiveness, pointing to China's major push to electrify its economy and expand its electric vehicle industry.
