noticias.titulo: India lodges complaint against Palestinian footballer after under-17 match
noticias.resumen: Palestinian player Taha Soueidan 'deeply surprised' by criticism following accusations that he made a racist gesture.
noticias.texto:
India lodges complaint against Palestinian footballer after under-17 match
Palestinian player Taha Soueidan ‘deeply surprised’ by criticism following accusations that he made a racist gesture.
Indian football’s governing body has lodged a complaint with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) over an alleged racist gesture made by a Palestinian player towards India’s captain during an under-17 qualifying tournament.
The All India Football Federation (AIFF) asked the AFC, on Wednesday, to “review the incident, examine the available match footage, and take appropriate action under the applicable regulations” during the teams’ match in the qualifying stage for the AFC Under-17 Asian Cup 2027.
“AIFF considers any form of racism or discriminatory behaviour extremely serious. There is no place for racism or discrimination in the game, and such behaviour must not be accepted or tolerated,” the organisation said in its statement.
The incident occurred during a qualifying match for the 2027 AFC U-17 Asian Cup between Palestine and India in Kuala Lumpur. India won the match 4-1.
Match footage showed Palestinian midfielder Taha Soueidan fanning himself as he walked next to Indian captain Dallalmuon Gangte on the pitch.
It has been deemed a racist gesture by the AIFF but Soueidan denied the accusation and said the reaction on social media took him by surprise.
The 15-year-old, who plays for FC Union Berlin’s under-17 team in Germany, said he approached Gangte to “assure him that I had never intended to offend him” after being made aware of the social media furore.
Soueidan said he was “deeply surprised by the wave of criticism and accusations” as he acknowledged the incident late on Tuesday.
“There was no dispute, confrontation, or exchange of offensive words between us. The gesture was simply a spontaneous reaction to the discomfort I was experiencing due to the high humidity in Malaysia, weather conditions that I am not accustomed to,” Soueidan wrote in a post on Instagram.
“I also encourage anyone seeking clarification to speak directly with Dallalmuon himself and ask whether I made any racist or offensive remarks towards him during the match, or whether there was ever any dispute or confrontation between us,” Soueidan said.
He added that both teams are staying in the same hotel and have had “friendly and respectful” interactions with each other. “I firmly reject racism in all its forms, and I am saddened that a spontaneous and innocent gesture has been interpreted in this way,” he said.
Indian football club Northeastern United FC said it was “deeply concerned” by the incident involving Gangte, who plays for them, and supported AIFF’s decision to lodge a complaint with the AFC.
“Every young footballer deserves to step onto the pitch knowing they will be treated with dignity and respect,” the club said in a statement on Wednesday.
“We are proud of Gangte and the way he leads his country. He has the full support of his club.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Palestine Football Association (PFA) for a comment on the incident but had not received a response when this article was published.
The AFC has not acknowledged AIFF’s complaint publicly and did not reply to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Palestinian player shown red card for aggressive tackle
Earlier during the match, another Palestinian player was involved in a disciplinary episode after being shown a red card for a harsh tackle on an Indian opponent.
Mohammed Jamhour appeared to kick Raj Singh Wahengbam twice while attempting an aggressive tackle in the first half. Jamhour grabbed and pulled Wahengbam’s shirt, kicked him in the shin after he fell, and then stamped on his arm.
He was immediately shown a red card by the referee as Indian players ran towards their teammate who was still lying face-down on the pitch.
Following the match, the Palestinian team’s coach Yousef Sharbaji apologised on behalf of his player and, recalling the episode, said “there was no reason to do that”.
The qualifying matches for next year’s tournament continue this week.
India lead Group E with three wins in as many matches, while Palestine are second with two wins and a loss. Both teams will play their final group match on Friday.

noticias.titulo: Tim Hortons accused of sharing user data with firm linked to Israeli army
noticias.resumen: Research into Tim Hortons’s app finds that it began transmitting information to Forter as soon as it opened.
noticias.texto:
Tim Hortons accused of sharing user data with firm linked to Israeli army
Research into Tim Hortons’s app finds that it began transmitting information to Forter as soon as it opened.
The application of the popular Canadian coffee chain Tim Hortons has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertechnology company founded by former members of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200 intelligence division, according to a Canadian advocacy group.
Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) identified Forter as the third-party company receiving data from the app after a recent investigation by the CBC News broadcaster that raised concerns about the app’s data collection and sharing practices.
CBC News did not identify the recipient in its report.
The CJPME said on Tuesday that it contacted Joel Reardon, a computer science researcher at the University of Calgary whose findings informed the CBC investigation, to establish the identity and location of the company.
The research into Tim Hortons’s app found that it began transmitting information to an overseas third party as soon as it was opened.
Extensive information transferred
The data included unique device identifiers, camera specifications, lists of device sensors, and the names of users’ ringtones and alarm sounds. It also included the names of nearby wi-fi routers, which Reardon told the advocacy group could be used to determine a user’s location.
Researchers said the information could be used to create a digital fingerprint of individual devices.
Israel has been facing growing international isolation over its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.
Tim Hortons said its app collects information for fraud prevention, account protection and payment abuse prevention and not marketing or advertising. The company also said neither it nor the third-party recipient of its app data sells users’ personal information.
Forter’s founders – Michael Reitblat, Liron Damri and Alon Shemesh – are alumni of Unit 8200, Israel’s signals intelligence and cyberwarfare division. The company says it uses machine learning technology to identify potentially fraudulent transactions, flaunting that its expertise draws from Israeli military intelligence.
Mass surveillance on Palestinians
Unit 8200, the largest single military unit in Israel, has faced scrutiny over its role in mass surveillance of Palestinians in occupied territory.
Microsoft last year barred the unit from using its technology after discovering that its systems had been used for surveillance operations against Palestinians.
“Canadians ordering coffee should not have their unique and sensitive user data shared with an Israeli cyber-tech company whose infrastructure was built by alumni of a foreign military intelligence agency engaged in human rights violations,” said Michael Bueckert, the CJPME’s vice president.
“The company’s ties to an Israeli military unit that oversees the mass surveillance of Palestinians pose significant ethical issues, raising alarm bells for anyone concerned about cyber-security. Tim Hortons must cut ties with this company immediately,” he added in a statement.

noticias.titulo: Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
noticias.resumen: The NYT faces backlash over report suggesting a possible link between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities.
noticias.texto:
Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
The New York Times faces backlash over report suggesting a possible link between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities, raising fears US could use the claims to target vital infrastructure.
A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators warning the report could help justify further attacks on civilian facilities.
The controversy comes as Washington threatens renewed military action against Iran, following months of war that have already left the country’s energy facilities, bridges, water infrastructure and other civilian sites damaged.
“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a post on X.
The newspaper has defended its reporting, insisting it accurately represented the views of its experts.
However, several experts quoted by the publication have publicly challenged the implications of the investigation, questioning the evidence behind the proposed link between dams and military installations.
The controversy has also revived memories of the NYT’s reporting in the lead-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, when the paper’s journalists helped amplify claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that later proved unfounded.
What did the NYT report say?
Published on Tuesday, the story, headlined “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason”, examined whether Iran’s extensive network of dams, pipelines and water-transfer projects could be connected to its underground missile programme.
The report cited researchers who observed geographical similarities between the locations of dams and sites targeted by US and Israeli air strikes.
According to the report, some of the water and military experts the NYT spoke to concluded that the “water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup”.
However, the newspaper itself acknowledged, “Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.”
Why is the report causing a backlash?
Critics fear that portraying dams as potentially serving military purposes could provide a justification for attacking infrastructure essential to millions of civilians.
US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have damaged oil facilities, power plants, water reservoirs, bridges, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened further attacks, saying last week that key Iranian infrastructure could be destroyed within three days.
Political analyst Rami Khouri called the NYT report “troubling”, saying it reaffirmed his concerns about US mainstream media being “complicit in the US-Israeli criminal attacks on Iran, just as it was during the war on Iraq decades ago and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”.
“The telltale sign of non-credible wobbly journalism is when conditional words like ‘speculative’, ‘suggestive’, ‘may have developed’, ‘may shed light’, ‘suspect’, and ‘long-term riddle’ occur more often than any definitive, evidence-based facts.”
Khouri said it was “not definitive and verified reporting” and “another attempt to support the US-Israeli urgency to find any reason to carry out more war crimes against Iran” by attacking critical infrastructure.
“Another sad day for US mainstream journalism,” he added.
Why is the story falling apart?
Aside from online criticism from readers and commentators, experts cited in the story have themselves come out against aspects of the report.
Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University’s water institute and a former senior Iranian environmental official, one of the experts cited in the story, challenged the report’s reasoning.
“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” he wrote on X.
“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles! This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure. The New York Times should know better.”
Madani also questioned the newspaper’s claim that seven experts had supported its analysis. “I’m one of the people quoted in the article, but my comments had nothing to do with dams or missiles!” he added.
Nima Shokri, a water-security expert at Hamburg University of Technology, whose research featured prominently in the investigation, also issued a clarification.
“The proximity of dams to military targets does not establish why those dams were built, nor does it justify attacks on them,” he said on X.
A third researcher quoted in the article echoed Shokri’s comments.
“I fully agree [with Shokri],” Amir Aghakouchak, a water expert at the University of California, Irvine, wrote on X, sharing Shokri’s X post.
“Dams and water infrastructure are essential to civilian life and must never become targets of military attacks. Regardless of their location or potential strategic significance, their primary roles in water supply, food security, energy, and environmental sustainability must not be overlooked. Protecting these critical resources should be a priority, regardless of politics or conflict.”
The newspaper rejected accusations that its investigation could provide a pretext for military attacks.
“Our report on Iranian dams accurately cited research and analysis by seven international experts on Iran’s environment and military presence,” spokesperson Nicole Taylor said.
She added that the NYT’s journalists had sought to explain Iran’s infrastructure investment and the effects of US and Israeli attacks on civilians.
“Framing the independent reporting as a pretext for violence is dangerous,” Taylor said.
One of the story’s co-authors, Sanam Mahoozi, said that “neither I nor our report endorses or justifies attacks on dams or other infrastructure”.
“As a journalist, I welcome rigorous, constructive criticism, but I hope some users will critique the report fairly, based on what was actually written,” she posted on X. The story was co-written with Erika Solomon, the NYT bureau chief for Iraq and Iran.
What has Iran said?
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish”, accusing what he suggested was pro-Israel media of promoting narratives reminiscent of the run-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.
“Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it,” he wrote on X.
Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, accused the newspaper of preparing the ground for further attacks on civilian infrastructure.
“New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” he posted on X.
Why are people questioning the NYT’s credibility?
The controversy has revived widespread criticism of the newspaper’s reporting before the US-led invasion of Iraq, when claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction helped build public support for war.
Judith Miller, a former NYT journalist, was among the reporters whose coverage amplified claims about Iraq’s weapons programmes that subsequently proved unfounded.
In September 2002, Miller co-authored a report claiming Iraq had intensified its pursuit of nuclear weapons, citing US officials who alleged that Baghdad was seeking aluminium tubes for uranium enrichment.
Former Vice President Dick Cheney cited the newspaper’s reporting on aluminium tubes to bolster President George W Bush’s administration’s case against Iraq. The claims were later discredited.
Two months after the invasion of Iraq began in March 2003, Miller co-authored a report citing that US intelligence agencies had concluded that two mysterious trailers found in Iraq were mobile units to “produce germs for weapons”.
However, a year after the US war on Iraq began, the NYT acknowledged serious shortcomings in its reporting on the build-up to war, including its reliance on Iraqi defectors and exiles seeking regime change.
“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” it said.

noticias.titulo: Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
noticias.resumen: Anguish caused by conflict sees a growing number of young people turn to drugs.
noticias.texto:
Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
Anguish caused by conflict sees a growing number of young people turn to drugs.
Khartoum, Sudan – Mohammed Awad never imagined that his life would change so dramatically when war broke out in his home city of Khartoum in April 2023 when he was aged 17.
He found himself displaced and forced out of school, moving from one state to another accompanied by his cousins and searching for a safe place where he could escape the horrors of war.
But what began as a journey in search of safety became the beginning of a personal tragedy, one experienced by millions of people in Sudan who are in the midst of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in which killing and displacement have become routine.
“I started taking drugs to forget what I have seen and the horrors I have been through in Khartoum during the first months of the war. My friends and my cousin were killed in front of me,” he told Al Jazeera. “I am trying to recover now, so I can proceed with my education and life.”
The conflict between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group saw the capital become one of the initial epicentres of this power struggle between the two former military allies.
The war trapped thousands of people in Khartoum State in their homes for weeks or forced them to flee, but since the SAF expelled the RSF from the region in May last year, it has now become a haven for millions of people fleeing fighting elsewhere in Sudan. The war has led to a humanitarian catastrophe with at least 59,000 people killed and 14 million people forced to leave their homes in a country with a population of 52 million. Displacement is more than the simple act of moving from one place to another but a journey marked by fear, anxiety and instability with increasingly limited options in life.
For those such as Awad caught in the pressures of displacement and the absence of a supportive environment, drugs have become a way of dealing with an unbearable reality.
“I entered rehabilitation centres many times, and I quickly returned to addiction. I take pills and sometimes weed. I want to stop, but I keep failing over and over again,” Awad said.
The war in Sudan has not only severely impacted individual civilians’ lives but has also torn apart the social fabric of the country. The lack of security and poverty have also led to a proliferation of drugs manufacturing and trade, particularly the highly addictive amphetamine Captagon. According to government officials, areas currently or formerly under RSF control are a particular problem.
Treatment and care
The Qadreen Center for Addiction Treatment is one of the few charitable institutions dealing with the problem in Khartoum, and doctors in the capital told Al Jazeera there is growing demand for their services.
“The centre continues to provide its medical services both before and after the outbreak of the war,” the centre’s director, Lubna Ali, said.
“Following the war, it witnessed a significant increase in the number of cases seeking treatment amid growing needs for mental health and addiction recovery services.”
Since the war has broken out, the centre has treated 10,100 cases ranging from patients in need of psychological support for war-related trauma to those with drug addiction. Ali said 135 such individuals have been treated “in their recovery journey”.
Young people are particularly affected by the war, witnessing horrific violence, displacement, the loss of friends and relatives, interrupted education and quickly declining employment opportunities.
Weakened institutions and a deteriorating security situation have undermined oversight efforts and the ability of health services to respond to the addiction crisis.
Dr Aisha Almobasher, a psychiatrist at the Bitmakaly National Organization, which provides psychological and therapeutic support to individuals affected by war and addiction, told Al Jazeera that some areas of Sudan are worse affected by the drug problem than others.
“The growing number of people seeking treatment suggests that this is more than a passing phenomenon. Many of those struggling with addiction come from areas previously controlled by the Rapid Support Forces, RSF, where, following their withdrawal, drugs reportedly became more widely available and trafficking networks expanded,” she told Al Jazeera.
“In some states, drugs also became a means of attracting and recruiting young people, particularly into the ranks of RSF fighters, drawing many of them onto a dark path.”
Drug seizures
According to a report published by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker in March, 19 incidents involving the seizures of drugs or manufacturing facilities were recorded in Sudan from 2015 to 2025 with a notable acceleration since the outbreak of the war.
These figures refer to seizures and estimated production capacity not actual drug consumption. Nevertheless, they reveal the scale of the problem and the transformation taking place in the country’s illicit drug trade.
Major-General (Legal) Mohamed Al-Moatasim Okasha, director of Sudan’s General Directorate for Anti-Narcotics, said its teams have dealt with an increase in drug manufacturing and production since the war began.
They have found advanced drug production facilities in areas retaken from the RSF by the SAF, including areas in and around Khartoum. El-Radom, an area in South Darfur State in western Sudan, has become a well-known cannabis-growing region, he said.
“It remains under RSF control and is expected to return to the control of the Sudanese armed forces soon. Throughout the past three years of war, antinarcotics operations in this area have been suspended with no other authority able to effectively address the problem due to its inaccessibility under RSF control,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Meanwhile, the use and circulation of other narcotic substances have been increasing, particularly Captagon, crystal methamphetamine (ice) and drugs such as tramadol. However, these substances remain less widespread than cannabis and other traditionally prevalent drugs.”
A huge facility for manufacturing Captagon pills was recently discovered by the SAF north of Khartoum, close to an oil refinery that was formerly under RSF control.
SAF forces uncovered drugs manufacturing equipment valued at about $3m. The facility was capable of producing 100,000 Captagon pills per hour with raw materials potentially able to produce 700 million pills.
“These are not merely allegations of drug trafficking, smuggling or distribution. They are evidence of industrial-scale drug production taking place in areas that were under RSF control,” Okasha told Al Jazeera.
“As for drug use among combatants, there have been reports and testimonies indicating that quantities of narcotic substances were found in the possession of captured militia members. This highlights how widespread these substances have become and how readily accessible they are to fighters.”
Drug trafficking and manufacturing have become weapons of war, not just illicit sources of income, and they are directly impacting the conflict between the SAF and RSF, he said. Captagon has become a regional issue with facilities producing the drug in Syria during the rule of former President Bashar al-Assad flooding the illicit market.
While the new government in Damascus is trying to crack down on these facilities in southern Syria, Captagon production is a growing problem in other regional conflict areas such as Sudan.
“Sudan faces this growing threat amid the ongoing conflict,” Okasha said. “Through strong nationwide coordination, we are intensifying seizures and disrupting smuggling, trafficking and production networks. Our mission is to stop the spread of narcotics, protect our youth and safeguard future generations. Combating drugs is a national security priority.”
“The drug problem in Sudan cannot be viewed in isolation. It is a regional challenge, and Sudan is part of a region experiencing a growing drug crisis.”

noticias.titulo: What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
noticias.resumen: Deutsche Bank leaks expose ties to Trump, Epstein, and global elites amid scrutiny over past financial misconduct.
noticias.texto:
What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
Files show Epstein-linked payments at $582m, far more than previously known, and tie Trump business dealings to suspected money laundering networks.
A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerful figures.
The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation, published on Tuesday by a consortium of international news outlets, has put Germany’s biggest bank back in the spotlight after years of trying to rebuild its reputation following its failures to prevent money laundering.
Here is what we know:
What was leaked and how did it happen?
Files containing millions of emails, minutes of meetings and internal reports were leaked by two whistleblowers whose identities and links to the institution have been withheld for their protection, according to Le Monde, one of the participating news outlets. The pair told the media groups they believed the bank was engaging in criminal activity and that releasing the documents was in the public interest.
An Indian journalist and a South African journalist obtained the cache, then shared it with more than 230 reporters from about 50 news organisations, including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and The New York Times, in an internationally coordinated effort.
The material includes some nine million emails, as well as meeting minutes, due diligence reports and financial crime reports dating back to the early 2010s, many of them from the bank’s internal investigations.
The whistleblowers also passed the data to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities, and could be eligible for a reward if Washington prosecutes the bank based on their leaks. Le Monde said the whistleblowers were not paid by the journalists and placed no conditions on how the material was used.
Deutsche Bank said concerns raised by the investigation “date back many years” and that it had since strengthened its controls, adding that it did not expect any meaningful financial impact. The bank’s chairman reaffirmed the board’s support for chief executive Christian Sewing, who has run the institution since 2018.
“Deutsche Bank is a different bank today,” the bank said in a statement.
What do the leaks reveal about Trump?
The files identify more than $3m in transactions involving Trump-owned companies, including payments linked to suspected Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks.
Deutsche Bank extended loans to Trump for years, even after a string of bankruptcies and defaults at his businesses from the early 1990s. By January 2021, it was his biggest creditor, with about $340m in loans to his company outstanding.
That month, following the January 6 assault on the US Capitol by protesters wanting to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s win in the presidential election, the bank ceased doing business with him, according to The New York Times. Trump had claimed the election had been rigged against him, of which there has never been any proof.
The Financial Times reported that the bank inadvertently sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term in office, and never told him about the error. Asked about the disclosure during his visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit on Tuesday, Trump said the bank should not have released that information.
“They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his remarks.
The leaked records also reveal special monitoring that the bank applied to Trump’s accounts, and its handling of them has drawn scrutiny before.
In 2019, The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank had failed to alert US authorities to suspicious transactions linked to Trump. The bank said at the time that none of its investigators had been prevented from escalating such concerns.
What do the leaks reveal about Epstein?
The leaked files list about $582m in transactions linked to Epstein, which were flagged internally as suspicious. That is more than double the amount previously identified as being overlooked or not reported by banks during US Senate investigations. When the Senate findings were released in August, a Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank regretted its “historical connection” with Epstein.
Epstein, who was a US financier, became a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, and remained a client until 2018. He died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
Internal emails in the newly leaked cache indicate that senior executives approved Epstein as a client despite his conviction, and kept his accounts open even after warnings about the activities of Ghislaine Maxwell, his former girlfriend and associate. Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein sexually abuse teenage girls. She is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The files also reveal information about payments linked to wealthy Epstein associates such as private equity billionaire Leon Black and Wall Street financier Glenn Dubin.
A review commissioned by Black’s firm previously found he had paid Epstein $158m between 2012 and 2017 for tax and estate planning advice. Black has sought to distance himself from Epstein, repeatedly denying wrongdoing or any knowledge of his abuse of girls and young women.
The leak comes years after the bank paid fines and settlements of more than $200m over its handling of Epstein-related finances. In 2020, regulators fined it $150m for compliance failures linked to Epstein and other high-risk clients, finding that he had held more than 40 accounts at the bank. In 2023, it agreed to pay $75m to settle a suit brought by women who alleged they had been abused by him.
Who else is named in the leaks?
The documents also detail Deutsche Bank’s business dealings in Russia up until Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite concerns raised by some managers.
They include previously undisclosed internal warnings about the bank’s continued dealings with wealthy Kremlin-connected clients despite sanctions and money laundering concerns.
Those named include Russian billionaires Roman Abramovich, the former owner of English football club Chelsea, and aluminium tycoon Oleg Deripaska. Both men were sanctioned by the United Kingdom in 2022. Suleiman Kerimov, another billionaire whose name appears in the files, was sanctioned by the US in 2014 and 2018.
Transactions associated with Rifaat al-Assad, the uncle of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, also appear in the files. Rifaat, who died in January, was convicted in France in 2020 of acquiring millions of euros’ worth of property with funds diverted from the Syrian state.
Other files concern figures connected to the Sarkozy-Libya affair, in which former French President Nicolas Sarkozy was convicted in 2025 of criminal conspiracy over efforts to secure funding for his 2007 campaign from the government of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

noticias.titulo: Why Democrat Mary Peltola’s US Senate win in Alaska matters
noticias.resumen: Peltola’s Alaska win gives Democrats 56 Senate seats and a buffer in Republican states ahead of the 2028 elections.
noticias.texto:
Why Democrat Mary Peltola’s US Senate win in Alaska matters
Peltola’s Alaska win gives Democrats 56 Senate seats and a buffer in Republican states ahead of the 2028 elections.
Democrat Mary Peltola has won the United States Senate seat in Alaska, unseating two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. It is the Democrats’ first US Senate win in the state in more than a decade.
As of early Wednesday, The Associated Press news agency’s count gave her 50.1 percent of first-choice votes against Sullivan’s 45.8 percent, with an estimated 99 percent of votes counted.
Clearing the 50 percent mark matters. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a candidate who wins a majority of first-choice votes is elected outright, with no further rounds of counting.
The vote has been closely watched, not just because it is the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections, but because of a Republican legal challenge to the election over the listing of two candidates with nearly the same name – Republican Dan Sullivan and independent Daniel Sullivan. The legal challenge was thrown out just days before the election.
The Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Dan Sullivan to divide Republican votes in the state – a practice known as “ballot stacking“.
But on Tuesday, it was clear that even if the “official” Dan Sullivan had received all the votes of his namesake, he would not have gained enough to beat Peltola.
Peltola’s win brings Democratic control of the Senate to 56 seats, against the Republicans’ 44.
Who is Mary Peltola?
Peltola, a Yup’ik Alaskan, became the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress when she won a special election for the state’s sole House of Representatives seat in 2022. She served from September 2022 to January 2025, losing her re-election bid in 2024.
On the Senate campaign trail this year, she played down her Democratic label, which remains unpopular in the state, and focused on local issues such as energy jobs, border security and gun rights.
Scott Lucas, a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told Al Jazeera that Peltola is viewed as a “safe pair of hands”.
“Alaska is a very small population, with a very, very large landmass, so it’s very important that you try to build up, across that large landmass, ties and community ties,” he said. “Peltola was seen as someone who had represented Alaska’s interests very well.”
Lucas described her as “a pragmatist, very much in that centre line of Democratic politics”. “Not too provocative, doesn’t really play identity politics,” he said. “She didn’t play on the idea this is all about Native Americans, even though she happens to be a Native American.”
Sullivan, by contrast, “was tarnished because he was there on Trump’s ticket, as it were”, Lucas said, though “he was very much a local candidate”. “Had the Trump administration done a better job on the issues, then I suspect Sullivan holds his seat,” he added.
Why was this race so tense?
For one, it was the last Senate seat to be counted.
But also, there were two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
In late May, Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, entered the race. On June 15, the state elections division removed him from the ballot. It said he had chosen the name to cause confusion with the senator, and pointed to his use of a political consultant who had previously worked for Peltola.
The courts reversed that decision. A superior court judge ruled he was eligible, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling on June 29. The two candidates appeared on the ballot as “Daniel J Sullivan Jr”, with no party affiliation, and “Dan S Sullivan”, Republican and incumbent. The retired teacher finished in the top four of the August primary, earning a place on the November ballot.
Republicans claimed he was a decoy. The New York Times later reported that Peltola campaign staff and Democratic operatives had worked to get him to contest. At Trump’s urging, the Department of Justice (DoJ) sued to delay certification if Senator Sullivan lost and to separate ballots cast for his namesake. Federal Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on November 1. The DoJ said it would appeal.
Lucas said this kind of “ballot stacking” – backing a minor candidate to pull votes from a rival – is not uncommon, and both parties have engaged in it in the past. If the second Sullivan had taken 2 percent of the vote, he explained, he could have pushed the incumbent below the 50 percent mark and forced a ranked-choice count. “You drain enough support from the Republican that you give yourself a better chance of winning,” he said.
In the end, he said, “I don’t think it made that much of a difference.” AP’s count gave Daniel J Sullivan Jr 1.7 percent, and Peltola won more than 50 percent of the vote.
Why is this result significant?
Peltola is the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since Sullivan unseated Mark Begich in 2014. Her win is not a deciding factor in which party controls the chamber – Democrats already had enough seats to control the Senate – but Lucas said it is “significant in a wider context”.
Alaska is the latest in a string of Republican strongholds to switch to Democrats.
On election night, Democrats flipped seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. Later-arriving counts then confirmed that Mississippi had flipped, electing its first Black senator in 150 years, and now Alaska has taken the tally to nine.
Texas went Democratic for the first time since 1988, and Kansas for the first time since 1932.
“Alaska was one of the seats that it was thought that the Democrats might win,” Lucas said. “So that in itself is not as surprising as, say, Mississippi, which is really, really surprising. South Carolina was quite a surprise as well. But still, it reaffirms the extent of this Democratic surge.”
Those wins also give Democrats a buffer. Senators serve six-year terms, with about one-third of the 100 seats contested every two years, so the seats won this month will not be on the ballot again until 2032. By holding seats in states they would not normally carry, Democrats can make it much harder for Republicans to retake the Senate in 2028.
Finally, the win brings Democrats closer to the magical two-thirds majority. They now hold 56 seats, which Lucas called “a pretty good majority when even the most optimistic analysts regarding the Democrats were looking at 53 seats at most”. They will still need Republican support on issues to secure the two-thirds majority needed to overturn a presidential veto in both chambers.
A two-thirds vote in the Senate is needed to convict an official in an impeachment trial. The more seats Democrats hold, the fewer Republicans they need to win over to reach that threshold. For now, Lucas said, “They cannot pass legislation because Trump can veto it. So they still have to try to work with Republicans if they want to get any legislation across.”
What happens next?
Lucas expects the new Democratic majorities to propose legislation and hold hearings on accountability, “whether that be with respect to AI and technology, whether it be with respect to the Epstein case”, or the wealth of Trump and his family, including through cryptocurrency. “Meanwhile, the Republicans are a fractured party,” he said.
In North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, Trump’s inner circle imposed candidates on the party, and all three were lost. Democrats, by contrast, “went for more organic candidates, and Mary Peltola was one of them”, Lucas said.
“Diversity has become a bad word with the Trump camp,” Lucas said. “It’s interesting that in this very diverse election, you have your first US Muslim senator, you have your first US openly gay man in the Senate, and you have two Native American women who have won: Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and then Peltola. In this case, it was the party with the diversity of candidates that did better.”
Lucas predicts “a fairly chaotic couple of years, primarily because of the executive”, with Democrats needing to “show that they can provide some at least potential for stability” before the 2028 presidential race. Rising health insurance premiums and disputes about data centres, which have proved unpopular in part because of the drain they impose on local resources, are among the next tests.
“This isn’t really a right-versus-left issue any more,” he said. “This is an issue of who governs effectively when they’re in office.”

noticias.titulo: Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way
noticias.resumen: Separate regional conflicts are increasingly linked by the interests of rival powers.
noticias.texto:
Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way
Regional conflicts and emerging alliances are creating a global confrontation that international institutions are failing to contain.
Many commentators in the Middle East and the West warn that the world is witnessing the early stages of another world war. I disagree, at least if we are talking about a war on the scale of the two world wars fought in the last century. Nuclear deterrence makes such a conflict all but impossible.
The United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France, the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), all possess nuclear weapons, as do India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel. Iran may yet join them. An all-out war involving these powers would produce neither victors nor vanquished, but destruction on a scale that could threaten civilisation itself.
Yet while a world war in the traditional sense may be impossible, a different kind of global conflict is already under way. Some longstanding disputes and rivalries have already erupted into war, while others threaten to do so. Much as in the years preceding World War II, competing national interests are driving countries into opposing camps.
The alliances that emerged during World War II were shaped by the ambitions and strategic interests of the countries involved. Hitler’s Germany sought territorial expansion and revenge for its defeat in World War I. Mussolini’s Italy pursued imperial ambitions, while Japan sought to expand its dominance over China and Southeast Asia. Together, they formed the core of the Axis powers. Britain and France stood against them, later joined by the Soviet Union following Germany’s invasion in 1941 and the US after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor. Despite their different political systems and objectives, these countries were ultimately brought together by their interests and the threats they faced.
The question today is whether we are witnessing a similar alignment of interests among the world’s major powers, particularly among nuclear-armed states. Could Russia, China, North Korea and Iran form a bloc capable of confronting the US and its allies, and could their regional conflicts become part of a wider global war fought with different weapons and methods?
Russia
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, it appeared that US-led capitalism had triumphed. But under President Vladimir Putin, Russia has sought to rebuild its economic and military strength and reclaim its position as a global power. Despite abandoning communism, Moscow has once again emerged as a rival to the West.
The war in Ukraine is therefore far more than a conflict between two neighbouring countries. It is a confrontation between Russia and Europe, while Washington’s position has shifted from President Joe Biden’s efforts to weaken Moscow to the reluctance of his successor, Donald Trump, to regard Ukraine as a vital US interest or Russia as a principal adversary.
This is already one front in a wider global conflict. On one side stand Ukraine and Europe; on the other, Russia, supported by China, Iran and North Korea, which see its defeat as a threat to their own interests and regional standing.
China
China’s economic and military might represents the greatest challenge to the US and the West. Its economy is already the world’s second-largest, and many expect it to overtake that of the US within a decade or so. China has successfully used the tools of free-market capitalism championed by Washington to its own advantage, flooding US and global markets with its products and securing a major commercial victory.
Although Beijing has largely avoided direct military involvement in international conflicts, preferring diplomatic support for Russia and the Palestinian cause, as well as engagement on trade, development and climate change, Taiwan remains a major unresolved objective.
The principle of “one China” and the goal of bringing Taiwan under Chinese control, much as Hong Kong was returned to China, remain central to Beijing’s ambitions. If China decides to make this objective an immediate priority, it could trigger a major political and potentially military confrontation between China and its allies on one side and the US and its allies on the other.
North Korea
North Korea’s nuclear arsenal makes the Korean Peninsula another potential flashpoint in a wider global conflict. Despite its economic superiority, South Korea faces a serious military threat from the North.
Any confrontation between the two Koreas could quickly become an international crisis. Historically, Korea was a battleground for competing powers. Following Japan’s defeat in World War II, the peninsula was divided into Soviet and American occupation zones, which subsequently became two states: one backed by China and the Soviet Union, and later Russia, and the other by the West. A renewed conflict could therefore draw in these powers and become another front in a wider global confrontation.
Iran
Iran’s far-reaching ambitions are rooted partly in the legacy of the Persian Empire. Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Tehran has also sought to export its sectarian ideology, fuelling divisions and conflict among Muslims.
More importantly, Iran’s pursuit of nuclear capabilities is regarded by the US and Israel as a direct threat, particularly to Israel. The continuing cycle of military confrontation, diplomatic brinkmanship and economic sanctions is pushing Tehran towards an increasingly clear alignment with China, Russia and North Korea.
A world war fought in parts
Although other rising powers, including Brazil and India, must also be considered, the clearest emerging alignment places China, Russia, North Korea and Iran on one side, and the US and Europe on the other, despite the weakening of political and ideological ties between Washington and its European allies.
As for Japan, despite its longstanding tensions with China, I doubt it would be prepared to participate directly in a regional or global conflict, given its bitter experience of World War II and the atomic bombings it suffered.
I therefore do not believe we are heading towards an all-out world war in the traditional sense. Instead, we are witnessing what might be called “piecemeal wars”: a series of regional conflicts, some already raging, such as the war in Ukraine and the confrontation involving Iran, the US and Israel, and others that remain unresolved, such as the Taiwan question and the tensions between the two Koreas.
Taken together, however, these seemingly separate conflicts amount to a global war, one being fought piecemeal rather than through a single, openly acknowledged confrontation between opposing blocs.
The collapse of international safeguards
There is another factor making the current international situation particularly dangerous: the declining authority of the UN, including the UNSC.
Throughout the Cold War, these institutions helped contain crises that might otherwise have escalated into wider wars. The leaders of that era also understood the devastating consequences of a global conflict, particularly given advances in conventional and nuclear weapons.
Unfortunately, the UN’s authority has steadily eroded. Its weakness became glaringly apparent when the US invaded Iraq in 2003 on the spurious pretext that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, disregarding the UNSC and proceeding without its authorisation.
Today, the UNSC has effectively surrendered its authority over the Palestinian question to President Trump and his so-called Board of Peace. Yet this body has failed to implement even one of the 21 provisions intended to restore peace to Gaza. Instead, under its watch, what was a Palestinian-Israeli war in Gaza has given way to continuing Israeli aggression against civilians in the enclave, the occupied West Bank, Jerusalem, Lebanon and Syria, without any meaningful deterrent.
In my view, the paralysis of the UN today resembles that of the League of Nations on the eve of World War II. Perhaps the clearest illustration of this failure is the disregard for the decisions of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. Those responsible for genocide in Gaza face none of the accountability imposed on war criminals in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo or conflicts in Africa.
The international community must therefore strengthen the institutions and mechanisms designed to protect international peace, giving them the authority and effectiveness they need to prevent a wider collapse of the international order.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: As Trump arrives in China, low expectations for breakthroughs in rivalry
noticias.resumen: Analysts expect few concrete outcomes from talks between the leaders on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
noticias.texto:
As Trump arrives in China, low expectations for breakthroughs in rivalry
Analysts expect few concrete outcomes from talks between the leaders on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
For more than a year, the United States and China have maintained an uneasy truce in their intense technological and economic rivalry.
As US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for his third meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping since hitting pause on the US-China trade war last year, expectations for major breakthroughs are low.
At the Shenzhen airport, Xi greeted Trump — Chinese presidents rarely welcome visiting guests when they land — even as journalists travelling with the US president waited on Air Force One.
Yet despite the red carpet welcome, analysts expect few concrete agreements out of Trump and Xi’s meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
Instead, the two leaders are expected to focus on stabilising ties between Washington and Beijing at a time when their differences are in full view amid claims that chip giant Nvidia’s former CEO was targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.
Trump and Xi each benefit from “projecting a sense of having things under control in the US-China relationship,” said Ryan Hass, director of the John L Thornton China Center at Brookings.
“I do not expect that dynamic to change in the coming period,” Hass told Al Jazeera.
“Their ability to continue to guide the relationship will be challenged in the coming year, though, since they will not have as many opportunities for direct leader-level diplomacy as they did in 2026,” he added.
Ahead of the talks, Trump has sought to downplay the controversy surrounding Nvidia, which revolves around former CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Megaspeed executive accused of being a Chinese spy.
The scandal has highlighted tensions within the Trump administration over China’s access to AI chips amid suspicions that Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore, diverted Nvidia GPUs to the country in violation of US export controls.
On Monday, US prosecutors confirmed that it had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed amid recriminations over the US Department of Commerce’s failure to place the firm on its export control list.
“We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump, who will also join an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at APEC, told reporters on Monday.
Beijing has denied the spying claims, calling them “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”.
Rana Mitter, S T Lee Chair in US-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, said he expected “little mention” of Nvidia in public.
“China denies involvement, and Trump has stated that he doesn’t intend to raise it,” Mitter told Al Jazeera.
“Also, the US administration is still divided on the best course of action,” he said.
“Overall, the Trump administration will look to maintain the current detente, but the underlying competition remains strong.”
Renewed trade war
Trump and Xi have held three face-to-face meetings aimed at lowering the temperature in the US-China rivalry since the US president kicked off a renewed trade war against Beijing upon his return to the White House.
Amid tit-for-tat trade salvoes, tariff rates for Chinese and US goods rose as high as 145 percent and 125 percent, respectively, until Trump and Xi agreed to a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, in October last year.
The truce is currently set to expire on January 10, 2027, after Washington and Beijing agreed to extend the agreement beyond its original expiration date of November 10.
Speaking at the opening of the two-day APEC summit on Wednesday, Xi reiterated Beijing’s opposition to protectionism and unilateralism, urging countries to support “free and open trade and investment” and “inclusive and balanced development”.
“The primary focus of this meeting is the management of risks among major powers; it does not aim to produce any groundbreaking, sweeping agreements,” Wang Wen, dean of the School of Global Leadership at Renmin University of China in Beijing, told Al Jazeera.
“China’s primary expectation is to steer major power relations back toward a path of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence, preventing a slide into a Cold War-style bloc confrontation,” Wang added.
While Trump and Xi’s September meeting in Washington was heavy on pomp and ceremony, it produced only a handful of tangible outcomes, apart from the truce extension, including commitments to establish a communication channel for AI-related security incidents and lower tariffs on $60bn worth of goods.
Among the major outstanding areas of contention is China’s restriction of rare earth exports to the US, which remain about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, said the once “reasonably high” expectations for the talks had been dimmed by recent events.
“Now, particularly with the midterm election results and Nvidia fallout, if they manage to shake hands without incident, it will be viewed as a win,” Elms told Al Jazeera.
“Part of the issue on the US side is growing uncertainty about US positions. The Nvidia chip movement has broken open disagreements among Trump’s own team,” Elms said.
With a new crop of US lawmakers entering Congress in January, Elms added, “there is also no clarity on what the Democrats might want to see happen and I think the returning Republicans are also less clear about how closely to align with Trump on China”.
With Trump and Xi only expected to talk for about two hours, they will have much less time to hash out issues than during previous meetings and are unlikely to announce an extension of the trade truce at the summit, said Dennis Wilder, a former US national security official who is now an adjunct professor at Georgetown University.
“There are many protocol events, thus the time is very limited to a few topics,” Wilder, who worked on China at the CIA and the White House’s National Security Council, told Al Jazeera.
“The Chinese will voice their concerns over new export controls on high technology, the US will voice concerns that China is not lifting up to agreements on agricultural imports and rare earth exports,” Wilder said, adding that discussions would likely address AI generally but not touch on the Nvidia scandal.
“Trump’s goal is to continue the strategic stability that he and Xi announced at the Washington summit,” he added.

noticias.titulo: Photos: Thousands march in Haiti in support of Salvadoran troops
noticias.resumen: Haitians take to the streets to praise El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and his soldiers for fighting gangs in their country.
noticias.texto:
In Pictures
Photos: Thousands march in Haiti in support of Salvadoran troops
Haitians take to the streets to praise El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and his soldiers for fighting gangs in the country.
Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections of the capital.
Protesters on Tuesday carried signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele”.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from El Salvador went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The latest Salvadoran deployment, although separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought additional reinforcements to combat the gangs.
Bukele’s hardline crackdown on gangs in El Salvador has broad public support but has drawn accusations of human rights violations.
On November 10, he claimed to have destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs, releasing video footage of a helicopter attack.
Since then, Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have taken control of a football stadium in the capital.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to prioritise the protection of civilians and to use lethal force only as a measure of last resort.
In the first 10 months of this year, the UN recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deepening political and security crisis, with gangs tightening their grip on the country through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.

noticias.titulo: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia to open forum for players, rules out probe
noticias.resumen: Cricket Australia says it will establish a forum, likely led by a former judge, but there will be no new sanctions.
noticias.texto:
Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia to open forum for players, rules out probe
Cricket Australia says it will establish a forum, likely led by a former judge, but there will be no new sanctions.
Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening an investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal but said it would launch an independent forum for players to share their version of events as a “circuit breaker”.
Festering wounds over what happened in the third Test at Cape Town eight years ago reopened last week when Usman Khawaja released his autobiography.
In the book, Khawaja alleged the whole team knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing, an allegation strenuously denied by current captain Pat Cummins.
A Cricket Australia probe at the time concluded that only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were in the know, with all three sent home in disgrace and banned.
Warner, who has backed Khawaja’s version of events, over the weekend accused Cricket Australia of conducting “a shoddy investigation”, claiming not all players had been interviewed.
Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said the past week had been an “incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved”.
However, speaking in Hobart ahead of Australia’s one-day clash with England on Wednesday, Greenberg was adamant that “the investigation has been completed” and ruled out making it public, citing confidentiality.
“We’ve got almost everyone’s version of events, and they differ markedly,” he said.
“This is the greatest challenge with this project is people’s version of events at the time differ substantially, and we have to give enormous respect for each individual.
“Looking for the perfect truth doesn’t exist, and we’re not chasing that,” he added. “We’re giving people the opportunity to have their version of events played into a safe place.”
Interim chairman David Boon said instead that a forum, likely led by a former judge, would be established.
But there would be no new sanctions coming out of it.
“After careful discussion, we agreed to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and their perspectives,” he said.
“We believe it is time for a circuit breaker. This is not about litigating the past. It is about giving the opportunity to those involved to have their voices heard.
“Australian cricket is at its strongest when we’re united, and we owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together with understanding, respect and perspective.”
‘Game needs to move on’
Cricket Australia (CA) would not commit to making public the contents of the forum, which it hopes can be wrapped up within a month.
“We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, while at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward,” Greenberg said.
He denied the forum was to appease Warner, who has been vocal in his support of Khawaja.
“This is not about appeasing any individual. This is about the game; it’s about the sport,” Greenberg said.
“The game needs to move on somehow from this. These events were eight years ago. They caused enormous pain and hurt for lots of people, and are doing it again now.
“And at some point we have to move forward. And we can’t move forward without putting some of the steps in place.”
Greenberg, who took over at Cricket Australia in 2025, said the governing body also had to take some responsibility for the environment that existed in the team in 2018.
“You’ve heard a number of times through different players that the culture at that time was quite toxic,” he said.
“It was a difficult dressing room. It was a win-at-all-costs mentality, and that doesn’t just start with a group of players. It comes from an entire organisation.”
Warner said he agreed there should be no new sanctions for anyone involved, but would prefer to have an open inquiry.
“I would’ve liked an open inquiry, and the people that were there at the time actually can come forward and speak,” he said while commentating on the Australia-England match.
“It’s not about penalties. It’s about transparency and accountability – which Todd’s acknowledged, on CA’s behalf, about the culture at the time with the players and CA.”
Khawaja, also on commentary for the match, said he welcomed a “safe space to chat”, but voiced concern that it would be behind closed doors.
“The biggest question I have is [that] the board makes the decisions of what comes out at the end,” he said.
“How is that an actual way of trying to present what people have said?
“I can go in there and say something, but then the board can decide they’re not going to release that.”

noticias.titulo: India-UK ties outride Modi’s ‘decolonisation’ rhetoric
noticias.resumen: Prince William's visit highlights growing partnership between New Delhi and London, despite their colonial history.
noticias.texto:
India-UK ties outride Modi’s ‘decolonisation’ rhetoric
Prince William and Princess Catherine’s visit this week highlights the growing partnership between New Delhi and London, despite their colonial history.
Delivering a lecture in November 2025, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke of the lingering legacy of British rule that the country suffered for two centuries. Though India gained independence in 1947, it still needed to “decolonise the mind,” he said, laying out a decade-long plan to achieve this goal.
But on Wednesday, almost exactly a year after those comments, Modi will host Prince William and his wife, Catherine, the Princess of Wales, in New Delhi, after they also visited Mumbai — playing street cricket alongside Indian legend Sachin Tendulkar to kick off a three-day visit to India.
The British royals, visiting India for the first time in a decade, are attending the Earthshot Prize ceremony, one of the most prestigious environmental awards in the world, founded by William.
Modi’s conversation with the royals is expected to focus on the deep bonds, past and present, between their nations — a reality that analysts say is more powerful than the rhetoric politicians turn to.
The prime minister’s residence is no longer on Race Course Road: Modi renamed the street Lok Kalyan Marg (Public Welfare Street in Sanskrit). Several landmarks and towns named after British colonial-era figures across the country have been renamed under Modi, as have the country’s British-era criminal and penal codes.
Yet beyond that symbolism, India’s relations with the United Kingdom have blossomed over the decades, just as India’s bureaucracy, legal and political systems still remain rooted in institutions set up by the British.
Under Modi, New Delhi has also pursued increasingly close economic ties with London, culminating in a landmark free trade agreement that came into force in July.
“I don’t see an inherent contradiction. India has been moving away from its colonial legacy while building a relationship with Britain ever since 1947,” academic Jaideep Prabhu told Al Jazeera.
“I believe that a more confident India can reclaim its historical narrative while engaging Britain as an equal. The relationship can acknowledge the past without being defined by it,” Prabhu, professor of business and enterprise at Cambridge University, added.
Strategic interests
Economic and strategic interests are at the heart of the growing partnership that has seemingly taken precedence over the countries’ complicated history.
Britain’s search for new trading relationships following Brexit has made India an increasingly important partner, said Kate Sullivan de Estrada, associate professor in international relations of South Asia at the University of Oxford.
“As a post-Brexit UK has honed in on global trade and investment opportunities, pursued defence and technological cooperation, and sought partners to address global challenges such as climate change and health, India has emerged as an increasing priority in almost all areas of UK foreign policy,” de Estrada told Al Jazeera.
Echoing de Estrada, Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, said Britain’s post-Brexit ambitions, including its growing focus on the Asia Pacific, have converged with India’s economic and strategic priorities.
“Both are trying to transform their shared colonial legacy into a foundation for positive engagement, particularly through deeper economic integration and diaspora linkages,” he told Al Jazeera.
In July 2025, the relationship reached a notable high when Modi and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a multibillion-dollar trade agreement, which came into force a year later.
The agreement is expected to increase bilateral trade by £25.5bn ($33bn) annually in the long term, according to British government estimates, by reducing tariffs and removing barriers across a range of industries. Trade between the two countries had already reached nearly £48bn ($63bn) in 2025, reflecting the growing economic stakes for both sides.
Oxford’s de Estrada said the agreement also reflected growing global trade uncertainty, particularly following US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, which encouraged both countries to diversify their economic relationships.
Beyond trade, India and Britain have also increased cooperation in areas of defence and security, as well as emerging technologies and clean energy.
In October 2025, London and New Delhi signed a $465m deal to supply India’s military with UK-manufactured lightweight multirole missiles built in Northern Ireland.
That same month, India’s Ministry of External Affairs announced that New Delhi and London had agreed to establish centres for connectivity, innovation and artificial intelligence, alongside a critical minerals industry group aimed at strengthening supply chains and advancing green technologies.
But Cambridge’s Prabhu noted the relationship between India and the UK is defined by much more than “ties between governments”, pointing to longstanding cultural, sporting and historical connections, as well as Britain’s large Indian diaspora.
“Britain’s large Indian diaspora is an important bridge between the two societies, while Indian parents continue to invest in a British education for their children. There is also an institutional familiarity, given the similarities in our legal, parliamentary and administrative systems,” he added.
About two million people of Indian origin live in the UK today.
Simmering yet minor tensions
Despite their growing partnership, several disagreements between New Delhi and London continue to flare up from time to time.
“One point of tension is diaspora politics,” Edward Anderson, associate professor at Northumbria University and senior fellow at SOAS, the South Asia Institute, told Al Jazeera.
“India sees its diaspora as a potential ally and asset – the huge rallies Modi has held in New York, London and elsewhere clearly illustrate that. But India simultaneously sees the diaspora as a possible threat and liability.”
One of the most contentious issues involves the Khalistan movement, which seeks the creation of an independent Sikh homeland in India’s Punjab region.
Britain is home to a large Sikh diaspora, including supporters of the separatist movement, whose activities have repeatedly drawn criticism from Indian officials.
New Delhi views Khalistani separatism as a threat to its territorial integrity and has accused British authorities of failing to adequately address the activities of groups it considers extremist.
The issue came to the forefront in March 2023 when protesters supporting the movement removed an Indian flag from the country’s diplomatic mission in London, prompting stern condemnation from New Delhi and the summoning of the UK’s deputy high commissioner in India.
Two years later, in March 2025, a pro-Khalistan protester breached a police cordon during a visit by Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar to London and tore an Indian flag.
Other disagreements have also tested bilateral relations.
India’s human rights record, including its treatment of religious minorities and policies in Indian-administered Kashmir, has drawn criticism from some British politicians and human rights organisations. New Delhi has rejected such criticism as interference in its internal affairs.
According to Cambridge’s Prabhu, these tensions between the countries often arise when “domestic political concerns meet the bilateral relationship”.
“Immigration and access for Indian students and professionals are sensitive issues, as are extradition cases and India’s concerns about potential anti-Indian activities in Britain,” he said.
“Such disagreements matter and should not be dismissed. But the relationship is sufficiently broad that friction in one area need not determine what happens in others.”
‘Building together’
Despite the tensions, analysts say the two governments have developed sufficient shared interests to manage their disagreements.
Oxford’s de Estrada says both sides have demonstrated a willingness to “compartmentalise their differences in pursuit of shared economic and strategic interests”.
“While disagreements over Russia, Pakistan and occasionally the activities of Sikh separatist groups in Britain remain potential sources of friction, neither country appears willing to allow these issues to overshadow the broader relationship.”
Similarly, Cambridge professor Prabhu warned that while a serious security incident or sustained loss of trust could damage the relationship, both governments increasingly recognise the benefits of working together.
“Their expanding cooperation in trade, technology and security gives them strong reasons to manage their differences,” he said.
Moreover, Prabhu said Prince William and Catherine’s visit, with its emphasis on sustainability and innovation, reflects the changing nature of the relationship.
“I see Prince William’s visit in that light,” he said. “Its emphasis on sustainability and innovation symbolises a relationship that acknowledges its history but is increasingly concerned with what the two countries can build together.”

noticias.titulo: Myanmar-linked arsenic pollution prompts clean water scramble in Thailand
noticias.resumen: Thai authorities race to provide safe water to villagers after arsenic from Myanmar mines contaminates Mekong River.
noticias.texto:
Myanmar-linked arsenic pollution prompts clean water scramble in Thailand
Thai authorities race to provide safe water to villagers after arsenic from Myanmar mines contaminates Mekong River.
Thai government authorities have raced to provide clean water for more than 20,000 households in northern Thailand after unsafe levels of arsenic, linked to rare earth mining operations in Myanmar, were found in the water supply.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul late on Tuesday ordered government agencies to find alternative water sources and closely monitor tap water quality in the province of Chiang Rai, according to deputy government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana.
Tap water supplies to thousands of homes in 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times over the safe limit.
Government authorities also found arsenic contamination in untreated water from the Sai River, a tributary of the Mekong River, at 25 times the limit for drinking water.
Authorities have deployed two trucks to supply residents with clean drinking water, while the government is also considering alternative river water sources.
Rare earth mining in Myanmar blamed
Researchers at Naresuan University said last week that chemical analysis and satellite modelling traced much of the arsenic-laden sediment in the Sai River to gold mining operations across the border in Myanmar.
A surge in rare earth mining in rebel-held pockets of Myanmar supplying Chinese processing plants is being blamed for toxic levels of heavy metals in Thai waterways, including the Mekong River.
Myanmar’s longrunning civil war enables unregulated exploitation of natural resources, including rare earth elements used in smartphones, wind turbines and electric vehicles.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow raised the issue of what he said was a “dramatic” increase in pollution in the Sai River during a visit last week to Myanmar to meet government officials.
He blamed “wastewater from mining”, adding that it was an “urgent matter that needs urgent attention”.
The Thai government says it has also discussed the issue with Beijing, with researchers saying many of the mining operations in Myanmar are Chinese-run.
There are fears the pollution is being washed far down the Mekong River, a waterway supporting millions of people across several countries.
Thai officials said arsenic had been found in the urine of 17 out of 177 people tested in October in the northeastern province of Nong Khai, on the border with Laos.
