If you don’t want two-tier justice, stop legislating for it. Stop training people for it. Last year the Home Office belie
noticias.texto:
Lammy claims 'many' Tory voters could switch to Labour at next election if party committed to rejoining EU
David Lammy has claimed that Labour could win the support of pro-European Tories by proposing rejoining the EU at the next election.
Speaking at an event at the Chatham House foreign affairs thinktank, Lammy also argued that Andy Burnham should run the campaign to rejoin the EU out of No 10 North in Manchester to avoid it being seen as a project based in London and the south-east.
Lammy has explicitly said that rejoining should be a manifesto commitment for Labour at the next election. (See 9.49am.) He is the second senior figure from the Keir Starmer government to say this, after Rachel Reeves recently said being out of the EU left Britain “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In his speech, Lammy pointed out that the Conservative and Reform UK proposals to leave the European convention on human rights meant that at the next election they would be arguing for their own renegotiation of the Brexit settlement – because the current post-Brexit trade deal with the EU is based on the UK remaining in the ECHR.
He said:
We may be in a position at the next general election where the Labour party is effectively arguing for rejoining and to get growth as a result, and Reform and the Conservatives are arguing effectively for a harder Brexit because both those parties want to pull out of the ECHR, which would mean a renegotiation of the TCA (trade and cooperation agreement), which is in fact a hard Brexit. I say bring it on.
He predicted there would be “a consolidation in the polls around progressives, around the Labour party” and he claimed:
I think you’ll also find that many Conservative voters, mainstream Conservative voters, vote Labour to get back into the European Union.
There is some polling to back this up. A recent poll by Lord Ashcroft found that 28% of people who voted Conservative in 2024 now say they would vote to join the EU.
Yvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England
Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced. Denis Campbell has the story.
Lammy claims 'many' Tory voters could switch to Labour at next election if party committed to rejoining EU
David Lammy has claimed that Labour could win the support of pro-European Tories by proposing rejoining the EU at the next election.
Speaking at an event at the Chatham House foreign affairs thinktank, Lammy also argued that Andy Burnham should run the campaign to rejoin the EU out of No 10 North in Manchester to avoid it being seen as a project based in London and the south-east.
Lammy has explicitly said that rejoining should be a manifesto commitment for Labour at the next election. (See 9.49am.) He is the second senior figure from the Keir Starmer government to say this, after Rachel Reeves recently said being out of the EU left Britain “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In his speech, Lammy pointed out that the Conservative and Reform UK proposals to leave the European convention on human rights meant that at the next election they would be arguing for their own renegotiation of the Brexit settlement – because the current post-Brexit trade deal with the EU is based on the UK remaining in the ECHR.
He said:
We may be in a position at the next general election where the Labour party is effectively arguing for rejoining and to get growth as a result, and Reform and the Conservatives are arguing effectively for a harder Brexit because both those parties want to pull out of the ECHR, which would mean a renegotiation of the TCA (trade and cooperation agreement), which is in fact a hard Brexit. I say bring it on.
He predicted there would be “a consolidation in the polls around progressives, around the Labour party” and he claimed:
I think you’ll also find that many Conservative voters, mainstream Conservative voters, vote Labour to get back into the European Union.
There is some polling to back this up. A recent poll by Lord Ashcroft found that 28% of people who voted Conservative in 2024 now say they would vote to join the EU.
Mahmood to tell police chiefs that leadership is ‘frankly inadequate’
In her speech today, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will also announce plans for a new fast-stream police leadership programme for up to 200 recruits a year. Vikram Dodd has the details.
Tories and Reform UK dismiss Mahmood's bid to assuage concerns about 'two-tier policing'
The Conservatives and Reform UK do not seem very impressed by Shabana Mahmood’s proposal to meet their concerns about two-tier policing.
This is fromNick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.
If you don’t want two-tier justice, stop legislating for it.
Stop training people for it.
Stop hiring people for it.
Two-tier justice comes from the equality duty, human rights laws, DEI policies, differential sentencing policies, conscious choices like the “Islamophobia” definition, the decision to use the Public Order Act as a de facto blasphemy law, the deliberate decision not to enforce the law during the anti-Israel marches, appointing communalist interests to police and CPS advisory boards, and more.
The issue is not training the police to treat people equally - it’s all the decisions that stop the criminal justice system treating us as equal before the law.
And this is fromRobert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.
Last year the Home Office believed claims of “two-tier” policing were “far-right”. Will they now apologise?
Even in her statement Mahmood still can’t bring herself to say it’s wrong.
Lucy Powell criticises media organisations for playing prison message from Russell Brand
Lucy Powell, the Labour deputy leader, has criticised media organisations for playing a message from rapist comedian Russell Brand.
As the Press Association reports, Brand’s wife Laura Gallacher shared the message from the jailed sex offender in which he insisted he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year term. Gallacher read out the message on a YouTube podcast on Sunday, prompting an official investigation into whether Brand has breached prison rules.
Asked about this in an interview on LBC this morning, Powell said:
I was appalled at that and actually I think mainstream media shouldn’t have transmitted that either.
Brand was “someone who’s not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims”, she said.
This is somebody who’s been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape.
Asked why she wanted to censor that message, she said: “It’s a platform I don’t think … should have been amplified, to be honest.”
Lammy rules out standing to be Labour's next candidate for London mayor
In his Today interview, David Lammy also said that he would not be standing to be Labour’s next candidate for mayor of London. He said he was still enjoying national politics. There had been speculation that he might apply if Sadiq Khan decided not to stand for a fourth term in 2028. Today voting ends in the Tory election to choose their candidate and James Cleverly (like Lammy, a former foreign secretary), is expected to win.
Khan had been expected not to seek a fourth term. But, with Andy Burnham beefing up the powers available to mayors, making the job more attractive, there is increasing speculation that he will try to stay on.
Lammy says he doesn't think there is two-tier policing in Britain, but he supports 'tidying up' guidance on this
David Lammy was on the Today programme this morning talking about his call for the UK to rejoin the EU. (See 9.49am.) Asked about Shabana Mahmood’s speech on two-tier policing (see 9.04am), Lammy, a former justice secretary, replied:
I don’t think that there’s two-tier policing in Britain.
But I think there’s a preception [of two-tier policing] because of too many guidelines that are not straightforward. If [Shabana Mahmood] is tidying that up – I haven’t seen the detail [of her speech later] – then I would welcome that.
Lammy says Burnham should put rejoining EU in Labour's next manifesto
David Lammy, the former foreign secretary and former deputy PM, has used an article in the Times to say that Andy Burnham should proposing rejoining the EU in the next Labour manifesto. He says:
Burnham has to show how joining the EU passes the Makerfield test. I believe to do that it should answer three questions. What will deliver the most growth? What will deliver the most security? And what will help prevent uncontrolled irregular migration?
The customs union doesn’t deliver major growth on its own. The single market without EU membership gives Britain economic growth but with little influence over the rules we follow. Only membership answers all three questions. On migration, it would put Britain back inside the EU’s asylum returns system, giving us access to the tools we lost in 2020 and have only been rebuilding piecemeal ever since. The ability for Brits to live and work in Europe and Europeans to live and work in Britain with free movement would return. But I believe, like Ireland, we can remain outside Schengen, and, like Sweden, we can stay out of the eurozone.
Burnham’s Labour should go into the next election clear that its intention is to rejoin the EU. Forming the next government would give it the mandate to begin formal negotiations. Once a deal is agreed, this should be put to the people against the status quo. Unlike the last referendum, the public should have the opportunity to decide between two clearly defined choices.
Lammy also says, towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, he tried to get Starmer to agree to abandon Labour’s red lines on Europe (ruling out rejoining, or joining the single market or customs union) at the next election. But Starmer resisted, he suggests.
Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households, Jillian Ambrose reports.
Mahmood to tell the police 'leave politics to the politicians'
Here is another quote from what Shabana Mahmood will say in her speech to the the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC).
Community engagement should mean going to a residents’ association meeting and discussing local issues. It can be over tea and biscuits, or tea and samosas, but it doesn’t mean engaging with activist groups and campaigners who are pushing an agenda and not representing a community.
Leave the politics to the politicians – and we will leave the policing to you.
Shabana Mahmood pledges to tackle ‘corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing’
Good morning. Shabana Mahmood has done two of the most difficult jobs in the government. With Labour under pressure from anti-migrant populists, in Reform UK, in the Conservative party and in the media, as justice secretary and home secretary she has been on the frontline in all the debates where the fight between the right and progressive politics has been most intensive. And she has developed a bold, novel, and largely successful strategy for winning these battles; she disarms her critics by agreeing with them.
Not entirely, of course. She is still a Labour cabinet minister. But sometimes she can sound a bit like Chris Philp.
And today we are going to get another example. In a speech to the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), she will tell officers that she wants to do something about so-called two-tier policing – the theory that, under pressure to be politically correct, the police have become biased towards leftwing causes and nervous about enforcing the law against minority ethnic people for fear of being seen as racist.
On the right, the existence of this version of two-tier policing is now an article of faith, even though most of the time actual policing is very different. This is how Robert Hutton from the Critic satirised the idea in a sketch two years ago, during 2024 summer riots when racists were trying to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers.
This is about fairness, Ed, and it’s a very important point. When I talk about two-tier policing, I’m talking about the way that different groups of marchers are treated. For instance, if you go to a Pride march, there are police with rainbow flags on their cars. During the Black Lives Matter protests, the police took the knee. But you go to these protests, and do you see the police waving swastikas? No you don’t. When was the last time you saw a film of a policeman kicking a brown-skinned person in the head? Well, OK, but when was the last time you saw a video of a policeman trying to set fire to a building full of refugees? Exactly. That’s what we mean by two-tier policing.
Here is a Guardian article looking at whether policing really is two-tier. In some respects, it is, the article points out. “Black people remained more likely than any other ethnic group to be subjected to almost every form of force, from handcuffing and dog bites to firearms and Tasers, when compared with population or arrest figures.”
In her speech today, from the extracts released in advance, Mahmood is not going to say that there is two-tier policing. But she will argue that it is important to respond to the “perception” it exists. She will say:
We must tackle head-on the corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing in this country.
Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed.
But there have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing people – often motivated actors – to whip up the idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.
In its report previewing the speech, the Press Association says:
Mahmood will lament the low levels of black officers in police forces, while also warning against “misguided attempts at course correction” that lead to “differential treatment”.
And she will warn officers against engaging with “activist groups”, telling them to “leave the politics to the politicians”.
She will also set out plans to fast-track talented recruits – including from outside policing – to senior ranks to address sometimes “inadequate” leadership.
A new “impartiality standard” is being developed to ensure all members of the public are treated equally, she will tell chief constables and police and crime commissioners.
This will bring guidance on key impartiality principles into one place and aims to give police more confidence in how they handle cases, regardless of someone’s race, faith or other characteristics, and to give the public confidence they will be treated fairly.
A third of Britons believe police treat people from ethnic minority backgrounds more favourably than white people, a More in Common poll found earlier this year, noting this marks a doubling in the last two years.
Mahmood will tell the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) that it is “shameful”, 33 years after the murder of black teenager Stephen Lawrence, that the proportion of black officers remains virtually unchanged.
But Mahmood will argue that some approaches intended to promote equality, such as the former police anti-racism commitment, have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing.
Mahmood will say:
We must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.
To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing does not mean treating everyone the same.
This is a reference to the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, a document that has frequently been criticised by the Conservatives and Reform UK. It says producing equality of policing outcomes “does not mean treating everyone ‘the same’”.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, gives evidence to the Commons Northern Ireland committee.
11am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives a speech at the King’s Fund conference.
1pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives a speech on policing.
After 12.30pm: MPs begin a debate on a Tory opposition day motion opposing most of the key features of the PM’s proposed UK-EU reset deal due to be agreed on Friday.
I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

noticias.titulo: Yvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England
noticias.resumen: Health secretary says 500,000 will benefit initially from ‘downpayment’ on PM’s national care service pledge UK politics live – latest updates Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced. Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive help from new joint teams of NHS and social care staff. Initially about 500,000 people by next April will benefit from new joine
noticias.texto:
Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.
Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive help from new joint teams of NHS and social care staff. Initially about 500,000 people by next April will benefit from new joined-up support teams providing personalised care.
In a speech on Wednesday, Cooper described the measure as a “downpayment” on the national care service promised by Andy Burnham to address the social care crisis. The approach will be expanded and eventually cover about 2 million people, the health secretary said in a speech at the annual conference of the King’s Fund health thinktank.
Once fully operational the major shift in how key care services work will help relieve the pressure on overcrowded hospitals by cutting 4.3m bed days and reducing the number of people – mainly the frail elderly and those with dementia – who experience “corridor care”, Cooper said.
It is a significant milestone in the government’s ambition to transform how the NHS works through “three big shifts” – from an analogue to digital-based service, prioritise prevention of illness over treatment and move a lot of hospital-based care into community settings and people’s homes.
The planned “neighbourhood support teams” come together to identify the most vulnerable members of their local community and devise a plan for keeping them as well as possible and provide care in their own home or care home – and out of hospital – for as long as possible.
They will receive regular check-ins to assess their health from teams who know them, to ensure they are receiving the right support. They and their family will also have access to a 24/7 helpline that will act as a single point of contact, though it is unclear when that part of the new service will start.
Everyone being helped by the joint teams of NHS and local council personnel will also have an individual care plan that makes clear what their needs are and who should be helping with them.
Cooper billed the creation of the teams as a way of providing proactive, personalised care that will make care much easier to access while also reducing the strain on the NHS, which has been struggling to meet the growing demand for healthcare caused by the ageing population.
In her speech, the health secretary was expected to say that the new way of working is “a downpayment on a national care service: a practical step towards bringing health and social care together around people’s needs”.
Wednesday’s speech builds on Cooper’s announcement last week that GPs in England will receive £40m this winter to help give 300,000 vulnerable patients better care at home, to reduce their risk of ending up in hospital.

noticias.titulo: UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high
noticias.resumen: Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January Business live – latest updates Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.
As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.
Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate.
“Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices respectively.”
Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global increase in energy prices.
The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.
Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.
At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20m households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.
The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October.
A new forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.
Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.
Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.
A spokesperson for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.
“The MPC raised bank rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there.”
Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could be forced to raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.
Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.
Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.
Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.
Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.
“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.
“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”

noticias.titulo: Shabana Mahmood to set out plans to tackle ‘corrosive’ perception of two-tier policing
noticias.resumen: Home secretary to tell police chiefs ‘misguided attempts at course correction’ can lead to ‘differential treatment’ UK politics live – latest updates Shabana Mahmood will set out plans to tackle the “corrosive and growing perception” of two-tier policing in a speech to police chiefs on Wednesday. The home secretary will say “misguided attempts at course correction” can lead to “differential treatment” while also warning officers against engaging with “activist groups”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Shabana Mahmood will set out plans to tackle the “corrosive and growing perception” of two-tier policing in a speech to police chiefs on Wednesday.
The home secretary will say “misguided attempts at course correction” can lead to “differential treatment” while also warning officers against engaging with “activist groups”.
Mahmood will announce that a new “impartiality standard” is being developed to ensure all members of the public are treated equally. This is intended to bring guidance on key impartiality principles into one place and aim to give police more confidence in how they handle cases, regardless of someone’s race, faith or other characteristics, and to give the public confidence they will be treated fairly.
Addressing chief constables and police and crime commissioners, Mahmood will say: “We must tackle, head-on, the corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing in this country.
“Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed. But there have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing people – often motivated actors – to whip up the idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.”
The home secretary’s remarks come after the murder of Henry Nowak prompted criticism of alleged two-tier policing in the UK. Nowak, who was fatally stabbed by Vickrum Digwa in December 2025, was handcuffed by police as he lay dying after his attacker falsely accused him of racial abuse.
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, subsequently delivered an emergency address calling for the public to respond with “pure cold rage” and demanding an end to what he described as “two-tier policing”.
A third of Britons believed police treat people from minority ethnic backgrounds more favourably than white people, a More in Common poll found this year, noting this marked a doubling in the last two years.
On Wednesday Mahmood will tell the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) that it is “shameful”, 33 years after the murder of the black teenager Stephen Lawrence, that the proportion of black officers remains virtually unchanged.
But Mahmood will argue that some approaches intended to promote equality, such as the former police anti-racism commitment, have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing. “We must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment,” she is to say. “To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing does not mean treating everyone the same.”
The new standard, to be developed by the College of Policing and subject to consultation next year, will also give officers guidance on scenarios such as wearing symbols on badges and lanyards, and advise them how to behave at community-led events.
Mahmood will urge officers to avoid becoming drawn into political activism. She will say: “Community engagement should mean going to a residents’ association meeting and discussing local issues. It can be over tea and biscuits, or tea and samosas, but it doesn’t mean engaging with activist groups and campaigners who are pushing an agenda and not representing a community.
“Leave the politics to the politicians – and we will leave the policing to you.”
Mahmood will also set out plans to fast-track talented recruits – including from outside policing – to senior ranks to address sometimes “inadequate” leadership.
Gavin Stephens, the chair of the NPCC, said: “Public trust depends on the police being seen to act fairly and impartially. Barriers to justice remain, discrimination still exists within our own ranks, and we rely on the trust and confidence of all communities to do our job. A diverse service is a stronger service.
“Equally, there have been occasions where well-intentioned approaches and our language have led some people to question whether policing has remained focused on its core purpose. We should take those concerns seriously.”

noticias.titulo: Burnham considering cuts to national insurance to create more youth jobs
noticias.resumen: PM hints he is open to suggestion in Milburn report to lower NICs contributions paid by companies for under-25s Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”. The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”.
The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government.
On Tuesday, a report suggested national insurance contributions (NICs) paid by firms for under-25s should be gradually lowered, starting with retail and hospitality companies, to help create more jobs.
The independent report, by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, also proposed doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.
Asked if he believes the last government was wrong to increase NICs, Burnham told LBC: “I think it’s something you’ve got to consider very carefully going forward. Obviously, I’ve come in [and] inherited the situation.
“I think the last government was right to offer support to employers to take on young people. So, that was one of the things that they did through the Youth Guarantee.
“I will want to look at all of the evidence in relation to it, but also the affordability of making any change to national insurance. There is an exemption for young people up to 21, so there is some [movement] that’s been done in that area.
“But I can’t give you a firm commitment today because obviously these matters are matters for the budget more broadly.”
Currently, businesses do not pay employer NICs for workers younger than 21 nor for apprentices under 25 unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. For non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.
 
Official figures show there are nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK.
On the backbench rebellion to the last proposed reforms to welfare, Burnham told LBC: “Well, it is a very different proposition. First and foremost, it’s about support for young people, opportunity for young people.
“It’s not about an arbitrary number for cuts within the system. You’ve got Conservatives and Reform who are going that way. It’s the crude cuts approach, and it just doesn’t work. It’s why they left office with a million Neets, and we’re going to have to do something fundamentally different.
“I think Alan Milburn has laid out what that looks like. It is also about a very different way of providing support, so not the old top-down tick-box system of the past, but a much more localised approach.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio
noticias.resumen: US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state. Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state.
Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.
In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.
Rubio’s comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, a programming language used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500, a ranking of the largest companies in the US. The researchers at US-based Calif used AI to discover the flaw and recently unearthed glitches in PHP, another computer language.
Calif said the Java flaw could allow to remotely execute code, allowing them to place malicious software on a target’s systems.
The US director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, said the incidents were caused by security upgrades – such as plugging the flaws in PHP – that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
“Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” he told the Fox Business news channel.
Tal Be’ery, a cybersecurity expert, said he did not believe the incidents were linked directly but had a common underlying theme: AI. IT systems are buckling under the pressure of adding AI or tackling flaws uncovered by AI, he said.
“Our IT infrastructure is brittle, and when AI puts massive extra pressure on it, whether through upgrades to accommodate AI or through the rapid patching that AI-driven vulnerability discovery demands,” Be’ery said.
Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which had a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eightfold – while OpenAI has also released models capable of finding previously unseen flaws. Researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw.
“[Java] is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blogpost. “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”
Rubio made the comments as he travelled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila.
The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, affecting millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the problem to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”.
Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest “ground stop” since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related”.
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”. Apple also confirmed problems with its iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday but said it had resolved them.
The Democrat Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, supported the assessment that the outages were not caused by a “coordinated effort” but by attempts to shore up systems.
“The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

noticias.titulo: Gun control activist faces long recovery after Washington DC mass shooting
noticias.resumen: Susan Thurston Hamerski was shot in the face by gunman who killed one and injured several others in Logan Circle A gun control advocate is grappling with a grueling recovery after being shot in the face during the recent mass shooting at a Washington DC condominium building – an ordeal that she began with a handwritten note from her hospital bed reading: “Gun control is a public health crisis”. Susan Thurston Hamerski had traveled to the nation’s capital from her home in Minnesota’s Twin Cities for her daughter’s wedding when she was shot by a gunman who killed one person, injured five others
noticias.texto:
A gun control advocate is grappling with a grueling recovery after being shot in the face during the recent mass shooting at a Washington DC condominium building – an ordeal that she began with a handwritten note from her hospital bed reading: “Gun control is a public health crisis”.
Susan Thurston Hamerski had traveled to the nation’s capital from her home in Minnesota’s Twin Cities for her daughter’s wedding when she was shot by a gunman who killed one person, injured five others and evidently died by suicide on 12 November at a condo building in the Logan Circle neighborhood near the White House, according to her friends and family.
Hamerski had stayed back to take care of her daughter’s dog while the newlywed bride, Madeleine, and her husband went on their honeymoon, family friend and spokesperson Tina Wilcox said. She was walking the dog, Wrigley, when the mass shooting erupted in and around the condo building, and the attacker – who was locked into an ongoing legal dispute with the complex’s management – shot Hamerski.
She survived after being brought to a hospital in critical condition. But she was left needing to undergo multiple surgeries to restore her jaw and tongue’s function as well as to repair her face. The procedures require months of rehabilitative therapy, Madeleine and her family wrote in a statement online after the daughter cut her honeymoon short to be at her mother’s side.
As Wilcox put it, there is a dark irony to the plight confronting Hamerski, who spent six years voluntarily managing the social media in her community for the non-profit group Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America.
Susan Hamerski’s role with Moms Demand Action saw her share news and research about gun safety in the US, where as of Tuesday there had been more than 415 mass shootings reported nationwide. Mass shootings are colloquially defined as ones in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed – and the high numbers of such cases reported perennially in the US have prompted many, including those aligned with Moms Demand Action, to call for more substantial federal gun control.
But Congress in Washington DC over the years has not implemented such measures, creating an environment in the US where sometimes it seems “you can’t go anywhere [outside your home] and feel safe”, Wilcox said.
It feels as if “it can happen to any of us”, Wilcox said. “And it’s happening so frequently that more and more innocent people are losing their lives or suffering massive injury.”
After the mass shooting victimizing Hamerski drove that reality home as closely as possible for her and her family, she made clear that her advocacy remained as top of mind for her as her looming recovery journey.
Hamerski did that by writing a note from her hospital bed that said, “Gun control is a public health crisis” – words that she couldn’t speak because of her injury.
Her son, Sam Hamerski, shared a picture of the note with the Minnesota news station KARE.
“It’s ironic that … the people [who] do the most and care the most are often the people that are affected,” Sam Hamerski told the outlet.
In a social media post, Moms Demand Action said Susan Hamerski’s handwritten words are a reminder that gun violence doesn’t just change lives – it “reverberates throughout families and communities, leaving survivors and their loved ones to navigate unimaginable physical, emotional, and financial hardships”.
“We are in awe of Susan who, through her pain and suffering, found a way to make her voice heard,” Moms Demand Action’s post added. “We hold Susan and her loved ones in our hearts as they come to terms with their new reality as survivors of gun violence. We will keep fighting in her honor, working toward a future where no family has to endure this kind of horror and devastation.”
As word about Hamerski’s shooting has circulated, there has been substantial public support for the novelist and poet who has worked as a Minnesota state public health department communications specialist – and has served as a governing board member of the Illusion Theater in Minneapolis, too.
An online campaign meant to help Hamerski cover her medical expenses as of Tuesday had raised more than $210,000 from about 2,600 individual donations.
The campaign’s page noted that Wrigley was back home and safe. The page also said that the money raised would be used to pay costs described as “enormous”, including getting Hamerski back to Minnesota from Washington DC, ongoing medical care and financially supporting her while she is convalescent and unable to work.
Wilcox said that has certainly been a boon for Hamerski and her loved ones as she musters all the strength she can to navigate her recovery.
She also remarked: “Susan is the type of person who you say, ‘If it had to happen to anyone.’
“Because she’s doing the best she can, and she’s a really strong individual – and she’s going to need to be to survive this.”

noticias.titulo: Fresh off recent wins, the left has a new goal: get AOC to run for president
noticias.resumen: With its policy priorities more mainstream than ever, the left is directing its momentum toward 2028 A week after the US midterms elections swept an unprecedented number of leftists into office across the country, about 600 people joined a Zoom call. The goal: to convince rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president. On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer w
noticias.texto:
A week after the US midterms elections swept an unprecedented number of leftists into office across the country, about 600 people joined a Zoom call. The goal: to convince rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president.
On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer with the group. “We are more ready than we have ever been.”
Ocasio-Cortez, the millennial New York congresswoman whose improbable defeat of an establishment candidate eight years ago helped usher in a renaissance for the US left, has not declared her intention to run, saying recently that she will take some time to decide “privately”. (She is also reportedly considering a primary challenge to Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer.) But the work to build a field operation behind her is already underway. On Saturday, at their biannual convention, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, the insurgent group backing many of the leftist candidates who won office last week, also voted to encourage the longtime member to run. Within 24 hours of Ready for AOC’s launch last Monday, more than 10,000 people across 50 states had signed a pledge to support her, and nearly 4,000 had registered for organizing calls to jumpstart a field operation to get her elected.
“The goal is to get her to run,” said Ravi Sahai, an organiser with the group who also worked on the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani’s, odds-defeating campaign last year, who stressed Ready for AOC is an independent, volunteer operation with no affiliation to her team. “It’s clearly a very personal choice – and we want to respect that, but also demonstrate that there is real, widespread support behind such a run.”
In an age of soaring costs of living, seemingly endless wars, and an ever-widening distance between a small set of oligarchs and everyone else, the left is having a moment. Calls for universal healthcare, affordable housing, free childcare, and getting money out of politics have been on the ascent since Bernie Sanders’ history-making 2016 run. Today, they have never been more mainstream.
Eager to seize the momentum, not everyone is waiting for Ocasio-Cortez before lining up alternatives. Just two days after the midterms, former democratic socialist rep Jamaal Bowman and progressive activist Nomiki Konst launched a committee urging California rep Ro Khanna to run. Mamdani, whose winning endorsements of fellow democratic socialists have crowned him a kingmaker of the left, has been meeting with union leaders – including United Auto Workers (UAW) president, Shawn Fain, and Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA – to make the case for a leftist, labor-aligned leader to jump into the race.
But, virtually no viable candidate on the left has Ocasio-Cortez’s name recognition, fundraising skills and deep relationships both in Washington and within working class movements.
“Her victory in 2018 shook national politics in a way that we hadn’t seen,” said Sahai. “There isn’t really anyone else that has that kind of profile.”
A transformed landscape
When she first ran for Congress, in 2018, Ocasio-Cortez said she wasn’t running “from the left” but rather “from the bottom”. As both progressive and moderate Democrats swept to victory this month, that’s the grassroots, populist message her supporters are evoking, stressing policy – Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, raising the minimum wage – rather than ideology.
“The focus is on what we’re going to deliver for the American people, and that transcends whether it’s left or establishment,” said Sahai.
That approach may run up against the group most associated with this leftist resurgence. The DSA, the left’s largest national organization, is not always known for adapting its positions or rhetoric for a mainstream audience.
By January, six new democratic socialists, include pro-Palestinian activists and labor and community organizers, will join Ocasio-Cortez and rep Rashida Tlaib in Congress. Four new democratic socialist mayors will join Mamdani at the helm of US cities. And more than 100 socialists will sit in state and local offices across the country. Buoyed by the wins, socialists who for years have prioritized down-ballot races and local organizing are increasingly urging that the time is now – maybe now or never – for a socialist president.
“In a time of rising fascism and historic levels of inequality, the stakes of the 2028 presidential election for the direction of US politics and world history are monumental,” read the resolution to back AOC passed by the group’s New York City chapter over the weekend. “A winning presidential campaign creates enormous opportunity to deliver a democratic socialist agenda that puts working-class people back in control of their own lives.”
Whoever runs in 2028 will face a transformed political landscape. The DSA now counts more than 130,000 due-paying members nationwide, and more than 200 local chapters, and growing numbers of Americans are viewing socialism favorably.
“Democratic socialism is becoming part of the mainstream of American politics,” Eric Blanc, a professor of labor studies at Rutgers University and DSA member, said on election night. “Now, we have an opportunity to do something much bigger, and much bolder.”
The recent wins would have, not long ago, been unthinkable for a left that has historically existed outside the US’s bipartisan political system. While long-shot socialist candidates have run in presidential elections throughout US history, they have always done so on third party lines. The most votes a socialist candidate got was 6% – in 1912.
That candidate was Eugene Debs, a labor organizer, anti-war activist, and founding member of the Socialist Party of America. From a peak of 120,000 members that year – a record the DSA surpassed this summer – socialism retreated to the margins of US politics, beaten down by repeated Red Scares, the cold war, runaway US capitalism, and the internal strife that often characterizes movements on the left.
It’s against that backdrop that the DSA was founded in 1982 by the longtime activist Michael Harrington. The vision was to promote a pragmatic approach to radical leftwing aspirations, what Harrington called “the left wing of the possible”.
DSA had limited political impact politics even as its members occasionally rose to elected office – David Dinkins, New York’s first Black mayor, was also its first democratic socialist one. Still, the group remained largely obscure.
Then came Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run, which came within inches of the Democratic nomination with a raucously socialist, anti-billionaire message. Sanders was never a member of the DSA but many within the organisation view him as its political muse.
Sanders inspired young political newcomers like Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani to launch their anti-establishment campaigns. Others followed their stunning upsets. The group’s once dormant membership soared with its wins.
“We have a world to win” is the DSA’s pitch to would-be members.
‘What’s needed is a broad coalition’
As DSA has grown in prominence, the group’s tensions have been on display – about pragmatism vs ideological rigidity, Israel, policing and other issues. Even committed members like Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani have at times distanced themselves from its most more radical positions, like abolishing borders of the US Senate.
And while the group is coalescing around Ocasio-Cortez, there remains plenty of internal opposition. A faction opposes her on the grounds that she has compromised on some of the organization’s values, most notably on Israel. The national DSA, which has been more critical of Ocasio-Cortez and has not taken a position yet on a potential presidential run, rescinded its endorsement of her in 2024 over her failure to vote against funding for Israel’s Iron Dome and after she hosted a panel featuring supporters of the controversial IHRA definition of antisemitism. The NYC-DSA resolution to back her passed with 291 votes – but 123 delegates voted against it.
“The biggest danger is that DSA doesn’t live up to this moment that the left is not used to, engaging in mass politics, talking to millions of people and not just thousands of people,” said Blanc, the Rutgers professor and DSA member. “The biggest danger is that we don’t seize this moment and that we stick with the routines and internal, inward-looking purity politics of the last decades.”
It’s also not clear that the rest of the Democratic party is ready for a socialist presidential candidate. The DSA is not a political party – and the fact that DSA candidates are running as Democrats has irked both party centrists and some of DSA’s own members who view the party as too compromised. Already, centrist Democratic funders fearful of the group’s impact on the 2028 election have pledged to spend millions to fight the group.
While the recent midterms may have been historic for the left, many of their wins came in solidly blue states, while more moderate Democrats broke through elsewhere. A successful presidential candidate will need a broader reach – at the very least in swing states.
In Michigan, for example, Abdul El-Sayed explicitly distanced himself from both socialism and the DSA, even though he is broadly aligned with the left. In Florida, Angie Nixon, a progressive who joined DSA during the campaign, lost to the Republican candidate by a small margin. (Many blame the Democratic establishment for failing to rally behind her.) Francesca Hong, a DSA candidate who this summer came close to clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in the swing state of Wisconsin, also fell short.
“Of course, the growth of DSA in the last eight years or so has transformed the way that the left holds power in this country – and that’s not an insignificant thing,” said Sahai. “But this project goes beyond that, because what is needed to win on the national level is a coalition of the left, labor, progressives, liberals – a broad coalition that can bring all these groups together.”
Ocasio-Cortez is the only left candidate with “the ability to communicate to such a large group”, he added. “[She] has the kind of vision, experience, and connections to the movement that no other candidate has.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives
noticias.resumen: Peltola, the first Alaska Native in the US Senate, ran a campaign that drew universal issues from her own Indigenous politics Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters. noticias.texto:
Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.
It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
Before she could speak, a volunteer shouted out from the back of the hall: “Aarigaa!” Peltola picked up the refrain, and threw it right back:
“Aarigaa! Can we just chant aarigaa? Aarigaa! Aarigaa!”
It was just one word. But it encapsulated something special about Peltola and her insurgent’s campaign to unseat the incumbent Republican US senator, Dan Sullivan.
“Aarigaa” is an Iñupiaq word that is commonly understood across Alaska’s 229 federally recognised tribes. It is a word of celebration, of relief almost, that roughly translates to: “Way to go!” or “Attaboy!”
Now, Peltola genuinely has a reason for exclaiming it. On Tuesday – two weeks after the midterm elections – the tortuous count was finally completed, and she was declared winner.
In prevailing, she becomes the first Alaska Native to take a seat in the US Senate.
“I was so happy at that moment,” said Ana Hoffman, a lifelong friend of the senator-elect’s who was present in the Sheraton ballroom. “Aarigaa! It demonstrated through language what her campaign is all about: inclusion, representation, identity.”
The last US Senate race of the 2026 cycle to be called, Peltola’s victory carries with it several layers of significance. For US politics as a whole, it awards Democrats comfortable control of the upper chamber of Congress, with 56 seats to Republicans’ 44.
For Native Americans across the union, it marks the first time that seven Native people will be serving simultaneously in Congress – representatives Josh Brecheen and Tom Cole from Oklahoma, Sharice Davids from Kansas, Sean McCann from Michigan and Claire Valdez from New York; and senators Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota and Peltola from Alaska.
And for Alaska Natives, there is their own resounding cause to roar aarigaa: since Congress was convened 237 years ago, there have been more than 20,000 seats filled in the US House and Senate.
Among them, only 29 have been occupied by Native Americans, and of those Peltola is the only Alaska Native to have served in Congress. She won Alaska’s only House of Representatives seat in 2022, losing it two years later to the Republican Nick Begich, and in January she will take her Senate seat as part of the new intake.
Hoffman, who is president of the Native Corporation in Peltola’s home town of Bethel in western Alaska, said that her friend’s victory would uplift a people “who have been marginalized and underrepresented throughout generations. ‘Alaska Native’ will no longer be a concept in the Senate, it will be a colleague.”
The gaping lack of representation of Alaska Natives is no small thing for Alaska or the US. Alaska is home to about 40% of all federally recognized tribes in the union, and the one in five voters who are Indigenous amount to the largest proportion of the electorate in any state.
“Alaska Natives have played pivotal roles in US history, around decisions on land, resources and development. Yet their centrality to US decision-making still takes many people by surprise,” said Sonja Castañeda Dower, a congressional fellow with the American Political Science Association who has studied the power of Alaskan tribes.
Peltola is a Yup’ik Alaskan from Bethel, a town of fewer than 7,000 people that acts as the hub of 56 villages scattered along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers. Her Yup’ik name is Akalleq, or “the one who rolled”. Her mother was from the nearby community of Kwethluk; her father, a German American, came to Alaska from Nebraska to work as a pilot.
As a young girl, Peltola began fishing the Kuskokwim river with her father from the age of six. “We’d pass each other on the river,” said Hoffman, who lives in Bethel and is also Yup’ik. “We had fish camps near one another along the same slough.”
Peltola put Alaska Native issues and sensibilities at the center of her election campaign. She made exceptional efforts to reach out to communities that have rarely been included in the political process, travelling by floatplanes, four-wheelers and snowmachines to far-flung parts of the last frontier – a state that is larger in landmass than California and Texas combined.
Peltola showed up in more than 50 communities, some with a population of fewer than 300 people.
Yup’ik symbolism was embedded in her campaign. At campaign stops, she wore mukluk boots and Indigenous kuspuk shirts. The campaign’s circular logo was modelled on the Yup’ik eye, a traditional sign that also alludes to the eyewear made from wood or walrus ivory worn by Yup’ik people as protection against the blinding glare of the arctic snow.
“Peltola leaned into her Yup’ik identity as a qualification for advancing policies that appealed to a broad base of Alaskan supporters,” said Elise Blasingame, a political scientist specialising in Native American representation at Emory University, and a citizen of the Osage Nation. She added: “Look at her campaign’s merchandise. Who else would market a baby onesie saying: ‘I teethe on dried salmon’?”
You might also ask, who else would put salmon at the heart of an electoral contest for national office? The official mantra of the campaign was “Fish, family, freedom” – a slogan that neatly captures the dual nature of Peltola’s message and can be read in equal measure as an appeal to Native tribal people and as a paean to Alaskan and American patriotism.
Fish embody that double-edged message. As Peltola explained in an interview in October, about 80% of the diet of Yup’ik people has traditionally been fish, of which about half is salmon. “Our generic word for fish is the generic word for food,” she said. “Neqa.”
The devastating decline of the catch of chinook salmon, or king salmon, along the Kuskokwim river in recent years, partly as a result of the climate crisis and partly through over-trawling in international waters in the Bering Sea, is an existential challenge for Alaska Native tribes. Their villages are sited on riverbanks along the salmon run.
“Fish, and our access to them, are the reason our communities exist,” Hoffman said.
But fish are also central to the entire economy of Alaska, Indigenous or not. The state accounts for about 60% of all wild seafood harvested across the US, and the combination of subsistence fishing, industrial fish processing and tourism is critical to Alaska’s 740,000 residents as a whole.
So when Peltola made a central pitch of her campaign that her rival, the incumbent Republican senator, was selling out the people in favor of big trawler companies, it spoke not just to the 20% of the electorate who are Alaska Native, but to all Alaskans. Without that, she would never have stood a chance – she had to reach the independent and wavering Republican voters who overwhelmingly elected Donald Trump in 2024 and for whom Native issues are not top priority.
Peltola, like Democrats across the country, hammered the issue of affordability on the campaign trail. When a gallon of milk costs as much as $21 in the most isolated parts of the state, and grocery prices are sky-high as a result of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, that is a concern for all Alaskans.
For Hoffman, that is the key to Peltola’s agonisingly delayed victory – she drew out of her own Indigenous politics what was universal for every voter.
“That’s the beauty about Mary, that she understood the universality of who we are as Alaskans. So the focus on access to fish, for Alaskans, that is like the pursuit of happiness.”
In the end, though the race was tight, Sullivan could not overcome that universal appeal. The furor over the appearance of a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, which the New York Times revealed just weeks before the election had been a ruse cooked up by Democratic operatives aligned with the Peltola campaign, provided the Republican incumbent with ammunition late in the cycle.
Sullivan backers also rolled out their own dirty tricks. In September, the Republican-linked Senate Leadership Fund Pac put out an ad titled: “Who is Mary Peltola?” It featured a middle-aged white man saying: “They dress her up, throw her out on a stream somewhere, make her look like an Alaskan.”
In case the racial undertone of that comment was too subtle for some viewers, the ad went on to hear from a white woman: “Every time Mary Peltola gets in a room with her people, she’s not with our people,” the woman said.
That pandering to Alaska Native otherness ultimately failed. Though detailed figures are not yet available, anecdotal evidence suggests that a surge in Alaska Native turnout contributed to Sullivan’s loss.
In her election night speech Peltola name-checked one of her fellow Yup’ik residents in Bethel, Susan Murphy. The Guardian reached out to Murphy, 85, by phone.
She said that on election day she passed the polling place near her house several times. It was in a parking lot, and each time she walked by she saw the lot full of voters standing patiently in line.
It was reminiscent of a scene in Bethel on 26 August 1958. She was 17 on that day, and still in high school. The town was much smaller then. “There were only about 500 Bethel residents then,” she said.
A similarly impressive proportion of the town turned out to the polls that August. They were voting for statehood, for Alaska to become the 49th state of the union.
Now there is a chance of forming a more perfect union with the arrival of Peltola in the US Senate. “It is important, of course it is,” Murphy said. “It is a start.”

noticias.titulo: Mary Peltola beats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska to give Democrats 56 Senate seats
noticias.resumen: Republican incumbent beaten in race dominated by controversy over second candidate named Dan Sullivan Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country. Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.
Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement on Tuesday.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she said. “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families.”
Alaska was the last Senate race remaining to be called, and with Peltola’s victory, Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber, after winning campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi. The party gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year, when they are expected to embark on an aggressive campaign of both lawmaking and investigating.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.
Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit another Republican challenger, also named Dan Sullivan, to appear on the ballot.
Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run, and after state election officials tried to remove him, Alaska’s supreme court in June ruled he be allowed to appear on the ballot. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the apparent ruse, and Alaska’s top federal prosecutor announced that criminal and civil inquiries were under way, while the state’s governor separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme.
Under Alaska’s voting system, the top four candidates from the nonpartisan primary advance to the November general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives more than 50% on the initial round of counting, the last-place finisher is eliminated and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had secured 50.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, while the incumbent senator received 45.8%. The other Sullivan had received just 1.7% while a third Republican, Gerald Heikes, received 2.1%.
Though Alaska is a Republican stronghold in presidential years, Peltola was viewed as a uniquely potent challenger to Sullivan, a two-term senator first elected in 2014 after defeating a Democrat.
A former state legislator who grew up in small communities along the Kuskokwim River in Alaska’s interior, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022, when she won a special election to replace the longtime Republican at-large congressman Don Young following his sudden death, and became the first Alaska native elected to Congress.
Peltola won a full term later that year, but lost re-election to Republican Nick Begich in 2024.
In the race against Sullivan, Peltola’s fortunes appeared to rise as Alaskans grew frustrated with the price increases brought on by Trump’s tariffs and his decision to attack Iran earlier this year.
The state is the largest in the union, and dotted with cities and villages that are disconnected from the road system, and thus particularly hard-hit by the increases in oil prices the war caused. Gas prices in some interior Alaska communities jumped into the double-digits per gallon, while the rise in the price of diesel affected everything from groceries to alcohol, since many communities rely on shipments by sea.
Alaska is nonetheless a right-leaning state heavily reliant on its fishing and oil and gas industries. On the campaign trail, Peltola adopted the slogan “fish, family, freedom” to highlight how she would stand up for the state’s unique interests in Washington DC.
She has cast herself as an advocate for expanding oil production in the state, and addressing the issue of bycatch, or the accidental fishing of unwanted species, which some Alaskans believe is to blame for declining salmon runs.
Late in her campaign, Peltola posted a photograph of herself on Instagram from 1995, wearing the winner’s sash from the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant. “Then and now, Alaska is at the heart of who I am,” she wrote.
Sullivan, meanwhile, stuck to Trump’s side, even as the president’s popularity declined nationwide, and especially in Alaska, according to some surveys. He did not join other vulnerable Republicans in urging an end to the war with Iran, while accusing Peltola of disrespecting voters after a report emerged that she had used a homophobic slur and abused her staff.

noticias.titulo: Axes, cutlass and blunt objects: Nigeria's campaign trail of violence
noticias.resumen: As Nigeria's January 2027 polls inch closer, a spate of violence and political thuggery during campaign rallies and town hall meetings is raising concerns about the safety of citizens participating in the election.
noticias.texto:
Axes, cutlass and blunt objects: Nigeria's campaign trail of violence
November 18, 2026
Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering. "I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men got down and began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.
Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.
During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."
He was left groaning in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.
As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.
Election-related violence on the rise
Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja. Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.
Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation. On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwanso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.
Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.
Nigeria's history of electoral violence
Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria. Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."
Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.
The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.
"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.
The high cost of violence
A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."
Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority. However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.
"Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.
Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

noticias.titulo: Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?
noticias.resumen: El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible with human rights.
noticias.texto:
Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?
November 18, 2026
Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.
These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.
