More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.
What is a mega-prison?
De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.
But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.
High costs and a questionable track record
According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.
It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.
Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.
Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.
However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).
The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.
"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe. As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.
Security, propaganda and human rights
Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.
However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.
Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."
Can the Salvadoran model be exported?
Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.
Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.
However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.
What are the alternatives?
In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.
In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.
Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.
Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.
This article was originally published in Spanish.

noticias.titulo: APEC summit: Xi greets Trump on arrival in Shenzhen
noticias.resumen: US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen for a much-anticipated meeting with Russian and Chinese counterparts. Follow DW live.
noticias.texto:
APEC summit: Xi greets Trump on arrival in Shenzhen
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 18, 2026
What you need to know
- US President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen in southern China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit
- Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the airport
- Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks with Xi ahead of trilateral talks also involving Trump on Thursday
- Trump is on a three-day Asia tour, having first landed in the Philippines on Tuesday
- Trump vowed US support for India, Japan and Australia at his first Quad meeting in Manila and attended a dinner with ASEAN leaders
Here are the biggest headlines from Trump's Asia tour on Tuesday, November 18:
WATCH: Xi greets Trump at the airport
Trump's arrival was highly choreographed: He descended from Air Force One and stood on a red carpet lined with people waving colorful pom poms. Trump and Xi hugged before shaking hands.
Potential Trump talks touted in Shenzhen, even with Kim Jong Un
The White House, other countries and Donald Trump himself have all listed possible or probable bilateral or multilateral talks involving the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, beyond Thursday's highly-anticipated US-China-Russia meeting.
Some of the more notable examples are listed here:
- Kremlin officials said they expected a meeting between just Trump and Putin, but not one long or substantial enough for fully-fledged bilateral negotiations
- The White House said Trump would hold two separate meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum prior to the official APEC greeting ceremony
- While in Manila, Trump himself floated the possibility of a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un, but without voicing a solid intent
- China said it had no information on a potential Trump-Kim meeting
- Meanwhile, North Korean state media — which typically operates behind the global news cycle — has only released images of Kim visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu, making no mention of possible Shenzhen travel plans
Xi tells Trump China seeks 'strategically stable relationship'
Chinese news agency Xinhua has reported the first comments from Xi Jinping to Donald Trump following his arrival.
"I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape," Xi told Trump.
He said the talks would take place "with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations — one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity."
Despite Trump and Xi's efforts to regularly hold friendly face-to-face talks in recent months, the US and China are nevertheless embroiled in difficult trade negotiations as the two superpowers try to reconcile competing interests on various issues.
The two sides have been periodically extending a temporary tariff truce designed to bridge the gap until they can reach a more permanent agreement, which for now has proven elusive. China announced the most recent extension earlier this month, to run until early January.
Nvidia stops shipping US-approved chips to China
The interim CEO of US chip giant Nvidia says the company is not currently shipping Hopper-generation data center products to China.
These are some of the most advanced Nvidia products licensed for export by the US government; the company had sold such goods worth $2.4 billion (roughly €2.2 billion) in the previous quarter, Colette Kress said.
Kress replaced Jensen Huang following his resignation last week and amid the scandal over alleged Chinese attempts both to gain intelligence on the company's CEO and to circumvent import restrictions.
"Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said.
She did not specify why such deliveries had currently stopped or say whether the step would be permanent.
Huang was influential in persuading Donald Trump to allow sales of H200 Hopper processors used to train and run advanced AI models to China, reversing export controls the US had imposed in 2022 under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
China has called the allegations of espionage targeting Nvidia unfounded and threatened to respond in kind if restrictions on trade follow as a result of the fallout from Huang's resignation.
Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport ahead of summit
US President Donald Trump has landed at Shenzhen Airport on Air Force One and disembarked.
He left Manila in the Philippines a few hours earlier.
Trump will be attending the APEC summit but is also expected to take part in a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport on Wednesday, mirroring a gesture Trump had recently extended during the Chinese leader's state visit to the US in September.
Japan's Sanae Takaichi on first China trip since becoming PM
Sanae Takaichi arrived in China for the APEC summit, which is also her first official visit to the country as Japanese prime minister.
Takaichi's moves to bolster Japan's military and comments last year on Taiwan have upset Beijing and severely affected bilateral ties.
In particular, Takaichi's suggestion that Tokyo could intervene militarily if Beijing sought to forcibly take Taiwan — which China considers its territory — led to friction between the regional rivals with a troubled 20th century history and ongoing territorial disputes.
China imposed trade restrictions and urged citizens not to travel to Japan, which had become an increasingly popular tourist destination. Traffic is down by roughly half this year as a result.
A formal one-on-one meeting between Takaichi and China's Xi Jinping is considered highly unlikely, but Japan's NHK public broadcaster did report that Xi would "personally greet her" before Wednesday's banquet.
IN DEPTH: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
Read DW's full report on what Trump, Xi and Putin are hoping to extract from the trilateral talks.
Canada, China taking steps to widen access for financial firms, says Carney
Canada and China are moving to give each other's financial firms greater access to their markets, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said during a speech at the APEC summit.
"When our businesses depend on too few currencies or single payment channels, disruption, when it comes, can spread quickly," he said, adding that China and Canada had renewed the currency swap arrangement between their central banks and were issuing each other's currencies.
Carney's comments came a day after Carney and President Xi held talks in Shenzhen to produce deals to further reduce tariffs. Ottawa is re-engaging with China after years of strained relations as it looks to reduce its reliance on the US.
Trump says US concludes 'very big trade deal' with Philippines
President Trump on Wednesday said that the US has just concluded a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines, albeit without providing details. Manila has not yet confirmed any agreement.
"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries," Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace.
"We were very happy with that, and we didn't know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it's a magnificent deal for both," he said.
Trade negotiations were not listed in the schedules provided by Washington or Manila.
The Philippines' ambassador to the US, Jose Manuel Romualdez said, "The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements."
However, Romualdez told Reuters that nothing had been signed.
The man in the middle: Xi hosts APEC summit
The two-day APEC summit has kicked off in China's southern city of Shenzhen. DW's Rik Glauert in Taipei offers a preview of what host, Xi Jinping, is hoping to achieve.
Xi calls for 'free and open trade' as counter to US tariffs
President Xi pledged to stand against trade protectionism in his speech at the APEC summit on Wednesday, in a subtle slight towards the United States and the trade war waged by its president.
Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage in contrast with its main economic rival, the US, which has raised tariffs under President Trump.
His remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, further complicating a trade truce between the two superpowers.
Xi urged that China and Russia, together, take concrete measures to further cooperation and "lead and advance the trend toward a multipolar world."
Chinese and Russian news agencies reported at around noon on Wednesday that Xi and Putin had met for talks. That's the fifth time the two leaders have met this year, including once by video link.
Putin says he expects 'big potential benefit' from meeting with China, US
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday said he expected major benefits from his upcoming trilateral meet with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of the APEC summit, Putin called for partnership over isolation, citing a fragmented global economy and military-political risks.
"I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States, which is scheduled to take place on the sidelines of the APEC summit," Putin told the summit.
The Russian leader held bilateral talks with Xi ahead of the pair's trilateral talks with Trump on Thursday.
Putin said Chinese and Russian foreign policy was working "steadily and positively on the international stage."
Taiwan says in contact with US ahead of Trump-Putin-Xi summit
Taiwan's presidential office said that it was in close contact with the US ahead of meetings on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
US President Donald Trump is set to arrive in China on Wednesday.
Trump is then scheduled to take part in a highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
Taiwan "views positively any effort that helps manage the risks of authoritarian expansion and contributes to regional security and stability," office spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
This comes amid heightened tensions between Taipei and Beijing.
China has refused to talk to Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, whom Beijing sees as a staunch separatist. Lai has defended Taiwan's right to self-rule.
China's Xi calls for 'free and open' trade, deeper AI cooperation at APEC opening
China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called for more international cooperation on AI and "free and open" trade.
Xi made the remarks as he opened a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen, southern China, where he is expected to meet US President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who landed overnight, on Thursday.
Trump is due to arrive in Shenzhen later on Wednesday.
"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," Xi said.
"We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition," the Chinese leader said.
Trade tensions have loomed over the world's two largest economies as the summit neared.
Trump's wide-ranging tariffs have disrupted global trade.
China has responded with its own import levies and has threatened to withhold crucial exports.
Russia's Putin has arrived in China for APEC summit
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in China earlier to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit over the next two days.
Putin is expected to take part in a first-ever trilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

noticias.titulo: How a green economy could help reverse climate change
noticias.resumen: Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?
noticias.texto:
How a green economy could help reverse climate change
November 18, 2026
Human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.
If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.
Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.
"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.
Can economies grow while emissions fall?
In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.
Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.
The economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan and Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.
In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.
But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.
In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.
"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.
And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.
These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.
Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.
Emissions aren't the only problem with economic growth
There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.
Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.
But that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.
The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.
Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.
"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.
She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.
"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need."
Is degrowth the future?
Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.
Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.
That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.
Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.
Ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.
A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.
However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.
Is an environmentally friendly economy possible?
Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.
"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.
Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.
"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be."
An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.
Countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.
And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.
Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain."
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Merz's coalition agrees on electricity tax cut
noticias.resumen: The coalition government has agreed on an electricity tax cut for households amid energy shocks from the war in Iran. Meanwhile, the BSW party has failed to push for a recount of the 2025 election. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Merz's coalition agrees on electricity tax cut
Published November 18, 2026last updated November 18, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed on a tax cut for households and businesses for 2027
- A previous cut only applied to industry, agriculture and forestry
- A top court has rejected a recount appeal by the BSW party over the 2025 election
Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, November 18, 2026:
Governing coalition agrees to electricity tax cut
Germany's governing coalition has agreed to reduce electricity tax for households and businesses.
The cut will lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level.
The agreement between Chancelor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and his junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), was reached after multiple failed attempts.
Funding for the tax cut has only been secured for the year 2027, but the coalition stressed in a summary document of the agreement that it aimed to achieve a "permanent reduction." An extension is contingent on finding a way to fund it into 2028, according to the paper.
The coalition partners said that the tax cut will be funded by surplus funds from subsidies under the renewable energy bill, as the government anticipates lower demand for renewable energy subsidies next year.
The government is also to introduce a three-month cap on fuel prices in January.
The CDU/CSU and SPD promised in their 2025 coalition deal to cut taxes for all consumers, but initially only applied a reduction for industry, agriculture and forestry. Wednesday's agreement extends cuts to households and to businesses that did not qualify for the initial reduction.
Germany has some of the highest electricity prices in Europe, in part thanks to shocks following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and by the United States and Israel's war with Iran.
The Wednesday agreement still needs to be incorporated into the 2027 budget. The budget must then be cleared by the parliamentary budget committee, with the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, expected to give final approval on November 27.
The 2027 federal budget proposal marks a major shift in German fiscal policy, with Berlin taking on increasing debt, citing the need to finance repairs to the country's crumbling infrastructure, carry out the energy transition and expand and modernize the military.
Spike in holiday requests ahead of GTA6 launch
Germans are seemingly requesting days off work to play GTA 6 ahead of the videogame's Thursday release, according to data from the HR software company Personio
GTA 6 is part of the popular open-world, action-adventure series "Grand Theft Auto," in which the player can explore a city, commit crimes outside, and complete hours worth of missions.
The latest installment has been eagerly awaited by gamers for 13 years, having been subject to two delays and multiple leaks.
The Munich-based personnel software provider Personio said that Germany saw 38% more requests for days off than usual for the launch of GTA 6, and a 58% in requests for compensatory time off for overtime hours worked.
However, economists do not expect the rush to play the long-awaited game to have any impact on the German economy.
"The economy won't collapse because of GTA, just because some people decide to take a bit of time off," media economist Jörg Müller-Lietzkow was cited by ZDF as saying.
Net household incomes rising, but inequality remains — report
Real net household incomes in Germany are rising again following a period of high inflation, according to a report from the German economics research institute DIW Berlin.
The report revealed that overall income satisfaction has risen significantly as more and more people in Germany are managing to save.
However, the rise has not yet offset earlier losses from high inflation rates in 2022 and 2023, the institute said.
Incomes have grown by an average of nearly one-third since 1995, but inequality has risen significantly — while top incomes have risen by over 50%, those in the middle of the curve have risen by around a quarter and those at the lower end have largely remained stagnant.
DIW Berlin warned that the long-term risk of falling into poverty has risen to 17%.
However, the report's author stressed that the increase in inequality was due to a shift over a longer period and it had not significantly widened in recent years.
"While income inequality in Germany has risen over the long term, it has remained largely stable in recent years," DIW Berlin researcher Markus Grabka said.
Merz briefly left electricity tax cut talks out of irritation — report
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz left Tuesday night's coalition talks on an electricity tax cut out of frustration, German tabloid newspaper Bild reported on Wednesday.
Bild cited participants of the coalition meeting as saying that Merz left the talks in Berlin around midnight local time (2300 UTC) over demands made by his CDU/CSU conservative bloc's junior coalition partners, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Before leaving, Merz said "I'm not putting up with this anymore," according to Bild. He later returned to talks, reportedly after speaking to Markus Söder, who leads the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Merz's own Christian Democrats (CDU).
The coalition ultimately agreed upon a reduction in the electricity tax for households and businesses, bringing the rate for 2027 to the European minimum level.
According to Bild, the SPD had insisted on guaranteeing funding for the measure well beyond 2027.
The tax cut is to be funded by surplus funds from subsidies under the renewable energy bill and its extension is contingent on finding a way to fund it into 2028, according to a summary paper of an agreement reached between the two coalition factions.
Bild cited sources close to Merz as saying that the talks had been very difficult and intricate, with the CDU arguing that the issue could have been resolved within an hour, rather than extending deep into the night.
The two parties have regularly been at odds over key policy questions, particularly around budget and taxation issues.
Live lobster found on Munich train
Police were called to the lost and found for Munich's S-Bahn suburban rail network after a live lobster was found on one of the trains.
The lobster, weighing some 3 kilograms (around 6.6 pounds), was found in a Styrofoam box by S-Bahn workers on Tuesday morning.
He was initially treated with a saline solution and given the nickname "Günni."
Police determined that the crustacean had initially been purchased from a wholesale market for hospitality and retail in Munich and escorted it back to the point of sale.
Foreign Minister Wadephul visits Armenia, Azerbaijan
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Armenia and Azerbaijan on Wednesday.
He is set to make his way to Yerevan, Armenia after his visit to the Azerbaijani capital, Baku.
Discussions were to focus on implementing a joint strategic agenda signed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev in July, according to the ministry.
The leaders were also to discuss the supply of natural gas and crude oil from Azerbaijan.
They were also to touch on the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which fought wars over the Nagorno-Karabakh territory in 2020 and 2023.
Germany supports 'positive momentum' in Armenia-Azerbaijan peace
The ministry cited Wadephul as saying Berlin aimed to capitalize on the "positive momentum" between Baku and Yerevan that had developed since the 2025 peace summit in Washington.
Wadephul said that he also aims to examine Russia's influence in the southern Caucasus.
"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence — at the expense of the people and their future," the minister said on Tuesday before embarking on a flight to the region.
Armenia and Azerbaijan were part of the former Soviet Union and Russia maintains significant influence in the region.
Constitutional Court rejects BSW request for 2025 vote recount
Germany's Constitutional Court has rejected an appeal brought by the populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) against the February 2025 federal election result, dashing the party's hopes it could trigger a recount that would allow it to enter parliament.
The BSW party, formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance after the name of its founder, narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold to enter the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.
Having received 4,981% of the vote, it would have needed just 9,529 more votes to enter the chamber.
The BSW maintained that there had been an error in the vote count and that the party could be assigned some 35 seats.
If the party were to enter parliament, a rearrangement of seats could also threaten the majority held by the current ruling coalition made up of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left Social Democrats.
Lack of recount 'slap in the face of democracy' — BSW
"Everything points to the conclusion that Merz is an illegitimate chancellor and that the current Bundestag is not composed in accordance with the constitution," party founder Sahra Wagenknecht told Germany's DPA news agency before the court published its ruling.
"Without access to the actual ballots, it is impossible to provide further evidence or indications of counting errors to the detriment of the BSW."
She said that if the court were to rule against the party's appeal, this would be a "slap in the face of democracy."
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
Germany's coalition government, made up of the conservative CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), has agreed to an electricity tax cut.
Germany's Constitutional Court has rejected an appeal by the populist BSW party to do a recount of the 2025 election after they failed to top the 5% hurdle to enter the Bundestag.
Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting the southern Caucasus nations of Armenia and Azerbaijan.
The German Cabinet has nominated Germany's Markus Brunnermeier for the role of the European Central Bank's (ECB) chief economist.
Continue following this blog for more on that and other stories from Germany!

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Kyiv targets Krasnodar refineries after felling Kerch bridge
noticias.resumen: Reports that two industrial facilities were targeted overnight in Krasnodar, after the Kerch bridge was put out of action by Ukrainian strikes.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine: Kyiv targets Krasnodar refineries after felling Kerch bridge
Published November 18, 2026last updated November 18, 2026
What you need to know
- Two industrial facilities ablaze in Russia's Krasnodar
- Ukraine intercepts 126 drones in overnight Russian strikes
- Reported strikes come a day after the Kerch bridge was put out of action by Ukrainian attacks
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 18, 2026:
At least 4 killed in Russian strikes in Odesa
Regional officials say that at least four people have been killed in Russian strikes in the Black Sea port city of Odesa.
Regional governor Oleh Kiper said on Telegram that at least 13 people had also been injured.
Kiper said windows of residential buildings, cafes and shops had been broken, a car had been set on fire and several other vehicles had been damaged.
Both Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles, along with the continued use of drones, to strike inside each other's territories.
Odesa is a frequent target of Russian missile and drone strikes.
EU proposes €45 billion additional support for Ukraine in 2027
The European Commission has proposed a further €45 billion ($49.3 billion) in additional financial support to Ukraine in 2027.
"For 2026, Ukraine's needs are covered. And today we are proposing a further €45 billion to cover two thirds of its needs for 2027," European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Together, with our international partners, we will strengthen Ukraine. For as long as it takes to achieve a just and lasting peace," von der Leyen said.
According to the Commission, the proposed support would have up to €25 billion allocated to military support and up to €20 billion as general budget support in Ukraine.
The EU and member states have provided nearly €238 billion in support to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
Germany calls for Russia to be held accountable after chemical weapons probe
Germany's Foreign Office has called for Russia to be held accountable after a Ukrainian investigation concluded that Russia had used CS gas on Ukrainian forces.
"Russia continues its relentless war against Ukraine and commits grave breaches of the Chemical Weapons Convention," the Foreign Office said in a post on X.
"A Ukrainian investigation has found clear evidence of the use of prohibited chemicals. Russia needs to be held accountable," the statement read.
The Ukrainian probe was conducted with the help of the global chemical weapons watchdog, the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW).
The organization confirmed in 2024 that CS gas, which is banned on the battlefield, was found at several sites in Ukraine.
The new investigation now links the weapons used to the Russian military.
Ukraine focused on an incident from September 2024, in which Russian forces attacked a military post in central Ukraine.
Investigators found a video posted to a pro-Russian Telegram channel, which they say showed a grenade filled with tear gas being dropped from a drone onto Ukrainian forces.
Russia is party to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), having signed it in 1993 and ratified it in 1997.
Use of riot control agents on the battlefield is prohibited under the CWC.
WATCH: Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes
During a meeting of Ukraine's supporters in Brussels, US representative Elbridge Colby criticized Kyiv's use of deep strikes against Russian targets. But Germany's defense minister said the US's criticism was misguided.
Europe must be part of Ukraine peace talks — Wadephul
Germany's top diplomat is insisting that Europe should be involved in negotiations to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
"I expect, and have no reason to doubt, that talks on Ukraine's future will be held between Russia and Ukraine with Europe's participation," Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said during a meeting with his Azerbaijani counterpart, Jeyhun Bayramov, in the capital Baku.
Failing that, it would not be possible to achieve a sustainable solution that guarantees "that a new conflict does not emerge after this war, which we hope will end as soon as possible," Wadephul warned.
The comments come ahead of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China on Thursday.
Wadephul did welcome the planned trilateral talks in Shenzhen between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation, I say as a foreign policy expert," he said.
WATCH: Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea
The Kerch Bridge appears heavily damaged after a major Ukrainian strike. Footage released by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shows drones and missiles hitting the key link between Russia and occupied Crimea.
Reports of two industrial facilities struck in Russia's Krasnodar region
Ukraine has reportedly struck two industrial targets in Russia's Krasnodar region.
Media outlets in Ukraine are reporting that oil refineries have been struck, although this cannot be independently verified.
Telegram channels in the Krasnodar region warned of overnight drone strikes but it was not immediately clear what had been hit and whether damage had been caused.
Ukrainian online publication The Kyiv Independent reported that the Ilsky and Afipsky oil refineries had been hit and cited Telegram channel Exilenova, a pro-Ukrainian account that tracks developments in the ongoing war with the information.
The two refineries are the largest in the region and have previously been targeted by drone strikes.
The reported strikes come a day after Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge, linking occupied Crimea to Russia, putting the road and railway out of action.
The Ukrainian General Staff said an arch and part of the bridge's road section collapsed into the water, severing the link for vehicular traffic, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch.
Welcome to our coverage
We're following the latest developments in Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine has launched strikes on targets not far from the Kerch bridge, that up until yesterday, could be traveled by road and rail from the occupied Crimean peninsula to Russia's Krasnodar region.
The bridge is an arterial route for both Russia's military and civilian supplies to Crimea and is seen by Ukraine as a symbol of Moscow's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
There've also been more Russian overnight attacks, with Ukraine reporting dozens of interceptions.
Stay with us as we bring you updates related to Russia's war in Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: India news: Gandhi gives talk in New York, warns of 'looming crisis'
noticias.resumen: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's US remarks on the economy drew a BJP counterattack. Meanwhile, the Quad leaders pushed back on moves to undermine regional peace,
noticias.texto:
India news: Gandhi gives talk in New York, warns of 'looming crisis'
Published November 18, 2026last updated November 18, 2026
What you need to know
- Rahul Gandhi warns of economic crisis at a talk in New York, BJP accuses him of 'anti-India propaganda'
- Modi, Trump meet with Quad leaders in the Philippines
- William and Kate, the Prince and Princess of Wales, honor Earthshot winners in Mumbai
Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Wednesday, November 18:
Delhi rolls back pollution curbs after air quality improves
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) lifted Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) across Delhi-National Capital Region on Tuesdayafter the capital's air quality improved, local media reported.
The commission's sub-committee withdrew its November 6 order – issued two days before the festival of Diwali – with immediate effect after Delhi's daily average Air Quality Index reading reached 204 (indicating "poor" air quality), the cleanest this month.
Stage III was imposed on November 6, when the AQI hit 382. The 50% cap on office attendance has been withdrawn. Meanwhile, rules on older petrol and diesel vehicles have also been eased.
Stage I and II measures and the CAQM's October 30 order, which covered November 5 to 20, remain in force. Curbs on construction and demolition also continue.
The decision followed several days of steady improvement.
WATCH — As glaciers retreat, Ladakh innovates for its water
In the remote Himalayan village of Ursi in Ladakh, farmers depend on snowmelt. But climate change is both altering seasonal rainfall and reducing snowfall, forcing locals to get innovative.
Watch to learn more:
Quad leaders meet in Manila ahead of Trump's China talks
Leaders of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, which groups India, the US, Japan and Australia, met in Manila on Tuesday for their first summit in more than two years. It was the first Quad leaders' meeting of Donald Trump's current term.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Trump, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese held closed-door talks on the sidelines of the ASEAN meetings.
The joint statement said the leaders "strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," which local media called a signal to China.
The Deccan Herald said the language largely repeated earlier Quad statements but Trump avoided a strong message to Beijing ahead of his Thursday talks with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
The statement also condemned terrorism "in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism." It was the Quad's first summit since the 2025 Pahalgam attack.
A new initiative called the Quad Business Leaders' Forum is set to be hosted by India in early 2027. Additionally, a joint Quad exercise by maritime patrol aircraft in 2027 and a new maritime surveillance collaboration have also been planned.
"From maritime security to supply chains, new technologies to disaster response, the Quad provides trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific," Modi said. Meanwhile, Trump praised Modi as a "great leader."
William and Kate honor Earthshot winners in Mumbai
The Princess of Wales made a rare speaking appearance at the Earthshot Prize awards in Mumbai on Tuesday. "Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come," Catherine said of the winners.
Prince William, who founded the prize, said in his keynote speech that history is shaped not only by challenges but also by the people who rise to meet them. The prize is now at the midpoint of its planned 10 years.
Each winner received £1 million ($1.3 million, 1.2 million euros). They included Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, the maker of the electric rickshaw William drove earlier with Catherine as a passenger.
Catherine presented the Protect and Restore Nature award to Bhutan, which has written nature protection into its constitution and keeps nearly 70% of its land under forest.
Actor Rami Malek and cricketer Sachin Tendulkar were among the presenters. The royal couple wore outfits by Indian designers: a Mahima Mahajan "anarkali" for Kate and a Manish Malhotra "bandhgala" jacket for William.
Rahul Gandhi warns of economic crisis during talk in New York
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, during a conversation at Columbia University in New York City on Tuesday, said that India faces a looming economic crisis.
Answering a question about India's youth, the opposition leader said: "The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That's the reality. One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside, but India's got a massive unemployment problem. India's got a massive problem with its education system."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party responded sharply, calling him the "leader of anti-India propaganda."
Gandhi also reiterated his vote theft charge.
"140 million people who would have voted in 2024 have been removed from the electoral roll. We ask the Election Commission: how can an election be considered valid under these circumstances?" he was reported in Indian media as saying.
The Election Commission has rejected allegations of wrongdoing over the voter-roll revision.
In response, BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari took to social media to say: "His inherent hate for India's progress and Indian democracy makes him speak ill about India every time he goes abroad!"
Gandhi, on a two-day US visit, is also due to visit the University of Chicago on Wednesday.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello again!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest news from India.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has once again found himself on the receiving end of the BJP’s criticism after warning of a deepening economic crisis in India during an interaction at Columbia University.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi met with US President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Quad leaders' summit in Manila, Philippines.
Finally, the Prince and Princess of Wales were in Mumbai to celebrate this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
For this and more, keep reading.

noticias.titulo: US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
noticias.resumen: The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.
noticias.texto:
US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
November 18, 2026
The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.
Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.
The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.
Peltola promises to deliver for 'Alaska's working families'
"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.
"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.
Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.
Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.
Vote siphon allegations
The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.
The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.
The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.
"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.
Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.
The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

noticias.titulo: Pakistani man gets 27 years for foiled plot to kill Trump, Biden
noticias.resumen: A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison for his role in plotting to kill US politicians, including President Donald Trump.
noticias.texto:
Pakistani man gets 27 years for foiled plot to kill Trump, Biden
November 18, 2026
A US court sentenced a Pakistani man to more than 27 years in jail for plotting to kill US President Donald Trump and other prominent politicians at the behest of Iran, authorities said on Tuesday.
"Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a US president or other senior government official," said US District Judge Eric Komitee while reading out the sentence.
The 48-year-old man was handed 330 months in prison for "attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire," the US Department of Justice said in a statement. That's 27 years and six months.
A US jury had already convicted the man in March of traveling to the US to arrange political assassinations on American soil.
The trial had begun in late February, days before the Trump administration ordered strikes on Iran that it carried out with Israel. The war has killed thousands, mostly in Iran, Lebanon and Yemen, but also in countries around the Persian Gulf.
It is still ongoing.
A plot to kill Trump: What prompted it?
Prosecutors said the convict tried to recruit people in the US for a plan to kill Trump and other US politicians in retaliation for Washington's killing of Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani in January 2020.
Trump was in his first term as US president at the time.
Other targets in the 2024 plot included then-US President Joe Biden and Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump for the Republican presidential nominination, prosecutors said.
What else do we know about foiled plot to kill US politicians?
During his trial, the man testified that he had joined the plot with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps but did so unwillingly to protect his family in Tehran.
Tehran has denied targeting Trump or other US officials or plotting attacks against them.
The Pakistani man bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump's rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally to an acquaintance. He then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he had borrowed from a relative.
The man also said that he assumed that US authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward.
The DOJ said that a person contacted the man in April 2024 to help with the plot, only to report his activities and become a confidential informant.
The convicted man was arrested in Texas in July 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump's life in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

noticias.titulo: Slovakia: Thousands protest against pro-Kremlin leader Robert Fico
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister Robert Fico has been under fire over his ties to Russia. The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that toppled communism in Czechoslovakia.
noticias.texto:
Slovakia: Thousands protest against pro-Kremlin leader Robert Fico
November 18, 2026
Thousands of people protested across Slovakia on Tuesday to demonstrate against Prime Minister Robert Fico and his pro-Russian government.
The demonstration was organized by opposition parties and non-governmental organizations (NGOs).
The largest protest was on SNP Square, which was the site of the main anti-Communist protests during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, in the capital, Bratislava.
Organizers said 25,000 people had gathered there.
Other rallies were also held across the country, which is an EU and NATO member, including in the cities of Kosice and Banska Bystrica.
Why are people protesting in Slovakia?
The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended decades of communist rule in what was then called Czechoslovakia.
Protesters commemorated the fall of the communist dictatorship, which ruled Czechoslovakia for 41 years. They also called for more support for Ukraine.
The demonstrators mostly focused on Slovakia's prime minister, however, chanting slogans such as "We've had enough of Fico!"
One banner told the prime minister to "Go to hell."
Why are Slovaks angry with Fico?
Since Hungary's Viktor Orban was removed from power in April, Fico stands as Europe's most pro-Russian leader.
He opposed military aid for Ukraine and has maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite European Union sanctions against Russia.
Fico, who has served as prime minister four times in over two decades, has faced numerous protests since returning to power in 2023.
Fico has also repeatedly clashed with the EU. Last year, Slovakia's constitution was amended to state that national law takes precedence over EU law.
He has also been criticized for trying to exert greater control over the media and culture, and curbing LGBTQ+ rights.
"We're the last ones in the European Union to be negotiating with the Russians... It's a disgrace," Igor Vico, a 74-year-old doctor, told AFP.
"We're at the bottom of the world, not just in Europe, and it makes me sad," he said.

noticias.titulo: Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
noticias.resumen: Children frolic around the ever-watchful and calm Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze, in a square named after the German artist, whose work often depicted children in the wake of World War I.
noticias.texto:
Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
If you were listening to this, you'd hear what isn't pictured: the whoops and wails of children playing on the swings and slides behind me, all under the watchful eye of Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze. The German expressionist lived just off this square in Berlin — named after her, Kollwitzplatz — and, at the turn of the 20th century, her children probably played here, too.
In the wake of World War I, Kollwitz's lithographs, woodcuts and sculptures fixated on the suffering and futility of war. They depict undernourished, wide-eyed children in the protective arms of mothers whose anguish is etched into their faces. Her statue, The Grieving Parents, stands in Belgium where her son Peter died at the front, aged 18.
As I turn my back briefly on the playground and aim my camera at Kollwitz, a boy jumps into the shot, up onto the statue's plinth. Playing hide and seek, he conceals himself behind Kollwitz. His friend finds him quickly and the two boys chase each other around the statue, inadvertently embracing Kollwitz like she does her own boys in her lithograph renderings.
The Kollwitz statue's presence is calm. She sits, charcoal in hand, poised to draw the happy hubbub of children growing up in a city that is safe. But with wars not so far away and Germany bringing back military service for a new generation, I feel a sudden urge to wrap my arms around my own child, just as Kollwitz did.
For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph
noticias.resumen: An inspired synthesis of violent satire and contemplative storytelling, Grand Theft Auto VI is more mature and ambitious than any prior game in the record-breaking franchise.
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph
I want to tell you about the time I saw Bigfoot. I want to tell you about sitting in the rain on a city street in a muscle car and prepping to rob a bank while lightning split the sky between high-rise condo towers in the distance and the drum fill from In The Air Tonight played on the radio. I want to tell you about gunfights and fistfights, the perfect satire of radio commercials and how the sunrise looks over Ocean Beach. But more than any of that, I want to tell you about the time an alligator bit my mom.
It happened in the backyard of an abandoned house with a rotting inground pool. My mom, Mia Caminos (mother of Lucia Caminos, one of the two leads in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI, probably the most highly anticipated video game sequel of all time), was thrilled by the pool. Standing there, amid the artfully rendered weeds and trash, she spread her arms and told me to use my imagination, to see her vision for this ruin of a house with its upmarket water feature, in a scabby neighborhood on the outskirts of Vice City. She speaks in tones of increasingly frantic desperation because she has already put money down on this house, sight unseen. All of her money, actually, in hopes of flipping it and selling it fast to keep her startup real estate business afloat.
The pool is still half full of water. There's a dirty, sodden mattress floating in it. And as if this is the main thing standing between her and success, Mia is fixated on getting it out of the pool.
Help me, Lucia, she says.
And, dutifully, I do. Playing as Lucia, I grab hold, mash buttons, help my mom drag away the wet, heavy, stinking mattress. And just as we get it up and over the lip of the pool that's going to be the thing that makes this wreck of a house suddenly desirable – that's when the alligator lunges out of the murky water, grabs my mom by the arm and tries to drag her back in.
This is a story about folly, fixation, unrealistic expectations of success at the ass-end of late capitalism, and the vicious, whip-crack cruelty of predators who lie in wait for anyone trying to improve a terrible situation.
But then I shoot the alligator in the head before it can eat my mom. Because this is also a story about violence, and how sometimes (maybe all the times), the loud, cathartic rip of gunfire is the only solution left for people who have already lost so much and can't bear to see one more thing taken from them.
It's a story about my mom and an alligator, sure.
It is also the story of GTA6
But let's back up a little. For anyone who has somehow missed the shrieking, neon-and-swamp-water marketing onslaught over the past several days, weeks, months and years, Grand Theft Auto VI is the newest release from Rockstar Games. It is a Bonnie and Clyde love story, a knife-edged satire of modern American culture and politics, an unapologetic murder simulator, a love letter to 50 years of crime movies, and a thoughtful, emotional meditation on the sacrifices, small and large, that we make for family. A massive open world game set in the fictional state of Leonida (based on the very real state of Florida), it represents a return to a location that Rockstar hasn't visited in-depth since its 2002 release of GTA: Vice City, and is the first new game in the franchise since GTA5 launched in 2013. According to estimates, it already earned over $1.5 billion in pre-sales and will likely make a total of $3 to $5 billion in its first week, which could make it the largest single entertainment product launch ever.
Fans have been waiting years for it. They have created libraries worth of lore and theories and dissected trailers frame-by-frame. To discount the overheated environment into which this singular work of art is being released would be doing a disservice both to it and the legions of salivating prognosticators who have made guessing the number of bird species included in-game, or speculating on the square mileage of its map, their entire personalities.
Now, though, they know it all. We all do. We know that GTA6 is expansive, covering everything from the Keys (where the game starts) to the hilly, forested north, with Vice City in all its grimy, pastel-colored splendor at the beating heart of it. It is a playground, equal parts gorgeous and maniacal, and in all that space the developers have given us a thousand different things to do. You can rob a bank or take a bike ride, go fishing, hunt trophy animals, visit strip clubs, rob random civilians, street race, fly drones, eat a sandwich, work out, manage your family savings account, jump a sports car off the top of a building, steal a plane, punch out a convenience store clerk, fight a bear or, yes, just wander out toward the horizon and study the birds. And while some of that is fun and all of it is diverting (at least for a little while), none of it is the ostensible point. The game-y part of the game — the hundred extras and time-wasters that players have come to expect from open-world projects in general, and GTA specifically — is not what makes it matter.
What matters is Mia and the alligator, Lucia and the gun. It's the multi-pronged, exquisitely balanced narrative about poverty and rigged systems that makes it hard to turn away from GTA while you're playing and impossible not to think about when you're away.
Lucia is an ex-con, a car thief and a small-time criminal who got caught trying to rob a payday loan joint and starts the game in jail. Her partner, Jason Duval, is a veteran, dishonorably discharged, now making a living flying loads for a local coke dealer down in the Keys and living rent-free in one of his properties. Jason skims a little on the coke deals, wears flip-flops and drinks beer in the sun, and goes fishing with his best friend Cal (played with genius-level goofy, drunken paranoia and dopey bravado by Bobby Moynihan). Jason and Lucia have a kid, Tomás, who is currently living with Lucia's family, and every plan they have is about getting right by the law, making a few bucks and grabbing a chance at finally being a family.
Only there are complications — surprisingly banal ones at first (like not being able to open a checking account because of their bad credit) — that slowly ramp up into huge ones across 60-odd hours of main story gameplay that see Jason and Lucia (both of whom are playable characters) graduate from knocking over liquor stores in a beat-up El Camino, to pulling off elaborate heists in the middle of Vice City which will have you dangling from a net suspended from a cargo helicopter hauling 200 tons of cocaine. It goes from Badlands to Die Hard with the speed of a muscle car, all bright chrome and barking straight pipes. From True Romance to Heat like that's just the natural arc of any American love story.
And what's remarkable about the whole bloody delight is that it remains, until its final operatic moments, so surprisingly grounded. This is a somewhat more mature GTA than its predecessors, trading aliens, cannibal cultists and whacked-out drug trips for wellness influencers, local politics and the music industry. Jason and Lucia's relationship is the superstructure around which the entire narrative is built, and it's a dynamic thing that must be maintained in a dozen little ways — making coffee in the morning, opening doors for each other, date nights (even if that means robbing a jewelry store together), or holding hands as you walk toward yet another betrayal by someone you thought you could trust. You can switch freely between them, or just call the other one to come drive the getaway car. Let their relationship dwindle and the narrative shifts, flattens. But when they're together, the two of them talk and talk: In bed, in the car, by the pool. They reveal pieces of themselves in quiet moments, joke, tease, flirt, make plans for a future that always seems right around the next corner. And you love them for it. You can't help but love them for it, and root for them, and want good things for them, because they're just two hard-luck kids trying to do right in a world where "right" sometimes means petting a dog or helping a farmer spray manure all over his boss's house, and sometimes means stealing $10 million from South American drug lords.
In so many ways GTA6 is an example of inspired synthesis. Rockstar made a killing with the sunlit beauty and craziness of GTA5 more than a decade ago, a game built on deconstructing Hollywood myths and male friendships. Then it made art with a slow-burn meditation on loyalty, death and obsolescence in Red Dead Redemption 2. And this? It is the middle path charted between those two bright stars. It has seriousness and weight and something to say. And also, you accidentally end up starring in a porno movie. Through mechanical tweaks and narrative railroading, the game trades abject chaos for consequences that force you to actually live in its world rather than just murder your way through it, but then makes the dullest, most quotidian chores (like going grocery shopping or answering your mom's texts) feel like a long, slow breath taken between gasping moments of panic.
Yes, you have to sleep. Yes, you have to eat. Yes, you have to work out and put gas in the (stolen) car. But after a while, I found myself actually wanting to do those things because doing them felt like roleplaying; like added opportunities to fully exist within the fiction of Jason or Lucia's world. And in what will no doubt enrage a million over-testosteroned 15-year-olds who want nothing more out of GTA6 than a shinier, brighter, higher-resolution playground in which to jack a Lambo and mow down pedestrians, certain mechanical adjustments in the game (like cars that exist without the tools immediately available to steal them, or how you no longer carry every gun you've ever touched, but store them in the trunk of your ride) have made it harder to jump right in and create mayhem from hour one.
Plus, the police response has been overhauled. Commit brazen crimes and cameras will capture your appearance. Witnesses will describe your clothes or getaway car. Wanted levels now measure not just the size of the armed response, but its sophistication, so speed and stealth become vital. Do a job cleanly, destroy the evidence, get out fast without tripping alarms or blowing stuff up and you're golden. Go loud and cops will search whole regions for you, using helicopters and canine units. They'll hunt you until you change your appearance, swap cars, or simply flee.
To call the game a masterpiece seems like a cheap, throwaway declaration because after years of development and hundreds of millions of dollars spent, a masterpiece feels… expected, right? Like if it wasn't a masterpiece, that would feel somehow personally insulting. Like they just didn't try hard enough. But the truth is, these things can go wrong so easily. They are enormous, unwieldy, lumbering projects that can fall apart for any number of reasons — and do all the time.
But this one didn't. There is a gloss on it that feels like love. A polish so fine that if you're not looking for it, you might not even notice the way the palm fronds move in the wind when there's weather coming in, or the light on the edge of a storm; how Lucia hangs her head out of a convertible when Jason is driving, or the way the sound of your tires changes depending on whether you're cruising on macadam or blacktop. Does it drag a little in the third act? Sure. Are there NPC glitches, targeting hang-ups and moments where you have to stop to puzzle out exactly who is betraying whom and how they're all connected? Absolutely. But at almost any point, you can walk away from the narrative for a while, call your better half, hop in your car and just drive. Everywhere you go, Leonida is alive around you in a way that no game has ever been before. There are a million stories here just waiting to be discovered or created. Pick one. See where it leads you.
But remember Mia and the alligator. Because at its core, GTA6 will always be a story about predators and prey. And no matter where you go or how powerful you think you are, you can never, ever be sure which one you are.
Jason Sheehan knows stuff about food, video games, books and Star Blazers. He's the restaurant critic at Philadelphia magazine, but when no one is looking, he spends his time writing books about giant robots and ray guns. Children of the Flying City is his latest book.

noticias.titulo: Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
noticias.resumen: Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's visit to Washington in September.
noticias.texto:
Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
