"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
What's on the agenda for Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."
Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

noticias.titulo: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
noticias.resumen: A federal judge is keeping East Potomac Park open for now, but hasn't ordered the government to keep the municipal golf course operational.
noticias.texto:
How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.
Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.
But Sunday marked the last day of the government's lease with the National Links Trust, which had operated the golf course since 2020. And Reyes did not order the government to keep operating the golf course — though she has since signaled she may consider it.
"Whether and how Defendants do so is solely within their discretion, but Defendants cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course," Reyes wrote in her 30-page order.
Reyes criticized the government's "pretextual" justification and "arbitrary" timeline for closing the park, which she said would "irreparably harm" the people who enjoy it on a daily basis — including the local preservationists and golfers who first sued to protect the course in February.
In comments on social media and to the press, President Trump slammed her decision and said his administration will appeal. The White House referred NPR to those comments.
"What she's done is she stopped it for 15 days," Trump told reporters when asked about the case on Monday. "You can't stop that."
The National Park Service and Interior Department did not respond to NPR's questions about the future of the course.
Trump has his sights set on redeveloping the golf course — which he has repeatedly decried as decrepit and dangerous — into a championship-level venue. Administration officials are due to present that vision to the federal Commission of Fine Arts on Thursday.
According to the government's 64-page submission, architect Tom Fazio's design would replace East Potomac's three courses of varying difficulty levels with one 18-hole layout stretching across almost the entire peninsula.
The plan is broadly unpopular in D.C., as it would eliminate the perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists, and the grassy areas where people picnic and birdwatch. Critics worry the new course would be less accessible for beginners and less affordable for everyone. Prices currently range from $17 to $48 per round, and the Trump administration has not said what a round at the new course would cost, only that locals would be able to play at a discount.
Locals agree that East Potomac could use some improvements, including to its long-eroded seawall. But that's very different from overhauling the course entirely. Reyes pressed government lawyers at a Friday hearing on why the National Park Service chose the latter.
Officials pointed to Trump's social media directives, but also argued that the park needs to be closed for other reasons: to repair the seawall (for which it acknowledged Friday there is no plan yet) and because of the lack of a golf course operator (a situation Reyes described as "entirely self-inflicted"). And it says there are nearby recreational areas people can use instead — though critics say there is no substitute. Reyes seemed to agree.
"Plaintiffs' harms are tied to 'East Potomac's beauty, historic layout, and historic designs,'" Reyes wrote. "While there are other parks in Washington, D.C., there is no other East Potomac Park."
The East Potomac golf course is known for its history of accessibility
East Potomac is a man-made peninsula, originally dredged from the Potomac River to facilitate shipping channels. Congress designated the land a public park in 1897, declaring it should be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." It houses many forms of recreation, including a tennis complex, a perimeter road and a 220-acre golf course.
The golf course at East Potomac is one of seven that the federal government built in D.C. between 1917 and 1948, according to a 2017 National Park Service historical report. It calls that "a testament to the rise in popularity of the sport of golf and the demand for public golf courses for those who could not [afford] private memberships to exclusive golf clubs in the early decades of the 20th century."
That number has since dwindled to three. East Potomac is the busiest, especially after a renewed interest in golf during the COVID-19 pandemic: It hosted some 125,000 rounds of golf in 2025 alone.
"In a city where politicians are constantly focused on what separates us, East Potomac is one of the few remaining spaces where no matter who you are, what you do, or the state of your game, everyone is welcome and everyone is treated the same," plaintiff Dave Roberts said in a statement when the lawsuit was first filed.
Its first 18 holes were designed by Walter Travis, one of the top amateur golfers in the U.S., who shaped dozens of courses during the "golden age of golf" (which ended around the onset of the Great Depression).
He modeled East Potomac after Scottish "links-style" courses, which are known for their coastal terrain and relative lack of trees — in this case offering clear views of the Potomac River and the Washington Monument. And, in a unique twist, Travis designed the course to be reversible, for the durability of the grounds and to the delight of those who played them.
"Travis captured a design style that characterized the era's greatest courses, including East Potomac: difficult for aggressive elite players, yet playable for unskilled beginners," plaintiffs wrote in their February complaint.
The first portion of the course opened to the public in July 1920. It cost 25 cents to play a round, including locker room privileges. The course was a huge hit, drawing 16,345 golfers in its first year. That number nearly quadrupled by 1921, according to the National Park Service.
The links grew to meet demand over the next decade, ultimately expanding into three courses (red, white and blue) plus one of the first miniature golf courses in the U.S., which features tiny replicas of the White House and U.S. Capitol and is now the country's oldest continually operating mini-golf course.
But despite its broad appeal, East Potomac initially allowed Black players access only during limited hours one day per week. A separate course, Langston, opened to serve Black residents in 1939 — on the site of a former city dump — but suffered from neglect and downright hazardous conditions.
One day in June 1941, three Black golfers showed up at East Potomac and demanded to play.
According to historical accounts, they had a "fair-skinned" friend purchase their tickets but were turned away. They returned with some powerful government allies, and park police ruled that the men should be allowed to play since they had tickets. The trio completed 18 holes, accompanied by police and amidst the "boos and chorus of insults" from white onlookers.
The next day, the interior secretary issued an order opening the course to all players, regardless of race.
Harassment and other forms of segregation persisted at the city's municipal courses for over a decade, but the golfers' 1941 protest is seen as a turning point in the fight for equal access to public spaces. The National Park Service says it "opened the door for the full integration of all national park facilities in 1945."
Judge Reyes has nodded to that part of the park's history throughout the case, including while grilling government lawyers at a mid-October hearing.
"We're not just talking about some putt-putt thing that went up by the beach you take your kids to," she said, adding that the course holds a rich history and "deep amount of meaning" to locals. "There was bravery in the people who first desegregated this golf course."
The course has only closed — temporarily — a few times in its history, including for a portion of World War II and for a few days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, in 1968, when National Guard troops responding to riots set up camp at East Potomac.
What would change?
There have been changes at East Potomac over the decades, like the addition of a two-tiered driving range in the 1990s.
But, as the National Park Service said in its 2017 report, the city's courses continue their original intent "to allow golfers of all ages and skill levels to play at an [affordable] cost compared to private and even semi-private clubs in the area and remain extremely popular."
Plaintiffs note in their lawsuit that a weekend round at East Potomac's blue course costs $48, compared to $89 for a Sunday morning round at the Laurel Hill Golf Club, a municipal golf course in nearby Fairfax County, Va.
Critics worry a championship-style course would be even less affordable — especially one that Trump described over the weekend this way: "All over the World it will be acclaimed as being the Best Golf Course anywhere."
Trump said locals will get a 50% discount. But the administration has not said how much it will cost to play. The administration's proposal only points to "benchmark" championship courses in California, Texas and New York, where locals pay up to $90 per weekend round, even with a discount. The government admitted Friday that those were merely illustrations.
There's also the question of how beginner-friendly the redesigned course would be.
Reyes pointed out last week that under the administration's proposal, even from the shortest tee at every hole, the course adds up to 6,013 yards. She asked the government how that compares to recommended course length averages for different types of players, including seniors and young players, and did not get an answer.
The administration said repeatedly that its plan is not yet final, as it still needs to undergo various federal reviews that require input from experts and the public. Lawyers told Reyes that there is no contract between the government and Fazio, the architect — despite Trump's repeated social media posts saying work would begin on Nov. 15.
Even so, the government said it had to close the park that day in part because there was no one left to run the course.
The nonprofit National Links Trust had entered into a 50-year lease to operate the city's municipal golf courses in 2020. But the government terminated its East Potomac lease last December, accusing it of failing to make capital improvements. The trust continued to manage the course on an interim basis — and still manages the city's other courses — but announced last month that its role would end at East Potomac on Nov. 15.
Reyes said that timing was no coincidence.
"[The National Park Service] claims that it would be unable to safely manage the course itself. In other words, the Government's hands are tied," she wrote in her order. "But the Government tied the knot itself."
Reyes has been openly hesitant to take the administration at its word at this point in the increasingly inflammatory case. She ordered an inquiry into potential misconduct by government lawyers and officials after they cut down hundreds of trees on short notice in October and repeatedly contradicted the president's social media announcements in court.
At Friday's hearing, Reyes questioned why the National Park Service couldn't renew its lease with the operator, especially since it has already entrusted it to manage two other municipal golf courses for another 50 years. She mulled whether the government could theoretically step in to run the golf course, at least until it finds another party to do so.
Reyes appears to be weighing whether she has the legal authority to compel the Trump administration to do that. On Monday, she ordered both parties to submit briefings discussing "whether the Court may require the Government to operate East Potomac Golf Course in order to maintain the status quo."

noticias.titulo: OpenAI announces new AI safety program; researchers worry it won't be enough
noticias.resumen: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he would grant "employee level" access to outside researchers to evaluate AI safety. The pilot program appears much more restrictive.
noticias.texto:
OpenAI announces new AI safety program; researchers worry it won't be enough
AI safety researchers say OpenAI's new third party evaluator program falls far short of what the company promised, raising concerns about its effectiveness.
The company announced Monday that staff from four AI safety and research organizations will become "embedded assessors" to "give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing [potential] risks."
"Getting an outside opinion on the safety work and the robustness of these systems is going to be increasingly important and valuable," CEO Sam Altman said at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.
However, many AI safety researchers say the new program is a far cry from Altman's vow in September that independent evaluators would have "employee-like access" to internal company systems.
Altman's promise came after details of the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI's autonomous systems shook the AI field. Worries of the technology's catastrophic risk captured public attention, and rival Anthropic said it would set up such a program.
"We are giving deep access to some of the most sensitive tools and models our researchers use...that are the most important for assessing key, relevant and timely safety claims," said Lama Ahmad, OpenAI's frontier assurances lead, on X.
Prior to these new embedded evaluation programs, AI companies have brought in outside researchers to assess the capabilities of AI models and identify safety loopholes the companies have missed.
The work of outside evaluators have already helped shed light on the companies' work, and have raised public awareness of safety risks that the technology poses. One recent report about Anthropic using AI to significantly speed up model development has prompted concerns in the field about how close the top companies are to using AI to autonomously build even more powerful models, a stage known as recursive self-improvement. Some in the field worry that if this happens, the velocity of development could lead to catastrophic consequences for humanity and are calling for new regulation against the practice.
Researchers say the actual announcements of how these programs will work suggests something more limited than what Altman promised.
"The assessors have very narrow scopes to their access, and only two of them seem to really be allowed to talk to employees," said Sydney Von Arx, founder of AI safety research group Nightingale.
One of the announced assessors, Apollo Research, outlined its limited access to OpenAI employees. If employees that haven't been whitelisted, or pre-approved, reach out to the embedded assessors, then the assessors will have to loop OpenAI in before having substantive conversations with the employees.
It's important for outside researchers to be able to interview employees, Von Arx said. "They help you find your blind spots. They tell you what you're missing."
Another glaring omission: "Nobody has access to internal Slack," Von Arx said, referring to the corporate messaging tool, which would allow assessors to see what employees are talking about with one another. "Imagine being an 'employee' and only being allowed to talk about company information with whitelisted coworkers and having no Slack."
In a statement to NPR, OpenAI said there's currently no standards for embedded evaluations. "We expect to deepen these relationships over time and share what we learn to help establish best practices for effective embedded assessments across the industry," OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila said. The company also said assessors can ask to talk to employees that haven't already been whitelisted, and that there is a process in place to get statements from OpenAI about things they've learned informally.
The third-party organizations will focus on various aspects of AI safety, according to OpenAI. Some of the work is related to preventing models from trying to engage in undesirable behavior, and other parts are related to catching bad behavior when it happens. The assessors will have access to some internal models, training processes and some OpenAI employees. The assessors will be able to publish their findings after OpenAI redacts confidential information, the company said.
OpenAI's commitment to embedded evaluations was questioned when three employees who worked on safety were fired. They subsequently said they were worried OpenAI is walking back from its promise of having embedded evaluators.
One of the fired employees, Tomek Korbak, was OpenAI's technical point of contact for two outside evaluators that investigated the Hugging Face attack.
"Embedded auditing will only fulfill its aims if the auditors really get employee-level access as opposed to being hired to do a specific job," he posted on X in response to OpenAI's announcement. "Sadly, OpenAI makes it clear now that [Sam Altman's] September tweet about 'employee-like access' was just an awkward overpromise that the company wants to quietly walk back."

noticias.titulo: Iran-backed militias tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist refuses to quit
noticias.resumen: Iran-backed militias kidnapped and tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist is still on a mission to save marshes, and a way of life stretching back to the dawn of history.
noticias.texto:
Iran-backed militias tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist refuses to quit
Drought threatens Iraq’s marshes, risking one of the oldest ways of life
CENTRAL MARSHES, southern Iraq — For all he's been through, environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi still approaches each sighting of wildlife in Iraq's marshes as if it's the very first time — even though he has seen them thousands of times before.
"Do you see?" he asks excitedly, pointing out a white egret perched on the back of a water buffalo as his long, narrow boat glides by. "It's a buffalo! With a bird on its back!"
Kingfishers with bright flashes of blue on their wings perch on reeds rising up from the shallow water. A wild boar and her piglets dart in front of the boat and disappear into the tangled grass.
Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes, monitoring water levels and talking to fishermen and buffalo herders to find out what difference a season of rain has made in the biggest wetlands in the Middle East.
Five devastating years of drought dried out some of the marshlands. In places where water remained, it was brackish, stunting the reeds and grass. Water buffalo were dying from lack of food and contaminated water.
Residents who make their living from breeding the animals and selling milk and cream headed with their remaining herds in search of water or to the outskirts of southern Iraqi cities.
They have now begun to return, repopulating some of the tiny floating islands where, aside from some modern technology, marsh residents live a way of life little changed since Sumerian times, more than 4,000 years ago.
Loading...
Reflooding the marshes Saddam drained
Asadi is a leading environmental figure in Iraq. In the 1990s, in retribution for a Shiite uprising in southern Iraq, Saddam Hussein drained the marshes and set parts of them on fire to flush out resistance fighters.
After Saddam was toppled in the U.S.-led invasion in 2003, Asadi and Iraqi-American environmentalist Azzam Alwash helped residents tear down packed earth embankments holding back water from the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and the water flooded back in.
The two engineers founded the environmental organization Nature Iraq in 2004.
Asadi has been a high-profile figure, working with embassies and government ministries to garner support for the marshes and helping successfully lobby for inclusion as a UNESCO world heritage site in 2016. The inscription recognized the marshlands' biodiversity and their legacy as the site of one of the world's oldest civilizations.
Gregarious, welcoming and with a zeal for showcasing his homeland, Asadi frequently took Western journalists through the marshes, often hosting them at the Nature Iraq offices.
Kidnapped, tortured and accused of working for Israel
In February 2023, Asadi was kidnapped by an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, which accused him and the journalists he met of being Israeli spies who had fomented anti-government protests that had rocked Iran a few months earlier.
He was returning from Baghdad to his southern hometown of Chibayish after a meeting with the Iraqi president to discuss help for destitute families in the marshes when gunmen in pickup trucks and SUVs cut off his car on the road south.
They blindfolded him and threw him onto the floor of a vehicle, and with their feet on top of him drove him to what he believed to be farmland. There he was beaten and told to confess to being a spy.
"They showed me a map of the world," he says. "They were showing it on a screen and there were networks on it, connecting all the countries of the world — in Europe, Africa, Asia, America — to Tel Aviv. They said 'You are not just a spy, you lead a spy network from all the capitals of the world to Israel.'"
They accused him of ferrying journalists, whom they also accused of being spies, across the marshes into Iran. Nature Iraq, like almost all non-governmental organizations, often takes journalists and others on tours in Iraq to raise environmental awareness.
Asadi, who is 69 now, was born in the marshes — literally in a boat when his mother went into labor two months early while she was collecting reeds and grass.
"When I opened my eyes the first time, I opened my eyes to the blue sky, to the water, to the reeds and also birds," he says. "My mom returned home with the grasses, reeds and a baby."
At the age of 6 he rowed his own small boat to school. In the rainy season he says, the students would collect reeds to put on the classroom floors and when the school flooded there would be fish swimming under their desks.
In 1978, he was jailed for nine months for refusing to sign allegiance to Saddam Hussein's Baath party.
Asadi says when he was kidnapped three years ago and refused to admit to being a spy after being beaten, his captors decided he should be tortured.
They held him for two weeks. Asadi says they placed a plastic bag over his head until he thought he would suffocate and plunged his head underwater over and over.
"When the oxygen ran out I felt like I was going to die," he says.
They ran electric shocks through his body.
"They started from my feet, to my head, my genitals, my chest, my nose," he says in his office in Chibayish, on the edge of the central marshes. "They suspended him from the ceiling "like a sheep being slaughtered."
"They took my left arm behind my neck, and my right arm next to it, and beat them with metal chains. You feel like you're being pulled apart," he says. "I would scream, I would be on the verge of fainting, then they would stop and say, "So will you admit it?""
Then they would throw him back into his cell to await the next torture session.
Poetry helped save him
He says the waiting was also a form of torture.
"You think about your family, you think about your children and you think of your fate in the coming days and your fate in the coming sessions."
Asadi is also a poet. He wrote his first poem when he was 13 and has memorized many hundreds of other Arab poets' writings.
"I found a way to recite poetry to myself, so I didn't have to think about anything but poetry," he says. "When I hear the sound of the cell door opening — it means they are coming to take me, they are going to torture me."
Even now, in the boat three years later, he recites poems to himself — over several minutes — start to finish.
The one he told himself hundreds of times in captivity is called In Those Days, by Saadi Youssef, an Iraqi poet from the southern port city of Basra jailed in Iraq decades ago before he went into exile in Algeria and the U.K.
"I left the court with the guards' beatings and the judge's ridicule," reads part of the poem in translation. "I have a wife whom I love and a book made of date palms." Asadi recites it in Arabic like a mantra. It comforted him, he says, to imagine that he himself was the prisoner in Youssef's poem decades ago.
"Sign a confession or write your will"
After two weeks, his masked captors, dressed in military uniforms and using phrases that Asadi said were uniquely Iranian, told him he could either sign a confession that he ran spy networks and smuggled journalists into Iran, or he could write a will.
They placed a pen and a piece of paper in front of him and gave him an hour. If he didn't confess, they said, "We are going to kill you today."
"So I wrote my will," Asadi says. "I wrote that I love Iraq very much. That I have not done anything wrong, not to Iraq, not to anyone else. And I said that I wish for our country to be independent and strong and at the same time I am against all hatred and division."
He asked his wife not to be too upset.
"And I wished for my children to follow in my footsteps and in my path," he says he wrote.
"Yes, though that path led to my death, we only have one life so let us live that life honorably."
Instead of killing him, his captors ended up throwing him onto the floor of a vehicle and leaving him by the side of a road in Baghdad near where his family had been told to wait for him.
Loading...
Tribal threats and a deal for his release
Asadi, injured and weak, insisted on returning home to the marshlands the very next day. There, hundreds of marsh residents walked for miles to welcome him back, many waving celebratory posters and Iraqi flags.
Asadi says he knows the militia that kidnapped him and he believes the government did as well while he was being held. His cousin, who was driving, had memorized the license plate number of the kidnappers.
"Within two hours they found who owns the car and the name and who he works for," says Alwash, the Nature Iraq co-founder.
The Iraqi government had pledged to secure his release. But in certain areas, some of the Iran-backed militias that flourished in the security vacuum and the subsequent civil war after the U.S. invasion have grown more powerful than Iraqi security forces. And in some parts of Iraq, tribes are even more powerful still.
In the end it was Asadi's powerful Bani Asad tribe that won his release after mobilizing hundreds of armed tribal fighters to drive home their demand that he be freed.
"Four hundred members of the Asadi clan — all with guns. They surround the guy's house and say 'Ok, if he dies, you're dead'," says Alwash. "Jassim was known — I mean everybody was like, 'What the hell? Why mess around with Jassim?'"
As part of the deal for his release, Asadi says he did not pursue the case in court. He says it never occurred to him he was in danger of being kidnapped because Nature Iraq is purely environmental and not affiliated with any political party.
He was offered asylum in Europe after he was freed. He refused, saying it was what his captors wanted — for him to leave the country and stop his work. Instead he asked for asylum for two of his children, who are now in Sweden.
"He basically told people, 'Take my children away so I can work for the marshes without putting them in danger,'" says Alwash. A third child lives in the United States.
Alwash, speaking to NPR in Amman, was told by intelligence services of three different countries after Asadi was seized that he was also at risk of being kidnapped and has not returned to Iraq since.
"Iran's operating theory is that we are a Mossad operation," Alwash says of Nature Iraq. "They cannot understand why Western governments would give money to the environment."
He says Iran's suspicions about the organization go back to 2016, when Nature Iraq began a project with Iranian conservationists working on the endangered and elusive Persian Leopard in the mountains between Iran and Iraq. Two years later Iran arrested nine Iranian conservationists related to the project, accusing them of espionage.
The Iranian-Canadian co-founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation died in detention while the rest spent years in prison.
Protecting Iraq's environment
Nature Iraq has raised a generation of environmentalists working mainly from southern Iraq and Iraq's Kurdistan region. In the marshlands, the group has built floating islands for water buffalo breeders and reed guest houses intended for tourists. They have lobbied the Iraqi and regional governments to implement water policies that would revive the marshes — primarily Turkey whose huge dams have reduced the water flow downstream.
Because there is no water treatment plant, the organization has constructed a pond to naturally clean marsh water contaminated by sewage pumped from towns into the marshes. The collection pond is now full of reeds that naturally remove toxins from the water before it is pumped back out.
They are a small fraction of the cost of water treatment plants but they are still waiting for the Iraqi government to make a decision on constructing two more ponds needed near Chibayish, Asadi says.
At its peak, the environmental organization had 94 people on staff, operating in Iraq and the Iraqi Kurdistan region.
"Anyone who works on the environment in Iraq has gone through Nature Iraq," Alwash says. In 2018, after secret allegations that the environmental organization was misusing public funds, Iraqi prosecutors froze the group's bank accounts. They dropped the investigation four years later due to lack of evidence. Only four staff members who could afford to work without being paid, remained.
Asadi's arrest and Iran's imprisonment of Iranian environmentalists who worked with Nature Iraq have had a chilling effect on environmental activism.
"After the kidnapping people were like — 'Why are you working with Jassim? It's dangerous,'" says volunteer Muntadher Abedali, 21.
"Nature Iraq has been teaching me how to protect the marshes, the biology, the biodiversity and even the culture," he says. "I will stay with Jassim forever, no matter what. Why should I feel afraid? We are the next generation to protect nature."
To help raise awareness internationally, Abedali taught himself English and now speaks it fluently, contributing stories to a platform called Climate Stories. He sees himself as part of the voice of largely impoverished marsh residents who do not have the political power to advocate for themselves.
Water returns to Iraq's parched marshland
On a recent day Asadi and Abedali travelled through the marshes in long narrow boats called mashoufs. Without the motor, they are the same designs portrayed in Sumerian art more than 4,000 years ago.
"How is the water?" Asadi asks everyone he meets. He keeps track of water levels rising and falling to the centimeter. With rains last winter, after five years of devastating drought, the levels have risen by more than one third.
But the real gauge is the health of the water buffalo that are the backbone of the marsh economy.
During the drought the very landscape changed. Spiky desert plants that do not normally grow in the marshes took the place of reeds. Lakes used by migrating birds dried up entirely. Many buffalo herders moved away and turned to agriculture — scraping a subsistence while living on other people's lands.
There are some signs of recovery. At one of the tiny islands near sunset, Muamel Raad was milking one of his buffalo, the creamy milk sloshing into a pail to be turned partly into a luxuriously high-fat cream sold along with the milk, in town.
Raad, 23, says he and his family moved constantly over the last five years.
"With the drought, every two or three months I had to move," he says. Seven of his water buffalo sickened and died during the drought and he sold others he could not afford to feed. From a herd of 50, he now has fewer than 20 left.
Raad says he is getting twice the amount of milk from each animal as he did during the drought – up to four quarts a day. A small, barefoot boy shoos 2- and 3-month-old calves away from their mothers as his father milks them.
In Amman, Alwash stands near a map he obtained in 2003 from the Iraqi water ministry, showing the elaborate system of embankments and canals Saddam built to divert water from the rivers.
Alwash, who won the prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2013, speaks about the marshes with the expertise of a professor and the zeal of a preacher.
He explains the flood cycle that fostered what he calls 'a symphony of bio-diversity' ended in 2019 when Turkey's huge Elisu dam project began capturing water that would have run downstream.
"The pulse of the floods is no longer there," he says. "Does that mean the marshes are over? No, the marshes are changing. Everyone knows that the only constant in nature is change."
Environmentalist's return to the marshes
Out on the water, Asadi calls out to fishermen standing up in boats to cast wide circular nets into the water. They tell him the fishing is still bad — there are few fish, and most of them are small.
He asks children swimming in the canal — their clothes plastered against them — how the water is.
For all the trauma he has experienced, he seems to have lost none of his energy or his passion for every facet of the marshland.
He jumps in and out of boats, bursts into song, composes poetry. With boatman Razzak Jabar, whom he has known since childhood, he sings old songs – sad ones mostly about lost places and people.
"It was a horrific experience, it is true," he says of his kidnapping. "But also it showed me and us that yes, this isn't an easy path — it requires sacrifices and strength. This is your country, this is your nature, this is your environment. Work hard for your country and your land."
Awadh al-Ta'ie, Ahmed Qusay and Fatima al-Kassab contributed reporting from Chibayish and Baghdad, Iraq.

noticias.titulo: Project Gryffindor: Meta's plan to get more school kids using Instagram
noticias.resumen: Meta said it launched its "school partnership program" to keep teens safe, but internal documents tell a different story.
noticias.texto:
Project Gryffindor: Meta's plan to get more school kids using Instagram
Internal Meta documents show the company planned to boost Instagram use among teens by targeting schools in an initiative it named "Project Gryffindor."
The project focused on growing what it called "school communities" in the U.S. by encouraging teens to include their school banner on their profiles and establishing a student directory that allows users to see and connect with others from their school who use the platform.
Meta launched the initiative in 2025, calling it a "school partnership program," and significantly expanded it in September 2026. The company said almost 17,000 schools had signed up for the program at the time.
Meta said the program sought to provide a safer experience on Instagram for children, including protecting them from bullying and online risks by allowing educators to report safety concerns to the company.
Another feature gives school-related accounts the ability to post stories and notes visible to all verified students and parents in a school community. Meta said these features would help students and parents stay informed about happenings at school. The announcement gave an example of a school using the Instagram Stories feature to share a notice of basketball tryouts.
However, in internal documents prior to the program's public launch, the company discussed more explicitly commercial motivations for establishing school networks. In a 2024 presentation on Project Gryffindor, Meta said that embedding in schools was a way to increase user "acquisition," "friending" and "invites" to join Instagram. Gryffindor is one of the four Hogwarts school houses from the Harry Potter books.
"We believe network connections will fuel organic and unattributed acquisition," the project's presentation states, referring to adding new users.
In another internal presentation from 2023, titled "Unlocking New Networks Through School Communities," Meta stated that its school program would "give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram]."
"Our current strategy of relying on power user teens to get less active friends onto IG may not be effective if there are full communities of teens that have not yet joined IG," the presentation stated.
The previously unreported Meta documents are part of evidence obtained by lawyers through discovery in a multidistrict lawsuit alleging that social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks they failed to disclose. Meta, alongside TikTok, Google and Snap, are defendants in the cases, which were brought by children and their families, school districts and state attorneys general.
Online safety experts interviewed by NPR said that rather than boosting online safety, Instagram's school partnership program could make teen users more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase their likelihood of being targeted by predators.
"Meta's own documents refer to this very program as a mere way to get more teens addicted to Instagram and Facebook," said Sacha Haworth, the executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on tech policy. "Meta's latest attempt to trojan-horse their tech into the school day shows the business strategy remains the same: maximize their profits at our kids' expense."
According to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity investigator, Instagram's school partnership program could create privacy and security vulnerabilities to teens' accounts that could be "a loophole that scammers, sextortion scammers, as well as groomers, would obviously exploit."
Using schools to recruit teen Instagram users
Meta has long focused on boosting Instagram's popularity among teenagers. The social media giant viewed the slowdown in teen Instagram user growth since TikTok's US launch in 2018 as "an existential threat for not just IG [Instagram] but the company overall," according to other internal documents submitted as evidence in the multidistrict lawsuit.
Internal documents show that as early as 2015, the company was making plans to form relationships with schools to acquire new teen users.
One company presentation from 2023 stated: "Our competitors in social connection are leveraging school integrations as a way to keep in touch with their community. Can we take things a step further and use school networks as a lever for acquisitions?" Snapchat also has a school and college community program, where users can apply to have their school badge displayed on their profile, which has faced criticism for facilitating inappropriate posts and bullying.
Another Meta document discussed how acquiring teen users would have the knock-on effect of introducing younger children to the platform. "Teens strongly influenced preteens' understanding of what and how frequently to share on Instagram," the document said. Meta's own policy states that Instagram users must be at least 13 years old to have an account.
In another internal Meta presentation focused on the long-term retention of users on Facebook, a bullet point stated: "Tweens (approximate age 10-12) are special. People who join Facebook as tweens have the highest long term retention out of all age groups." Facebook also has a minimum age requirement of 13 to use the platform.
Targeting schools may also have served as a strategy to increase the amount of time teens spent on Instagram. In a 2025 legal brieffiled on behalf of school districts and boards of education across the country, lawyers cited a 2015 internal comment from a Meta employee describing the company's engagement goals: "One of the things we need to optimize for is sneaking a look at your phone under your desk in the middle of Chemistry :)."
Meta targeted push notifications to students within specific schools, which it called "school blasts," the same legal brief states. The aim of these "blasts" was to "tip schools from inactive to active via network effects and incrementally increase teen MAP [monthly active persons] in those schools," the brief said.
The legal brief also outlined how the company developed the technical capability to determine when teen users were at school, "using location and school-specific information collected through data harvesting."
This contrasts with public statements Meta has made about teens' use of Instagram. "We don't want social media to be a distraction from school," the company said in its September 2026 announcement the school partnership program was expanding.
Meta spokesperson, Liza Crenshaw, said in a statement to NPR: "This story completely mischaracterizes a positive program that helps thousands of U.S. schools protect their students online, communicate with them safely about extracurricular activities, and easily report safety issues. In the past year, we've reviewed over 90% of bullying and harassment reports from participating schools within 48 hours. We don't want Instagram to be a distraction during class."
Through its Instagram Teen Accounts program, parents have been able to block their teens' access during the school day, since 2022, Crenshaw said.
Program could increase risk of predators targeting teens
Children participating in the school partnership program are verified by a third-party app and can display their school badge on their profile, which is visible to other teens they follow. "To help stay connected to classmates, students can see a directory of other students at their school, or make a school banner," Meta said in its September 2026 press release.
However, online safety experts interviewed by NPR say that rather than making teen users safer, the school partnership program could increase their vulnerability to being targeted by predators and scammers.
"This goes against all the internet safety training that parents and teachers have been trying to instill in their kids all these years," said John DeMay, whose 17-year-old son Jordan DeMay died by suicide in 2022 after being targeted in a sextortion blackmail scam on Instagram.
Teens in the U.S. are frequently targeted by sextortionists — scammers who typically pretend to be a romantic interest about the same age as their target, who then groom the teen and convince them to send sexually compromising photographs of themselves. Once the pictures are sent, the scammers reveal themselves to be blackmailers, threatening to send the pictures to their victims' contacts if they don't comply with their requests for money.
Many victims are teen boys, dozens of whom have died by suicide because of their victimization by sextortionists, according to the National Center of Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC).
One of the first pieces of information scammers want to extract from their victim is where they go to school, said Raffile. Because scammers often pose as teenagers online themselves, they would be able to see their victim's school banner if the victim starts to follow them on Instagram.
Identifying where a victim goes to school is "actually written into the script that the scammers use," he said. "Later on, when it comes time for the blackmail, they will use that information, threaten to send it to everybody in the school. They will find teachers and coaches at the school and threaten to send this content to them."
While Meta uses a third-party to verify students' email addresses before they are admitted into their school's partnership program, the student's accounts could easily be breached, experts said.
"There's nothing to say that you know a student's account can't get hacked and then taken by a criminal and then used for all sorts of nefarious purposes, whether it be sextortion, grooming," said Raffile. "Once an account is embedded within a school and has an active school profile, they can see all sorts of things like directories of the different clubs, different groups on campus, and that's a sextortionist's dream."
Teen Instagram accounts are often targets of hacking and security breaches, which can include social engineering and account takeover schemes, child safety advocates and experts said.
In one case, in February 2026, an online child predator hijacked hundreds of young people's social media accounts, including Instagram and Snapchat, before threatening to release sexually explicit images, according to a Department of Justice announcement.
"Facebook and Instagram and most of these social media platforms are not secure. They do not have enough security measures in place to keep the bad actors out. As we know, how easy it is for literally anybody, even a child, a 10-year-old child, to go and create an account and start using it," DeMay said. "Bad actors and adult criminals can do the same thing."
Meta did not provide a response to NPR about sextortion and cybersecurity concerns.
Partnership claims disputed by education nonprofit
In a September 2026 press release, Meta said its School Partnership Program was developed "in partnership" with the International Society for Technology in Education and the Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development (ISTE+ASCD), an education nonprofit.
ISTE+ASCD disputed the characterization that it is a partner on the project, and said it undertook "contract work" for the project to develop a process for educators to report inappropriate posts and accounts. That work concluded in 2025, the organization said.
When asked by NPR why Meta referred to ISTE+ASCD as a partner on its school partnership program a year after their contract concluded, Crenshaw said: "We were proud to work with ISTE on the initial development of the School Partnership Program."
Crenshaw said the program has since evolved and "ISTE has not been part of that work."
Both Meta and ISTE told NPR that ISTE initially reached out to Meta.
"School leaders had been telling us they needed more options to remove disruptive posts and accounts on Instagram," said ISTE spokesperson Daniel Obregon. "We shared that feedback with Meta and were contracted to help collect educator feedback and test the new [account reporting] functionality in schools."
This year, Meta has settled and lost several lawsuits alleging its products are harmful to children.
In August 2026, Meta agreed to a settlement worth up to $17.1 billion to resolve claims brought by dozens of state attorneys general alleging that Facebook and Instagram were designed to encourage compulsive use among children and teenagers and that the company misled the public about the risks. As part of the settlement, Meta denied the allegations against it.
In a landmark trial in Los Angeles in March 2026, a jury found that co-defendants YouTube and Meta designed their platforms to be addictive to young users. Meta also lost a two-phase lawsuit brought by the New Mexico attorney general, in which a jury found the company had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms and knowingly harmed children. Meta is appealing the verdict.
"How irresponsible for a company who has just been held liable in multiple lawsuits across the U.S. for intentionally harming teens and putting their privacy and safety at risk," said Raffile. "Now they're trying to get embedded into the schools.

noticias.titulo: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
noticias.resumen: The two largest emitters of greenhouse gases are China and the United States. Now, the countries' stories are diverging: many Chinese provinces are reducing coal use, while the U.S. is falling behind on climate technologies.
noticias.texto:
China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
China’s emissions have plateaued -- and may even be falling
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.
For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.
"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.
This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.
The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.
" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.
Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.
China had long-term planning
China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.
Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.
"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."
The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.
"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.
These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.
In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.
Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say
While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.
Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.
The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.
Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."
This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.
"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."
A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.
Chinese exports equal emissions reductions
Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."
Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.
Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.
The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.
"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

noticias.titulo: Special education teachers shared their stories. You told NPR you felt seen
noticias.resumen: NPR is following along as about a dozen special education teachers navigate this school year and share their joys and challenges. Listeners say they're not alone.
noticias.texto:
Special education teachers shared their stories. You told NPR you felt seen
"From one special education teacher to all of you others, we are in the trenches. We are overworked, understaffed, and GROSSLY underpaid … I stand with each of you, I'm glad I'm not alone."
That's some of what Wendy Campbell, a special education teacher in Jacksonville, Fla., wrote on Instagram after reading NPR's story about special education teachers in America.
She was one of many teachers who wrote in to commiserate after NPR launched a series that aims to follow special educators from all over the country to answer half-century old questions: Why are these teachers always in short supply and what does it take to do this work?
Special education reaches over 8 million public school students in America — a number that continues to grow, yet the educators who teach these students remain some of the hardest to hire and keep.
NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear what it's like to do this job day to day directly from some of these teachers over the course of this school year.
Some of their stories so far recount joyful moments involving students meeting their goals sooner than expected, while others detail challenges like teaching without solid walls in their classrooms or managing the ripple effects of disruptive student behavior. Almost every teacher has mentioned wrestling with individualized education programs (IEPs), which involve legally required paperwork for students in special education.
Recently, Emily Ellis, one of the teachers NPR has been following and who works at an elementary school in Cayce, S.C., sent a voice memo on her way home from work, after wrapping up her first quarter of teaching. "A big happy moment was just seeing how much growth my students have had," she said. "Just seeing where they started and where they are now. Some of them are on their way to mastering their IEP goals. It's just wild and so exciting, I'm just so proud of them."
One of her students came into her kindergarten classroom not knowing how to count. "Now, he's able to count to 10 on his own," she said, and has learned the sounds of the alphabet. "Even when I feel like nothing is working, everything is failing, the data shows that I am doing the best I can for my kids and that they are making progress."
But reaching that payoff is no easy task. As Kathleen Tejeda, a veteran teacher in Riverside, Calif., said in a recent voice note, "Special education teachers have two jobs." There's the academic instruction part of the teaching job, and then, there's the case management. "That involves the creation and implementation, the goal setting, the goal reaching of their IEPs, collaborating with teachers, helping with social and emotional needs. It's a whole lot to do."
Tejeda said the work can feel so important that it can consume teachers' entire lives. It took her years to find a balance, she said. "It is a fine line between both parts of the job, and then yourself. You don't want to lose yourself in the job."
What teachers told us
Special educators from around the country heard what these teachers shared with NPR and shared their own stories. These are excerpts from some of those messages:
From one special education teacher to all of you others, we are in the trenches. We are overworked, understaffed, and GROSSLY underpaid. Florida (where I am) is short on teachers as a whole, and with [special education], it's tenfold … Additionally, we aren't only managing our caseloads, which are insane, but trying to support Gen Ed teachers … I stand with each of you, I'm glad I'm not alone." — Wendy Campbell, Jacksonville, Fla.
"I have been a [special education] teacher for almost 9 years in Southern California, and everything the team has written has proven true in my own work. I could not believe how strongly I connected with what you wrote about the balance between paperwork, meetings, and teaching, and how little teaching gets accomplished in a day at times … What your team wrote about SPED teachers feeling isolated from every other teacher due to the workload rang so true I began to tear up." — Jacob Meraz, Montclair, Calif.
"First year elementary sped teacher here. I'm glad I'm not alone. The comments here are 100% spot on. I thought I was a failure, but it turns out, I'm not incompetent. It's an onslaught of chaos that's relentless." Fung added via email, "I'm grateful for the support I get from my team." — Russell Fung, Los Angeles
It's no secret why there is a shortage of SPED teachers. … it is an impossible job to do well if you want to have a life outside of contract hours. Pretty much every SPED teacher I know puts in long hours before and after school, on weekends, over breaks, etc and still feel like they can't get it all done. I did this for 9 years at the preschool/elementary level and got so burned out and disillusioned I almost left teaching altogether … but decided to give general education a shot and love it. Don't get me wrong, it's still hard, but special education is a whole other beast. — Emily Clausen, Alexandria, Va.
Second year [special education] teacher here. It's an emotional rollercoaster minute to minute and day to day. I love my students and I started to seek therapy again this year due to the amount of second hand trauma in my class. It wasn't until I started to ask for concrete examples or advice from my peers and colleagues that I started to see changes really support my students. I started to take time to regulate my own emotions after work and it's been a tremendous help for me to carry out my daily workload. — Erica Otero, Sacramento, Calif.
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
"I feel excited to work with these special kids, but this job has a high burn out rate because of many of the issues mentioned in other comments: unreasonable work load involving IEPs, scheduling, curriculum planning, data collection, physical trauma from the students, etc. I work with the most incredible teacher who has taught special ed for 18 years and just last year suffered her 6th and 7th concussions due to student violence. At some point, teachers just can't stay in this environment for their own health. It might be a child with severe disabilities that we have so much care and empathy for, but when we get hurt by them, our bodies and brains register it as trauma."   
— Natalie Jeffs, Provo, Utah
Many of us who are special education teachers have two jobs: teaching subjects, and IEP case management. This means that in addition to preparing lessons, grading, managing the classroom, i.e. teaching content and managing behaviors, we have to manage our students' SPED services, work with providers, track goal progress, assess, write assessment reports, and hold at least one yearly IEP meeting. … Most of us have 25+ students on our caseload. We feel like terrible teachers because our priority has to be the legal aspects of the IEP. I am truly grateful for an incredible team of caring people that make it bearable. We all love the students or we wouldn't do this job. But it's simply too much most of the time. — Kara Grabendike, Ventura, Calif.
After 12 years teaching special education, I had to leave the profession to maintain and preserve my own mental health and well-being. This job has its rewards, but over time, it will wear you down unless you have a very supportive admin and parents that work with you, not against you … I fully support any teacher who goes into this field—they are not doing it for the money, I can assure you that. — Emily Zacarias, Santa Barbara, Calif.
And teachers, we heard from some of your former students about the impact you made on them, too.
Andrew Regopoulos emailed to say the story "hit home" for him because he was a special education student from second grade until he graduated high school. He has ADHD and dyslexia and said his special education teachers made a world of difference for him. "I overcame so much with them. I'm now the Deputy Fee Manager at Grand Canyon National Park," he wrote. Now 38, he has a family and said if it weren't for his special education teachers "knowing how to care and support me I don't think I ever would have made anything of myself."
Many special educators say that while the work begins in the classroom, seeing their students succeed beyond school is their guiding star.
As this school year rolls on, NPR's education team will stay in touch with about a dozen special educators, and visit some in their classrooms to continue bringing you their stories.
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Steve Drummond
Visual development and design by LA Johnson

noticias.titulo: She retired early to care for family. New work rules for food aid disrupted that
noticias.resumen: The Trump administration's sweeping changes to SNAP food aid mean older adults up to age 65 must work or volunteer to get the benefit.
noticias.texto:
She retired early to care for family. New work rules for food aid disrupted that
CAPITOL HEIGHTS, Md. – Over nearly four decades of working — at a liquor store, cleaning apartments and in hospitality — Lisa Reese never received government assistance. Now, after her decision to retire at 62 and apply for SNAP food aid, her plans to take care of family members in need became complicated.
It felt like the right time to retire, she said, sitting on the front porch of a gray clapboard house in Maryland, just outside Washington, D.C. The home has been in the family since her grandparents owned it, and three generations live here now. Her 2-year-old granddaughter peeks through the front door.
Reese spent the past 25 years at Marriott, where working at the front desk, in room service, and at events meant "there was no sitting down … I was tired!" she said with a soft laugh. But more than that, she chose to retire because she was needed at home.
Her 80-year-old mother is in senior living and Reese visits often. She shares the house with her uncle, who's had surgery for liver cancer, as well as her daughter and granddaughter, whom she helps care for. "Daycare was expensive," she said. "So I decided to retire to take care of everybody. I don't know if that's crazy."
Reese's daughter also gets SNAP and is exempt from the work rule since her child is young — but she has a job in childcare. There's also a waiver for those who care for someone incapacitated, but Reese's uncle is not.
After leaving her job, getting by mainly on Social Security was tough. The price of everything seemed to go up this year, especially the gas bill which "went through the roof," she said. "One of my bills was $500. Five hundred!"
She scrimped as much as she could, stuck to a tight budget, and went to a nearby food bank. But it wasn't enough.
This summer, Reese was approved for a small amount from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP. But to get $63 a month in food aid, she must work, train or volunteer for 80 hours a month.
That requirement is part of sweeping changes and cuts to both SNAP and Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill that President Trump signed last year. It slashed funding and expanded work rules, including for people aged 55 to 64.
Some 5 million people nationwide have lost federal food benefits since then, estimates the left-leaning Center for Budget and Policy Priorities. Newly empowered Democrats want to roll back the changes, but Trump administration officials have said repeatedly that they are helping to tackle waste, fraud and abuse.
"People are being punished"
Not far from where Reese lives, the nonprofit Mission of Love Charities has been swamped with need this year. It serves people who are homeless or low-income, and had to reduce food pantry visits from once a week to every other week. It also hired a third case worker to help people sign up for SNAP and Medicaid, and connect them with housing and jobs.
"We see it every day, people get cut off" from food aid, said CEO Adenia Bradley. Sometimes it's for red tape or a small error, sometimes people lose benefits because of the new work rules.
Maryland has tried to make it less complicated for people to get and stay on SNAP. It's created one application for multiple benefits that works on a smartphone, and made it easier and quicker to verify eligibility to renew the program. The decline in enrollment has been less sharp here than in some other states. And when officials do inform people their aid is being cut off, they connect them immediately with a job assistance center. "They say that you have this appointment at this time. If you need to reschedule, call this number," said case worker Brooke Wright.
But the labor market is still tough. "One of our volunteers, she did three work applications already and she cannot find a job yet," said case worker Jatmna Cabrera.
Bradley has allowed a few people to meet the new work requirements by volunteering at the Mission. They include Lisa Reese.
On a recent day, in a corner of the high-ceilinged warehouse, she filled crinkly bags with food for people who would line up later to pick them up. "Snacks, water, drinks and they get two sandwiches," Reese said.
Her four-hour shift is in the morning, so she can still watch her granddaughter in the afternoons. And she loves helping people this way. "I feel better when they walk past and they wave at me, "Hey, Miss Mission of Love!" she said. "It makes me feel good that they're eating."
But CEO Bradley can only let so many people volunteer here, and she worries the need will only grow. "So now we are researching places for people to volunteer, other than us, so we can give them referrals," she said.
She noted the expanded work rules apply to people who had long been exempt from them: Able-bodied older adults, parents of adolescents, veterans, homeless people and some noncitizens including refugees.
"I'm always for a case-by-case basis, but what they're doing now is lumping them all in one pot," she said. Certainly for older people, she does not think a blanket work rule makes sense. "I think people are being punished for being on the help that the government has said" someone is qualified for, she said. "They don't deserve that."
In a statement to NPR the Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, said "an expectation to work, train, or volunteer for 20 hours per week, as few as four hours per day, is not punishment. Industriousness and contribution to community should be applauded, not used as scare tactics." And on calls to roll back the rules, the USDA said, "Democrats and their pervasive advocacy arm have never met a welfare program they don't want to bloat, overfund, or exploit."
President Trump's larger approach to tackle waste, fraud and abuse "has brought down costs significantly," said White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster in a statement to NPR. As for SNAP specifically, "the program's mission to be temporary help for those in tough times was a total failure, but President Trump's historic legislation began the process to halt fraud and ensure that it only serves eligible Americans who need it most," she said.
Lisa Reese agrees that SNAP use should only be temporary.
"The ones that's been on it for 10, 15, 20 years, yeah, they do need to get off of it. It's hurting folks like me," she said. "I'm sorry if that sounds cruel. But go after them, not the retirees."
Reese will soon face a double whammy. Since retiring, she's been on Medicaid, and new work rules for that program kick in next year. But she isn't sure she can keep up volunteering 80 hours a month.
"I have arthritis in my hand real bad. My thighs hurt so bad, and sciatica, high blood pressure, you name it," she said.
Her thinking now is to get off SNAP and Medicaid if, hopefully, she can find a part-time job to pay for a private health plan. She and her daughter are researching plans they could split the cost of. It could be another hit to her budget, but only until she turns 65. Then she could fully retire, and spend more time helping out family, like she hoped to be doing now.

noticias.titulo: AI finds security flaw in Java, world’s third-largest programming language
noticias.resumen: The company that found the PHP flaw in October has used AI to uncover another security flaw in the widely used Java programming language.
noticias.texto:
The company that found the PHP flaw in October has used AI to uncover another security flaw in the widely used Java programming language.
The US-based security firm Calif, which was involved in uncovering the PHP flaws patched in October, has used AI to find another critical vulnerability, this time in OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime.
US-based startup Calif announced the discovery on Tuesday of a bug in Java’s memory functions, one which could be used by attackers to completely take over a vulnerable computer server over the internet without needing a password or login.
Java is the world’s third most popular programming language, used by 90% of Fortune 500 companies.
It is used to power services including banking and finance, cloud and big data infrastructure, critical public sectors like aviation, telecommunications and healthcare, as well as smartphones and all kinds of connected devices.
While newer languages like Python, Go, and Kotlin have gained market share in areas like data science and mobile apps, Java continues to serve as the backbone of global enterprise infrastructure.
Before Calif made the announcement, they coordinated with the Five Eyes intelligence partners (the US, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand) and major cloud providers so defenders could prepare patches ahead of criminals.
In Europe, national cybersecurity authorities are coordinating emergency response teams to track the rollout of patches from Oracle, the company that leads Java maintenance globally, as well as other open-source maintainers.
What is the Java vulnerability?
Java4Shell has been described by Calif as a memory corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is one of the internet’s most popular runtimes, software environments that allow users to execute code and run programmes.
Base64 decoder, on the other hand, is used to carry out authentication protocols, to encode file uploads and deliver network messages, and operates by representing binary data as text, says Calif.
The bug was found in the process where OpenJDK tries to use the Base64 decoder more quickly to carry out commands by using specialised instructions to process many bytes at the same time, known as x86064 CPU instructions.
Calif found that this mechanism, which optimises the code to use Base64 decoding more quickly, is vulnerable to exploitation, allowing attackers to send scrambled code to overwrite memory, tricking Java into thinking they are an administrator.
With this level of access, hackers can then run their own malicious software and operate with the same controls as the company’s own IT engineers, making sensitive data vulnerable and giving attackers the ability to take control of vulnerable platforms and services using Java.

noticias.titulo: Trump ordered to give sworn testimony in BBC defamation case by January
noticias.resumen: The broadcaster says the US president has been avoiding its lawyers, and both sides have been told to be ready for trial in May.
noticias.texto:
The broadcaster says the US president has been avoiding its lawyers, and both sides have been told to be ready for trial in May.
US District Judge Jeffrey T. Kuntz, sitting in Florida, on Tuesday extended an earlier deadline of 11 December for depositions, giving Trump and the BBC more time to prepare their cases.
Trump must testify under oath by January 22 the judge ruled and both sides must be ready for trial by 3 May, 2027.
A deposition is out-of-court testimony given under oath before a trial. It’s part of the "discovery" stage of a US civil case, when each side gathers evidence from the other.
A witness or party is questioned by the opposing side’s lawyers, usually in a lawyer’s office rather than a courtroom. A court reporter records the answers, and the session is often filmed too. No judge is present.
The witness’s own lawyer can object to questions, but in most cases the witness still has to answer.
Trump accuses the BBC of misleadingly editing a documentary so that it looked as if he was inciting violence when he urged supporters to march on the US Capitol in Washington on 6 January 2021.
The Panorama programme, "Trump: A Second Chance", joined together two separate parts of his speech that day. This Trump claims gave the impression that he had directly called on his supporters to attack the building.
A crowd later stormed the Capitol in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 presidential election.
The BBC has apologised for the edit, which led two senior executives to resign, but it denies that Trump suffered any real harm as a result.
Trump sought at least $5 billion on each of two claims: one for defamation and another under a Florida consumer protection law. Earlier this month, Kuntz rejected the BBC’s attempt to have the defamation claim thrown out, although he dismissed the consumer protection claim.
The BBC has accused Trump of dodging its efforts to obtain his sworn testimony while Trump's lawyers argue the president has been engaged campaigning for the recent mid-term elections rather than avoiding the deposition.
