noticias.titulo: Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins
noticias.resumen: Cameron Bancroft claims the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
noticias.texto:
Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins
- Published
Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.
"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
- The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what? 
  - Published4 hours ago
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:
- Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa â the match before Bancroft was caught
- Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers â Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
- Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
- When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
- Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".
Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us â Steve Smith, David Warner and I â who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."
Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."
Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.
In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.
"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.
"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."
In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".
In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.
"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.
"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."
Analysis: Potentially the decisive intervention
For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.
Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.
His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.
In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.
Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.
It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.
But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.
Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.
What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?
Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.
Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

noticias.titulo: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
noticias.resumen: Tyler Buchanan, from Dundee, was a member of the notorious Scattered Spider group and began hacking when he was a teenager.
noticias.texto:
British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
- Published
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (Â£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.
Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.
For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
Threatened with a blowtorch
Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.
"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.
In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.
They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.
Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused Â£39m of damage.

noticias.titulo: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
noticias.resumen: The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless vehicles from operating on the state's highways following a series of traffic incidents.
noticias.texto:
Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
- Published
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.
California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.
Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.
California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".
In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.
The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.
In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.
In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

noticias.titulo: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
noticias.resumen: Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of trying to hire undercover FBI agents as hitmen to assassinate US officials, including the president.
noticias.texto:
Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
- Published
A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other officials.
Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire after trying to hire hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley.
The hitmen were instead undercover FBI agents.
In court, he said he was acting under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 US assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Iran's topmost military commander.
New York US federal judge Eric Ross Komitee sentenced Merchant on Tuesday to 330 months (27 years and six months) in prison, months after a jury handed its guilty verdict.
Although other US officials were potential targets, the assassination plot was largely focused on Trump because he was president at the time Soleimani was killed. Trump has spoken publicly about ordering the US airstrike that killed the Iranian general while he was travelling in Iraq.
In response to the killing, Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said "severe revenge awaits the criminals" behind the attack.
Prosecutors said Merchant initially travelled to Iran for religious pilgrimages and he was then introduced to an IRGC handler. He travelled to Iran 15 times where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, prosecutors said, before flying to the US in April 2024 to carry out the plot.
Prosecutors said Merchant paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as part of an initial payment. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he was about to leave the US.
In court, Merchant argued that he "had no other option" than to go along with the plot because his handler indicated that he knew who Merchant's Iranian relatives were and where they lived.
He said he had anticipated being arrested before anyone was killed and intended to cooperate with the US government, CBS, the BBC's US partner reported. He had hoped that would help him obtain a green card.
The jury deliberated for less than two hours before returning its verdict, US media said.
"An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
"The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."
Additional reporting by Nardine Saad.

noticias.titulo: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
noticias.resumen: The $60m (£45m) plane was destroyed in an hours-long raid by an anti-war protester, according to the FBI.
noticias.texto:
Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
- Published
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (Â£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.
Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.
American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.
"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."
Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.
He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.
"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.
He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.
He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.
The US charges say that he had planned well, because he avoided cutting a line that would have risked causing massive explosion.
According to the Limerick Post, external, O'Corrain is from Cork City. Supporters have described him as an anti-war activist.
Shannon Airport is a key hub for US military personnel, and is frequently the scene of anti-war protests. It was used by President Donald Trump in September for his visit to Ireland.
US prosecutors note that there have been several breaches there in recent years by protesters, including in May 2025 when three people drove a van through a perimeter fence, and then again later that month when a US airplane was sprayed with paint, making it temporarily inoperable.

noticias.titulo: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
noticias.resumen: Zookeepers say she cannot have surgery but are providing fluids and supportive care to help her pass the hat.
noticias.texto:
Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
- Published
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.
The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".
But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.
The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.
"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.
Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January 2017.
At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

noticias.titulo: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
noticias.resumen: Thursday's meeting between the leaders of US, China and Russia will give Vladimir Putin a big stage - but it does not bring him closer to winning the war in Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
- Published
The meeting hasn't even happened yet.
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.
Whatever the outcome.
Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.
Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down â just the three of them â for talks.
That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.
It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.
"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.
That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.
But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.
It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.
One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.
In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."
But what of those who are not at the table?
Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.
Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.
Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States â Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.
"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.
It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.
Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.
Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula â carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.
The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.
It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.
The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.
It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

noticias.titulo: Pakistan's solar revolution is so successful the national grid is lagging behind
noticias.resumen: People installing their own solar panels has helped boost the solar share of Pakistan's electricity from 1% to 28%.
noticias.texto:
Pakistan's solar revolution is so successful the national grid is lagging behind
- Published
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (Â£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eï¬ects.
The power grid death spiral
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.
When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [Â£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.
Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.
The solar power boom in Pakistan and the Philippines
Cheap solar panels, mainly imported from China, are transforming lives and slashing electricity bills across Asia.
Solar-powered business
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.
Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.
But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."
Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.
"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."
Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.
"Those profits were coming at the cost of the rest of the consumers of the grid. Had we not changed those regulations, the rest of the consumers would have been burdened by at least 150 to 200 billion rupees a year, say, two years from now."
Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.
Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.
But it's also at a crossroads.
"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.
Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.
"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.
"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

noticias.texto:
The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
- Published
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
Dario Amodei
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Daniela Amodei
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.
Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.
His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish
Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

noticias.titulo: US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
noticias.resumen: Letter alleges possible conflict of interest in commerce secretary not adding Megaspeed to US trade blacklist.
noticias.texto:
US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
Letter alleges possible conflict of interest in Lutnick not adding Megaspeed to US trade blacklist.
Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his position to help Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment firm controlled by his two sons, avoid financial losses amid the scandal involving Jensen Huang at artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia.
In the five-page letter dated November 17, House Democrats notified Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald and Howard Lutnick’s son, that they are requesting information to ascertain whether “any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.
Al Jazeera has reviewed the letter.
The letter was authored by Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, Gregory Meeks of New York and the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. It asks if the company’s financial exposure influenced Lutnick’s decision to keep Megaspeed off the US Entity List, a trade blacklist.
Megaspeed is attached to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who reportedly had an affair with now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.
The US adds companies to the Entity List if it determines they pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy.
“The Secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC,” a Commerce Department spokesperson said in a statement in response to the letter, which was first reported by the Financial Times.
Cantor Fitzgerald denied the claims in the letter, saying it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients, according to the Reuters news agency.
The firm also said it has no role in US export control or Entity List decisions.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four government agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.
Reuters also reported that senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out.
On Tuesday, Huang, in his first public statement after he stepped down from Nvidia, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO, but the company’s board during its earnings call later in the day ruled out bringing him back.

noticias.texto:
Trump and Putin to meet one-on-one in China Thursday
Coordinated US diplomatic effort underway to end the war in Ukraine, a US official tells Al Jazeera.
Washington, DC, USA – United States President Donald Trump is set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, a US official tells Al Jazeera.
The two presidents last met in Alaska in August 2025 for high-stakes negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, but failed to reach a settlement.
The US official said on Wednesday that, in addition to the president’s engagements in China, American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to meet with Ukrainian officials and European partners in Berlin on Thursday to develop post-war security guarantees and a comprehensive economic recovery plan for Kyiv.
“The Berlin meetings and President Trump’s engagements in China are part of a coordinated diplomatic effort,” the official said.
“President Trump remains committed to ending the fighting and the tremendous human suffering, while helping establish the conditions for a sovereign, secure and prosperous Ukraine.”
On Thursday, Trump and Putin are also scheduled to join their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, for an unprecedented trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, marking the first-ever gathering of the leaders of the world’s three major powers.

noticias.titulo: Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge
noticias.resumen: An Israeli court extended the detention of Abu Safia nearly two years after Israel's army detained him.
noticias.texto:
Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release.
Abu Safia’s lawyer said that a court in Beersheba decided on Wednesday to extend the physician’s detention for a further six months, according to Abu Safia’s account on X.
The court said that Abu Safia “poses a threat to the State of Israel”, his lawyer reported.
“Dr Hussam questioned why his detention order was being renewed once again, expressing that he is being punished for fulfilling his humanitarian mission and professional duty as a doctor at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza,” the social media post added.
The Israeli army detained Abu Safia in December 2024, along with other staff members and patients, during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza.
International agencies and rights groups have called for the physician’s release on multiple occasions, highlighting reports that he is being subjected to abuse in detention.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said in July that Israel “must immediately release Dr Abu Safiya, or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offence and grant him a fair trial”.
OHCHR added that it received information indicating Abu Safia “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care”.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said last week it had obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a significant loss of weight, a drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated.
“Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said.
Last week, the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking the release of 14 doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, who are being held in Israeli prisons without being charged or brought to trial.
PHRI argued that the prolonged arbitrary detentions – in some cases for more than two years – constitute a violation of their individual rights and further undermine Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical professionals.

Donald Trump meets ‘longtime friend’ Imelda Marcos during Philippines visit
Trump told Philippine President Marcos he knew his ‘parents very well’.
US President Donald Trump reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Trump got to know the Philippine first couple while partying in New York decades ago.
Wednesday’s brief encounter happened at Manila’s Malacanang presidential palace, where Trump was received with a red-carpet welcome and full military honours.
On Tuesday evening, before a speech to Asian leaders, Trump praised Marcos and his parents, saying, “I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” adding that Marcos Jr had “good genetics”.
Imelda Marcos now 97, was known for her lavish lifestyle and vast collection of expensive shoes accumulated while her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was in power as president for more than 20 years, at a time when many Filipinos lived in poverty-stricken conditions.
Since Marcos was ousted in the 1986 “people power” revolution, Imelda has faced several charges of embezzlement, corruption and tax evasion.
Once seated inside the sprawling palace for their meeting, Trump told Marcos their countries’ people have a lot in common and stressed “architectural tastes”.
“I love what you’ve done here,” Trump said, referring to the palace. “You’ve done a fantastic job.”
Marcos said he sent Trump a delivery from Jollibee, the Philippines’ biggest homegrown fast-food chain, so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital.
Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday night to join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) at their annual summit meetings.
On Wednesday, Trump shook hands and exchanged greetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin before a group photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.

noticias.titulo: What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?
noticias.resumen: Billions have been pledged for Gaza since a 2025 'ceasefire', but rebuilding hasn’t begun and Israeli attacks continue.
noticias.texto:
What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?
Billions have been pledged for Gaza since an October 2025 ‘ceasefire’, but rebuilding has not begun, and Israeli attacks continue.
Donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza through US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. But more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin, and nearly 1.4 million Palestinians are still living in makeshift shelters.
Even preliminary reconstruction efforts have stalled. The board had asked for $280m to fund the initial building phase, but in September it said most of that money remained unspent.
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board warned that the truce between Israel and Hamas could collapse unless immediate steps are taken to carry out the ceasefire deal, according to The Associated Press.
The next day, on Wednesday, Israel began its first major military ground operation in the Gaza Strip since the ceasefire began, attacking refugee camps in the central part of the enclave.
Since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,658 Palestinians and injured 6,000, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Israel continues to block the entry of 60,000 mobile homes promised under the ceasefire deal and to severely restrict food and medical aid into the besieged enclave. It has also yet to allow the Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza to enter the Strip.
What is the Board of Peace?
United States President Trump proposed the board in September 2025 as part of his 20-point plan for Gaza.
On November 17, 2025, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, which recognised the board as a transitional administration responsible for setting the framework and coordinating funding for Gaza’s redevelopment.
The resolution authorises its role in Gaza until December 31, 2027, unless the UN Security Council decides otherwise. The board’s charter also allows it to work in other areas affected by conflict.
Trump chairs the board and can only be replaced if he resigns or is unable to serve. He also represents the US.
He appoints its executive board, whose members are Ajay Banga, Tony Blair, Martin Edelman, Robert Gabriel Jr, Jared Kushner, Marc Rowan, Marco Rubio, Steve Witkoff, and Susie Wiles.
Each member state has one vote. Decisions need a majority of those present and voting, and Trump’s approval. He can also veto executive board decisions.
Under the plan, Palestinian technocrats would run Gaza’s day-to-day affairs through the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, led by Ali Shaath. The committee reports to the board, but Israel has not allowed it to enter Gaza, and it operates from Cairo.
The board has 28 members: Albania, Argentina, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Belarus, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Egypt, El Salvador, Hungary, Indonesia, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Mongolia, Morocco, Pakistan, Paraguay, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam.
Germany, India, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union also attended the inaugural meeting as observers.
Countries join by invitation from Trump and normally serve up to three years. Countries that pay more than $1bn in cash in the charter’s first year are exempt from that limit.
Which countries have pledged money?
At the board’s first meeting in Washington, DC, on February 19, Trump announced about $7bn in pledges from nine countries, plus a $10bn US pledge. He did not say what the US money would be used for.
The UAE pledged $1.2bn. Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia pledged $1bn each, with Saudi Arabia saying it would pay over several years. Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Kazakhstan, Morocco, and Uzbekistan also pledged.
What happened to the funding earmarked for Gaza?
At a briefing in New York on September 23, the board said donors had made about $18bn [pdf] in early funding commitments. It said it had called in $280m from donors for the building phase so far, and that most of it remained unspent.
Board of Peace officials previously told the Washington Post that the money couldn’t be spent on projects until Israel allowed international troops or newly-trained Palestinian police to enter Gaza and begin the process of disarming Hamas.
The board puts the cost of rebuilding Gaza at about $71bn, close to the UN’s estimate of $71.5bn, a figure that could rise as more damage is recorded. The board has identified $6bn in projects. It says its six-month recovery plan needs $2.45bn for 66 programmes, plus about $200m in in-kind support.
What does the six-month recovery programme cover?
The 66 programmes are divided across six areas:
- Infrastructure development: 24 programmes
- Human development: 17 programmes
- Peace and security: 11 programmes
- Economic acceleration: 7 programmes
- Digital transformation: 6 programmes
- Legal: 1 programme
Who has pledged to help Gaza?
The Board of Peace highlights five countries helping Gaza’s recovery on the ground. Others have pledged money, but the board has not said how much each has pledged.
- Egypt: Training a civil guard
- Kazakhstan: University scholarships
- Morocco: Disarming fighters and helping them return to civilian life
- Romania: Medical evacuations
- United Arab Emirates: Resources, support and its own programmes

noticias.titulo: Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
noticias.resumen: Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries draw condemnation from across the region.
noticias.texto:
Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries draw condemnation from across the region.
Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
Gulf and Arab condemnation
The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.
The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.
Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.
Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.
Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.
He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

noticias.titulo: World Bank official says Lebanon reconstruction making slow progress
noticias.resumen: Beirut blames Israel's occupation and attacks on southern Lebanon for reconstruction delays.
noticias.texto:
World Bank official says Lebanon reconstruction making slow progress
Beirut blames Israel’s occupation and attacks on southern Lebanon for reconstruction delays.
A senior World Bank official says Lebanon has been slow to use international aid to rebuild areas destroyed during the 2024 war and the renewed fighting since March 2026.
World Bank managing director of operations Anna Bjerde said she had to be “honest” about the pace of reconstruction during a visit to southern Lebanon on Tuesday.
The international financial institution approved $250m in June 2025 to help Lebanon clear rubble and repair “damaged critical public infrastructure” after the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war. But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026.
The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b.
“Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”.
Israel has continued to occupy and attack parts of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River since March, claiming to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure, while demolishing civilian homes.
On Wednesday, Israel fired artillery shells towards the towns of Baraachit and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). The towns of Rashaf and Sarbine, extending to Wadi al-Hujair, were also targeted. And Israeli earth movers demolished residential homes in the town of Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah and Haddatha.
The United Nations estimates at least 304,500 Lebanese remain internally displaced in the country, down from 1.2 million. Up to 4,500 have been killed in Israeli attacks.
Last month, Hezbollah announced it will pay up to $14,000 to families whose homes were destroyed or made uninhabitable by Israel, as the group accused the government of failing to carry out its duties to help the displaced.
Israel has refused to withdraw from southern Lebanon, citing security concerns connected to the delayed disarmament of Hezbollah and other groups, which the United States and the Lebanese government have insisted on, as part of the trilateral ceasefire framework launched in April.
“Israel will not withdraw from the current lines of these security zones, nor will it redeploy its forces,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that if tensions escalate on the various fronts, “we are fully prepared to seize additional territory”.
Bjerde said that “institutions in Lebanon are very thinly stretched” and the security situation required “very careful planning around where you can start and where you don’t start” to remove rubble and repair infrastructure.
The World Bank projected Lebanon’s economy to shrink by 6.4 percent this year, in its Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor report, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy.
“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said.
According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than one million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of hunger.
Despite this, Lebanon’s western-backed government insists it is doing all it can, given the circumstances, such as the distribution of approximately $100m in housing loans granted to 1,500 families, according to NNA.
Bjerde said the World Bank needs to be “insistent” and “very close to monitoring on a daily basis” to make sure the work gets done “because you cannot let the people down”, adding that the World Bank wants to see the reconstruction work go more quickly.

noticias.titulo: Largest US egg producer to cull 1.8 million birds after bird flu outbreak
noticias.resumen: Cal-Maine reports avian influenza at Florida site, with 2.7 percent of its total flock affected.
noticias.texto:
Largest US egg producer to cull 1.8 million birds after bird flu outbreak
Cal-Maine reports avian influenza at Florida site, with 2.7 percent of its total flock affected.
Cal-Maine Foods, the largest egg producer in the United States, has said it would cull 1.8 million birds after avian influenza was detected at one of its facilities in Florida.
On Wednesday, the company said the 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 young hens being culled account for 2.7 percent of its flock. Production at the facility will be temporarily halted.
Cal-Maine said in a statement that it would coordinate with other production and distribution facilities to minimise disruption across the company.
The risk bird flu poses to human health is low. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there have been 74 human cases since February 2024, with no evidence of human-to-human transmission.
However, the virus continues to pose a significant challenge to the US poultry and egg industries. Some 21.5 million birds have been affected this year, following a historic surge in outbreaks in late 2024 and early 2025 that sharply reduced the number of egg-laying hens.
Approximately 50.7 million laying hens were lost between mid-October 2024 and early March 2025, when egg prices in the US reached a record high of $6.23 per dozen.
The current average retail price of eggs is $2.32 per dozen, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Despite the announcement that production at the Florida facility would be temporarily halted, Cal-Maine’s stock rose 5.3 percent in early trading.

noticias.titulo: Pax Silica is the new face of US imperialism in the Philippines
noticias.resumen: Behind promises of jobs and investment lie threats to ancestral lands, water security and national sovereignty.
noticias.texto:
Pax Silica is the new face of US imperialism in the Philippines
Behind promises of jobs and investment lie threats to ancestral lands, water security and national sovereignty.
The Philippine government is promising jobs and billions in investment through the United States-led Pax Silica initiative. But protesters see a very different future: threatened ancestral lands, environmental destruction and deeper dependence on Washington.
On November 15, ahead of Donald Trump’s visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit, Philippine police arrested more than 200 demonstrators opposing the initiative. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on protests against a project that critics see as another form of US neo-imperialism.
The Pax Silica initiative is a US-led coalition aimed at securing supply chains and countering China’s strength in critical minerals, semiconductors and other technologies essential to AI infrastructure. The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with a proposed industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac province, forming part of it. The Philippine government has promoted the proposed industrial hub as essential to economic development, projecting that it could generate more than 130,000 jobs and attract up to $70bn in investment once fully developed, a process expected to take decades. The proposed Pax Silica industrial hub, which covers approximately 1,618 hectares, raises concerns not only about national sovereignty but also about the displacement of local communities, environmental repercussions, Indigenous land rights and human security.
Critics see the project as taking land from local communities and farmers to serve foreign interests. The Aeta Hungey community in Sapang Kawayan, for example, faces relocation from land it has occupied for generations. Around 200 residents could lose access to their homes, farmland, water sources and burial grounds, while the community’s efforts to secure formal recognition of its ancestral land, dating back to 1994, remain unresolved.
Another major concern is water consumption. According to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), the proposed industrial hub could require 65–90 million litres of water daily. Although the BCDA plans to meet this demand through surface-water harvesting, concerns remain about the pressure on water resources, particularly during droughts. The Philippines is already vulnerable to drought, water shortages, agricultural disruption and climate change. On November 4, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) confirmed that a very strong El Nino was present and expected to persist into the first half of 2027.
The Philippine government must respond to the pressing needs of Filipinos instead of becoming a pawn of the United States in its geopolitical rivalry with China. Southeast Asia is a focal point of competition between the two major powers, with the Philippines serving as a key US ally. Pax Silica would position the Philippines as a central node in an emerging AI Cold War with China.
Projected as an avenue for economic progress, Pax Silica could also serve as a tool for the military expansion of the US in the region, particularly in the Philippines. Semiconductors are used in modern military production and are essential components of weapon systems in modern warfare. During his November 17 ASEAN speech, Trump highlighted US agreements across the region involving critical minerals, energy and technology, while describing the Philippines as a longstanding key ally. He also pointed to increased defence cooperation between the two countries. This cooperation already rests in part on the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), which allows US forces access to agreed Philippine military facilities.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr also emphasised the depth of the relationship between the two countries, rooted in shared history and values. Describing the extent of US influence in Philippine life, he said, “There is no part of our lives in the Philippines that is not involved with the United States in some way, in some shape or form or another.”
An unexamined alliance compromises national interests, particularly those affecting the lives of the Filipino people. Economic development should not come at the expense of human security, sovereignty and environmental sustainability.
Against this backdrop, a broad, multisectoral opposition movement against Pax Silica has emerged and is gaining momentum. It brings together diverse sectors, including Indigenous peoples, farmers, workers, scientists, environmentalists, faith leaders, students, and progressive activists.
The protests have also spread to university campuses. On November 13, university students staged coordinated campus walkouts across the Philippines. Among the major participating universities were the University of the Philippines, De La Salle University, Ateneo de Manila University, University of Santo Tomas, and Far Eastern University, among others. United in their opposition to Pax Silica, protesters repeatedly chanted slogans denouncing US imperialism. Drawing on the Philippines’ history as a former US colony, they associate the initiative with another neocolonial project by an imperial power.
In the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Mindanao, where anti-Pax Silica demonstrations took place in Marawi City and Tawi-Tawi, the opposition is particularly significant. For protesters in this predominantly Muslim region, opposition to the initiative intersects with longstanding grievances rooted in the historical dispossession of local communities whose ancestral lands were taken by settlers, reinforced by imperialist wars and oppression. They see Pax Silica as another project that could displace local communities and facilitate land-grabbing by an imperial power.
Equally important is the movement’s expansion beyond the Philippines into transnational solidarity. According to organisers, solidarity demonstrations have taken place in 23 cities across 14 countries, bringing international support to the opposition against Pax Silica and US imperialism.
As the movement gains momentum, the Marcos administration must address the legitimate grievances of the people directly affected by the proposed project. Moreover, this is not merely a concern of the Indigenous Aeta communities; it carries broader regional implications. Marcos’s reference to shared history does not necessarily mean that the two countries stand on equal footing. There is no symmetrical relationship between a coloniser and a colonised. Those subjected to imperial domination are not equal to those imposing control.
The ASEAN Way, characterised by the principle of consensus, must prevail over the competing interests of major powers. Fostering multilateralism will pave the way for cooperation, collective security and economic progress that will eventually empower ASEAN and the Global South. It is through this approach that the three major priorities of the Philippine ASEAN chairship can be realised: Peace and Security Anchors, Prosperity Corridors, and People Empowerment.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
