noticias.titulo: Hakeem Jeffries formally nominated as first Black US House speaker
noticias.resumen: The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month's midterm elections.
noticias.texto:
Hakeem Jeffries formally nominated as first Black US House speaker
The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month’s midterm elections.
Washington, DC, United States – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history.
In a closed-door vote on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination for the post just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress.
After voting concluded, Jeffries took to social media to thank his fellow Democrats for their support.
“Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!” he wrote in a post on X.
Amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote on Wednesday.
Some of those members, most of whom were elected this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries. Several said they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on.
One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.
“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.
Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. During an interview with The Atlantic magazine on Tuesday, Jeffries addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution.
Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the House Democratic Caucus with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed it.
Seven of those who voted against Jeffries included newly-elected Democrats Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.
Those members released a statement, which was shared with Al Jazeera, detailing their opposition they said was over failure to receive commitments from Jeffries on policies like “Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics or ending the genocide in Gaza”.
“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership”, the soon-to-be lawmakers wrote. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no”.
Another future member, Frederick Haynes of Texas, was included in the joint-statement against Jeffries’ nomination, but clarified later, in his own statement, he “narrowly” missed Wednesday’s vote due to illness.
Most Democrats, however, praised Jeffries’ nomination for speaker, which will put him on track to become one of Donald Trump’s top political opponents during the final two years of his presidency.
Outgoing Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi, who served for eight years as the first female speaker during two non-consecutive terms, marked the historic moment with a social media post, which included a photo of her holding Jeffries hand.
“Congratulations, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries!” she wrote.
Just before the vote, Jeffries took to social media to post a Bible verse from the book of Corinthians reading,” For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
In 2023, Jeffries was put forward by Democrats as their pick to succeed former US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, who was ousted by his fellow Republicans in favour of the chamber’s current speaker, Mike Johnson. Wednesday’s vote, however, means Jeffries has now been formally nominated by members of his party.
Jeffries is poised to replace Johnson as speaker when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3 with a Democratic majority and a vote on the new speaker is held in the full chamber.

noticias.titulo: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least five people
noticias.resumen: Most of the casualties were in strikes on Odesa that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as 'brutal'.
noticias.texto:
Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least five people
Most of the casualties were in strikes on Odesa that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as ‘brutal’.
Russian air attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, authorities said, a day after a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Kerch Bridge killed two and caused part of the structure to collapse.
In the southern city of Odesa, at least four people were killed and 13 others wounded in Russian air strikes, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the “brutal and deliberate” attack also targeted first responders.
Oleg Kiper, the head of the Odesa region’s military administration, said three Russian strikes hit the city’s “historic centre”. Odesa city council said one of the strikes hit a UNESCO-protected area, causing a car to catch fire and blowing out hundreds of windows in at least seven buildings.
Ukrainian emergency services shared images showing wounded people on stretchers, buildings with shattered windows and firefighters extinguishing a blaze on a rooftop.
“There were double-tap strikes after first responders and police officers had already arrived at the scene,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
He said the attack served as “further proof of what the Russians really want and how they truly regard diplomatic efforts”.
In the southeastern Zaporizhia region, a Russian drone strike killed a woman and injured a man in the town of Kushuhum, local military administration official Mykhailo Semykin said.
Attacks on the region also forced local authorities to order families with children to leave the village of Balabyne, he said.
“We are talking about 85 children from 80 families. In total, the evacuation affects 184 people,” he wrote on Telegram.
In northern Ukraine’s Rivne region, 80 settlements were left without electricity after a Russian attack, authorities said. No deaths or injuries were reported.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. New power outages had been recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Sumy, Rivne, and Cherkasy regions in the last 24 hours, Interfax reported on Wednesday. Russia has increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the lead-up to winter, in a strategy the United Nations said amounted to war crimes.
“The situation in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions remains extremely difficult. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power supply as soon as possible, but repeated attacks are significantly complicating repair work,” Ukraine’s energy ministry said.
The attacks came a day after Ukraine attacked Russia’s Kerch Bridge – a symbolic road-and-rail link from Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula – killing two people.
Europe proposes $45bn loan for Ukraine
As the warring sides continue to trade long-range attacks, the European Commission has proposed a new 45 billion euro ($49.5bn) loan to Ukraine to help fill a 70 billion euro ($76.8bn) funding gap for next year.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused since it launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
“We very much hope for the swift adoption of this decision by the European Parliament and the Council and count on the support of all EU member states,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Although Ukraine is not officially on the agenda during a tripartite meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Beijing, the talks are being watched closely in the Ukrainian capital.
Reporting from Kyiv on Wednesday, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said there were concerns in Ukraine that the meeting “could place the Russian President in a similar category of world powers and world leaders as the United States and China and what the optics mean for Ukraine”.
MacAlpine said parallel meetings to negotiate the end of the Ukraine war were due to begin in Berlin on Thursday. “The US delegates are reportedly travelling there to meet with the Ukrainian delegation, potentially with some of the leaders of Europe,” she said.
The agenda is expected to address Ukrainian demands for security guarantees and the prisoner swap agreed in Abu Dhabi last week, MacAlpine said.

noticias.titulo: Hegseth boasts about Maduro’s capture while vowing to deepen US military cooperation with Venezuela

noticias.texto:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.
“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.
Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”
Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.
But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

noticias.titulo: Anthony Albanese defies critics for Apec summit photo with Vladimir Putin
noticias.resumen: Despite pleas from pro-Ukraine Australians, the prime minister accepts wishes of Chinese hosts with group picture Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese has appeared in a leaders’ photo with Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit in China, despite Australia’s Ukrainian community urging the prime minister to protest against Russia’s war. After arriving in the Chinese tech capital, Shenzhen, on Wednesday, Albanese said he would respect the wishes of China as the hosts of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and take part in the photo. noticias.texto:
Anthony Albanese has appeared in a leaders’ photo with Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit in China, despite Australia’s Ukrainian community urging the prime minister to protest against Russia’s war.
After arriving in the Chinese tech capital, Shenzhen, on Wednesday, Albanese said he would respect the wishes of China as the hosts of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and take part in the photo.
He appeared in a group shot that included Putin, the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping at the summit banquet on Wednesday night. The traditional leaders’ “family photo” is due to be taken on Thursday morning.
“I will bear in mind the wishes of our host,” Albanese said before the event. “China are our host here, I respect that, but we also make our position very clear when it comes to Ukraine.”
Other leaders including Canada’s Mark Carney said they would take part, despite foreign affairs ministers at this month’s G20 talks in the United States refusing to pose with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov.
It is the first time Putin has had a place at the forefront of a grouping of world leaders in nearly a decade.
A professor of international law at Australian National University, Don Rothwell, said posing with Putin risked undermining trust in the international criminal court, where the Russian has been indicted as a war criminal over his invasion of Ukraine and the four-year war.
“For the Australian prime minister to appear in a photograph with Vladimir Putin is not consistent with the international values Australia is seeking to espouse,” Rothwell told Guardian Australia.
The Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations chairwoman, Kateryna Argyrou, had urged Albanese to boycott the event.
“Vladimir Putin is not just another world leader attending an international summit,” Argyrou said.
“He is an indicted war criminal and the architect of a brutal war against Ukraine – a war that has brought death, destruction and unimaginable suffering to millions of people.”
China is the latest stop on Albanese’s intense diplomatic tour.
After Quad leaders’ talks in Manila on Tuesday night, the prime minister attended a business event and toured a supermarket selling Australian-made products in Shenzhen.
The city – known as a major hub for electronics, drones and companies including Huawei and electric vehicle brand BYD – is seeing intense security as world leaders gather. Many of the streets have been cleared of local residents, allowing motorcades speedy access to the summit hubs and nearby luxury hotels.
Spruiking investment in Australia, Albanese recalled first visiting Shenzhen in the 1990s and said AI could help bridge economic divides and allow for sustainable growth in the region.
“The economic potential and opportunity of artificial intelligence is enormous,” he said. “Not just for the Asia Pacific, but for the world.”
As well as the main summit, Albanese will take part in bilateral meetings on Thursday, including with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. He will attend a lunch with Carney and the leaders of Singapore and New Zealand.
But the trilateral talks with Trump, Xi and Putin on Thursday are set to dominate conversations in Shenzhen and in capitals around the world. Already likened to the Yalta summit after the second world war, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned against decisions about his country’s future being made without him.
Albanese will make a diplomatic call on Xi on Friday, before a meeting in Beijing with the Chinese premier, Li Qiang.
On the agenda with both leaders is a push for China to remove 55% tariffs for Australian beef exports, imposed after the country hit an annual quota for sales. Albanese said he would lobby in Australia’s interests.
“Of course we’d rather not have any quotas on Australian goods anywhere in the world, but the fact they’ve hit it is a signal that Chinese consumers want to buy Australian beef because of its quality.”
He said he would raise trade issues as the federal government works to stabilise trade with China after Beijing imposed a major diplomatic freeze on Australia during the former Coalition government.
Albanese praised Xi’s engagement and knowledge of Australia, noting the Chinese leader had visited every state and territory.

noticias.titulo: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
noticias.resumen: Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas supplies Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies. The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over
noticias.texto:
The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.
The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.
Analysis by the London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition, where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.
InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.
“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.
“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”
InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.
That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.
For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.
Of those members assessed, 69% backed stronger climate policies than the BCA, a gap that widened to 78% on energy transition issues.
Herring said the BCA does not disclose who sits on its internal climate and energy committees, obscuring how its policy positions are formed.
“We obviously do know who’s on the association board but, beyond that, there’s no transparency around those internal committees,” he said.
A spokesperson for the BCA said the association supported the “national goal of achieving net zero by 2050 and the setting of interim targets, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy and ensuring we don’t undermine our international competitiveness along the way”.
“The BCA has long advocated for gas as an essential part of the net zero transition – ensuring grid stability – while we move to greater reliance on renewable energy,” the spokesperson said.
The BCA declined to comment on the makeup of its climate and energy committee.
‘Technology agnostic’
The analysis comes as industry groups ramp up lobbying over the “safeguard mechanism”, Australia’s main policy for curbing emissions from its largest industrial facilities, which is under federal review.
While the BCA and most big resources companies publicly support the Paris agreement and Australia’s net zero 2050 carbon emissions target, they interpret what those commitments require in radically different ways to what is widely regarded as climate best practice.
Several oil and gas producer members, including Woodside, argue that increased gas supply is required to support the shift to renewables and enhance energy security in language that has been adopted by the BCA.
This rubs against those BCA members aligned with the findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which found greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure were more than enough to push the world beyond its climate goals.
InfluenceMap also found that the business council frequently lobbies for a “technology-neutral” or “technology agnostic” energy transition, which is the same language used by the fossil fuel sector designed to steer renewable energy funding toward gas.
Persephone Fraser, the ethical research and climate policy lead at fund manager Australian Ethical, said misaligned lobbying was a significant risk for companies and their shareholders, and a major risk to the economy.
“Companies must be scrutinising what is being advocated for in their name and actively correcting the record when it is inconsistent with their own positions, and interests,” Fraser said.
“Membership of an industry association cannot mean outsourcing responsibility for climate lobbying.”

noticias.titulo: EU ‘to close door’ to talks on long-term UK ties until Burnham has decided on Brexit
noticias.resumen: Diplomats say piecemeal approach of resets is coming to an end and Europe wants clarity on whether Britain wants to reverse its exit The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said. European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal “reset” summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said.
European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal “reset” summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed.
But they suggested a joint statement after a summit this Friday would signal that further discussions would follow on the UK’s entry to the EU’s energy single markets, irregular migration and a closer defence and security relationship.
“Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK. Don’t come back until you know what you want. Work out what your options really are and then come to negotiate,” one EU diplomat said.
“The prime minister needs to bring the public with him. We can’t have another negotiation based on just half the country. We’ll only put the effort in if we know it’s not going to change down the line.”
Burnham is expected to set out his own next steps after the summit on Monday, including his hopes for a “national conversation” on what a closer relationship might look like.
With less than 48 hours before the Brussels summit, negotiators were still racing to finalise Friday’s agreement. A leaked draft seen by the Guardian shows continued disagreement over demands by the EU that the UK commit to aligning with the bloc’s trade defence measures, such as tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, in exchange for inclusion in Made in Europe legislation.
The text shows the UK is pushing for a weaker commitment, only promising an “aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention”.
A Cabinet Office source said Made in Europe language was “the highest jeopardy” in the negotiations, while an EU official suggested it was the part of the discussions most likely to go “down to the wire” on Friday.
Though there is a formal commitment to annual reset summits, senior EU diplomats say the current approach, designed by Keir Starmer, will quickly “reach its limits” and more “mini deals” do not make sense.
One said the “piecemeal approach is coming to an end” and that Burnham’s intentions for the UK’s long-term relationship created a natural juncture for the EU too.
Another said: “It is like a buffet: you can choose to nibble on one or two dishes to start, but at a certain point you have to go for the whole of the buffet.”
One EU diplomat said there would be a “pause for reflection” after the Friday summit.
Burnham has said there is no rush to decide on the longer-term relationship, as he comes under pressure from within his own party to slow the pace of pursuing of closer ties.
He is not now expected to set out the full range of options for the future relationship – the status quo, customs union, single market or full rejoin – until he announces his 10-year plan in December.
Sources said the government was considering holding a year-long “national conversation” in 2027, including town halls and citizens assemblies, before deciding which route to pursue in advance of the next election.
However, the potential length of that debate has alarmed Brussels officials, who were caught off-guard by the launch of the new pro-Brexit campaign group Stay Out, set up by architects of the Vote Leave campaign.
One EU diplomat said: “The government would spend the year making evidence-based arguments about each of the four options, while Boris Johnson and Michael Gove and Nigel Farage will spend it shouting about traitors.”
After the reset deal is agreed on Friday, it will be enacted by the European partnership bill, covering the deals on food and agriculture, emissions trading and youth mobility. It is expected to be introduced before Christmas, with legislation laid possibly as soon as next week.
EU diplomats said the two sides were expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 people a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each other’s territories. Originally, the UK had pitched for 50,000 and then 80,000, while Brussels has consistently sought a higher number.
Both sides have agreed that tuition fees for European students coming to the UK should be discussed at a later date, although there have been attempts by some member states to link the debate to the ratification of the whole reset deal.
Senior Labour figures are already beginning their push to have a full rejoining on the table. The former business secretary Peter Kyle said Burnham should fight the next election on a promise to rejoin the EU, with voters given a referendum on the outcome of any deal.
Kyle, who was a key member of Starmer’s cabinet, said the “only way through” the challenges of the domestic political debate was for the government to offer voters the choice to accept or reject any agreement.
He is the latest senior Labour MP to publicly wade into the Brexit debate, after the former foreign secretary David Lammy said the party should go into the next election clear that its intention was to rejoin.
Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, has also said Britain’s future should be back in the bloc, arguing that leaving had made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.

noticias.titulo: The leave campaign has been resurrected, so how should Burnham respond?
noticias.resumen: No 10 is confident the PM can make the case for closer EU ties, while others worry about leaving the campaign solely in his hands The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even if the arguments were straight out of a familiar playbook. The video launched on X over the weekend, with scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians saying how desperate they were for Britain’s cash. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even if the arguments were straight out of a familiar playbook.
The video launched on X over the weekend, with scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians saying how desperate they were for Britain’s cash.
Among Westminster’s anti-Brexit veterans, there was immediate chatter about whether a counteroffensive was needed. “I think the immediate reaction was – are they off to the races while we are still putting our pants on?” one said.
For now, the rebuttal of Stay Out’s claims – including that returning to the EU would cost £750m a week – is mostly being done on social media by interested pro-rejoin freelancers, without any kind of central organisation.
One MP said: “It is hard for us to begin any kind of new pro-rejoin campaign until we know exactly the direction the government is heading.
“There are organisations that exist already, like Best for Britain, but I think making the case to the public would need a fresh movement. I think we want to stay away from the kind of marches that People’s Vote movement did with the blue berets if we can possibly avoid it.”
Inside No 10, there is a confidence that Andy Burnham can make his own case for a closer relationship with Europe, without the need for any external pressure group. Stay Out – which is run by the former deputy chief Brexit negotiator Oliver Lewis – will be dubbed “the status quo campaign”.
There is reason to be confident. Strategists have seen Labour polling that shows almost three-quarters – 71% – of all voters support a closer relationship with Europe if it helps bring down prices and grow the economy.
It will be the prime minister, they say, who can front any campaigning that is needed, who can argue that Brexit has done more harm than good, damaging the economy, making it harder for British people to travel and businesses to trade and fuelling the small boats crisis.
However, there will be some fears that this has been tried before when David Cameron attempted to make the case for remain in 2016. But Labour strategists say this is a fundamentally different political moment. “Cameron could not make this kind of emotional connection with people, it was business leaders, facts and figures, and he was arguing for the status quo,” one said. “We are the change campaign now.”
While some cabinet members urged caution last week over Burnham’s uncertain direction on Europe, most trust the prime minister can set out a viable post-summit plan. “All of us, honestly, are slightly running to catch up with a different way of doing things,” one said. “We all easily lapse into the worries about leave-voting seats.
“But there is obviously an argument to be made that the old rules don’t apply. And Andy’s way of doing things is laying out political argument. And we have to believe in that as the way to affect public sentiment.”
There are some close to Labour who worry about leaving the argument solely to Burnham. “Can they do this from the bowels of Downing Street?” one asked. “You do need rebuttal out there and people ready to go out and fight and say, this is bollocks. And it felt like that infrastructure is not there yet.”
Another veteran of the remain campaign said there was concern about being “left out on a limb” if a rejoin campaign was resurrected. “I think whether they like it or not, there will be an apolitical campaign trying to push the maximalist position on Europe. They have people willing to help but it’s not organised in any way.”
Many of those who worked on the remain campaign and the subsequent People’s Vote are scarred by the experience, particular the final months which descended into bitter infighting. But the same is also true for some of the most high-profile veterans of Vote Leave – who also want to steer clear of Stay Out.
As in the pro-Brexit campaigns, there are often willing funders to push pro-European campaigning. “It will happen because there will be money for it,” one campaign veteran said. “But you could not pay me any money to go back to that issue.”

noticias.titulo: Cheese, pet passports and youth mobility: what’s in the UK-EU ‘relationship reset’ draft?
noticias.resumen: Leaked text of 72-paragraph second draft shows agreement has largely been reached before expected signoff on Friday The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday. A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Wensleydale cheese on the shelves at a North Yorkshire dairy. The sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) agreement on cheese exports to the EU will not be implemented until 1 March 2028. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Observer
Wensleydale cheese on the shelves at a North Yorkshire dairy. The sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) agreement on cheese exports to the EU will not be implemented until 1 March 2028. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Observer
Cheese, pet passports and youth mobility: what’s in the UK-EU ‘relationship reset’ draft?
Leaked text of 72-paragraph second draft shows agreement has largely been reached before expected signoff on Friday
The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday.
A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points.
Here’s what is and isn’t addressed in the 72-paragraph joint communique, from pet passports and cheese imports to student fees and artist touring visas.
I’m 29 – will the under-30s youth mobility scheme help me live in an EU country?
You may not make it. The deal states it will “allow people from the EU and the UK to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling”.
But the deal may not be active until 2030 because work permits are the preserve of national governments, not something Brussels can solve.
The youth mobility scheme allowing under-30s to work, study and travel across the UK and EU for up to three years may not be in place until 2030. Photograph: PhotoAlto/James Hardy/Getty Images
“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” the draft says.
I am an EU student. I want to apply for a year’s study in the UK. Will I pay home fees?
This has yet to be agreed. The two options in the draft text are a halfway house between international and home fees, or a concession from the UK to allow EU citizens pay the same as British students (or Irish ones, who are also eligible for home fees under a separate longstanding agreement).
The choices, according to the draft, are “significantly reduced undergraduate” or “equal treatment” with UK nationals on tuition fees.
Will there be a limit on the youth mobility scheme?
The British government wants to cap youth mobility at between 50,000 and 80,000 places to reduce impact on overall migration numbers. The EU is pushing for at least 100,000.
Some EU states, including Germany, are open to the idea of allowing unlimited numbers of British young people to work, live or study in their countries regardless of UK reciprocation.
Will the government finally get a deal to help UK artists touring in the EU?
Elton John has long been among those demanding the government fix a flaw in the Brexit deal which saw gigging bands or theatre groups unable to tour Europe without major bureaucracy (and its associated cost) since 2021.
The EU has resisted negotiating on the issue because, like youth mobility, it touches on work permits which are a national remit. But in what appears to be a win for the UK, touring artists do feature in the draft text.
This takes into account primary legislation that is needed on the UK side to dynamically align with EU standards.
Any mention of pet passports?
No. These are tied to the SPS deal, meaning British travellers will still have to fork out up to £200 every time they take their dog or cat to an EU country.
Pet passports are tied to the SPS deal. Photograph: Javier Brosch/Alamy
Travel and transport officials are hoping relevant changes to the SPS agreement can be brought forward.
“Around 15% of our customers have pets with them. For them it will make a huge difference,” Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, told the Guardian.
Has the UK agreed to tariffs on Chinese EVs?
No. The EU has pressed the UK to follow its trade defence measures which include quotas on Chinese hybrid-electric cars and tariffs on fully electric cars.
The UK has said it will not be coerced into a decision but is demanding that British manufacturers are not locked out of the upcoming Made in Europe legislation in exchange for forming a kind of trade club with the EU on autos.
Both sides agree to protectionist measures in “a particular supply chain” but there is no agreement yet on how that will apply. According to the text, the EU proposes that “the UK would be bound to ensure in its policies and national legal order the same outcomes” as measures imposed by the EU. The UK’s proposed text says: “We will aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention.”
Nio electric vehicles on a production line in Hefei, China. Nio exports to the EU and hopes to launch its models in the UK. Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty Images
What about the new ‘trusted partnership’?
It’s gone. Instead of a vague “trusted partnership”, both sides commit to a “partnership for economic resilience”.
The language in the latest draft agreement has also been tightened up in a concession to the UK, say diplomats.
What about migration and security?
The UK wants to restore pre-Brexit access to EU databases but this will not be agreed on Friday. The EU will instead explore giving the UK access to its proposed Prüm International scheme “on data exchange for police cooperation to chosen third-country partners”.
And what about the EU’s biometric database?
There is no mention of Eurodac, the database that stores biometrics of asylum seekers in the EU, and diplomats say sharing this data, which was not collected for law enforcement purposes, could be tricky.
But according to the draft, the EU will “continue exploring ways to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third-country nationals”.

noticias.titulo: Alexander Zverev notified of abuse lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals
noticias.resumen: Men’s world No 1 allegedly violated terms of settlement Lawyers say Zverev will ‘defend himself against lawsuit’ Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her. The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an intervie
noticias.texto:
Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.
The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with the French sports daily L’Equipe earlier this year that “it has been proven that the accusations were false” and “my innocence has been proven”.
Zverev’s Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement that they were formally served with Patea’s lawsuit on Wednesday.
“Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit,” Zverev’s lawyers said. “If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion” – which would be protected by the German constitution. They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.
Patea’s lawyer, Michael Scheele, said that Zverev’s claim over his innocence “triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client”. He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.
“Quite apart from the fact that Zverev’s claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form,” he said. “Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement.”
Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and that he be fined up to €250,000 (£208,500) every time if he does.
Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing. The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. The case officially declared no verdict and the settlement entailed no acknowledgment of guilt on Zverev’s part. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.
The German player this month ascended to the world No 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two grand slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin.
Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.

noticias.titulo: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
noticias.resumen: Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area. Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street . Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but b
noticias.texto:
Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.
Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.
She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.
The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.
Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”
The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.
Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.
The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.
Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”
Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.
If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.
The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.
Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

noticias.titulo: Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform
noticias.resumen: Home secretary says ‘routine two-tier policing’ does not exist, but public trust in impartial law enforcement must be restored Shabana Mahmood has backed a ban on police officers marching in pride events in uniform as she said there had been a “few examples” of two-tier policing . Although she said there was no systematic or routine two-tier policing, the home secretary said “a new impartiality standard” was necessary to reverse the fall in the public’s faith in law enforcement. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Shabana Mahmood has backed a ban on police officers marching in pride events in uniform as she said there had been a “few examples” of two-tier policing.
Although she said there was no systematic or routine two-tier policing, the home secretary said “a new impartiality standard” was necessary to reverse the fall in the public’s faith in law enforcement.
She said one example had been when police officers took part in a pride event in Northumbria last year, which a court found had breached a duty of impartiality. Mahmood said: “The judgment found that they got the balance wrong … and that marching … was not acceptable and not impartial.
“Today at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act.”
Nik Adams, the deputy commissioner of City of London police who is also the LGBTQ+ lead for police chiefs, said: “Using the language about LGBTQ issues being contested makes LGBTQ people in policing and wider society feel less safe, makes their lives feel less valued.
“LGBTQ is a protected characteristic in law. The rights are hard won.”
Wiltshire police faces a court challenge next week for setting up a stall at a pride event in Swindon after claims it had exposed a lack of neutrality amid disputes over transgender rights.
Asked if she was accepting there was two-tier policing, Mahmood said: “There’s no systematic, systemic, routine two-tier policing in this country. I reject that charge.
“What Reform and others will have you believe is every single day officers go out and they practise a thing called two-tier policing. That is utter, complete, ridiculous rubbish.
“But there have been examples of differential treatment, and those have had an impact on confidence in policing, and they’ve allowed that false perception of two-tier policing to take hold.
“I accept that there are few examples, and I know that actually the best way to deal with that is to make sure we have a new impartiality standard.”
One police leader told the Guardian this rhetoric was concerning as forces tried to navigate the culture wars buffeting Britain while serving all communities.
She said police had to improve its record on recruiting more black officers, noting there were barely any more than there had been 30 years ago.
Mahmood added: “We must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment. I believe we see this in examples like the old police anti-racism commitment, which was a well-intentioned attempt to address racism that ended up achieving the opposite of its stated goal.
“It made statements that are clearly wrong: to the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing ‘does not mean treating everyone the same’. So was the document’s guidance that officers should not be ‘colour blind’.”
The home secretary also said officers should engage with the community to discuss local issues, but not with activist groups and campaigners who were pushing their own political agenda.
But one source said Mahmood’s soundbites did not take account of the complexities: “It’s an easy slogan, but dig into the details and it becomes more complicated.”
For instance some oppose the red poppy as part of Remembrance Day celebrations, believing it glorifies militarism, but these are worn by officers and chiefs.
Mahmood decried police talking to activists, but policing has been given money to boost the protection of Jewish people in Britain, while some groups that police may want to consult have been accused of extremism by pro-Palestinian groups.
Gavin Stephens, the chair of the National Police Chiefs Council, said: “Public trust depends on the police being seen to act fairly and impartially. Barriers to justice remain, discrimination still exists within our own ranks, and we rely on the trust and confidence of all communities to do our job. A diverse service is a stronger service.”

noticias.titulo: Ex-Tory MPs barred from shaping Reform UK’s immigration policy, says Zia Yusuf
noticias.resumen: Comments by Reform’s home affairs spokesperson raise questions about unity at top of the party Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy, its home affairs spokesperson has claimed, excluding in effect the majority of the party’s MPs. “If you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy,” Zia Yusuf told a podcast by the Spectator magazine. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy, its home affairs spokesperson has claimed, excluding in effect the majority of the party’s MPs.
“If you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy,” Zia Yusuf told a podcast by the Spectator magazine.
Michael Gove, the Spectator editor and former Conservative minister, challenged Yusuf over how Reform intended to bring down migration numbers, given there were so many former Tory MPs in its ranks – including the former immigration minister Robert Jenrick – who had failed to do so while in government.
Yusuf said: “There’s a reason why Nigel’s given me this brief and not them.”
Yusuf was embroiled in a feud with Jenrick before the former Tory minister made the jump to Reform earlier this year, becoming its economics spokesperson.
In addition to Jenrick, the former home secretary Suella Braverman, the former DWP shadow minister Danny Kruger and the former Foreign Office shadow minister Andrew Rosindell are among the Tory MPs to have defected to Reform.
Yusuf qualified his comments by saying Braverman and Jenrick had either been sacked or resigned “over immigration policy or issues around culture”. The comments raise questions about unity at the top of Reform.
Braverman, Reform’s education spokesperson, and Jenrick have waded into immigration and cultural issues since joining Reform. The claims that former Tories have no role in immigration policy for Reform also appear to be at odds with, for example, Jenrick’s announcement in June of plans for a levy on migrant labour.
Reform’s grassroots members have long appeared suspicious of former Conservatives in their midst. Farage himself has frequently had to push back against claims that his party had become “the Conservative party 2.0” and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections were held on 7 May. Jenrick and others who defected nonetheless maintain a strong influence within Reform.
Tom Milford, a former spokesperson for Jenrick, has become Reform’s head of press, while the MP himself continues to generate slickly produced videos for social media covering a range of topics including law and order.
Jenrick is often mooted alongside Yusuf and Richard Tice as the most likely successor to Farage if he was to stand down.
The Labour party said Yusuf had “admitted that most Reform MPs can’t be trusted on their migration policies”.
Anna Turley, the Labour MP and minister of state for border security and asylum, said: “They don’t trust two-thirds of their MPs to work on their immigration policies, yet they expect the country to trust them to secure Britain’s borders.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Neighbourhood support teams’ to pave way for national care service, Cooper announces
noticias.resumen: Health secretary said programme would help about 566,000 vulnerable people in England by April More than half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will be offered help from joint NHS and social care teams that will pave the way for the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced. Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive assistance from the new programme. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
More than half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will be offered help from joint NHS and social care teams that will pave the way for the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.
Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive assistance from the new programme.
By next April about 566,000 people – 1% of the population – will benefit from joined-up “neighbourhood support teams” providing personalised care.
In a speech on Wednesday at the King’s Fund health thinktank, Cooper described the measure as a “downpayment” on the national care service promised by Andy Burnham to address the social care crisis.
The service will be expanded and eventually cover about 2 million people with particular health needs, including parents and babies, and under-25s who are not in education, employment or training.
Once fully operational, the major shift in key care services is expected to help relieve the pressure on overcrowded hospitals by cutting 4.3m bed days and reducing the number of people – mainly the frail elderly and those with dementia – who experience “corridor care”.
“The most frail and vulnerable, 4% of the population, account for 70% of emergency bed days in hospital, even though for many of them, an extended hospital stay is not where they want to be,” Cooper said.
The teams will be made up of GPs, district nurses, occupational therapists, geriatric consultants, physiotherapists, clinical pharmacists, mental health workers and social workers.
Age UK welcomed the announcement as “fantastic news for older people, especially those living with frailty and in declining health”.
The pledge to create the new teams is a major milestone in the government’s ambition to transform how the NHS works through “three big shifts”: from an analogue to digital service, from treatment to prevention of illness, and from hospital-based care to much more help being provided in community settings and people’s homes.
The teams will identify the most vulnerable members of their local community and devise a plan for keeping them as well as possible, including providing care in their own home or care home for as long as possible.
They will receive regular checks to assess their health, from teams who know them, to ensure they are receiving the right support. Patients and their families will also have access to a 24/7 helpline that will act as a single point of contact, though it is unclear when that will start.
Everyone being helped by the joint teams of NHS and local council personnel will also have an individual care plan that makes clear what their needs are and who should be helping with them.
The teams will review patients’ medicines, check they are having physiotherapy and that they have a care plan in place, for example.
Cooper said the teams would provide a more proactive and personalised approach that would make care much easier to access while also reducing the strain on the NHS, which has been struggling to meet the growing demand for care from the ageing and increasingly sick population.
Remote monitoring, “virtual ward” rounds and face-to-face visits to patients in their own homes in west Hertfordshire has led to people spending three fewer days in Watford general hospital, saved the local NHS £3.8m, and proved very popular with those cared for in that way.
The health secretary cited the NHS founder Nye Bevan’s belief in local community services, not just hospitals, and the then Labour health secretary Barbara Castle’s ambition in 1976 to reduce dependence on hospitals and promote integration of health and social care, as well as Burnham’s attempt as health secretary in 2009-10 to reform social care.
Sarah Woolnough, the King’s Fund’s chief executive, cautioned that while “bringing care closer to home has been an ambition for successive governments”, it had not happened – and may not happen now – because money had not been provided to enable the switch.
Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “To bring hospitals back from the brink we need more care at home, but a phone number isn’t a care package. With no new money and nothing starting until April, this does little for the thousands of frail patients facing a winter stuck in hospital.”
The creation of the new teams builds on Cooper’s announcement last week that GPs in England will receive £40m this winter to help give 300,000 vulnerable patients better care at home, to reduce their risk of ending up in hospital.

noticias.titulo: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s
noticias.resumen: Scientists tell Commons exposure to colibactin in early life is potential driver of early-onset colorectal cancer Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer among those under 50, MPs have heard. Cases of early-onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved. noticias.texto:
Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer among those under 50, MPs have heard.
Cases of early-onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved.
Dr Karl Smith-Byrne, a senior molecular epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, told the Commons science and technology committee that known risk factors for colorectal cancer, such as obesity, smoking and alcohol, can explain only about half of the cases doctors diagnose.
He said he did not find it “plausible” that the rise in early onset bowel cancer could be entirely explained by risk factors that researchers were already aware of.
Last year scientists identified a toxin called colibactin, produced by some variants of E coli bacteria in the gut, as a potential driver of early onset colorectal cancer. Hallmark mutations caused by the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those from people over 70.
More work is needed to understand whether colibactin actually drives bowel cancer, but it is a question scientists are now actively pursuing. “That’s probably the leading explanation at the moment,” Smith-Byrne told MPs.
Prof Mike Stratton at the Sanger Institute, who was not at the hearing, has said that colibactin causes mutations in some children but not others, with evidence of mutations appearing as early as infancy. By the age of 10, affected children can have a similar “mutational burden” to a 50-year-old, his work showed.
“If it is causing mutations, it’s causing mutations at a sensitive period earlier in life, and that can give that person’s colon or their rectum a head start on its journey towards being cancerous or developing these tumours,” said Smith-Byrne, who is himself a survivor of early-onset rectal cancer.
Some suspect that particular variants of E coli that normally live harmlessly in the gut have evolved in recent decades to produce colibactin. Prof Elio Riboli, a cancer epidemiologist at Imperial College London, told the committee: “This colibactin is essentially found in people born after 1960. Something has happened in the E coli bacteria … There must have been a mutation, and there is a new bacteria.”
Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer in the world, accounting for about one in 10 of all cases. The disease is still far more common in the over-50s, but global figures suggest diagnoses are rising steeply in younger people.
Prof Helen Coleman, a cancer epidemiologist at Queen’s University Belfast, told MPs that colibactin was “the first new clue that we’ve had in quite some time”, but that its potential role in bowel cancer was still under investigation.
“Even though we’re talking about adults that are being diagnosed with cancer between 18 and 49, it’s quite likely to be very early life exposures,” she said. “It could be something you were exposed to in very early childhood, possibly even in the prenatal period, and that makes it very difficult to study.”
Riboli said that while scientists needed to uncover the unknown drivers of different cancers, people should minimise risks that are already clear. In the UK and US, drinking and smoking are both falling, but obesity is rising and physical activity is in decline. “The quick win could come from applying what we know,” he said. “We could prevent about 60% of the cancers occurring now, but we are not applying in society what we know.”

Mullin defends move to take government plane to college football game amid nationwide grounding in House hearing
During today’s hearing Markwayne Mullin defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas on Saturday, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend.
“You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the committee’s top Democrat.
Mullin went further, and said that had he not traveled to the game it could have created “confusion” because he was due to meet Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.
Mullin added that his absence might have shown “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly” after the FAA reopened the airspace.
“We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it,” the homeland security secretary said. “We were saying our skies were completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours.”
Mullin noted that he paid for the trip himself because it was for non-official business, even though he is required to use the government aircraft for security reasons, and scolded Democrats for their line of questioning.
“The hypocrisy from you and from the members that want to make a big deal out of it … you guys would have done the same thing, but you would have called it a campaign event,” he said.

Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated. This, Scharf highlighted, “should not be surprising” to Democrats, noting the party took the “same position” in 2022, when they were relegated to the minority in the House.
In the majority, Democrats have vowed to launch sweeping investigations into a variety of issues and officials when they have subpoena power.

“It’s half a cubicle, but I have an extra seat for one staffer,” Massie said. “It’s traditional to kick non-returning members out of their offices early and ship them to this cubicle farm. The assumption is lame duck members just quit working … not me!”
A reminder that Massie lost his primary in May, after bucking with Donald Trump on several occasions. Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

noticias.resumen: DoJ cites three examples of alterations from English into Spanish for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after Guardian report US authorities have admitted altering the translation of an extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers from English into Spanish, attributing violent and illegal actions to the wealthy activist and philanthropist that were not in the original. noticias.texto:
US authorities have admitted altering the translation of an extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers from English into Spanish, attributing violent and illegal actions to the wealthy activist and philanthropist that were not in the original.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
In a notification sent to Spain’s ministry of justice, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) cites three of the examples of legally significant alterations revealed in the Guardian’s reporting on the issue, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”.
The notification arrived to defense attorneys, the prosecutor and a three-judge panel on Tuesday as the judges were deliberating whether to grant the US extradition request, leading the defense team to file a motion calling for a halt in the proceedings and a new translation.
The US has now admitted to three of the alterations detailed in the Guardian’s reporting, and calls the fourth “an acceptable translation”. One of them involves introducing the word “fire” in describing late 2023 protests against Elbit, an Israeli weapons manufacturer. Two of the three charges in the criminal complaint against Chambers are related to the protests – where nothing was set on fire.
Other changes involved adding the Spanish words for “violent” and “detonate” when the original English text did not have them.
According to documents seen by the Guardian, the Trump administration notified Spain of the alterations on 12 November, the day before a hearing involving Chambers’s attorneys, the three judges and the prosecutor – but the notification only reached all parties on Tuesday.
The unusual chain of events caps off weeks of unsuccessful efforts by the defense team to get the high court to pay attention to the issue and order a new translation.
The Guardian’s reporting on the issue was based in part on a 3 November motion that Chambers’s attorneys filed with the court, identifying a dozen alterations to the original criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request.
However, the judges responded to the motion by saying “the translation offered by the requesting country’s authorities should be considered trustworthy” and that no action was required, according to Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team.
Then, during the hearing, the judges denied the defense team’s request to admit into evidence a 345-page report prepared by a certified Spanish translator identifying what were now 30 “incriminating changes” the US had made to a machine-made translation.
The judges also denied the attorneys’ request to present the translator as a witness in the hearing. Meanwhile, the prosecutor dismissed the issue dismissively, referring to “supposed translation errors”.
These and other prejudicial notions with specific legal implications form part of the prosecutor’s report on the case, which in turn influences the judges deciding on the extradition request, Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian.
“I think the fact that the US recognizes what it has done shows that they were trying to fool the judges,” said Martínez. “This should touch the pride of the Spanish justice system.”
Spanish law and the extradition treaty between the US and Spain require extradition requests to be translated into Spanish by the requesting country. Martínez notes in the defense team’s motion filed on Tuesday that a 2003 extradition request from Turkey wound up being denied due to errors in translation – after defense attorneys took the case to Spain’s constitutional court, alleging violations of due process.
“We might wind up doing the same,” Martínez said.
A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers is also heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises. He sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023 and has been funding an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries since then.
Chambers’s views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media, including his public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
If the court’s decision on the US request is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the outcome. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.

Flood advisories have been issued for much of the Bay Area , according to the National Weather Service (NWS), while southern California may see coastal flooding, heavy surf, wave damage to coastal piers and parking lots , and beach sand erosion. noticias.texto:
Heavy rain or snowfall is predicted across California this week, as an “atmospheric river” dumps precipitation across the state.
Flood advisories have been issued for much of the Bay Area, according to the National Weather Service (NWS), while southern California may see coastal flooding, heavy surf, wave damage to coastal piers and parking lots, and beach sand erosion.
Areas of the state still recovering from recent wildfires are at risk for flash flooding, with specific warnings issued for “burn scar” areas including in Big Sur and the Napa valley.
The heaviest of the rainfall is expected north-east of San Francisco, from Santa Rosa to Chico and Redding in the state’s Central valley, and in the southern part of the Bay Area, along coastal mountain ranges from Santa Cruz to San Jose and Palo Alto, according to the NWS.
“Travel delays, localized flooding and hazardous conditions are possible, especially along the coast and on mountain pass roads,” Accuweather warned in an online forecast.
Atmospheric rivers, massive currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric rivers provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.
In southern California, the NWS predicted 1-3in of rain in many areas, with 3-5in in some mountain and foothill areas, and a 20% chance of thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday. As much as a foot of snow was expected in higher-elevation areas above 6,000ft. There was a high risk of “significant road flooding” and a moderate risk for rockslides and mudslides, the NWS said.
The risk of coastal wave damage was expected to peak in southern California on Thursday, with additional risks expected next week, with seasonal high tides overlapping with storm risks during Thanksgiving week.
Waterspouts were spotted over the San Francisco Bay earlier this week, and the NWS flagged the risk of additional waterspouts over the ocean east of San Francisco on Wednesday.

noticias.texto:
The head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) took responsibility for the nationwide ground stop that affected more than 12,400 flights on Friday, urging people to “lay off” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.
“I take full responsibility for it,” Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, said at an event featuring aviation officials and lawmakers on Wednesday, Politico reported.
“I wish people would lay off the secretary,” Bedford added. “He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody. Blame me.”
The FAA administrator’s comments arrived as Duffy, the top transportation official in the US, faces scrutiny from former officials and lawmakers over his handling of the tech outage crisis, which left tens of thousands of travelers stranded over the weekend.
In a press conference on Friday, Duffy refused to accept responsibility or apologize for the crisis, blaming Democratic lawmakers and his predecessors for not providing the funding to upgrade outdated systems.
The FAA said it grounded all flights after a newly installed router flooded communication systems, causing issues between aircraft systems and radar feeds.
