The Mexican president took a South China Airlines flight from Mexico City to Shenzhen, with posts going viral on China's Weibo social media site seemingly showing Sheinbaum chatting with other passengers on board.
She posted a short video on social media showing her being greeted by Chinese officials and schoolchildren after getting off an airport bus, as well as an earlier post showing her waiting in Mexico City's airport departures lounge.
A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival attracted more than 10 million views, with users voicing admiration for her low-cost intercontinental travel.
"It's commendable to spend taxpayer money frugally and ensure it's used where it's most needed, rather than squandering it on luxurious private jets or official travel expenses," the AFP news agency cited one user as saying.
Sheinbaum is promoting an austerity program launched by her predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who put the Mexican presidential plane up for sale in 2023.
She traveled with a large delegation of ministers to Shenzhen.
China has become particularly sensitive to the idea of corruption and wasteful public spending in recent years amid high-profile and long-running anti-corruption measures launched by President Xi Jinping, seemingly at least partly as damage-limitation efforts following a series of scandals.
Canada's Carney, Mexico's Sheinbaum hold talks with Trump
The leaders of Canada and Mexico have both reported on separate meetings with the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit, amid difficult trade talks with the main economic power in the Americas.
"The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada's languages, culture, and sovereignty," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office said. "They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact."
Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum published a photo of her "very good meeting with President Donald Trump and his team" online, saying "we continue to make progress on our shared agenda."
Trump, Putin shake hands in first face-to-face encounter since Alaska summit
The presidents of the US and Russia have shaken hands in their first in-person meeting since August 2025, when Putin was invited to Alaska for talks primarily concerning Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shook hands in the presence of host Xi Jinping ahead of the leaders' welcome banquet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
The encounter follows a rare sign of progress in the US-led efforts to broker an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, a conflict Trump repeatedly claimed he would settle in "a day" if reelected.
The two are expected to have a private meeting on Thursday.
Talks took place last week in Abu Dhabi involving Russia, Ukraine and European representatives, with Trump's negotiating team subsequently traveling to the Kremlin for a meeting with Putin and other Russian officials.
WATCH: Xi greets Trump at the airport
Trump's arrival was highly choreographed: He descended from Air Force One and stood on a red carpet lined with people waving colorful pom poms. Trump and Xi hugged before shaking hands.
Potential Trump talks touted in Shenzhen, even with Kim Jong Un
The White House, other countries and Donald Trump himself have all listed possible or probable bilateral or multilateral talks involving the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, beyond Thursday's highly-anticipated US-China-Russia meeting.
Some of the more notable examples are listed here:
- Kremlin officials said they expected a meeting between just Trump and Putin, but not one long or substantial enough for fully-fledged bilateral negotiations
- The White House said Trump would hold two separate meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum prior to the official APEC greeting ceremony
- While in Manila, Trump himself floated the possibility of a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un, but without voicing a solid intent
- China said it had no information on a potential Trump-Kim meeting
- Meanwhile, North Korean state media — which typically operates behind the global news cycle — has only released images of Kim visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu, making no mention of possible Shenzhen travel plans
Xi tells Trump China seeks 'strategically stable relationship'
Chinese news agency Xinhua has reported the first comments from Xi Jinping to Donald Trump following his arrival.
"I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape," Xi told Trump.
He said the talks would take place "with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations — one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity."
Despite Trump and Xi's efforts to regularly hold friendly face-to-face talks in recent months, the US and China are nevertheless embroiled in difficult trade negotiations as the two superpowers try to reconcile competing interests on various issues.
The two sides have been periodically extending a temporary tariff truce designed to bridge the gap until they can reach a more permanent agreement, which for now has proven elusive. China announced the most recent extension earlier this month, to run until early January.
Nvidia stops shipping US-approved chips to China
The interim CEO of US chip giant Nvidia says the company is not currently shipping Hopper-generation data center products to China.
These are some of the most advanced Nvidia products licensed for export by the US government; the company had sold such goods worth $2.4 billion (roughly €2.2 billion) in the previous quarter, Colette Kress said.
Kress replaced Jensen Huang following his resignation last week and amid the scandal over alleged Chinese attempts both to gain intelligence on the company's CEO and to circumvent import restrictions.
"Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said.
She did not specify why such deliveries had currently stopped or say whether the step would be permanent.
Huang was influential in persuading Donald Trump to allow sales of H200 Hopper processors used to train and run advanced AI models to China, reversing export controls the US had imposed in 2022 under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
China has called the allegations of espionage targeting Nvidia unfounded and threatened to respond in kind if restrictions on trade follow as a result of the fallout from Huang's resignation.
Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport ahead of summit
US President Donald Trump has landed at Shenzhen Airport on Air Force One and disembarked.
He left Manila in the Philippines a few hours earlier.
Trump will be attending the APEC summit but is also expected to take part in a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport on Wednesday, mirroring a gesture Trump had recently extended during the Chinese leader's state visit to the US in September.
Japan's Sanae Takaichi on first China trip since becoming PM
Sanae Takaichi arrived in China for the APEC summit, which is also her first official visit to the country as Japanese prime minister.
Takaichi's moves to bolster Japan's military and comments last year on Taiwan have upset Beijing and severely affected bilateral ties.
In particular, Takaichi's suggestion that Tokyo could intervene militarily if Beijing sought to forcibly take Taiwan — which China considers its territory — led to friction between the regional rivals with a troubled 20th century history and ongoing territorial disputes.
China imposed trade restrictions and urged citizens not to travel to Japan, which had become an increasingly popular tourist destination. Traffic is down by roughly half this year as a result.
A formal one-on-one meeting between Takaichi and China's Xi Jinping is considered highly unlikely, but Japan's NHK public broadcaster did report that Xi would "personally greet her" before Wednesday's banquet.
IN DEPTH: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
Read DW's full report on what Trump, Xi and Putin are hoping to extract from the trilateral talks.
Canada, China taking steps to widen access for financial firms, says Carney
Canada and China are moving to give each other's financial firms greater access to their markets, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said during a speech at the APEC summit.
"When our businesses depend on too few currencies or single payment channels, disruption, when it comes, can spread quickly," he said, adding that China and Canada had renewed the currency swap arrangement between their central banks and were issuing each other's currencies.
Carney's comments came a day after he and President Xi held talks in Shenzhen to produce deals to further reduce tariffs. Ottawa is re-engaging with China after years of strained relations as it looks to reduce its reliance on the US.
Trump says US concludes 'very big trade deal' with Philippines
President Trump on Wednesday said that the US has just concluded a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines, albeit without providing details. Manila has not yet confirmed any agreement.
"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries," Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace.
"We were very happy with that, and we didn't know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it's a magnificent deal for both," he said.
Trade negotiations were not listed in the schedules provided by Washington or Manila.
The Philippines' ambassador to the US, Jose Manuel Romualdez said, "The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements."
However, Romualdez told Reuters that nothing had been signed.

noticias.titulo: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
noticias.resumen: In a statement celebrating the historic drop in drug deaths, the White House pointed to successes since President Trump took office. In fact, the biggest progress happened under the Biden administration.
noticias.texto:
As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.
But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.
"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.
Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.
What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.
"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."
Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths
According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.
Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.
"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.
Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.
Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.
The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.
Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.
White House on Biden role in declines
NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.
"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.
Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."
According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.
"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.
But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.
"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."
Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.
Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.
The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.
"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

noticias.titulo: Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story
noticias.resumen: On NPR's Morning Edition , fashion designer Karl Kani talks about his new memoir, dressing some of hip-hop's biggest stars and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.
noticias.texto:
Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story
Hip-hop streetwear pioneer Karl Kani shares how he built his brand in new memoir
Fashion designer Karl Kani believes hip-hop needed its own clothing brand, one that reflected the music, culture and style of the artists who were changing fashion in the 1990s.
"Hip-hop needed the clothing brand that fit that look, who was from the culture," Kani told NPR's A Martínez on Morning Edition. "And I felt like the marriage between Kani and hip-hop was, like, heaven-sent."
Kani, born Carl Williams, started designing clothing in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He was inspired by watching his father, a Haitian tailor, make matching linen suits to sell around the neighborhood.
At the time, hip-hop artists were already wearing names like Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein. But they weren't necessarily wearing the clothes as their designers intended. They favored oversized fits, mixed colors and created looks of their own.
Kani understood the appeal. He began making clothes as a self-taught designer in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He helped turn that emerging streetwear style into a brand worn by some of hip-hop's biggest stars, including Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah and The Notorious B.I.G.
But the designer's ambitions extended beyond dressing famous musicians. He wanted to build an international fashion business that could last.
In his new memoir, Karl Kani: A Life By Design, Kani reflects on the creative instincts and business decisions that helped his brand survive long after the decade that made it famous.
Even his name reflects his ambitions. Kani, pronounced like "Can I?," came from the doubts he faced while building his business.
"Can I really come from the inner city and build a clothing brand?" he recalled asking himself. "I didn't know the answer to that question, but I knew if I call myself Kani, then every day I have to answer that question. Yes, I can."
After more than three decades in fashion, Kani also has some thoughts about what hasn't aged quite so gracefully: men in skinny jeans.
"I feel like a lot of guys kind of messed up when the skinny jeans phase came in," he said.
His advice? "Keep it simple, keep it slick and all black. You can never go wrong in all black."
In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Kani discusses his new memoir, the rise of his streetwear empire, hip-hop's influence on fashion and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

noticias.titulo: Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
noticias.resumen: Flying somewhere for Thanksgiving or the holidays? Travel insiders explain what to do if your flight gets canceled or delayed — so you can quickly get to your destination.
noticias.texto:
Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025.
This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November.
If you plan on being one of those travelers in the coming days, make sure you know what to do in case your flight suddenly gets delayed or canceled.
Life Kit
Listen to an audio version of this story here
Air travel has gotten notably worse over the past decade. In 2025, cancellations and delays surged, creating the worst on-time performance for airlines in the United States since 2014, according to a 2026 report by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, a consumer advocacy group.
So, with holiday schlepping season kicking off this week, what's a weary traveler to do? Ahead, travel experts explain how to make rebooking flights less painful. Because what's worse than a canceled holiday flight is missing the holiday altogether.
Multitask! While standing in line, rebook your flight online
Most people react to a cancellation by heading straight to the nearest customer service desk and queuing up to rebook their flight. The problem with that approach? Everyone else on your flight is doing that too.
"You have 300 people getting off the plane. There's maybe one, two people trying to help everyone. That clearly is the least efficient way," says travel reporter Chris Dong.
While standing in line, open up the airline app and rebook yourself, he says. There's often a seamless way to get it done, no customer service conversation necessary. During the holiday rush, when hundreds of other passengers may be trying to rebook at the same time, getting a head start on the airline's app can make an especially big difference.
See if an agent can help you at the airport lounge
If you have a travel credit card that gives you lounge access, head there to get one-on-one customer service. "Lounge agents are much more inclined to help you and are usually not as short-staffed," Dong says. "That can get you help quickly."
If you don't already have lounge access, see if you can purchase a day pass on-site. It may be well worth it depending on your flight cost and timeline.
Know what you're entitled to from the airline
All ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they don't accept whatever the airline is offering, such as a later flight and/or travel vouchers or vouchers for hotels or meals. However, most airlines in the U.S. aren't required to compensate you for delays or cancellations unless it's the airline's fault (think maintenance issues or staffing problems).
To find out what you're entitled to, check the Department of Transportation's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard. Many major airlines have committed to giving passengers cost-free rebooking, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, hotel transportation and more.
Once you know what your airline offers, say, a hotel, you can rest easy about what to do that night — and focus on rebooking for the next day.
Check what your travel insurance covers
Once you know what your airline will cover, check what your travel insurance will cover. Many credit cards include some travel insurance coverage, which can provide everything from trip cancellation to luggage insurance to any medical needs that might arise en route.
When rebooking, choose a flight earlier in the day
If you have flight time options when rebooking or flexibility in your travel schedule, choose the early-morning flight. They're your best bet to avoid delays or cancellations, Dong says.
If you're on the first flight out, there's little chance you'll have to wait for that aircraft coming in from another city because it's likely been sitting at the airport overnight.
This is especially worth considering during the holidays, when a single disruption can have a domino effect on subsequent flights. An early departure gives you more opportunities to get rebooked on another flight that same day if something goes wrong — because nobody wants to miss that family Thanksgiving dinner!
If you want refunds or flight credits, be nice to your customer service rep
If the airline significantly delayed, significantly changed (see DOT website for details) or cancelled the flight and you originally booked your ticket directly with your airline, getting your money back should be no problem, even if the ticket is nonrefundable. But if you booked through a third party such as a travel agent or travel website, you'll have to go through them.
Remember that customer service representatives are likely dealing with hundreds of frustrated passengers during the holiday rush. Being patient and polite won't guarantee an exception, but it certainly won't hurt your chances, suggests Eulanda Osagiede, director of operations at Black Travel Alliance and chief operations officer at Black Travel Summit.
The best approach, she says, is to be "very nice, very friendly" with the customer service representative on the phone. So don't start yelling at them. Treating reps like the human beings they are can make all the difference.
Have a backup plan before you leave home
When you're traveling for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas, a delay doesn't just mean missing a few hours of vacation. It could mean missing the big family gathering or a favorite kiddo's holiday performance.
So before you leave, take a few minutes to research alternative routes to your destination. Are there other airports nearby? Could you drive part of the way? Are there trains or buses that could get you there if your flight falls through?
It's also worth saving your airline's customer service number, downloading its app, and keeping your confirmation numbers somewhere accessible offline. If you're traveling with kids, pack enough snacks, medications, entertainment and other essentials to get through an unexpected overnight stay.
You can't plan for every possible disruption, but you can make sure you're not starting from scratch when one happens.
This story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter. Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit.

noticias.titulo: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
noticias.resumen: The New York Democrat moved a step closer to becoming the first Black lawmaker in U.S. history to serve in the job, after House Democrats voted overwhelmingly to support him.
noticias.texto:
Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.
Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.
"Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.
Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.
"Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.
The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.
Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.
It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.
While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.
He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.
Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.
"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."
Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York; New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.
After the vote, Jeffries told reporters "the results of today's election speak for themselves."
"We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism — not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people."
Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.
Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.
Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.
Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.
Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.

noticias.titulo: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
noticias.resumen: Among the recipients of letters from Robert Garcia, incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, are Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Jared Kushner and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
noticias.texto:
House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.
"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."
The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.
The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.
In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
Here's a closer look at the letters Garcia sent: 
- Donald Trump Jr. — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, and the financing of his wedding after-party by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin. President Trump later told reporters the costs for the wedding celebration was later paid back. "You have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father's presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people," the letter reads.
- Eric Trump — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture. "Oversight Democrats have found that your roles as a co-founder of World Liberty Financial and a key player in the Trump family's pay-to-play schemes have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years," said the letter. 
- Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law — allegations of conflicts of interest, his investment firm Affinity Partners, and using his government role to enrich himself and his companies. "Directly or indirectly, you have received billions of dollars in fees and investments with particularly troubling ties to Middle East states where you also have a government role," the letter reads. "This raises urgent questions about transparency, conflicts of interest, and the abuse of what appears to clearly be a government position—with influence over war, peace, and nuclear proliferation as well as direct access to President Trump—for personal profit." 
- Former Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle. She was previously engaged to Trump Jr., and was contacted by Garcia over allegations of pay-to-play schemes. "As ambassador, you appear to have been intent on leveraging your position to cash-in," said the letter. 
- Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend — construction and donations for the White House ballroom, financed in part via private donations to the Trust. 
- White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — allegations of abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement under his direction. "Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the 'linchpin' and 'architect' of the Trump Administration's most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties," reads the letter. "We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses."
- Former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski — allegations of abuse of DHS funds, corruption and self-dealing. 
- Vice President J.D. Vance — allegations of secret meetings inside the White House Situation Room about the administration's handling of the Epstein files. "Reportedly, you were even the first to suggest that Ghislaine Maxwell be interviewed in hopes of using her testimony to distance President Trump from Epstein, despite President Trump's well-documented decades-long friendship with the notorious abuser and sex-trafficker," the letter reads. "These discussions appear to be directly linked to an apparent quid pro quo in which Maxwell was moved to a minimum-security prison camp after she made favorable statements about President Trump in a highly unusual prison interview conducted by then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche."
-  Former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — allegations of secret White House meetings surrounding the Epstein investigation. "Reporting describes you as refusing to release documents concerning allegations against President Trump to the public," the letter said. 
- Attorney General Todd Blanche — allegations of a cover-up of the Epstein files, failure to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and the decision to transfer Maxwell to a minimum-security prison. "You have refused to cooperate with our investigation, or to fulfill your legal responsibilities to be transparent with the Committee and the American people," the letter said. "This obstruction is even more concerning given your direct involvement in the broader cover-up, as well as your history as President Trump's personal attorney."
- Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Federal Prison Camp Bryan Warden Tanisha Hall — regarding Maxwell's transfer to a minimum-security prison camp days after she was questioned about Trump and his relationship to Epstein. "Committee Democrats will not tolerate the Administration's refusal to respond to our inquiries and, in the future, will not hesitate to compel information from individuals enabling the cover-up of Maxwell's and Epstein's crimes," the letter said.

noticias.titulo: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
noticias.resumen: After dismantling the United States Agency for International Development, the Trump administration is restarting foreign aid. In Zambia and Zimbabwe, there are different approaches but similar worries.
noticias.texto:
The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
This is a story that starts with a remarkable success story. However, the ending has become a cliff hanger — with potentially grave consequences.
The success is clearcut and remarkable: Both Zambia and Zimbabwe are beating back devastating HIV/AIDS epidemics. These neighboring countries in southern Africa are on the cusp of controlling the virus.
Between 2000 and 2025, new infections dropped by 76% in Zambia and 80% in Zimbabwe. In both countries, more than 95% of infected individuals are identified and 95% of them are on treatment, according to data from the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.
This progress is thanks, in large part, to billions of dollars in U.S. aid over the past two decades.
However, President Trump's new global health strategy is scrambling the landscape. After dismantling without warning the U.S. Agency for International Development in 2025, the administration is now hammering out government-to-government aid agreements as a new framework for how aid is provided.
That process leaves these two countries on very different paths and heading toward uncharted territory.
Just last month Zambian and U.S. officials signed an agreement — albeit for far less annual U.S. health aid than the country received in the past. Zimbabwe, in contrast, lost all U.S. health aid this fall after negotiations collapsed. To get an on-the-ground assessment of what has happened and what the future may hold, NPR interviewed a health worker in each country with experience in the HIV/AIDS world.
Zambia's aid agreement
When the aid agreement was announced on ZNBC — Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation on October 8 — it was branded as "a new chapter" in which the U.S. aid dollars flow primarily through the government and aims to build up the national health system.
The negotiations behind the aid agreement were secretive and became contentious, explains Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP "There was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," Russell told NPR. Her organization helped expose this situation. Ultimately, the discussion about mineral rights was decoupled from the health agreement.
"I felt a bit relieved," says the Zambian health worker. But, with the aid agreement finally signed, she says, "the work now begins."
The health worker asked NPR not to use her name because she helped make public that mineral rights were in play and fears government retribution. She worries the Zambian government is ill equipped to face down the obstacles of the HIV/AIDS epidemic.
For example, homosexuality is illegal in Zambia. "Because [people are] scared of being arrested when they go to the public health facility, they would rather just stay home and face the consequences of their illness," she says, adding that such a decision not only leaves them without treatment it also lets the virus spread further via unprotected sexual relations, drug activity and other routes.
Under the previous system, huge amounts of U.S. aid went through international and local non-governmental groups who have staff specially trained to reach those vulnerable populations. This new agreement sidelines those groups and instead aims to build up the government's health systems rather than a parallel system, according to the U.S. strategy.
The Zambian health worker is also concerned the country could trumpet success in addressing HIV/AIDS but that thorough outreach and treatment records won't be kept and the right infrastructure may not be in place. For instance, she says, the government may say: " 'We've employed 5,000 community health workers!' "
But, she asks: "What is the quality? What capacity do they have? Who will they be serving? Which district? "
This health worker says many in the medical field have not received answers about what the future health systems will look like.
"It feels like a big mess, honestly. It's scary," she says, "It feels like doing it right is not the priority, but people's lives are at risk."
The Zambian Ministry of Health did not respond to requests for comment. But in the press conference announcing the agreement, Health minister Roma Chilengi said the department plans to recruit up to 40,000 health care workers, including 15,000 front line workers such as doctors, nurses, midwives, scientists, pharmacists, as well as community health workers.
However apprehensive this health worker is, she says that what's happening in Zambia is still better than the situation in neighboring Zimbabwe.
Zimbabwe's agreement collapses
In February, negotiations over the future of health aid between U.S. and Zimbabwean officials fell apart.
There was plenty of fingerpointing. Zimbabwean officials said the proposed agreement was lopsided. For example, Zimbabwe would have been obligated to provide data and biological samples of pathogens for research but would not have been guaranteed access to any treatments that result from that information. The U.S. Embassy in Zimbabwe said in a press release that the breakdown was regrettable. Whatever the reason, the result was clear. The country went from receiving well over $100 million in U.S. health aid each year to having none.
The health worker in Zimbabwe is baffled by this: "The U.S. put [in] 20 years of support — 20 years of support! — that's a huge investment which I think you cannot just throw away?" But he says that's what he's seeing.
This health worker also asked NPR not to use his name because he fears government retribution for speaking out. Without aid, he says, in his community, people's HIV medications are dwindling. "Within a period of six months or so, you will start to see a very huge impact," he predicts.
But he's concerned the world may never know the real impact. The U.S has had the best data collection and monitoring system for tracking and understanding the HIV epidemic and the response. Going forward the data coming out of Zimbabwe will be hard to verify or trust, he says. "We may not even know…if it's true or not."
The Ministry of Health and Child Care in Zimbabwe did not respond to NPR's requests for comment but this past summer, Zimbabwe's health minister, Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, pledged to expand the health workforce and infrastructure.
In a statement to NPR about the status of aid to the two countries, the U.S. State Department did not address the specific concerns of the health workers but said it's committed to working "with partner governments to define and advance shared global health priorities."
A subdued domestic response
As for public reaction in the two countries? It's been muted, the health workers say.
Both say that in their communities people are mad but that a public outcry has been muted because they fear reprisal from their governments. Russell, of Health GAP, echoed this experience saying many people who she works with are afraid to speak publicly: "The problem is retaliation" because they lived under authoritarian regimes.
"People are trying to not lose more than they've already lost," the health worker in Zambia says. "So even the anger is there, the frustrations are there, but you do not see this very publicly."
Similarly, the health worker in Zimbabwe says, "you can be mad, you can be angry, you can be whatever. But if you talk, you know the consequences of what will happen to you."
Public outcry or not, the global health world will be carefully observing how the next stage unfolds for these two countries.
Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at the research organization KFF, says her team is scrutinizing all the information it can get about the agreement and implementation of the aid agreement in Zambia. And Zimbabwe "is an important one to watch," she says. "It's made a lot of progress, heavily relying on the U.S." — and now the future is uncertain.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

noticias.titulo: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
noticias.resumen: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has won one of the U.S.' most watched Senate races. And, Nvidia's board says it doesn't plan to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang despite pressure from his allies.
noticias.texto:
Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
Trump-Xi-Putin Meeting, Nvidia Board Rejects Haung's Return, Computer System Outages
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Her victory gives Democrats 56 senators in the upcoming Congress. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola secured a majority of first-place votes, eliminating the need for ranked-choice calculations. Her win flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. The race's final days were tumultuous due to allegations that Peltola's team tried to recruit another candidate to the race to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement.
Trump has arrived in the Southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he is set to meet with China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday. This will mark the third time these two leaders have met this year. They are expected to discuss trade, investment and tariffs, which are currently on hold.
- 🎧 The meeting is about establishing a tone, as the U.S. and China have agreed to have constructive strategic stability, NPR's Jennifer Pak tells Up First. The two leaders will later be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting. The trio may discuss a peace deal for Russia's war in Ukraine, but China says that Europe must be included. Pak says China wants to show that a world leader won't make decisions without input from smaller countries. This is especially significant, Pak says, because these meetings take place on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), where many smaller nations seek a voice in regional matters.
Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in an earnings call yesterday that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct," according to Jones. Huang acknowledged he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency. The board unanimously accepted his resignation. Earlier yesterday, Huang said he would return as CEO if the board permitted it and agreed to testify before Congress regarding national security issues surrounding the company.
- 🎧 NPR's John Ruwitch said that Jones clearly wanted to dispel rumors, and showed support for interim CEO Colette Kress. He said she "has been at the center of the company's extraordinary growth." Kress also participated in the call, maintaining a business-as-usual demeanor, Ruwitch says. Nvidia posted revenue exceeding $115 billion for the quarter, which isn't surprising, as the numbers were secured before Huang's recent departure. Tech analyst Gaurav Gupta from Gartner tells Ruwitch that any impact from new leadership won't be reflected in the numbers for several months. Jones said the board would try to decide on a permanent CEO as soon as possible without rushing the decision.
Major organizations have been experiencing widespread crashes of computer and online systems. Apple reported significant outages yesterday, and the U.S. National Security Agency also experienced a breakdown. As of this morning, no major disruptions seem to be occurring. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that these incidents are related to one another or involve a malign actor or cybercriminal.
- 🎧 Cyber experts tell NPR's Greg Myre that artificial intelligence is uncovering previously undetected software flaws at an unprecedented pace. Companies are racing to patch or upgrade to address these vulnerabilities, but working under tight deadlines often leads to mistakes. As many systems undergo upgrades, people should anticipate disruptions along the way, Myre says. However, the optimistic perspective is that computer networks are expected to become more robust and resilient within the next year or two due to the improvements.
Deep dive
In recent years, highly concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) have emerged online and at smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. These products, available as tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolates, contain one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom. Unlike kratom leaf products, 7-OH acts more like an opioid in the human brain. Some people use kratom to maintain long-term recovery from opioid addiction. Others say it helps them feel energized or focused. Users of 7-OH and kratom can show signs of addiction, and unclear product labeling makes it hard to determine the quantities consumed. Over the past decade, the U.S. government has tried to restrict these products, but public opposition has kept them legal. Recently, this situation has started to change.
- ➡️ In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration restricted the manufacture and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids from 7-OH and other related compounds. They were classified under the Controlled Substances Act alongside drugs like heroin and LSD.
- ➡️ Kratom advocates were concerned that new rules would impact products with "trace amounts" of the opioid MGPI. The American Kratom Association filed a federal lawsuit against the DEA on Aug. 26, seeking to keep natural kratom products with MGPI legal.
- ➡️ On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI, leading the DEA to revise its stance to focus on restricting products with higher concentrations of these substances.
- ➡️ Opponents of the restriction argue that the products helped them avoid traditional opioids. Some point to the decrease in opioid deaths in the U.S.
- ➡️ The National Institute on Drug Abuse says that early studies indicate kratom and its compounds deserve more exploration as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder.
Real Talk With a Doc
Family physician Mara Gordon answers reader health questions monthly for NPR's special series Real Talk with a Doc. Send in your question to thrive@npr.org.
Artificial intelligence scribes help doctors take notes in various settings, from gynecologist visits to emergency rooms. Dr. Gordon says the technology saves time and allows her to focus entirely on her patients without the distraction of multitasking. But she also understands why patients might feel uneasy about new technology, and says she shares their concerns about privacy. Here's what Dr. Gordon says you should know about AI scribes:
- 🩺 The scribe uses "automatic speech recognition" technology to record the conversation between the doctor and the patient. After the visit, the recording is transcribed and turned into a medical note of the exam's findings and the doctor's decisions.
- 🩺 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance is crucial for AI scribe services to ensure they protect patient privacy. Software companies must safeguard data by encrypting it, controlling access and implementing systems to prevent data breaches. Most companies delete recorded conversations after a specified period.
- 🩺 AI scribes can make mistakes, which is why doctors must review AI-generated notes before signing them and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software requires doctors to sign a user agreement, making them liable for all content in the medical record.
- 🩺Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates have raised concerns that this could widen health disparities.
- 🩺 You can always opt out of using an AI scribe during your doctor's visit. But opting out of AI in medicine more broadly could be tricky.
3 things to know before you go
- NPR's Breakfast Around the World series is spotlighting Lebanon's man'ouché, a beloved breakfast flatbread. It's a U.N.-certified part of intangible cultural heritage, with a unique twist crafted by generations of Lebanese.
- The Pan American Health Organization announced yesterday that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. It is now considered endemic because a strain has persisted in the country for more than a year.
- The oldest survivor of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Freeman Johnson, died this weekend at his Cape Cod home at the age of 106.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

noticias.titulo: Faster electrification is essential for Europe to escape fossil fuel shocks, Jørgensen warns
noticias.resumen: Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said the latest EU agreement to accelerate permitting procedures is a step forward for clean power and infrastructure to revamp the bloc's obsolete power grid and boost electrification — even if financing the power grid remains yet another obstacle.
noticias.texto:
Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said the latest EU agreement to accelerate permitting procedures is a step forward for clean power and infrastructure to revamp the bloc's obsolete power grid and boost electrification — even if financing the power grid remains yet another obstacle.
Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen welcomed the recent deal struck by EU lawmakers on permits for energy infrastructure and clean power, describing it as a major win towards integrating more renewable electricity into Europe's energy system and allowing consumers to switch from gas and oil to electricity.
Speaking to Euronews' Europe Tonight, Jørgensen explained that getting those permits can take five years or even a decade, making lengthy approval processes one of the biggest hurdles to electrification.
The deal struck on Wednesday between the EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the European Council, seeks to bring those permitsdown to just six months for most projects, a significant push intended to unlock investment and help electricity networks keep pace with growing demand.
"This is about making sure that we have the infrastructure to actually electrify our societies, to get the renewable energy into our systems so that we can drive our cars on electricity, we can have heat pumps and so forth," Jørgensen said.
Critics argue that faster permits do not automatically mean cheaper electricity, citing the lack of investment in infrastructure and the fact that network expansion will still have to be paid for.
EU countries are currently discussing the proposal, which has raised some divergences. Sweden pushed back hard, arguing Brussels would redirect money paid by Swedish power consumers and grid operators to fund electricity grids elsewhere in Europe instead of benefiting Stockholm.
Hailing electrification as a new climate doctrine, the Commissioner argued that expanding renewables, improving energy efficiency and connecting national electricity markets would help bring down energy costs.
"The main way of bringing down prices is to deploy more renewables, because renewables are cheaper than the fossil alternative," he said.
Europe has saved more than €30 billion annually through cross-border electricity connections, Jørgensen added, arguing that the potential for further savings remains much greater.
MEP Niels Fuglsang (S&D/Denmark), leading the file in the Parliament, described the deal to speed up the granting of permits as a "very important step".
The Danish lawmaker said the agreement will allow for faster rollout of renewables and grid infrastructure, to the benefit of our citizens, to mitigate climate change and to boost the EU's competitiveness.
A difficult winter exposes Europe's fossil fuel vulnerability
Despite the celebrations in Brussels over the agreement on permits, the Commission's longer-term electrification strategy is unfolding against an immediate energy security challenge. The deal struck on Wednesday won't alleviate energy prices in the short term.
With tensions in the Middle East threatening supplies and markets, the energy Commissioner warned that Europeans should not expect energy prices to return quickly to normal, even if the geopolitical situation stabilises.
"We don't even know if they will come down. What we do know is that it's a very unstable winter that we are going into (...) We also know that even if there's a normalisation of the situation, it'll take months for the prices to normalise," Jørgensen added.
The warning suggests Brussels is preparing for another winter in which households and businesses could face sustained pressure from energy costs, reinforcing the political argument for reducing dependence on imported oil and gas.
The Commissioner urged consumers to switch from gas and oil boilers to heat pumps, replace combustion-engine cars with electric vehicles and improve home insulation.
"We probably have to prepare, or not probably. We unfortunately, for sure, have to prepare for a difficult winter," Jørgensen said.

noticias.titulo: Euronews Verify: Can the EU close Russia's sanctions loopholes?
noticias.resumen: Another batch of EU sanctions targeting Russian banks, oil refineries and Russia's "shadow fleet" is expected later this month. But are sanctions actually effective against Moscow?
noticias.texto:
Another batch of EU sanctions targeting Russian banks, oil refineries and Russia's "shadow fleet" is expected later this month. But are sanctions actually effective against Moscow?
The EU's foreign ministers have approved another sanctions package targeting Russian banks, oil refineries, and its "shadow fleet".
This latest batch of sanctions targets almost 150 additional individuals and entities, while the EU's 22nd economic sanctions package is expected later this month.
The EU has slapped sanctions on around 4,600 individuals and entities and frozen more than €28 billion in private assets since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
What sanctions are actually effective against Moscow?
Sanctions appear to be more effective against Russia than others.
Analysts say that oil import bans and export controls on Western tech hit the country hardest, because they deliver a blow to its economy and its ability to make sophisticated military equipment.
However, Russia can exploit trade loopholes and use its so-called illicit "shadow fleet" to export oil.
"If you are somebody who is inside Russia and who wants to get the sanctioned goods, it's not that difficult. A lot of this comes through third countries like Kazakhstan, Turkey, Armenia, Hong Kong and so on. And you don't even have to hide them, because on the Russian side of the border it's legal," Konstantin Egorov, associate professor of economics at the University of Antwerp, told Euronews Verify.
Who is really behind Europe's airline bomb scares?
Today's episode also focuses on the latest bomb threats.
In just five days, more than 50 flights across Europe were caught up in a wave of bomb threats.
Aircraft were diverted, fighter jets were scrambled, and passengers faced lengthy delays, but searches of the plane found no explosives.
"Unfortunately, there's very little hard evidence that it's sort of directly linked to Russia. We've got speculation in popular reporting, including some, you know, alleged reports from anonymous security officials close to the investigation," said Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at Osprey Flight Solutions.
"But what I think we can say is that it's consistent with the operational intentions and the sort of tactics we've seen from Russia previously."
What could these bomb threats achieve?
This kind of disruption affects different fronts.
The aim is to impose economic costs and undermine the political order of the countries affected.
"I think it does fit into a wider pattern. We can see that all kinds of infrastructure are being targeted," said Guntram Wolff, senior fellow at Bruegel.
"But more importantly, it's really about the political cost that comes with it. It is part of an information campaign, part of a political campaign against the political system, against the existing political order. And it really aims at destabilising our countries."

In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

noticias.titulo: French broadcaster faces backlash after revealing feminist guest's marriage live on air
noticias.resumen: An activist criticised a French public broadcaster after a presenter revealed her marriage to a senior TV executive, sparking controversy over transparency rules and political reactions.
noticias.texto:
An activist criticised a French public broadcaster after a presenter revealed her marriage to a senior TV executive, sparking controversy over transparency rules and political reactions.
French public broadcaster franceinfo has faced criticism after a presenter revealed feminist activist Anne-Cécile Mailfert's marriage to a senior television executive during a live broadcast on Monday.
Before she could speak, the presenter introduced her as the wife of the number two at public television giant France Télévisions.
Visibly outraged, Mailfert responded, "So what?", calling the disclosure "absolutely scandalous". She then challenged a male journalist on the panel, asking, "Who is your partner?"
Transparency rules spark controversy
The incident followed the introduction of new transparency guidelines aimed at preventing conflicts of interest within France's public broadcasters.
While franceinfo initially defended the disclosure as consistent with the rules, it later acknowledged that Mailfert should have been informed beforehand.
Mailfert, who was heard shouting as she left the studio, addressed the incident on Instagram on Tuesday, saying it had deeply affected her.
"Yesterday, I experienced something that hurt me deeply," she wrote.
The activist insisted that she is "deeply committed" to the principles of "professional ethics, transparency, and integrity".
"However, these principles must address a genuine risk of a conflict of interest - one that is clearly defined - and the individuals involved must be informed."
Yannick Letranchant, franceinfo's head of ethics and transparency, acknowledged the challenge of balancing "necessary transparency" and the risk of "relegating an individual" to the status of being the partner of someone else.
Political reactions ahead of French presidential election
The controversy has prompted reactions from across France's political spectrum, including hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon but also parliament speaker Yael Braun-Pivet.
"A woman holds her own convictions, fights her own battles, and speaks for herself. This should be a given in 2026," Braun-Pivet said.
The dispute comes ahead of France's presidential election next year, as France Télévisions faces continued scrutiny over its political impartiality.
The public broadcaster has repeatedly been accused of left-wing bias by the far right, while also facing criticism from Mélenchon's hard-left movement.

noticias.titulo: No heating or AC needed in France's first housing of its kind
noticias.resumen: French real estate company Nexity presented the first apartment building of its kind on Tuesday, which is designed to maintain an interior temperature between 20 °C and 26 °C without heating or air conditioning.
noticias.texto:
French real estate company Nexity presented the first apartment building of its kind on Tuesday, which is designed to maintain an interior temperature between 20 °C and 26 °C without heating or air conditioning.
Almost brutalist in style, this new white and cubic building is the first of its kind in France. Its cutting-edge design allows it to regulate its interior temperature without using heaters or air conditioning.
In Lyon, French real estate company Nexity and Austrian architectural firm Baumschlager Eberle presented on Tuesday their new seven-story-high project of 23 housing units in the ever-transforming Confluence neighbourhood.
No need for air conditioning in the summer or heating in the winter; that's the realtor's promise. The building is designed to maintain an interior temperature of 20 to 22°C in the winter and 26 to 28°C during heatwaves.
An Austrian concept
Seeking a response to the energy and climate crisis, Austrian architect Dietmar Eberle designed a building capable of letting sunlight in to retain the heat, called "22-26" in reference to the interior temperature it should maintain.
This cutting-edge technology that has yet to prove its effectiveness, is based on the building material's inertia.
"These play a major role and have been selected for a common characteristic: their ability to store and release energy," Anne Speicher, director of the Baumschlager Eberle agency, told online French media Vert.
"An insulating envelope, constructed from Monomur bricks (a hollow-core terracotta structure), concrete and a lime render, helps to retain heat or coolness inside homes," reports the French media.
The heat is "retained" by the walls and floors that are twice as thick as France's average, 61 centimetres compared to around 30 in average.
Two layers of hollow bricks interspersed with glass wool insulation give the building a quite massive appearance while also protecting it from direct sunlight thanks to large recesses.
The concept also relies on innovative construction planning and on an automatic slat system controlled by multiple sensors.
Wooden slats installed in each housing unit automatically open and close to air out the apartment regarding its "temperature, humidity, air quality and weather," explains Nexity in a press release.
"Residents can also monitor them themselves. Auxiliary heaters, which are required by regulation, only turn on during extreme weather events or following a prolonged period when the property has been unoccupied."
Residents act as heaters
The greatly insulated apartments retain the heat produced by the residents' bodies, "we are the heaters of the home — us and what we do," Cédric Hatat, Programme Manager at Nexity Auvergne Bourgogne told French broadcaster BFM Business.
The heat produced by cooking, showering or electric appliances will also be trapped in the apartments, reducing energy bills by 80%, according to Nexity's CEO Véronique Bédague. This would save every resident €380 a year for a three-room apartment.
Each apartment is still equipped with heaters and a double-flow mechanical ventilation system, as required by French law. The realtor claims this has raised the construction cost by 15% to connect the building to the city's heating system.
This technology is also supposed to cut energy consumption associated with thermal comfort by 73%, reducing carbon emissions by 65% over 50 years.
High construction cost
The Austrian agency has already built two of these "22-26" type buildings in Switzerland and Germany, but it's the first one in France.
Its reproducibility is uncertain because of high construction costs, "this project cannot be replicated on a large scale," elected ecologist metropolitan councillor at the Métropole de Lyon, Renaud Payre, told Vert.
"The cost of materials, the highly sophisticated home automation system on which it is based… The 22-26 is quite simply too complex to establish itself as a standard model for construction."
"It is designed to serve as a showcase for sustainable housing and to encourage the development of local supply chains," Payre told Vert.
The ecologist councillor claims that housing renovation remains the best way to improve apartments' energy consumption.
"Of course, you can pick up a few techniques or ideas here and there, but as things stand, you cannot turn a draughty building into an energy-efficient one using state-of-the-art, very expensive home automation systems," Payre told Vert.
Other cities have been won over by the concept; the building's realtor, Nexity, plans to complete the construction of a similar 22-26 project in La Garenne-Colombes, near Paris, in 2028. This other test project building that will host 80 housing units is set to gauge the effectiveness of this concept.

noticias.titulo: Europe Tonight: EU proposes €45bn Ukraine loan as Trump, Xi and Putin meet
noticias.resumen: Ursula von der Leyen unveils a new joint-debt package for Kyiv, an unprecedented US-China-Russia trilateral summit unfolds at APEC, industry figures warn Europe cannot sleep through the AI revolution.
noticias.texto:
Ursula von der Leyen unveils a new joint-debt package for Kyiv, an unprecedented US-China-Russia trilateral summit unfolds at APEC, industry figures warn Europe cannot sleep through the AI revolution.
On today's show:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed a new €45 billion loan for Ukraine for 2027, backed by joint EU borrowing against the bloc's budget. The facility (split between €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for budget support) is designed to cover roughly two-thirds of Kyiv's anticipated €70 billion financing shortfall next year.
Von der Leyen stated that Ukraine will only be required to repay the funds once Russia pays war reparations, calling it the best way to give Kyiv "a strong hand at the negotiation table." However, the proposal requires unanimous backing from all 27 member states ahead of next week's EU summit, where resistance from Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, and Bulgaria threatens to stall approval.
Trump, Xi, and Putin set for unprecedented trilateral summit in China
US President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit, where he is set to take part in a high-stakes, unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders are expected to discuss major global security issues, including regional conflicts such as Ukraine and Iran, alongside trade and nuclear and AI guardrails.
The summit gives Putin a major diplomatic platform alongside the world’s other two leading economic and military powers, while Beijing uses the APEC stage to project stability and economic cooperation. Speaking at a CEO summit on the sidelines of the gathering, Putin declared that “sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions” have “outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect.”
Joining us for analysis on this diplomatic development are S&D MEP Sakis Arnaoutoglou and MEP Toomas Hendrik Ilves.
Tech leaders warn Europe cannot sleep through the AI revolution
Meanwhile, in an open letter titled “An Urgent Call: Europe Cannot Sleep Through the AI Revolution,” 59 industry figures warn that Europe is currently competing against the United States and China with only a fraction of their capital, computing power, and scaling capacity. The tech leaders have laid out five urgent demands for European policymakers, stressing that the ongoing negotiations for the 2028–2034 EU long-term budget are critical.
According to the signatories, Europe must stop acting merely as a global regulator of technologies invented elsewhere and shift from “defence to offence” by deliberately backing European champions to compete and win globally.
We will examine this push with German Minister for Digital Transformation Karsten Wildberger.
When and where to watch Europe Tonight?
You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings the day's top stories through a European lens, with live analysis and debate with MEPs and leaders.

noticias.titulo: EPP ready to suspend Vučić’s SNS party in December
noticias.resumen: The party leadership will submit the proposal to the political assembly, where it is expected to secure approval. SNS could make a comeback, provided it meets certain conditions.
noticias.texto:
The party leadership will submit the proposal to the political assembly, where it is expected to secure approval. SNS could make a comeback, provided it meets certain conditions.
The European People’s Party (EPP) is expected to suspend the membership of Serbia’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) at its next political assembly, scheduled for December.
The EPP presidency, headed by Germany’s Manfred Weber, is set to propose the suspension following an internal scrutiny process launched more than a year ago, EPP sources told Euronews.
The centre-right political family has long been on a collision course with the party of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić over its ties to Russia and its violent crackdown on protests.
Frustration within the EPP has grown in recent months, culminating in renewed calls for action following the granting of state honoursand the presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral of Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić.
A convicted war criminal known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, Mladić died in a UN detention facility in The Hague in late August, aged 84.
The political assembly, comprising delegates from EPP-affiliated parties, must endorse the presidency’s proposal at its meeting in Brussels on 7–8 December. The number of delegates allocated to each party is determined by its performance in the most recent European elections, ensuring that national parties are represented in proportion to their electoral strength.
“An overwhelming majority of the EPP is in favour of the suspension,” a member of the presidency told Euronews, considering the outcome all but certain.
The presidency has been considering the move for several months but wanted to wait for the outcome of the Serbian elections before putting it forward.
SNS, which had dominated Serbia’s political landscape until this year, lost October’s parliamentary election to the Student List and is set to enter opposition for the first time in nearly 14 years.
If suspended, the party would have one year to meet certain conditions established by the assembly to be reinstated, an EPP official told Euronews.
SNS has been an EPP associate member since 2016. The party was contacted for comment but had not responded by the time of publication.
