noticias.titulo: Storms Bruna and Charles bring record rain and winds to Portugal and Madeira
noticias.resumen: The two storms combined meant that several records for maximum wind gusts and rainfall were broken in the first 12 days of November, according to the Portuguese Institute for the Sea and the Atmosphere (IPMA).
noticias.texto:
The two storms combined meant that several records for maximum wind gusts and rainfall were broken in the first 12 days of November, according to the Portuguese Institute for the Sea and the Atmosphere (IPMA).
Although storm Charles did not have the catastrophic consequences the Portuguese government had previously anticipated, this depression, together with the earlier system Bruna, led to record levels of rain and wind for the month of November, according to the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA).
IPMA has now published its report on the two depressions (source in Portuguese) that affected mainland Portugal and Madeira between 7 and 12 November and recorded several records. Both daily rainfall and maximum wind gusts reached new record highs for this month. Each of these records was broken four times during the period.
As for accumulated rainfall over the first 12 days of the month, it was well above the "climatological norm", that is, the average recorded between 1991 and 2020, at several weather stations, especially in the centre and south of mainland Portugal.
The stations at Mora and Mértola, both in the Alentejo region, stand out, where rainfall was more than 180% above normal, as does Tapada da Ajuda in Lisbon, with a 174% increase. At several of these stations, the rain recorded during the first 12 days of November accounted for more than 25% of the total measured so far in 2026.
Regarding the warnings issued for the 10th, when the entire mainland territory was placed on alert and people were advised not to leave home, IPMA considers that "the storm produced gusts that were lower than initially forecast, though still consistent with a yellow warning, in the order of 70 to 90 km/h along the southern coast. At some of the most exposed locations, according to IPMA stations at Cabo da Roca, Fóia and Loulé (Cavalos do Caldeirão), values compatible with an orange warning were reached, with the strongest gust of the event hitting 123 km/h at the Fóia station". As for rainfall, IPMA says that the figures "justified a red warning for six-hour accumulation (> 60 mm) at several stations in the Lisbon district".
On Madeira, a national record for rainfall was set at the Chão do Areeiro weather station, with 502.7 millimetres recorded in the 24 hours between 9 am on the 10th and 9 am on the 11th.
Across the stations at Chão do Areeiro, Funchal/OBS, Sta. Catarina and Santana on the island of Madeira, and Porto Santo on the island of the same name, rainfall during the first 11 days of November exceeded the 1991-2020 monthly average for this month by between 1.5 and 3 times.

noticias.titulo: Israeli military launches new operation on central Gaza despite ceasefire
noticias.resumen: The military says it is targeting Hamas infrastructure near two refugee camps, while Hamas has accused Israel of violating the truce in place since October 2025.
noticias.texto:
The military says it is targeting Hamas infrastructure near two refugee camps, while Hamas has accused Israel of violating the truce in place since October 2025.
Israeli tanks have advanced towards central Gaza as the military launched what it called a “precise operation” against Hamas, raising fresh tensions over a ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025.
An AFP journalist reported seeing tanks, driven by the Israeli military, position themselves east of the Nuseirat refugee camp, which is located in a Hamas-controlled area of central Gaza.
The AFP also heard from a security source in Gaza who said there was "intense Israeli artillery shelling" north of the camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza "amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday".
The Israeli military confirmed the attack, saying: “The IDF launched a precise operation within the Gaza Strip earlier today west of the Yellow Line... to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip.”
The so-called Yellow Line separates Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since an uneasy ceasefire began in October 2025. The Israeli military says it controls more than 60% of the Palestinian territory.
Confirming that the operation involved military and Israeli Security Agency personnel, the IDF said, “there is Hamas infrastructure in the area in the central Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, has warned international aid organisations not to move through the affected areas.
It said the operation would take place near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps, with traffic also halted along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza's main thoroughfare.
Hamas condemned the operation as a "flagrant violation" of the ceasefire agreement, accusing Israel of failing to honour its commitments.
The Israeli military, meanwhile, said it was responding to apparent violations of the truce by Hamas.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, according to an AFP tally based on figures from Gaza's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose data is considered reliable by the United Nations.
The Israeli military has reported seven soldiers and one civilian contractor killed over the same period.

noticias.titulo: EU has failed to curb harmful 'forever chemicals', auditors warn
noticias.resumen: EU auditors warn that slow regulation, patchy enforcement and outdated food and drinking water safety limits are leaving Europeans exposed to harmful chemicals, six years after Brussels pledged to phase out their non-essential uses.
noticias.texto:
EU auditors warn that slow regulation, patchy enforcement and outdated food and drinking water safety limits are leaving Europeans exposed to harmful chemicals, six years after Brussels pledged to phase out their non-essential uses.
The European Union has failed to deliver on its pledge to phase out harmful "forever chemicals", known as PFAS, because of sluggish regulation, weak enforcement and outdated safety limits, according to a damning report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA).
Six years after the European Commission vowed to eliminate non-essential uses of PFAS, thousands of substances remain largely unregulated, while national authorities are failing to check whether existing restrictions are being respected, the auditors said.
PFAS are widely used in consumer and industrial products, from non-stick cookware and waterproof textiles to medical equipment and food packaging. They break down extremely slowly and have been linked to cancer, reproductive problems and weakened immune responses.
An awareness campaign involving EU ministers and Commissioners last year found that everyone who underwent blood tests tested positive for PFAS. Yet Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has repeatedly declined to meet EU citizens affected by PFAS pollution in recent years.
“These chemicals may last forever, but there are ways to limit their harmful effects on people and the environment,” said Joëlle Elvinger, the ECA member who led the audit.
“The EU must tackle this problem firmly and without delay to defuse this ticking time bomb before it is too late.”
The auditors found that while the EU had made political commitments and funded research, it had failed to translate these efforts into effective protection for citizens.
The audit comes a day after a separate investigation by campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO) accused the chemical industry of stepping up its lobbying efforts to water down the EU's proposed PFAS restrictions, potentially leaving large parts of the sector exempt from the planned ban.
"The ‘forever pollution’ crisis caused by the manufacture, use, and disposal of PFAS is getting worse. It is clear that citizens across Europe (and beyond) are contaminated with these chemicals, some at far higher levels than is considered safe," reads the CEO's report.
Sluggish regulation and weak enforcement
Although the EU was among the first to restrict PFAS, its regulatory framework has struggled to keep pace with the scale of the problem.
The ECA audit said the regulatory process is "too slow" to address chemicals that can persist in the environment for generations. Assessing the hazards of individual PFAS takes an average of six years, the ECA auditors said, while adopting restrictions takes almost five years.
The substance-by-substance approach has also encouraged so-called "regrettable substitution", whereby banned chemicals are replaced with others with similar properties and potentially similar risks.
A proposal to restrict PFAS as a group, covering thousands of substances and uses, was submitted in 2023 by five European countries. But its complexity means the scientific assessment alone is expected to take around four years, before the Commission can move towards a final decision.
Even where restrictions are in place, enforcement is patchy. A third of EU member states carried out no targeted checks on PFAS compliance between 2020 and 2025, the auditors found.
Limited laboratory capacity, high testing costs and competing priorities were among the reasons cited by national authorities for the lack of enforcement.
EU chemicals agency split
Neither the Commission nor the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) has a comprehensive overview of national enforcement efforts, leaving implementation fragmented and heavily reliant on companies policing themselves.
ECHA has already backed a ban on PFAS, although the final decision rests with the Commission.
However, inside the Helsinki-based agency, two scientific committees — risk assessment and socio-economic analysis — held somewhat divergent views, with the latter seeking to ensure that industries reliant on some PFAS wouldn't be affected.
ECHA's socio-economic committee is expected to deliver a final assessment of the impact of a PFAS withdrawal soon. After ECHA's submission, Brussels is under pressure to propose a restriction.
Meanwhile, no new EU restriction procedures have been launched since the universal proposal, apart from measures covering firefighting foams and PFHxA.
Martin Dermine, executive director at the NGO Pesticide Action Network Europe, said PFAS pesticides, beyond their intrinsic toxicity to humans, contaminate groundwater with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a forever PFAS metabolite.
"TFA levels in drinking water are very high in intensive agriculture areas, and TFA was recently classified as Toxic to Reproduction. It is urgent that the Commission bans all PFAS pesticides," Dermine told Euronews.
PFAS in food and drinking water
The EU's food and drinking water rules are also lagging behind scientific evidence.
Food limits cover only four PFAS in certain products, despite more than 50 different PFAS having been detected in food.
The ECA auditors calculated that if certain foods contained the maximum permitted PFAS level, a person could exceed their tolerable weekly intake after eating only around 7 grams of anchovies, 39 grams of wild salmon, 181 grams of eggs or 237 grams of beef.
According to the ECA audit, five EU countries submitted no food-monitoring data between 2020 and 2024, while the Commission has yet to use the growing database to decide whether existing limits should be revised or extended to other substances and food categories.
"We are not naming and shaming. It’s our job to analyse the data and the legislation and to make our recommendation to the Commission," Elvinger told reporters on Wednesday, as all 27 EU countries were asked to reply to ECA's survey for the audit.
Denmark, Germany, France and the Netherlands account for more than half of all PFAS food-monitoring data submitted to the EU between 2020 and 2024.
Nonetheless, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia were urged to introduce PFAS checks in their 2026 national food-control plans.
The ECA auditors also found that the Commission had exceeded the five-year review timetable for drinking-water limits, waiting for new World Health Organization recommendations expected in 2027.
Eight of the 25 EU countries responding to the audit had already introduced additional national limits, exposing differences in the level of protection across the bloc.
The ECA is calling on the Commission to accelerate the universal restriction process, overhaul regulatory procedures, strengthen national enforcement and update food and drinking-water limits where justified by scientific evidence.
Most recommendations have deadlines stretching to 2028 or 2029, although the Commission is urged to reach a decision on the universal restriction proposal by 2027.
"Better and faster action is necessary to protect our citizens. We hope the Commission will implement our recommendations," Elvinger told reporters on Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: The Dardenne Brothers: 'We need to ensure that there remains a sense of humanity in cinema'
noticias.resumen: Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will receive the European Lifetime Achievement Award from the European Film Academy, in recognition of their body of work. Euronews Culture sat down with the filmmaking duo to discuss the prize, the perils of AI, and the evolution of European cinema.
noticias.texto:
Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will receive the European Lifetime Achievement Award from the European Film Academy, in recognition of their body of work. Euronews Culture sat down with the filmmaking duo to discuss the prize, the perils of AI, and the evolution of European cinema.
Celebrated Belgian filmmakers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardennes will be the recipients of next year's European Film Awards' Lifetime Achievement Prize.
The directing duo, famous for their humanist and compassionate dramas, have been two of the leading figures in European independent cinema for almost 40 years. They have won six prizes in Cannes over their illustrious career – including two Palme d'Or awards for Rosetta and L'Enfant (The Child).
Their most recent prize was last year for Jeunes Mères (Young Mothers), which won Best Screenplay on the Croisette.
Their recognition at the European Film Awards includes winning best documentary in 1997 for Gigi, Monica… Et Bianca and the European screenwriter award in 2011 for Le gamin au vélo (The Kid With A Bike).
Euronews Culture sat down with the Dardenne Brothers to discuss their upcoming EFA prize, the perils of AI in cinema, and the current evolution of European cinema.
Euronews Culture: You will receive the European Film Academy's Lifetime Achievement Award next January. What does this award mean to you?
Luc Dardenne: For us, it’s a great honour to receive this award. I think it reflects the fact that we’ve made films that have had a certain continuity. By that I mean a continuity in our artistic exploration. It’s a bit pretentious to say that about oneself, but anyway, there’s a body of work that’s trying to take shape, and I think that after a certain time, you can indeed say: ‘Well, there’s something rather unique about these two brothers who’ve been making films for about forty years’. Plus, we’re European, so the Academy probably thought: ‘Right, we should honour them!’ (Laughs)
I had the pleasure of speaking with Academy president Juliette Binoche, who told me that one of her aims was to rehumanise society through cinema. What do you make of that statement?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: One must always be careful with statements, even if they are important. There are many examples throughout history that show us that cinema hasn’t humanised anything at all… But, it can contribute to us being human. It can help us become more human. Certain films can do that. Charlie Chaplin’s films, for example, can help us become more human, that’s for sure. It’s true that in cinema, as well as other art forms can humanise us, even though culture has never put a stop to barbarism.
Her comment reminded me of a definition of cinema that I’ve always liked: that cinema is a machine for generating empathy. It’s a definition that fits your films well, and I was wondering if you can remember the first film that made an impression on you in that respect – one that generated empathy within you?
Luc Dardenne: Among the films that have made an impression on me, as you say, and which have sparked a desire for brotherhood, friendship and mutual support, I’d mention Kenji Mizoguchi’s Sancho The Bailiff. When I first saw it, quite a long time ago now, I did indeed feel a profound human sense of compassion, friendship and closeness to the victims, the oppressed, and the people trying to build a better life for themselves.
There are films like that - films by Bresson, for example. And then sometimes there are some love stories. If I think of Truffaut’s The Woman Next Door, it’s a tragedy, but it also captures human complexity… One can feel a deep friendship, a profound sense of closeness to human beings in a film such as The Woman Next Door. We feel close to these two lovers, close to their story, their inability to love one another and yet love each other. Beyond this impossibility, we experience something very profound and very human.
That is what cinema is all about. It is not a militant language, I would say; it is a complex language. These are complex emotions. Because when Mizoguchi made his film, it was political, as it's a film in which someone breaks free from slavery... But it's also a complex story about human relationships.
You mentioned Charlie Chaplin – any specific examples that spring to mind?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: All of Chaplin’s films. Because there is such generosity in his films, a constant spirit of civil disobedience in the character of the Tramp, and an enormous faith in life. That’s important too. It’s that sort of cinema that matters. The kind that believes in life – and that’s full of life. Chaplin’s films are full of life - they’re not like funeral dirges, and that’s beautiful. He’s not the only one, of course, but I mentioned Chaplin because he’s a bit of a benchmark for everyone. Everyone knows him, and everyone has seen at least one Chaplin film in their lifetime. Even if you don’t go to the cinema any more, you’ve seen at least one Chaplin film. It’s good that cinema lives on under the watchful eye of the Tramp.
Luc Dardenne: Then there’s Paulette Goddard in the films too, alongside Chaplin (in Modern Times and The Great Dictator). She’s brilliant as well. She brings such life in Modern Times. It’s magnificent.
Over the course of your careers, you’ve presented your films at several festivals, including, of course, Cannes. You’ve been ideally placed to bear witness to the evolution of European cinema. Do you think it’s heading in the right direction?
Luc Dardenne: We are, I would say, living through a time of great upheaval. The current situation is complex for European cinema, world cinema, but also for African cinema – because we always tend to forget about it. For them, however, the situation is more financial and practical in nature. But what is going to happen? I don’t know. As for what the situation actually is, I’m not entirely sure either.
There are several ways of looking at it. I think the perspectives of writers and filmmakers, men and women, will endure. The question is: Will they still have the technical, practical and financial means to express themselves, to criticise, to love, and to make the world love? Will that still be possible? Given the dwindling number of cinemas and the rise of streaming platforms which, whatever people may say, do require a fair amount of standardisation, I’d say that faced with such a complex situation, the only thing I feel certain about is that we’re going to have to fight.
We – the writers, filmmakers and film technicians, the cinema operators and the heads of television channels and streaming platforms as well – are people who love cinema and who do not want artificial intelligence to make films for us. We don't want actors and actresses to be replaced, or films to be edited by AI. We need to ensure that there remains a sense of humanity in cinema. We’ve got to fight for this. We’ve got to refuse to hand over all our data to artificial intelligence.
At the same time, we’ve got to use it as a tool as well, because it’s useful for certain things, but that’s the big issue today. I don’t think cinema is going to disappear as a medium. It’ll still exist – but it needs to reflect a truly human perspective from a woman or a man making a film with living beings. Making a film that’s alive.
Will that still be possible considering the maddening push towards more AI in every aspect of our lives?
Luc Dardenne: I hope so. But we have to fight for it. And freedom, too, because there is freedom in cinema. Filmmakers like Rossellini, Godard and Agnès Varda had great freedom. Will we still be able to find that freedom if the tools dictate the writing and structure of films? So I think we need to be wary of all these new tools. We can use them, but wisely and without believing we’re above them. Otherwise we'll end up being swallowed up by them. And maybe I interpret the award we’re about to receive in this light. We’re craftspeople. We work day after day on films. We do something, redo it, start again... I hope it’s that work, too, that’s being honoured.
It does feel as though there’s a new threat to cinema with each passing year – be it Covid, which closed down so many cinemas, or the rise of streaming platforms. Now, it's AI, a technology that could be described as posing an existential threat to cinema as an artform, as well as human creation in general.
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: I don’t know anything about AI, so we must be very careful not to turn conversations into pub debates, so to speak. The other day I heard a doctor from a Belgian hospital talking about how treatment for a certain type of cancer will become increasingly personalised. He explained how artificial intelligence enables them to process a whole range of data and analyse it. He said that without artificial intelligence, you couldn't do that. So, this technology could be something marvellous. But it’s the same with everything – it depends on how we’re going to use it. Of course, there are people whose sole obsession is profit at any cost. It’s propaganda at any cost. They were certainly like that before, so this artificial intelligence will be a means of amplifying their actions and their thirst for profit. But there are others too, for whom it can be a source of help, a working tool. I think that’s what it can be - a working tool.
Luc Dardenne: In medicine, in ecology, in all the areas we need to monitor in relation to climate issues… Artificial intelligence will play a real role, that much is certain. But when it comes to art, to cinema – which is most affected – for us, it’s a mechanical art form. If we ever confuse the simulacrum with reality, we’re done for – and society is done for too.
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: Yes, but the fact that we’re talking about it proves that this isn’t yet the case.
Luc Dardenne: But there are some who would do nothing to stop it because it’s very lucrative, and we have to stand up to them.
Thanks to your films, as well as those by directors such as Emmanuel Marre, Lukas Dhont and Michael Roskam, to name but a few, Belgium has been gaining an increasing amount of internation recognition. Would you say that Belgian cinema is in good shape?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: When I look back at when we started out, making our documentaries, I get the impression there’s more going on now. More richness. I’m not talking about financial wealth – I’m talking about the richness of films, of the variety of films available compared to 40 or 50 years ago. There’s certainly a wealth of filmmakers, including those whose names you’ve just mentioned. There are others too. And not just in fiction, but in documentary as well, which has always been an important movement in our cinema. Because, in Belgium, we had limited resources, and the documentary genre allows you to work with fewer resources. In that respect, I’d say it’s doing well, but it’s also a victim, like everyone else in European cinema, of the financial difficulties we face.
We’re lucky here to be close to France… And most of our films – even Dutch films – are largely produced in collaboration with the French film industry. All of us in Europe are incredibly fortunate to have the ‘cultural exception’ – which was championed by France. That is why it is also important that Europe awards prizes to filmmakers. If Europe were ever to decide to abolish the ‘cultural exception’ and treat culture as just another commercial product, it would be a real disaster. Our safeguard is really the cultural exception. It is this that still allows European cinema to exist today in all its diversity and richness.
Granted, but there are threats in France too. We’re seeing this with Vincent Bolloré and Canal+, who say they’re going to cut back on their support for the film industry. These budget cuts will, of course, have an impact on French film production. It feels as though cinema is at risk of losing its importance in society and that culture is increasingly becoming a commodity to be consumed – or worse, neglected.
Luc Dardenne: We have championed the cultural exception alongside Michel Hazanavicius and other French filmmakers, as well as German and Finnish directors... We’d already noticed that the commissioners responsible for cinema, industry, the economy would say to us: ‘Is it really a good idea to keep defending this cultural exception?’ There was Borgen, the series… ‘Look, the Danes have translated it into every language and everyone loves it. And it was done in Denmark. Tomorrow, it’ll be done elsewhere. Do we still need to defend individuals, filmmakers who create unique works? We’re moving towards a cinema of TV series', and so on... We fought against that.
We’ve got nothing against TV series – there are some very good ones, including the one I just mentioned, for that matter. But we said, ‘Ladies and gentlemen, you must understand that the film industry is about jobs.' There are economic considerations to think of and it’s important to talk about that. It’s also about perspective, shared by millions of Europeans, and others too. It’s millions of people who are watching a unique work. And when they come out of a cinema, after they’ve seen a film, people talk amongst themselves. They’ve seen the film, then they re-watch it whilst discussing it, and that sparks debate. It’s a public debate and that's part of democracy. Someone is offering you a vision of the world, of reality. Whether it’s a science-fiction or a realistic one, you talk about it. It’s an invitation to debate that they’re giving you.
If we abandon cultural exception, we’ll end up with a system dictated by profit. We’ll end up with the lowest common denominator, and we’ll have no more individuality. Let individuality exist! Give us the money, for goodness’ sake! Do your jobs as Europe’s political representatives! They need to remember that culture isn’t just another commodity. People think, reflect, are moved – and their emotion is thought.
Emotion is thought...
Luc Dardenne: People tend to forget that. It isn’t something we experience and then forget. No, it stays with us. We’ve all been moved by a scene in a film… And if these scenes all end up looking the same, we won’t be moved by them anymore. It’ll pass, we’ll consume them, then forget them straight away. I hope we really do hold on to this. Here, as my brother said, is where Europe has a major role to play. Maybe this award they're giving us is a way of saying: ‘Here are two unique individuals making unique films. This must continue.’
Are there any recent films that have stood out and made an impression?
Luc Dardenne: La Gradiva. That’s a very good French-Italian film by Marine Atlan. It’s a beautiful film that made an impression on both of us. We saw it a few days apart. But you see, there are two of us – my brother saw the film in Liège, I saw it in Brussels. We ring each other up and talk about the film. You can multiply that by hundreds of thousands of people. We watch a film, we talk, we discuss, and that gets people talking about society. So cinema contributes to the debate that, I hope, brings about change and moves things forward.
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: It’s the lastest one we’ve seen and I think it’s one of the greats. It’s one of the films which has moved me the most recently. And it’s a fine example of a film that’s truly alive.
Luc Dardenne: She worked, she edited, she researched, she slept poorly, she suffered… And then she was happy because she found a solution… That’s what art is all about. It’s not always pleasurable, far from it. Things don’t go to plan. We fail. We start again. And blimey, we’ve messed it up! What do we do? We’ll try to re-edit… We search and we find things. It’s marvellous. It remains a marvellous profession.
What advice would you give to young filmmakers who want to get started in this marvellous profession, as you put it?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: You need to be around other people. You need to have friends. These days, you can make films with groups of friends, and with a mobile phone. Get going and try things out. Watching films is good too - and I’d recommend to go see the film we’ve just been talking about… To see how a young female director today manages to retain that uniqueness, that richness and that freedom. Because it’s not easy, we know that full well, and you have to fight your way through. Then there's this excessive drive to succeed... We get it. Nobody wants to fail. But this obsession with success and recognition is terrible. Here, with La Gradiva, we see that amidst all that, there’s this woman who succeeds, who really brings something to the table. It’s not just another film.
Your latest film, Jeunes mères, was screened in Cannes last year and won the award for best screenplay. If I’m not mistaken, that’s your sixth award on the Croisette. Where do you keep them all?
Luc Dardenne: (Laughs) There weren’t as many awards in the past – there used to be certificates, scrolls of paper… We’ve had two Palmes d’Or, and then, it’s true, there are other awards for screenplays, for directing… They’re in the producer’s office!
**So it's not a timeshare / "three in one household, three in another" deal? **
Luc Dardenne: (Laughs) No, not yet!
Can you tell me about your next project?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: If things go as we’d like them to, we’re hoping to start filming next year… In September or October. That’s all I can tell you, but we’re not at all certain at the moment, given that we have zero euros.
Given what is happening in France, Italy and Belgium – I'm referring to student protests and demonstrations against the high cost of living... Considering your films, which deal with everyday life and survival in a society that exacerbates everyday problems, do these social movements serve as a source of inspiration?
Luc Dardenne: The script for our next film was finished before these events took place, so I can’t say they served as a source of inspiration. But the calls for greater justice help us a great deal. We draw a great deal of inspiration from reality, from these struggles, which are sometimes individual, unknown, even almost clandestine, if I may say so. So, naturally, we’re interested in them. And it’s excellent that young people in France and in Belgium are making concrete demands. It’s not just about being against this or that... They’re asking for concrete things that a democratic state should normally be able to provide. Education is a common good. This common good must exist, and it must exist in the finest possible way in a democratic society. There is a real problem, and it’s not just in France – it’s everywhere. Let’s not even mention the United States!
Social rights are, thankfully, being highlighted today - namely the right to food, to education, to healthcare. That's why the Democrats in the United States won. It’s because people remembered that social justice and economic justice do exist, and that they are fed up with living on the equivalent of €1,500 a month… A family with two children, who have to find a way to send them to school, put food on the table, go for a walk, take a holiday – it’s no longer possible. And people sense this, and they think: ‘They’re taking the piss, they’re no longer interested in us, they don’t care about us.’ Our films, whilst not being activist or political, etc., have always featured characters trapped in an economic and social situation linked to poverty and material hardship. That, for us, is very important. And the film we’re going to make is still part of that tradition, if I may say so. It’s about people who find themselves in a difficult situation that traps them, and they’re fighting to break free from it.
Finally, I recently had the pleasure of attending this year’s Lumière Festival, which honoured the Coen brothers. They work together but also separately. What about you? Are you or have you ever been tempted to go your separate ways for a while?
Jean-Pierre Dardenne: (Laughs) Clearly not so far! I don’t know what’s always going on

noticias.resumen: New footage shared by a Ukrainian Telegram channel appears to show extensive damage to the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia.

New footage shared by a Ukrainian Telegram channel on Wednesday appears to show extensive damage to the Kerch Bridge, a strategic crossing linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the bridge on Tuesday.
The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said road traffic across the bridge had been halted, while rail services resumed by Tuesday afternoon.
The Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea and carries major strategic and symbolic importance for Moscow, which annexed the peninsula in 2014.

noticias.titulo: Amazon pledges €6.3bn for renewable energy projects in India: Who will benefit from the clean electricity?
noticias.resumen: Some of the electricity generated will be used to power the company's data centres.
noticias.texto:
Some of the electricity generated will be used to power the company's data centres.
E-commerce giant Amazon will invest $7 billion (€6.3bn) in renewable energy projects in India. It will buy some of the electricity generated to power its operations, such as data centres.
The money will help India to reach its target of 500 gigawatts of clean energy capacity by the end of the decade, a goal the government estimates will require around $220 billion (€200bn) in investment. Coal and oil remain central to India's energy mix, with 54 per cent of the country's electricity currently coming from non-fossil fuel sources, including solar, wind and hydropower.
"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry," says Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer.
In 2022, Amazon emitted 51.17 million metric tonnes of CO2e – more than the likes of Switzerland, Hong Kong, and Denmark.
In 2025, Amazon's absolute carbon emissions increased by 16 per cent, mostly due to increased use of AI and data centres. In the same year, Google's emissions increased by 18 per cent and Microsoft's emissions jumped 25 per cent.
How is Amazon trying to cut its emissions?
The investments, to be made by 2030, will contribute to the Amazon's goal to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030.
The new target means that every unit of electricity the company consumes will be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions compared to a 2019 baseline. This is part of Amazon’s Climate Pledge goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040.
Amazon's transportation emissions have accelerated at an average of 18 per cent per year since it introduced its Climate Pledge in 2019, according to the Guardian newspaper.
Amazon is one of India's top corporate buyers of renewable energy
The pledge comes on top of $4 billion (€3.3bn) in renewable energy investments Amazon has already pledged in India, making it one of the country's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free electricity, the firm said in a statement on Tuesday.
Once operational, Amazon's contracted renewable energy projects in India will have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts (GW), enough to generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households.
Amazon is such an energy intensive company because: "Its business ventures produce massive volumes of packaging waste, emit many carbon emissions via shipping and logistics, and utilize large volumes of energy to equip its worldwide network of data centers," according to a study by Carolina Lisboa Sisnando in the Journal Of Humanities and Social Science published in 2025.
What are Amazon's solar and wind projects in India?
Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 megawatts (MW). They include a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka, Amazon’s largest wind project contracted in Asia to date; a 200 MW combined solar and wind project also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.

noticias.titulo: Robots serve ice cream and coffee in China's tech hub
noticias.resumen: In Shenzhen, China, humanoid robots serve coffee and ice cream while AI developers use human-recorded movements to train machines for everyday jobs.
noticias.texto:
Humanoid robots are serving ice cream and coffee in Shenzhen, China, as developers work to introduce artificial intelligence into everyday tasks.
At a park refreshment stand, one robot prepares ice cream while another makes coffee, attracting curious visitors who film them in action. Both are powered by AI, although staff still need to refill supplies and empty coffee grounds.
Chinese companies are also using data collected from workers wearing cameras and sensor gloves to train robots. These recordings help the machines learn tasks such as handling parcels and stocking shelves, as well as adapting to different environments.
Although they still struggle with complex household chores, robots are increasingly taking on repetitive work. Shenzhen's manufacturing network allows developers to test and refine their technology quickly.

noticias.resumen: GTA VI fever grips Australia, Japan and New Zealand ahead of its 19 November release, with record downloads expected.
noticias.texto:
Billboards advertising Grand Theft Auto VI appeared across Melbourne and Sydney, Australia, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026, as gamers worldwide counted down to its long-awaited release.
The latest instalment in the blockbuster franchise is set to launch on Thursday, 13 years after GTA V. In Tokyo, fans shared their excitement, with some looking forward to exploring the story and eventually playing online with friends.
Meanwhile, internet providers in New Zealand are preparing for a surge in downloads. Telecommunications company Chorus expects around 35 petabytes of additional data traffic as players download the 212-gigabyte game.
Network strategy manager Kurt Rodgers said the company had planned for the increased demand and did not expect any disruptions. GTA VI follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, as they navigate a fictional world inspired by Florida.

noticias.titulo: Singer Julio Iglesias under investigation for alleged sexual offences
noticias.resumen: The Spanish National High Court has admitted a complaint filed by two former employees of Julio Iglesias alleging sexual offences, bodily harm and degrading treatment. The singer has been summoned to testify on 3 February.
noticias.texto:
The Spanish National High Court has admitted a complaint filed by two former employees of Julio Iglesias alleging sexual offences, bodily harm and degrading treatment. The singer has been summoned to testify on 3 February.
A Spanish court opened an investigation into veteran singer Julio Iglesias on Wednesday after two former employees filed a complaint alleging sexual abuse, which he denies.
Madrid's Audiencia Nacional court said in a statement that it would investigate alleged "offences against sexual freedom", a category covering a range of crimes, including sexual assault, as well as bodily harm and degrading treatment.
The decision marks a reversal after an earlier complaint was dismissed on the grounds that Spanish courts lacked jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic.
The women, a domestic worker and a physiotherapist, allege they were subjected to sexual abuse and other forms of mistreatment while working at Iglesias' properties in the two Caribbean countries in 2021.
Judge finds sufficient grounds for investigation
Following the dismissal of the complaint, Women’s Link Worldwide announced last September that it would take the case directly to the National High Court by filing a criminal complaint against the singer.
The organisation accused him of alleged offences of human trafficking for the purposes of forced labour and servitude, offences against sexual freedom and sexual integrity, bodily harm, degrading treatment and violations of workers' rights through the imposition of abusive working conditions.
Antonio Piña, a judge at Spain’s National High Court, has partially admitted the complaint: he will investigate the alleged offences against sexual freedom, bodily harm and degrading treatment, but has excluded human trafficking and offences against workers' rights.
The judge considers that there is sufficient evidence to open criminal proceedings. In his ruling, he highlights that, in addition to the witness statements, the prosecution has submitted a photograph of one of the employees "showing a bruise on one of her arms, consistent with the possibility of having been grabbed forcefully".
In the same image, the investigating judge adds, "two marks can be seen on one of her thighs which may correspond to a bite mark from another person". According to the complaint, these injuries "are the result of her being forced to participate in acts of a sexual nature".
Iglesias, 83, a Grammy-winning singer who has sold more than 300 million records over his decades-long career, has described the accusations as "absolutely false", saying he has never "abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman".

noticias.titulo: Iraqi court jails six French Islamic State members for life
noticias.resumen: More than 5,700 Islamic State detainees whom the US moved from Syria to Iraq are due to go on trial from Sunday, while rights groups question whether Iraq’s courts are fair.
noticias.texto:
More than 5,700 Islamic State detainees whom the US moved from Syria to Iraq are due to go on trial from Sunday, while rights groups question whether Iraq’s courts are fair.
A court in Iraq on Wednesday sentenced six French citizens, among them the jihadist , to life in prison for belonging to the Islamic State (IS) group.
The six are among 47 French nationals who were transferred from Syria to Iraq last year and charged with membership of the extremist organisation. Their trials began in September. Ten of the group had already been sentenced, most of them to life imprisonment, before Wednesday’s verdicts, which were reported by an AFP journalist in the courtroom.
Barnouin, 45, told the court during his trial this month that he went to Syria because he believed it was his religious duty. He said he had not known that IS would go on to carry out attacks in France.
A convert to Islam in the early 2000s, he was gradually radicalised and became part of a jihadist network in southwestern France. The network included Mohamed Merah, who killed four people, three of them children, at a Jewish school in Toulouse, France, in 2012.
Barnouin joined IS in Syria in 2014. Three years later, Kurdish-led forces captured him.
Overcrowded prisons
Iraq’s jails were already holding large numbers of suspected jihadists when, in February, the United States moved more than 5,700 IS detainees from over 60 countries into Iraqi custody. They had spent years in prisons in Syria run by Kurdish-led forces. A court source said their trials would begin on Sunday.
Iraqi courts have issued hundreds of death sentences and life terms over the years to people convicted of terrorism, including foreign fighters. Some human rights groups have criticised the proceedings as hasty and say defendants are denied due process.
At its height, between 2014 and 2017, IS controlled swathes of territory across Iraq and Syria. During that time it carried out massacres and forced women and girls into sexual slavery.
Baghdad declared victory over the group in 2017 with the support of a US-led coalition. Two years later, Kurdish-led forces backed by Washington defeated IS in Syria. Iraq is still dealing with the aftermath: mass graves are still being discovered, and many accounts of IS atrocities have yet to be investigated.
Thousands of Europeans travelled to the Middle East to join IS. France has allowed relatives of French jihadists to come home, but it has refused to repatriate most of the fighters themselves, leaving them to stand trial abroad.

noticias.titulo: Meet the Kazakh artist who campaigns against nuclear weapons
noticias.resumen: Born without arms near the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, Karipbek Kuyukov became an artist and anti-nuclear activist. Today, he continues to campaign against nuclear weapons through his art and public appearances.
noticias.texto:
Born without arms near the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, Karipbek Kuyukov became an artist and anti-nuclear activist. Today, he continues to campaign against nuclear weapons through his art and public appearances.
In his apartment, behind a door marked "Art Studio", Kazakh artist Karipbek Kuyukov is working on a painting. He leans close to the canvas, holding a brush in his mouth. Every now and then, he rolls his chair back to look at the painting from a distance before moving closer again. He is painting a landscape. Autumn leaves cover a road leading towards mountains rising in the distance.
“I love painting landscapes. I want to show that wherever humans appear, they end up spoiling nature,” he says.
The mountains in his painting are Balkantau, near the village of Yegindybulak, about 100 kilometres from the former Semipalatinsk nuclear test site.
It is in this village that Kuyukov was born, without arms.
"When I was born, they showed me to my mother, and she saw that I had no arms. It was very difficult for her," he recalls.
Between 1949 and 1989, the Soviet Union conducted 456 nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk.
Kuyukov remembers the ground shaking after explosions, with shockwaves spreading like ripples in water. He recalls that many other children in the area were also born with disabilities.
Growing up, Kuyukov learned to use his feet instead of hands. One day, he came across a large box of coloured pencils and began experimenting with drawing. He started making simple childhood sketches, using his feet to hold the pencils.
Activism through art
In 1989, Kazakh poet and activist Olzhas Suleimenov founded the Nevada–Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement, which Kuyukov later joined. He took part in the movement's activities, but it was through his paintings that he found a powerful way to express his message.
His first painting on the subject, titled "The First Explosion", depicted a family inside a yurt caught in the force of a nuclear blast.
"The blast blows the yurt away, turning everything upside down. I wanted to show what the people living there went through and how the nuclear tests affected them," he explains.
He went on to create more works exploring the impact of nuclear testing, including "Nuclear Mushroom", "Atomic Childhood", "Radiation" and "Fear".
This year marks 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site in 1991. Kuyukov was invited to address a high-level meeting of the UN General Assembly about the human cost of nuclear testing.
"I wanted to shout, not just speak, because the time has come to make the whole world hear us," he says. "I addressed the leaders of countries that continue to make nuclear threats."
It was not his first appearance at the UN. Over the years, he has continued to campaign against nuclear weapons through his paintings and public speeches.
With nuclear threats once again part of international political rhetoric, Kuyukov's decades-long campaign remains relevant.
A life in his own words
Kuyukov has recently published his first autobiography, a project he began 35 years ago and only recently completed. With financial support from people who believed in the project, he recorded his memories as voice messages, which editors then turned into a manuscript.
Recounting his life brings him to tears. His sister Saule gently wipes them from his face. He calls her his "guardian angel". In the book, he pays tribute to her and others who have supported him over the years.
At the book launch, people line up to have their copies signed. Kuyukov patiently signs each one, holding a pen in his mouth. As he grew older, he gradually lost the ability to use his feet for drawing and writing. Today, he relies on his mouth for both.
Beyond the canvas
Back in his apartment, Kuyukov takes a break for tea. On the table is a specially designed stand. Saule places a bowl of tea on it, bringing it up to the level of his chin. He drinks without assistance.
Saule is often by his side, although she prefers not to be interviewed.
Later, sitting on the sofa in his living room, Kuyukov tucks one leg beneath him as he talks. His other foot moves in rhythm with his speech, gesturing almost as hands would.
Today, he increasingly turns to landscapes, painting mountains and scenes of nature untouched by humans. But his commitment to a world free of nuclear weapons remains unchanged. He continues to share his story through his art and public appearances.
Despite decades of painting, there is one person Kuyukov has never dared to portray: his mother. He says he is afraid to paint her portrait, but hopes that one day he will find the courage to do so.

noticias.titulo: Hungarian ethno-punk bands join forces for Brussels dance-floor show
noticias.resumen: Hungary’s Besh o droM and Bohemian Betyars will perform together for the first time in Brussels on Friday, at the request of the Balkan Trafik festival. Besh o droM founder Gergely Barcza promises a big party and says Central European and Balkan cultures are moving closer together.
noticias.texto:
Hungary’s Besh o droM and Bohemian Betyars will perform together for the first time in Brussels on Friday, at the request of the Balkan Trafik festival. Besh o droM founder Gergely Barcza promises a big party and says Central European and Balkan cultures are moving closer together.
The two leading bands of Hungarian world music, Besh o droM and Bohemian Betyars, are preparing for a special joint concert at the Beurse in Brussels on Friday 20 November.
At the invitation of the Balkan Trafik festival, the musicians will be performing together for the first time, with a 90-minute set.
Both bands draw on Balkan, Eastern European and Roma musical traditions, yet each has its own distinctive sound.
Since its formation in Budapest in 1999, Besh o droM has developed a virtuoso, highly danceable style in which Hungarian, Romanian, Roma and Balkan traditions are mixed with Greek, Turkish and Middle Eastern influences.
Formed in 2009, Bohemian Betyars describe their genre as "speed-folk-freak-punk": they fuse Hungarian folk, as well as Roma and Balkan melodies, with punk, ska and psychedelic rock.
Before the Brussels performance, Euronews Culture spoke to Gergely Barcza, one of Besh o droM's founders.
"The audience should get ready for a really big party," said Barcza. "Over the past 27 years, Besh o droM has always built on partying, dancing and a great atmosphere, and that has worked very well. Bohemian Betyars bring a very similar energy."
"The two bands are very similar, with a similar energy level. They are crazier than we are, though. What they do on stage is really intense."
Bands of brothers
Both groups have fan bases in Hungary that stretch across generations. There is constant demand for Balkan music abroad, both in Europe and beyond.
Barcza said that both bands represent Hungary and Hungarian music at their foreign shows, even though Besh o droM previously were shunned in folk-music circles, because, in his view, the band handled traditions disrespectfully.
"In the early 2000s we felt strong resistance from the traditional music profession: why we were treating Hungarian folk music disrespectfully, and why we were taking this abroad," he said.
"Besh o droM reworks Hungarian folk music and Hungarian folk songs. All our songs are in Hungarian or Romani. We represent Hungary, and we take Hungarian music abroad."
According to Barcza, from a Western perspective, Central European and Balkan cultures look very similar, so the peoples of the region could be more fond of their neighbours.
"When we are at home, we feel a big difference between Romanian, Serbian or Bulgarian culture and our own. But once you step outside this region, there is not such a big difference anymore."
He added that after people return home from concerts abroad they can also feel that these peoples and cultures "form one team".
"We can be proud of this, we can like one another, we can like our neighbours, because we come from the same culture."

noticias.titulo: Consumer screening tests make baseless health claims, UK study finds
noticias.resumen: Easy access to dubious health tests should be considered a “patient safety issue,” researchers said.
noticias.texto:
Easy access to dubious health tests should be considered a “patient safety issue,” researchers said.
You can find tests to screen for dozens of health conditions online — but many of them make baseless and potentially harmful claims, a new analysis has found.
Researchers in the United Kingdom analysed 50 health tests that were advertised online, including tests for the gut microbiome, blood counts, genetics, liver and lung function and cortisol levels, as well as pelvic and breast examinations, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.
Advertisers were both online retailers and in-person clinics. Prices ranged from £6.99 (€8.36) for an at-home “kidney albumin rapid test” to £14,000 (€16,751) for a “platinum assessment” that offered multiple tests, imaging and a physical exam. Some clinics offered a luxury hotel or spa package on top, with celebrities or influencers offering endorsements for other tests.
Yet many of these tests made unsubstantiated claims or offered screening that is not recommended by national health authorities, according to the study, which was published in the journal BMJ Open.
Sixteen tests claimed, without evidence, that they could help people live longer, while 36 promised earlier diagnosis and better health outcomes. Only 15 tests explained the potential downsides of testing, such as inaccuracy or risks from intimate physical exams.
In one example, a retailer cited death rates from a particular disease, saying they “could have been detected by one of our … health assessments. Just think of how many could still be here today”.
Among the 50 vendors in the study, 14 offered testicular exams, 13 offered breast exams and nine offered pelvic exams to people without worrisome symptoms. The UK’s national health system does not recommend these tests for everyone.
Consumer health tests are easy to access, with few regulatory guardrails, “despite their capability of harm,” wrote the researchers from the University of St Andrews in Scotland.
They said at-home health tests can help fill gaps in the medical system, but only if they are evidence-backed. Poor-quality screenings, they warned, can result in “false positives (false alarms), false negatives (false reassurance) and loss of personal resources with little or no value gained by individuals.”
At-home health tests are easy to find online. On Wednesday, the UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) upheld a ban on advertisements for an at-home testosterone blood test from Voy, an online provider that sells testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
The watchdog said Voy’s ads were “misleading” because they linked common symptoms, such as fatigue and irritability, to low testosterone to encourage men to buy a test kit.
Voy argued that the ads did not claim that low testosterone was the only explanation for those symptoms, according to the ASA. But the watchdog decided against the company anyway, ordering Voy not to “exaggerate” the connection.
Few cases make it to regulators, the new study found. “This should be considered a gap in regulation and a patient safety issue,” the researchers said.

noticias.titulo: Estado Novo interpretive centre opens in Salazar's birthplace in Santa Comba Dão
noticias.resumen: The Estado Novo Interpretive Centre occupies a former primary school in the town where the Portuguese dictator was born and is dedicated to studying the regime and resistance movements.
noticias.texto:
The Estado Novo Interpretive Centre occupies a former primary school in the town where the Portuguese dictator was born and is dedicated to studying the regime and resistance movements.
After two decades of stop-start progress and controversy, the former Salazar School-Canteen in Vimieiro, where dictator António de Oliveira Salazar was born, has been turned into the Estado Novo Interpretive Centre - Regime and Resistance (CIEN - RR).
The former primary school in the municipality of Santa Comba Dão, built between 1937 and 1940, reopened on 23 October to tell the story of the Estado Novo, censorship and resistance to the dictatorship.
The venue is under the scientific coordination of the Associação Ephemera, founded by historian José Pacheco Pereira, whose aim is to collect and disseminate collections, archives, books, periodicals, manuscripts, pamphlets, photos and objects from contemporary history.
The interpretive centre will host exhibitions, debates, conferences and research activities, as well as a thematic library and a reading room. The aim is to provide documents and materials that help to understand life under the Estado Novo, without hiding the building's historical link to Salazar.
The old school still retains elements associated with that era. For those responsible for the project, preserving this context is part of the work of historical interpretation, rather than turning it into a tribute.
The first exhibition, entitled "Only What Is Known To Exist Exists: Censorship under the Estado Novo", which brings together material from the Ephemera association's collection, looks at the mechanisms for controlling information and cultural expression during the dictatorship, including the press, literature and music.
At the formal opening session, the Secretary of State for Culture, Alberto Santos, argued, according to the Lusa news agency, that "studying the dictatorship is a responsibility of democracy".
According to the remarks by the Secretary of State quoted by Lusa, studying the dictatorship "in a place so directly associated with the figure of António de Oliveira Salazar", the central figure of the Estado Novo, increases the responsibility "to know the regime, to understand how it managed to last for so long, what it meant to live under its power" and what lesson it left for the future.
The opening of the centre brings to a close a process that spanned different municipal terms of office and generated debate on how to address the memory of Salazar in his home town. The new venue now seeks to establish itself as a place of historical knowledge and reflection on the dictatorship and the resistance to it, rather than a museum dedicated to the former ruler.
"We do not want to turn this interpretive centre into a museum to the dictator, we want instead to create an interpretive centre that studies not only the regime, but also the resistance to the regime", stressed the deputy mayor of Santa Comba Dão, Luís Nunes, in comments to Lusa.
The centre's scientific committee is made up of Marçal Grilo, Irene Pimentel, José Manuel Sobral, José Pedro Castanheira, Luís Nunes, Maria Inácia Rezola, Luísa Tiago de Oliveira and Rui Feijó.
At the inauguration of the facility, historian Pacheco Pereira stressed that most of them are people who "before and after 25 April played a role in defending freedom and democracy".

noticias.titulo: From the steppe to the global stage: Mongolia’s COP17 legacy
noticias.resumen: Mongolia hosts UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, showcasing its capacity, spotlighting rangelands and securing billion-dollar pledges for land restoration.
noticias.texto:
Hosting the UN’s land conference in Ulaanbaatar gave Mongolia an opportunity to demonstrate its organising capacity and put the future of rangelands and pastoral communities at the centre of international attention.
For Mongolia, land is inseparable from daily life. It sustains herding families, supports food production and carries a cultural inheritance shaped by generations of movement across the steppe. Bringing the world’s land conference to Ulaanbaatar gave those experiences an international platform.
From 17 to 28 August 2026, Mongolia hosted the seventeenth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, known as UNCCD COP17. Delegates from the Convention’s 197 Parties joined representatives of business, science and civil society under the theme “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.”
The gathering marked a milestone for the country: Mongolia became the first host of a UNCCD COP in East and Central Asia. For the government, it was an opportunity to connect the demands of organising a major multilateral conference with an issue of direct national importance. Nearly 77 per cent of Mongolia’s land is degraded, according to UNDP, placing pressure on livelihoods, ecosystems and the country’s pastoral heritage.
A national effort with international reach
Hosting a conference of this scale requires coordination across government, international organisations, local partners and the people supporting delegates throughout their stay.
The organising effort extended beyond the negotiating rooms. UNDP’s support included more than 400 UN Volunteers working alongside the National Organizing Committee, the Mongolian Red Cross and other partners across logistics, communications and delegate services. Their involvement also created opportunities to develop skills and experience that can serve future events.
Translating this high-level ambition into a seamless reality required unprecedented logistical coordination. At the core of organizing the event in Mongolia was Batbayar Shurenchuluun, State Secretary of the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. As part of the National Organizing Committee and the primary public servant spearheading the on-the-ground execution of the conference, he united domestic agencies, NGOs, and the massive volunteer force to accommodate over 10,000 delegates—twice the number initially expected.
"Hosting a multilateral gathering of this magnitude was a profound test of our national capacity and public service," State Secretary Batbayar noted. "The extraordinary dedication of our local partners, institutions, and volunteers created the vital, stable foundation needed to facilitate the complex international negotiations that followed."
By effectively translating international dialogue into actionable frameworks, the conference yielded concrete results—securing multi-billion dollar financial pledges and establishing targeted initiatives that will drive sustainable land management and herder resilience for decades to come.
The ambition of these global initiatives mirrored Mongolia's own domestic commitments. As a National Policy Advocate during the COP17 thematic sessions, State Secretary Batbayar officially presented Mongolia's domestic conservation strategies to the international community. He detailed the country's proactive goal to build a long-term foundation for natural conservation by placing 30 per cent of its total territory under state special protection by 2030, with a further ambition to increase this to 35 per cent by 2050.
The diplomatic task was equally demanding. Governments arrived with different priorities and expectations. Mongolia’s presidency supported negotiations through high-level consultations, helping create the conditions for 34 decisions to be adopted, including on rangelands, land tenure, sand and dust storms, and resource mobilisation.
That achievement gives the hosting story substance: Ulaanbaatar provided a setting in which countries could continue working towards shared responses to land degradation despite difficult negotiations.
Bringing the world’s rangelands into focus
Mongolia’s clearest contribution was to elevate an issue rooted in its own experience.
Rangelands cover approximately 54 per cent of the world’s terrestrial surface and support around 500 million pastoralists. Their condition has implications for food production, biodiversity and the resilience of communities far beyond Mongolia.
COP17 took place during the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, an initiative championed by Mongolia. Hosting the conference brought that international recognition into a country where pastoralism remains integral to livelihoods and national identity.
The decisions adopted in Ulaanbaatar encouraged stronger policies for the sustainable management, conservation and restoration of rangelands, alongside improved tenure security. The conference also saw the launch of the Rangelands Flagship Initiative, intended to increase investment in these landscapes.
For pastoral communities, this attention matters because the future of land depends on the people who manage it. Their knowledge and experience are essential to designing responses that work locally.
Connecting ambition with investment
A lasting conference legacy also depends on the partnerships and projects it helps advance.
In its closing assessment, the Mongolian government highlighted a portfolio of 45 land restoration, rangeland and drought-resilience projects across 23 countries, valued at approximately $1.3 billion. The portfolio illustrates the potential to connect international discussions with practical investment opportunities. Its value represents a project pipeline; delivery will depend on financing and implementation.
Mongolia’s Steppe Action Agenda reinforced that emphasis, bringing together priorities including rangeland management, nature-based infrastructure and the relationship between land and water.
The conference left further work ahead. Negotiations on several issues, including drought, will continue at COP18 in Egypt in 2028. The partnerships advanced in Ulaanbaatar must now translate into benefits for communities and landscapes.
For Mongolia, COP17 established a platform for that next phase. The government brought countries together, supported negotiations and placed the experience of the steppe within a global conversation about resilience.
The world came to Ulaanbaatar. Mongolia’s opportunity now is to carry that momentum from the conference halls to the land.

noticias.titulo: Europe cannot 'sleep through the AI revolution': Tech leaders urge EU to take action
noticias.resumen: Tech leaders, including Yann LeCun, Nobel laureate Philippe Aghion and the CEOs of ElevenLabs and Lovable, call on the EU to secure a dedicated AI allocation in its 2028-2034 budget.
noticias.texto:
Tech leaders, including Yann LeCun, Nobel laureate Philippe Aghion and the CEOs of ElevenLabs and Lovable, call on the EU to secure a dedicated AI allocation in its 2028-2034 budget.
Dozens of European tech founders and scientists are warning that the window to compete in artificial intelligence is closing and the European Union’s next long-term budget will be crucial to deciding the continent’s place in the future.
The open letter, signed by 59 leaders, including Nobel laureate and economist Philippe Aghion, one of AI’s so-called godfathers Yann LeCun, and the heads of DeepL, OVHcloud, ElevenLabs and Lovable, argues Europe risks losing its technological sovereignty and competitiveness.
“We share a deep belief in Europe’s potential, but also a growing sense of alarm: the world is undergoing a technological revolution, and Europe is competing in it with a fraction of the capital, the compute, and the scaling capacity of its rivals. The gap is widening every quarter,” the letter reads.
China and the United States are battling to take the lead on the technology that promises to transform healthcare, manufacturing, and global economies. Countries that lead in AI will not only define global power but also grow their economies.
Titled ‘An Urgent Call: Europe Cannot Sleep Through the AI Revolution,’ the letter released on Wednesday says the talent and ambition already exist in Europe, but what is missing is the political will and capital to match them.
They warn negotiations on the EU budget for 2028-2034 are under way, and what is not secured during the talks will not exist before 2035.
The five AI demands
The letter sets out five demands. The first is simplification: the authors say Europe is right to protect safety and fundamental rights, but that this should not bury innovators in bureaucracy.
They welcome the first Digital Omnibus, a legislative package introduced to simplify, streamline, and reduce administrative burdens across the EU’s digital rulebook. However, they say it must not be the last step, and they want the ongoing review of the digital rulebook to produce binding simplification.
They also call on the EU to create a true 28th regime, so that a company can incorporate once and operate under one set of rules in every member state.
Scale and data
The second demand is to help European tech scale. Europe, the letter argues, is good at producing ideas but poor at capturing their benefits, because too many founders start companies in the United States or relocate there during later funding rounds.
They call for the channelling of Europe's large pool of private savings through pension funds and insurers into scale-up funds, completing the single market for capital, and having governments act as anchor customers for European technology.
The letter also calls for broad access to data, which they say matters as much as compute or capital.
Investment
The third ask is a reality check on investment. While there are investments in the EU’s AI "Gigafactories", they say AI needs more investment, as American companies alone are putting hundreds of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure this year.
To fund this, they call on European leaders to secure a dedicated and ambitious AI allocation within the European Competitiveness Fund and the next research framework programme.
Talent
The fourth ask is to retain Europe’s talent and calls for institutions for talent.
'Ambitious strategy'
The final demand is a change of mindset in Europe, saying that the continent can no longer be content with regulating technologies invented elsewhere; it must move from defence to offence and deliberately back European champions with the scale, capital and market access to compete globally.
“Europe can no longer be satisfied with simply regulating the technologies invented by others. We need a far more ambitious strategy for technological competition with the world.
"We must shift our mindset from playing defence to playing offence, and eventually to win,” the letter reads.
Euronews has reached out to the European Commission for comment.
