noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy proposes 10 more humanitarian evacuations after Oleshky
noticias.resumen: Zelenskyy did not name the 10 settlements and said Ukraine’s delegation would raise the plan with US mediators, while Putin has separately suggested a similar operation in Kostiantynivka, which Ukraine says Russia does not control.
noticias.texto:
Zelenskyy did not name the 10 settlements and said Ukraine’s delegation would raise the plan with US mediators, while Putin has separately suggested a similar operation in Kostiantynivka, which Ukraine says Russia does not control.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has proposed 10 new humanitarian evacuation operations in the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, modelled on a recent ceasefire that allowed hundreds of civilians to leave the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday the proposal came up at a meeting where participants discussed the results of recent trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi.
"Ukraine proposed another 10 locations in temporarily occupied areas of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions where a similar humanitarian operation is required," he wrote on social media.
He did not name the settlements. Ukraine's diplomatic delegation will raise the proposal with US mediators.
A truce in Oleshky from 27 October to 1 November, initiated by US First Lady Melania Trump, allowed residents to leave through a safe corridor.
Melania Trump said almost 800 people were evacuated in total. Those who chose to move to Ukrainian-controlled territory were taken via Gomel in Belarus to the Chernihiv region, while others reportedly chose to evacuate to Russia. Neither Ukraine nor Russia disclosed the breakdown of figures.
Kyiv subsequently said Russia had used the ceasefire to rotate its troops on the left bank of Kherson region.
Verkhovna Rada Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said he had agreed with his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova to appeal to the US First Lady to extend the Oleshky model to other occupied settlements.
Russia's Vladimir Putin made a parallel proposal during his meeting with Trump and US envoy Steve Witkoff in the Kremlin on 12 November, suggesting a similar operation in Kostiantynivka in Donetsk region, which he said was under Russian "control".
Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said Russia was likely proposing a ceasefire there for the same reason as in Oleshky — to rotate its troops.
Ukrainian military statements and open-source intelligence research indicate that Russian forces occupy only parts of the city's eastern and south-western outskirts, with a significant portion in a contested zone and another part held by Ukraine's armed forces.
Putin has claimed Russian forces have occupied the city on multiple occasions.

noticias.titulo: Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of high-stakes trilateral summit in China
noticias.resumen: China’s Xi welcomed his US and Russian counterparts at the APEC summit as the three global powers’ leaders gear up for their first trilateral meeting. Trump shook hands with Putin, expressing hope about the chances of ending the war in Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
China’s Xi welcomed his US and Russian counterparts at the APEC summit as the three global powers’ leaders gear up for their first trilateral meeting. Trump shook hands with Putin, expressing hope about the chances of ending the war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin shook hands in China on Wednesday as they were welcomed by their Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping for crucial trilateral talks on Thursday — the first such summit between the leaders of three global powers.
In their first meeting since August 2025, Trump and Putin exchanged greetings and handshakes with Xi, then posed on stage for a family photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit gala dinner in Shenzhen.
This was Putin's first appearance in an APEC leaders' family photo in nine years, marking progress for the Kremlin amid Russia's isolation on the world stage following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Xi welcomed Trump at Shenzhen airport earlier on Wednesday, paying particular honour to Trump by greeting him with a hug, reciprocating a gesture the US president made during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding positive relationship.
Trump said that during the unprecedented trilateral meeting on Thursday he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about ending Russia’s ongoing all-out war in Ukraine, declaring on Tuesday that “I think it’s very close to getting it done".
“We are going to have a good meeting on that," Trump said.
The three leaders are also expected to discuss trade and nuclear issues as well as the Iran war.
Beijing announced the trilateral meeting as “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the APEC meeting, while Putin said that he expected the summit to be “highly useful”.
Trump has signalled that he wants to take an improvised approach at the APEC summit, betting that his unscripted brand of diplomacy, based on personal relationships, can create a legacy by reshaping world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
Europe and the world will be watching as Trump meets with two of Washington's largest geopolitical rivals after relations with US’ historical allies such as Europe and Canada have turned sour over the last months.
Trump raised the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, which had not yet been confirmed by the time the US president arrived in China.
During his first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders meeting since 2017, Putin met his Chinese counterpart on Wednesday and took aim at what he called “instruments of economic dominance,” such as the sanctions imposed on Russia following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
“Sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions” have “outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect,” Putin told a CEO summit on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
He highlighted his country’s desire to cultivate closer economic ties with the Asia-Pacific, saying the region accounts for more than half of its total trade.
Xi calls for open trade and equitable growth
In a speech on the sidelines of the APEC summit on Wednesday, the Chinese president told business executives that the Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
"China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further. We will carry out reform in challenging areas such as rules, regulation, and standards,” Xi said, reiterating Beijing’s pledges to improve conditions for global investors.
"While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said.
“It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticising the US shift toward protecting its own markets.
Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone, as Washington limits on Chinese access to cutting-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Trump is expected to seek to reinforce the US status as the world’s leading technology power.
His tariffs, intended to curb China's trade surplus, have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than it imported.
When answering reporters about US policies towards Beijing's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “we have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may extend the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
Trump has also said that during his talks with Xi, he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by US companies, but expects Xi to push him on Taiwan’s sovereignty.
“I’m sure he’ll raise it,” Trump said. “I won’t have to raise it.”
The 21 APEC economies account for 60% of global economic activity, half of global trade and 40% of humanity. The leaders will meet behind closed doors on Thursday, while holding other meetings on the event’s sidelines.
APEC does not take binding decisions, but over 37 years it has served as a forum for building a consensus on cooperation and more open trade.
The APEC summit is showcasing Shenzhen, which China has transformed in the past four decades from a fishing village into a skyscraper-studded centre for export manufacturing and technology.

noticias.titulo: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as petrol and diesel prices climb
noticias.resumen: Higher fuel prices pushed UK inflation up from 3.5% in September to 3.6% in October. Diesel hit a record high, while prices for food and non-alcoholic drinks rose at their slowest pace in five years.
noticias.texto:
Higher fuel prices pushed UK inflation up from 3.5% in September to 3.6% in October. Diesel hit a record high, while prices for food and non-alcoholic drinks rose at their slowest pace in five years.
Annual inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% the previous month, largely driven by the jump in the cost of motor fuels.
"Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate," said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Motor fuel prices rose by 33.2% in the year to October, up from 29.8% in September. It was the fastest rise since July 2022. Petrol prices rose to their highest level since August 2022, while diesel prices hit a record high.
Higher fuel prices meant transport contributed the most to the rise in the overall inflation rate. Transport prices rose by 7.5% in the year to October, up from 6.6% in September.
Meanwhile, inflation for food and non-alcoholic drinks eased to 0.9% from 1.3%, its lowest since September 2021.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was unchanged at 2.8%.
The overall consumer price index rose by 0.5% in October compared with the previous month.
Sanjay Raja, Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, said: "Overall, today’s print was far softer than we ourselves expected." He said food prices were rising slowly, although they were widely expected to rise faster in 2027.
What does this mean for interest rates?
"Today’s inflation data will give the Bank of England some breathing space," Raja said. He added that inflation was still uncomfortably high, but both the overall and core rates were 0.1 percentage points below the Bank’s forecasts. Services inflation, which held at 3.7%, was also lower than the Bank had expected.
The Bank raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% in early November to curb inflation. It was the first increase in more than three years.
"Looking beyond October, we still think the worst is yet to come," Raja said. He expects Ofgem’s cap on household energy prices to rise by more than 20% in January and food inflation to climb again. He also pointed to the expiry of two temporary tax cuts in July 2027, one on petrol and diesel and the other on household electricity in Great Britain.
The Bank of England’s November forecast put inflation at around 5% in mid-2027. In a separate scenario in which energy prices rose sharply and stayed high, the Bank projected that inflation could reach about 6.2% in the third quarter.
Raja expects inflation to peak well below the Bank’s forecast. He thinks higher energy costs will have less of an effect on wages and other prices than the Bank expects.
Raja said, "We see CPI pushing above 4% early next year – and sticking above 3% y/y all year."
He expects inflation to slow towards 3% by the end of 2027 as earlier energy price rises drop out of the annual comparison and gas prices ease. He said a sustained return to the Central Bank’s 2% target "looks unlikely before late 2028".

noticias.titulo: EU-UK summit: Leaked draft reveals ambition and limits of Brexit reset
noticias.resumen: A decade after the Brexit referendum, Brussels and London are poised to deepen ties on trade, defence and energy, but draft summit conclusions seen by Euronews reveal lingering political divisions.
noticias.texto:
A decade after the Brexit referendum, Brussels and London are poised to deepen ties on trade, defence and energy, but draft summit conclusions seen by Euronews reveal lingering political divisions.
EU and UK leaders meet in Brussels on Friday for a pivotal summit that could mark the most decisive political break with the Brexit era, a decade after the referendum that drove the two sides apart.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has made rebuilding relations with Europe a political priority since taking office in July, has been openly critical of Brexit, describing the current relationship with the EU as "not good enough" and even floating the prospect of rejoining the bloc.
With Europe under growing pressure to take greater responsibility for its own security and boost its economic competitiveness, there is also a political imperative on both sides of the Channel to put years of acrimony behind them.
Brussels and London are expected to unveil a package of agreements covering trade, defence industry cooperation, agrifood standards, youth mobility, economic security and access to the EU electricity market.
Draft summit conclusions circulated to European governments on Tuesday evening shed light on how the EU and UK intend to forge closer ties than at any point since Britain left the bloc in 2020.
But the document, seen by Euronews, also reveals the limits of the rapprochement, with negotiators still haggling over several politically sensitive issues just days before the summit.
Bilateral agreements
The two sides have all but finalised an agreement to align agrifood standards, which would scrap existing border controls and certification requirements for “the vast majority” of animal and plant products traded between the UK and the EU from 1 March 2028.
They are also expected to confirm a deal linking the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), which would remove the need for carbon border levies on trade between them, although the draft statement sets no date for its application.
Sticking points remain over a deal integrating the UK into the EU electricity market. Britain has some of the highest energy prices in Europe, while Brussels wants to make access conditional on a financial contribution to the bloc’s funding for its poorest regions. Both sides commit to concluding negotiations in 2027.
The EU and UK are also set to launch a digital partnership in early 2027 covering secure connectivity, artificial intelligence and digital identities. However, a commitment to apply the EU's AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act to Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework has been struck out.
Youth mobility
Youth mobility remains a key point of contention. EU countries want their students to receive equal treatment at British universities, notably on tuition fees, while the UK argues that it attracts far more European students than it sends to the continent.
The thorny question of fees has been moved into a parallel agreement. The draft statement currently contains two options: equal treatment for EU nationals or “significantly reduced undergraduate fees.”
The statement sets a clear timeline for the Youth Experience Scheme (TES), which would let young people live in each other’s territory for up to three years to work or study.
The aim is to seal the agreement by 2028 at the latest and have the scheme running by January 2030. The total number of participants has not been decided yet, although sources say it is likely to be around 100,000.
Defence integration
Defence industry cooperation has been a source of friction, with France pushing to restrict British firms' access to the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme over concerns about competition from across the Channel.
But the two sides are being pushed closer, as the US eyes a drawdown of its military presence in Europe, while also backing Ukraine’s war effort and attempting to fill the strategic gaps the Americans leave behind.
The UK has already been included in the Ukraine Support Loan, and the summit looks set to pave the way for closer defence industrial integration.
“Given the global security context, we intend to enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues and will identify ways to deepen capability collaboration, taking into account the objective of developing resilient European supply chains and capabilities and addressing critical capability gaps, including through the Capability Coalitions,” the text reads.
The Capability Coalitions allow EU member states to work together to address military shortfalls in strategic areas such as air defence, drones and ammunition.
Steel safeguards
Earlier this year, the EU adopted steel safeguards to counter Chinese overcapacity, which affected all exporters to the European market, including the UK.
The two sides now commit to exploring bilateral safeguards based on their respective quota allocations, to protect their industries from global overcapacity.
“A long-term sustainable solution for movement of UK originating steel to Northern Ireland would also be put in place,” the document states.
Economic security
London and Brussels will set up a dialogue on economic security, covering export controls, technology leakage in critical sectors and supply chain disruption.
A reference to coordination on market access, public procurement and subsidies has been removed. Discussions within the EU on whether a European preference in public procurement should also apply to the UK are still ongoing.
Notably, the EU wants the UK to ensure its national policies produce outcomes equivalent to the bloc’s, while London has proposed much softer language on protecting supply chains consistently and pre-empting circumvention.
Home affairs and migration
The EU's demand that the UK suspend its regime for deporting foreign national offenders has been dropped from the statement. Instead, the two sides commit to providing advance notice of such removals and exploring bilateral cooperation on prisoner transfers.
The two sides also acknowledge the difficulties law enforcement authorities face in obtaining electronic data from other jurisdictions. They commit to exploring ways “to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third country nationals, in the light of technical developments.”
The statement calls for more systematic, structured and reciprocal information exchange between EU member states and the UK to prevent migrant smuggling and human trafficking across the Channel, including by enabling the work of the EU border agency Frontex.

noticias.titulo: Marco Rubio says no evidence recent tech outages in US are linked or 'nefarious'
noticias.resumen: Air travel was disrupted because of what the Trump administration called outdated equipment, causing regulators to halt all flights from taking off for several hours on Friday evening.
noticias.texto:
Air travel was disrupted because of what the Trump administration called outdated equipment, causing regulators to halt all flights from taking off for several hours on Friday evening.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took time during a high-level diplomatic summit in Asia on Wednesday to try and soothe public US jitters over a spate of cyber-related disruptions.
Rubio insisted authorities have found "zero evidence" that recent outages across tech platforms are related to one another or due to the work of "nefarious actors."
His comments, on the sidelines of a Southeast Asia summit, follow multiple disruptions of everything from US air traffic operations to Microsoft email and messaging to banking and mobile pay, as well as the outage of a top-secret US government communications network.
"The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever, we have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other," Rubio told reporters in Manila while on a trip to Asia with US President Donald Trump.
"The second is that we have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind."
Rubio emphasised the ubiquity of technology when explaining why it could feel as if there was a growing wave of cyber incidents.
"The more technology becomes embedded into our everyday lives, the more the vulnerabilities become real," he said.
"There was a time when people used to physically go in with masks and guns and rob banks. Now they can do it from behind a computer screen halfway around the world and every major economy in the world is facing that same challenge."
NSA internal comms down
On Tuesday a top-secret network that the National Security Agency (NSA) uses for internal communications went down, the agency acknowledged.
The NSA said it had experienced "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," but that its capabilities remained operational and "our ability to defend national security continues."
The NSA, part of the US Department of Defence, is responsible for global monitoring, collection and processing of information for intelligence and counterintelligence.
The Trump administration has insisted Americans and their various systems remain secure, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin emphasizing that the wave of recent outages does not stem from cyber criminals.
"I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack," Mullin told CNBC. "There's no cyber threat that's taking place. The homeland is very secure."
Air travel was disrupted because of what the Trump administration called outdated equipment, causing regulators to halt all flights from taking off for several hours on Friday evening.
The mess of stranded travellers and aircrews spilled into the weekend and early this week.
Microsoft also suffered a major outage last week that affected Outlook and Teams users around the world, while several large banks saw disruptions to their banking apps and online portals on Monday.
Trump's rival Democratic Party, which just won decisively in US midterm elections earlier this month, blamed the administration's incompetence for the string of high-visibility outages and the lack of transparency around them.
"We've had the Microsoft incident, then we had the nationwide ground stop. Now we have concerns as it relates to highly classified servers over at the NSA," Hakeem Jeffries, a top Democrat in Congress, told reporters.
"I think it's time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves, so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken and we can inform the people of the United States of America."

noticias.titulo: Mexico owns the only non-Chinese panda in the world: President Sheinbaum asks Xi Jinping for a mate
noticias.resumen: Claudia Sheinbaum met Chinese president Xi Jinping at the APEC summit.
noticias.texto:
Claudia Sheinbaum met Chinese president Xi Jinping at the APEC summit.
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum has asked Chinese President Xi Jinping for a panda during a meeting in China.
The Chapultepec zoo, in Mexico City, is home to Xin Xin, a 36-year-old female regarded as the only giant panda in the world that does not belong to China. She is the last descendant of a line of giant pandas that arrived in Mexico in 1975.
"Next year marks the 55th anniversary of relations between Mexico and China, a very important date," Sheinbaum, a known environmentalist, told reporters in Shenzhen.
"We spoke about advancing in the field of tourism and we also asked for a panda for the Chapultepec zoo as part of this cooperation," she explained on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. "So it was a very good, very cordial and very frank meeting," added the Mexican politician.
What is panda diplomacy?
In the 1940s China began sending pandas to different countries abroad to strengthen diplomatic ties. But since the 1980s, the pandas came with strings attached: they are loaned to other countries for fixed periods in return for a financial contribution that goes towards programmes to conserve the species in the wild.
The contributions seem to be working - in 2021, China removed pandas from its endangered species list.
Native to the temperate forests of East Asia, these large black-and-white mammals do not usually roam over long distances in the wild. However, many have been moved to zoos around the world as part of the 'panda diplomacy' programme, a strategy Beijing has used for decades to strengthen relations with other countries.
Mexico's story is an example of this diplomatic dimension. In 1975, China gave the country a pair of giant pandas, Ying Ying and Pe Pe. The Mexico City government has said that this gift was part of a diplomatic agreement that symbolised friendship and cooperation between the two countries.
Earlier this year, Beijing demanded the return of the two pandas it had in Japan, amid a diplomatic dispute that began after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested that Tokyo could intervene militarily if there were an attack on Taiwan.
Sheinbaum also told Xi on Tuesday that relations between Mexico and China are entering a "new era". For his part, the Chinese president called for raising bilateral ties to "a higher level" in view of the complex international situation.

noticias.titulo: Iran’s army chief vows ‘more crushing’ response if US attacks again
noticias.resumen: Army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami said Iranian forces would strike the US “along with its supporters” wherever they were based, as CENTCOM confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt had joined two other carriers in the region.
noticias.texto:
Army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami said Iranian forces would strike the US “along with its supporters” wherever they were based, as CENTCOM confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt had joined two other carriers in the region.
Iran's army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami warned on Wednesday that if Iran were attacked again, its forces would deliver a "more crushing, harsher response, without geographical limitation," threatening to strike the US and its allies regardless of where they were based.
"If the enemy once again takes action, it will without doubt be dealt with more crushingly, more harshly and without geographical limitation, along with its supporters," Hatami said.
He said he hoped the other side would not "miscalculate," warning that if it did, "it will receive a lesson that will be a warning to everyone."
Hatami said the US had brought a new aircraft carrier into the region and that Iranian ground, naval, air and air defence forces were monitoring military movements and continuously raising their readiness.
He said the necessary preparations to counter possible attacks had been put in place under orders issued to senior commanders.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has confirmed the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the region, bringing the number of US carriers operating there to three.
Iran claims drone downed
The Iranian army's public relations department said its forces had destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz using domestically produced air defence systems deployed in the south-east of the country and operated through an integrated air defence network.
The claim has not been independently verified and Washington has not commented.
Yadollah Javani, political deputy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), claimed Tehran's forces could now strike or intercept advanced drones in areas including the Strait of Hormuz and Qeshm Island, citing advances in Iranian missile and electronic warfare capabilities.
On Tuesday, the US carried out air strikes on positions on Qeshm Island, following Iranian reports of attacks on US military installations in the region.
There have also been reports of attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has warned that any further attack would draw a military response not confined to targets within Iranian borders.
The US has said it will protect its forces and its allies' interests in the region.

noticias.titulo: Peru releases seven pelicans rescued from El Niño's effects
noticias.resumen: Seven rehabilitated pelicans return to the wild in Peru as the country opens its first state-run marine wildlife centre to protect seabirds affected by El Niño.
noticias.texto:
Seven Peruvian pelicans were released back into the wild near Lima, Peru, on Tuesday, 17 November 2026, after around a month of rehabilitation.
The birds returned to their natural habitat on a beach near Los Pantanos de Villa Wildlife Refuge, marking the opening of the country's first state-run rehabilitation centre for marine wildlife affected by El Niño.
Established by Peru's wildlife service SERFOR and Universidad Científica del Sur, the centre can care for more than 100 marine and coastal animals at a time. Staff provide veterinary treatment and supervised feeding before the animals are ready for release. Two Humboldt penguins remain at the facility.
The centre opens as warmer ocean waters linked to El Niño disrupt food supplies, leaving seabirds weakened along the Peruvian coast.

noticias.titulo: Burnham’s 10-year plan lined up for Dec. 17 publication
noticias.resumen: It would be the last possible date before MPs leave for their Christmas recess.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Downing Street officials have pencilled in Dec. 17 for the publication of Andy Burnham’s “10-year plan,” a person with knowledge of the conversations has told POLITICO. Britain’s prime minister promised the document when delivering his first speech in office and has said it will show his “clear vision for Britain,” including on energy and industrial policy and public control of utilities. Officials are looking at the Dec. 17 date in the hope of fulfilling Burnham’s pledge to publish it by the end of 2026, said the person, who was granted anonymity to discuss internal planning. Burnham suggested earlier this month that the plan might be delayed until January before recommitting to publishing it this year. It is the last date that he could publish the plan while sticking to his pledge, since it is the final sitting day of parliament before MPs’ Christmas recess. The person with knowledge of the conversations called it a “terrible decision,” since it would give MPs and the public little time to digest Burnham’s vision before the festive season. A second person with knowledge of the conversations said that the date was not set in stone. Downing Street declined to comment. An early draft for the plan has been circulating in Whitehall, and officials expect it to have around a dozen sections or chapters, including on Britain’s place in the world. In key areas, though, it is more likely to outline a broad vision than granular detail. This includes the future for England’s water sector, more details of which are set to follow in a cross-government spending review in 2027. Burnham has a mounting in-tray of issues to get through in the next month. Before Christmas, the prime minister has pledged to outline long-term options for moving closer to the EU, respond to two major reviews on reforming welfare benefits, and spell out more details of his plan to move power and resources to England’s regions.

noticias.titulo: Commission accused of withholding emails on killing patent law
noticias.resumen: Lawmakers suggested the U-turn came following a meeting between JD Vance and Ursula von der Leyen.
noticias.texto: LUXEMBOURG — The European Commission was accused Wednesday of withholding internal messages that explain why it dropped a contentious patent proposal, amid claims of pressure from U.S. Vice President JD Vance. At a court hearing in Luxembourg, judges were told that German center-left MEP Tiemo Wölken asked the Commission for internal notes on why the proposal was abruptly killed in early 2025. He was told there was only one relevant internal document: minutes of a private meeting between heads of cabinet, which the Commission refused to hand over. Wölken’s lawyers said the absence of information was hard to believe given how contentious the proposal had become. It was “unbelievable” that there were “zero emails on this highly-politicized, economically-relevant procedure,” Carsten Zatschler, Wölken’s lawyer, said at the EU’s General Court. “All of this apparently happened without any form of electronic communication,” Zatschler said. “That’s quite simply not credible.” In February 2025, the Commission announced it was withdrawing plans for a standard essential patents (SEPs) regulation on the licensing of patents, saying there was no “clear signal of support” from co-legislators. Negotiations between the European Parliament and EU countries were ongoing at the time. The proposal was officially killed in July that year. The proposal had triggered a fierce lobbying battle between patent holders — including Nokia, Ericsson, Qualcomm and Huawei — and companies that license their technology, from phone makers to carmakers. The withdrawal was announced on the same day that Vance met with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at an AI summit in Paris, where they discussed AI, Ukraine and transatlantic ties. The timing prompted questions in the European Parliament about whether their conversation played a role in quashing the proposal. Zatschler asked: “Why was it surprisingly withdrawn? Whether a meeting between Ursula von der Leyen and U.S. Vice President JD Vance played a role, that’s obviously not something we need to discuss here.” “But whether it can be clarified should not be dependent on whether the European Commission categorized emails as important or not, because otherwise we would be putting the fox in charge of the hen house,” he said. Wölken was part of the negotiating team blindsided by the decision. “My team had met the Polish presidency [of the Council of the EU] just days before, and they were gearing up to finalize the Council position,” the lawmaker told POLITICO. “No one was informed.” “That alone raises questions about the withdrawal, which for me turned into a real concern after hearing rumors about the meeting between Ursula von der Leyen and JD Vance,” he said. The Commission did hand over 14 documents to the German MEP, most of which were emails and position papers from outside stakeholders sent to the Commission after the decision to kill the proposal was announced. Lawyers for the Commission told judges that Wölken’s request didn’t specify that he was seekend internal emails predating the decision. “These are professional lawyers,” said Tim Maxian Rusche, representing the Commission (Wölken is also a lawyer). “They work directly in Brussels. If they want internal correspondence, they’re going to have to specify that.” He added that the Commission is “being exposed to more and more fishing expeditions” where it is asked “very general” questions in access to document requests. “They need to make [requests] clear, because otherwise we can’t do our work,” he continued. The Commission is also facing a lawsuit from the European Parliament over the decision to kill the proposal. Last year, lawmakers voted to sue the Commission over the decision, arguing that it had overstepped its competence. “The Commission’s right to withdraw a proposal … cannot be used as a political instrument to short-circuit Parliament’s work or to enforce a deregulation agenda from above,” German Social Democrat René Repasi said. “This is not in line with how the democratic processes in the European Union are meant to function.” The judges did not confirm when a decision would be made in the case.

noticias.titulo: German government recruits World Cup hero Philipp Lahm to teach financial literacy
noticias.resumen: The former international full-back will take part in a program teaching financial literacy to young Germans.
noticias.texto:
Philipp Lahm, the former international defender who captained Germany to victory at the 2014 World Cup, has been tapped by his country's government to tackle another challenge: helping young Germans find the best savings account.
Lahm will become a "financial education ambassador" alongside actress Tomomi Themann, the ministry announced Wednesday. Both will work pro bono.
“As an ambassador for financial education, I want to highlight its value in making informed choices about how we live our lives, and do my part to make it accessible to society at large,” the ministry quoted him as saying in a press release.
Advertisement
Lahm's new job description calls for him to act as a “bridge-builder,” reaching people online, in clubs and at schools to “explain financial topics in an accessible way and to encourage people to take an active interest in their financial future.”
The move is part of a new government strategy to strengthen financial literacy in Germany, particularly among young people and women.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pitching the strategy as a way to promote greater equality. “Financial education is a matter of fairness. Only with the necessary financial knowledge does everyone have the chance to build an independent life and decide their own future,” the minister said in the press release.
Klingbeil is set to meet with Lahm and students at a Berlin school on Friday.

noticias.titulo: France’s Philippe steps up attacks on Le Pen and Mélenchon as his poll numbers slide
noticias.resumen: The center-right presidential candidate accused his rivals of harboring an "unhealthy fascination" with Russia's Vladimir Putin.
noticias.texto: PARIS — Center-right presidential hopeful Edouard Philippe is sharpening his attacks on his 2027 election rivals, Marine Le Pen and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, in a bid to revive his flagging presidential campaign. In a speech on Wednesday presenting his platform and the high-profile allies supporting his campaign, Philippe accused both Le Pen and Mélenchon of an “unhealthy fascination” with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and dangerous economic plans — including their expensive proposals to lower the retirement age — that could push France into a financial crisis. “If we take the measures proposed by Mrs. Le Pen or Mr. Mélenchon, a financial crisis will end up happening,” he said. “The financial crisis has started. If we do not take as early as 2027 the measures needed to restore our finances, we will suffer a disaster.” Philippe, who served as President Emmanuel Macron’s first prime minister, also challenged Le Pen and Mélenchon on Europe and foreign policy, arguing they are hiding their ambitions to deliver “a slow Frexit” or “brutal break with Europe.” Philippe was once seen as the best-placed moderate to beat Le Pen , but he has slumped in the polls, which now show the far-right Le Pen and far-left Mélenchon advancing to the runoff next spring. Doubts about Philippe have also spread among his close allies since the summer. His struggle has put French moderates in a bind, as no one among the glut of candidates crowding the race has distinguished themselves from the pack. Centrist former prime minister Gabriel Attal and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau have also lost ground in recent polls. Macron, who remains unpopular, cannot seek a third consecutive term. There are also two relative newcomers to the race: Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner and Cannes Mayor David Lisnard. “Philippe is falling, and there’s only one end; he’ll hit the ground,” said a centrist former minister who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Riner’s candidacy “has finished off the job and killed the center,” they added. Attal, Retailleau and Lisnard met Tuesday to hammer out a deal to organize a primary that would give a single candidate the best chance of advancing to the runoff. While they agreed to hold the contest in January and stage a few televised debates, they have not agreed on who should participate, Retailleau and Attal’s campaign teams told reporters. Philippe has repeatedly said he would not take part in a contest that would likely deepen divisions. But it will be difficult for him to ignore the primary if preparations accelerate and he continues to fall in opinion polls.

Mit dem ehemaligen Fußballweltmeister Thomas Berthold schickt die AfD […]
noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Björn Höcke nutzt den Volkstrauertag für eine gezielte Provokation und präsentiert stark überhöhte deutsche Opferzahlen zu Flucht, Vertreibung und alliierten Luftangriffen. Die AfD fordert einen Schlussstrich unter die NS-Vergangenheit, doch wie funktioniert diese geschichtspolitische Umdeutung genau, und auf welche fragwürdigen Quellen stützt sich die Partei dabei? Mit dem ehemaligen Fußballweltmeister Thomas Berthold schickt die AfD zudem einen Kandidaten für das Amt des Bundespräsidenten ins Rennen, der offenkundig Verschwörungserzählungen und Reichsbürger-Thesen verbreitet: Von Schattenmännern, die die Welt regieren, bis hin zu bizarren Gesundheitstipps. Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren, wie die AfD mit gezieltem Geschichtsrevisionismus eine neue nationale Identität stiften will. Zudem beleuchten sie, warum die Personalie Berthold die Zerrissenheit der Partei offenlegt und welche strategischen Ziele die Parteispitze mit solchen Nominierungen verfolgt. Den WELT-Artikel von Frederik Schindler über Björn Höckes Rede vom „deutschen Volkstrauertag“ gibt’s hier. „Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands? Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch. Fragen und Feedback gern an insideafd@politico.eu . noticias.titulo: Moldova summons Russia’s envoy over multiple drone incursions
noticias.resumen: “This is what the 'peace' promoted by the Kremlin looks like," fumed Chișinău's foreign ministry.
noticias.texto:
Moldova’s foreign ministry summoned the Kremlin’s ambassador-designate in Chișinău, Oleg Ozerov, on Wednesday morning after Russian drones violated the country’s airspace.
Seven drones entered Moldova’s airspace Tuesday afternoon, the country’s defense ministry said, including one over the capital Chișinău. At least five of them crashed on Moldovan territory.
“This is what the ‘peace’ promoted by the Kremlin looks like: attack drones flying over the capital of a free and sovereign state,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “Russia does not respect the Republic of Moldova or its people and is putting their lives at risk.”

noticias.titulo: Deutschland und Österreich fordern europäischen Eigentümer für TikTok
noticias.resumen: Nach dem Vorbild der USA wollen Deutschland und Österreich eine Neuordnung der Eigentumsverhältnisse bei TikTok erreichen.
noticias.texto: Berlin und Wien wollen TikToks Europageschäft aus der Kontrolle des chinesischen Mutterkonzerns ByteDance lösen. Damit sollen Nutzerdaten geschützt und der chinesische Einfluss auf die Plattform begrenzt werden. Der gemeinsame Vorstoß von Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer und Österreichs Digitalstaatssekretär Alexander Pröll folgt auf die Entwicklung in den USA. Dort hatte Präsident Donald Trump im vergangenen Jahr die Abspaltung des amerikanischen TikTok-Geschäfts durchgesetzt. Der chinesische Mutterkonzern ByteDance hält an der neuen US-Gesellschaft noch rund 20 Prozent. Trump hatte sein Vorgehen zunächst mit Bedenken hinsichtlich der nationalen Sicherheit begründet. Nun verfolgen Berlin und Wien einen ähnlichen Ansatz. Mit rund 200 Millionen Nutzern in der EU sei TikTok ein zentraler Akteur mit erheblicher Bedeutung für die Meinungsbildung und gesellschaftliche Teilhabe, erklärten Weimer und Pröll am Mittwoch in einer gemeinsamen Stellungnahme. Die Rolle der Plattform bei Wahlen wird bereits im Rahmen des Digital Services Acts untersucht. Wegen der Übermittlung europäischer Nutzerdaten nach China hatten Datenschutzbehörden TikTok zudem mit einer Geldbuße belegt. Die Minister erklären, TikTok stelle eine „sichtbare Bedrohung für unsere demokratische Gesellschaft“ dar. Eine „grundlegende Lösung müsse daher dort ansetzen, wo die Bedrohung für Europa ihren Ursprung hat: bei der chinesischen Muttergesellschaft ByteDance, deren Ausrichtung auf chinesische Interessen und den daraus resultierenden, nach wie vor unklaren Zugriffsmöglichkeiten des chinesischen Staates auf die Daten von Millionen europäischer Nutzer.“ Die Erklärung wurde im Vorfeld eines Treffens der Kulturminister veröffentlicht, das am Donnerstag in Brüssel stattfindet. Weimer und Pröll riefen andere EU-Staaten dazu auf, sich ihrer Initiative anzuschließen. Wie eine europäische Eigentümerstruktur konkret aussehen könnte, ließen sie allerdings offen. Axel Springer, die Muttergesellschaft von POLITICO, hat erklärt , sie werde jede Initiative unterstützen, die darauf abzielt, TikTok unter europäische Kontrolle zu bringen – als Reaktion auf Berichte, wonach der Medienkonzern an einer Beteiligung an der Social-Media-Plattform interessiert sei. TikTok reagierte nicht auf Anfrage. Dieser Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

noticias.titulo: Germany, Austria demand TikTok’s European platform be sold to owners in EU
noticias.resumen: Proposal comes after President Donald Trump forced TikTok to split out U.S. app.
noticias.texto: Germany and Austria say Chinese-owned TikTok should come under European ownership to safeguard personal data, boost sovereignty and curb the platform’s “openly visible threat to our democratic society.” The joint proposal Wednesday by top government ministers of the two countries comes after President Donald Trump forced the separation last year of TikTok’s operations into a U.S.-based entity, with its original owner, Beijing-based Bytedance holding about one-fifth of the new entity. Trump’s campaign to initially ban and later split up TikTok cited national security concerns. Now, Berlin and Vienna are going down a similar route. With 200 million EU users, TikTok is “a central player with significant relevance for opinion formation and social participation,” Germany’s media minister Wolfram Weimer and Austria’s State Secretary for Digitalization, Alexander Pröll said in a joint statement. A TikTok spokesperson said there was “zero merit” to the proposal. The platform’s role in elections is being investigated under the EU’s Digital Services Act, while regulators have fined the firm for sending Europeans’ data to China, in breach of privacy rules. The ministers say that TikTok is a “visible threat to our democratic society” and that a “fundamental solution should therefore start where the threat to Europe originates: with the Chinese parent company ByteDance, its alignment with Chinese interests, and the resulting continuously unclear access possibilities of the Chinese state to the data of millions of European users.” The statement comes ahead of a meeting of culture ministers taking place in Brussels Thursday. Weimer and Pröll called on other EU capitals to join their bid, but didn’t clarify how the new structure would work. POLITICO parent Axel Springer has said it would support any initiative to bring TikTok under European control in response to reports that the media conglomerate was looking for a stake in the social media platform. This article has been updated with TikTok’s response.

noticias.titulo: What kind of ECB is Europe getting after Lagarde?
noticias.resumen: Now that Paris and Berlin appear to have lined up Spanish central banker Pablo Hernández de Cos for the ECB presidency instead of his Dutch counterpart Klaas Knot, whether a dove or a hawk sits at the top may matter less than it seems, including for France.
noticias.texto: This week, eurozone finance ministers are expected to choose who will replace Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB). Lagarde is stepping down early, on 7 February, to weigh in on the French elections and to allow EU governments to choose a new leadership team before next year’s presidential vote in France, which could well see the far-right Marine Le Pen take over the reins of power. Speculation has been going on for months, and the Dutch former central bank chief, Klaas Knot, as well as Spain’s ex-central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, quickly emerged as frontrunners. For a long time it seemed Knot, with conditional support from Paris, stood the best chance, but in recent days it has become clear that Paris and Berlin appear to have struck a deal, and that De Cos will almost certainly be Lagarde’s successor. Another southerner at the top This came as a disappointment in The Hague, where the feeling was that southern countries are overrepresented in European financial institutions. As the Dutch daily newspaper de Volkskrant said , “the Eurogroup is chaired by a Greek, the European Investment Bank is headed by a Spaniard, the European supervisory body for financial markets is chaired by an Italian, and the European Banking Authority has a Frenchman as president.” And now the ECB’s top spot will be filled by another Spaniard. The question is how a de Cos presidency might differ from one led by Knot. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: Xi keen to look ‘neutral’ on Ukraine at Shenzhen summit, as China risks spoiling EU relations by helping Putin to wage war
noticias.resumen: As Xi, Putin, and Trump gather in Shenzhen, Beijing is stretching its “neutral” pose to maintain a war‑fuelling trade lifeline for Moscow.
noticias.texto: Chinese president Xi Jinping and his Russian and US counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, are meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday (19 November) to discuss the war in Ukraine. China is seen as having considerable economic and diplomatic influence over Russia, but has so far shown little appetite to use this leverage to push the Kremlin towards concessions in peace talks. Xi and Putin began talks in Shenzhen on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, but whether Ukraine will dominate the agenda of Thursday’s trilateral summit remains uncertain. US officials had initially signalled that Ukraine might not be discussed, but Trump later said it would be. Beijing, for its part, has framed the summit more broadly, with China’s foreign ministry saying the three leaders would discuss “safeguarding world peace.” The meeting in Shenzhen comes after discussions in Abu Dhabi among the US, Russia, and Ukraine last week ended with an agreement to exchange 314 prisoners. And with peace talks gaining momentum, Beijing is positioning itself as an indispensable mediator, while avoiding responsibility for delivering a settlement. Beijing is trying to preserve a strategic relationship with Moscow, while maintaining its economic relations with Europe and presenting itself as a responsible global power. “These objectives are not always compatible, and the war in Ukraine has made those contradictions increasingly visible,” said Maria Adele Carrai, an international relations professor and a member of the Oxford School of Global and Area Studies ( OSGA ), at the University of Oxford. Dimitar Lilkov, a senior research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies in Brussels, also told EUobserver: “It is interesting to see if and how Xi Jinping is actually involved in a potential meeting, given that he considers Vladimir Putin as a junior partner.” Analysts have often called Russia China’s “junior partner”, given Moscow’s growing dependence on China for trade, energy, and technology after Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. China abstained from a United Nations Security Council vote denouncing the invasion in 2022, and Xi has maintained close political ties with Putin ever since. Portraying itself as an outsider to the conflict, Beijing has repeatedly said it is ready to promote peace talks and has conducted diplomatic shuttle missions and multilateral initiatives through its special representative Li Hui, but its diplomatic activity has not been matched by public pressure on Putin. “Its public support for talks stays at the level of general principles,” said Alicia García Herrero, a senior fellow at Bruegel Institute in Brussels. Status without responsibility China has consistently maintained that it is neither “the creator of the Ukraine crisis” nor “a party to it”, while calling for dialogue based on principles outlined by Xi, including respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the UN Charter, as well as attention to the legitimate security concerns of all sides. noticias.titulo: Centrist and leftwing MEPs boycott rightwing NGO funding probe, which found no wrongdoing
noticias.resumen: As rightwing MEPs present their 71-page NGO funding report, centre and left-wing deputies stay away in protest, accusing the scrutiny group of bending parliament rules and sidelining their input.
noticias.texto: Centre and left-wing MEPs boycotted another meeting of the European Parliament’s Scrutiny Working Group (SWG) on NGO funding on Wednesday (18 November), at which rightwing MEPs presented a 71-page report on their year-long probe that found no wrongdoing. In a joint press statement , MEPs from the S&D, Renew Europe, The Greens/EFA, and The Left accused the SWG, which was set up by the European People’s Party (EPP) and the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), of becoming “a political instrument” to undermine civil society. MEPs also accused the group of breaching parliament’s rules on confidentiality and democratic participation. No amendments to the report will be allowed when the Committee on Budgetary Control votes on it. “Having found nothing, the scrutiny working group has shown its real intent with its final document: attack civil society organisations and the democratic space they represent,” the statement of the cross-party group of MEPs said. Wednesday’s boycott follows a walkout at the group’s first meeting in November 2025, after which centre and left-wing MEPs refused to take part in its work. In the final report , authors Dirk Gotink, a Dutch centre-right MEP, and Carlo Fidanza, an Italian conservative, admitted they found no proof of wrongdoing or financial misconduct by NGOs or the commission. Nor did they find evidence that EU authorities had required NGOs getting EU funds to carry out advocacy, or whether they had any impact on policy outcomes at all. But the report still includes 23 recommendations to the commission, such as imposing five-year funding bans on organisations that lobby EU and national institutions, phasing out core operating support, and introducing administrative ring-fencing requirements. Read more Rightwing MEPs switch attack from facts to ‘perceptions’, after a failed witch-hunt against NGOs in Brussels Presenting the report to rightwing MEPs on Wednesday, after centre and left-wing groups stayed away, Gotink said some of these recommendations should apply only to a limited number of NGOs that “behave very much like the consultants”. “We want civil society to engage” but “they do not need to be here with amendments in their pockets and trying to influence our legislative outcomes,” he said. Still the gap in lobbying firepower between industry and NGOs remains huge. The EU’s biggest industry lobbyists, including Meta, Amazon, Apple, Shell and Bayer, spend at least €381.75m a year lobbying EU institutions, according to Corporate Europe Observatory and LobbyControl . By contrast, environmental NGOs receive roughly €15.6m a year in operating grants from the EU’s LIFE programme, according to media reports . Contracts between the commission and NGOs under the LIFE programme were among those reviewed by the scrutiny group, which examined over a hundred contracts. ‘Not a single euro’ One of the problems, Gotink said, was that EU money was going to NGOs that lobby MEPs and take legal action to enforce EU law. Pointing to what the report calls a “ persistent perception ” of closeness between the commission and the NGOs it funds, he argued that the EU executive does not need a “network of external actors to emphasise even more their proposals or make sure that they survive the legislative process.” Yet back in February, Gotink had said that “the problem that we’re pursuing here is not to establish whether things are illegal, it is to establish whether politically it is undesirable.” His co-author, Fidanza, also said the next long-term EU budget must have “all the tools possible to ensure that not a single euro of European public money is spent in a way that doesn’t bring benefits to European citizens,” calling for “reciprocal transparency between the institutions and civil society.” But centre and left-wing MEPs said in their statement that if transparency were the real concern, “the same scrutiny would apply to all beneficiaries.” What about the consultants? On Wednesday, Gotink admitted the group could have done “much more” on the commission’s consultancy contracts, warning that “if the big four stop working for the commission today, the commission simply stops working.” The centre and left-wing MEPs also accused the working group of “effectively seeking to penalise the defence of EU fundamental values,” arguing that implementing the report’s recommendations “would shut civil society out of the debate on EU and national legislation.” Read more Why rightwing inquiry into Europe’s NGOs was never about transparency The report by Gotink and Fidanza comes after the European Commission unveiled in November 2025 its strategy for civil society , in a bid to “ensure an open, safe and enabling civic space” and support organisations “with adequate, sustainable and transparent funding”. The UN special envoy on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association Gina Romero raised concerns ahead of the committee meeting on Wednesday, arguing that “restricting operating grants risks starving civil society and undermining agendas crucial for the EU”. “Weaponising budgetary scrutiny to sideline critical voices weakens democratic checks and balances at the exact moment Europe needs them most,” she also said.

noticias.titulo: EU auditors say rules ‘full of holes’ leave health at risk from toxic forever chemicals
noticias.resumen: Three eggs or a beef steak contain a dangerous amount of cancerous forever chemicals and yet it can take up to a decade before new harmful substances are banned under EU law.
noticias.texto: Three eggs or a beef steak can contain a dangerous amount of toxic forever chemicals and yet it can take up to a decade for regulators to ban new harmful substances under EU law, shows a study published on Wednesday (18 November). Regulations lack current data and chemical legislation falls behind producers, which are constantly introducing new substances to the market, a report from the European Court of Auditors (ECA) found. On top of that, many member states do not enforce existing restrictions. Forever chemicals, of PFAS, are a group of some 1,400 substances used for everyday products, such as clothing, kitchenware, cosmetics, or shoes, making them waterproof, resistant to heat, and more stain-resistant. They take hundreds, if not thousands of years to decompose, which means that over time, they accumulate in water, soil, and even the human body, causing cancer, infertility, and hormonal problems. The EU pays some €39,5bn a year for healthcare costs related to PFAS, according to a report from 2024. Tackling water and soil pollution and fixing issues stemming from it (such as disrupted pollination of fruits) can cost around €440bn by 2050, if the EU keeps using forever chemicals as much as it does now, according to commission estimates . Read more ‘Forever chemicals’ lobbyists met EU Commission 37 times in push to escape ban ahead of key decision And the PFAS build-up in food, potable water, and air, means “we are in a race against time,” said Joëlle Elvinger, auditor heading the report, during a press briefing on Wednesday. noticias.titulo: Bridge Wars: Putin’s iconic Crimean Bridge destroyed despite ‘elite’ air-defences, but vital Kyiv bridge also close to collapse (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,728)
noticias.resumen: The sudden collapse of the Crimean Bridge’s key span, combined with precision Russian strikes on Kyiv’s lifeline bridges, threaten to choke off entire cities on both sides.
noticias.texto: It was considered difficult to destroy, but its end ultimately took only minutes. What weapons the Ukrainians used and how they guided them to the target. What went wrong according to the Russians — on 16 November they were delighted with their top-tier defences and elite crews; on 17 November they were left wondering. Ukraine will receive 10 F-16s, two Mirage 2000s and air-defence systems by the end of the year. Maps of the day — the Sloviansk direction; where Kyiv’s Northern Bridge is located and where Russian missiles damaged it . Videos of the day — the bridge attack from various perspectives; weapons used in the attack; the attack on Kyiv’s bridges; traffic collapse in Kyiv; Prince Harry visited a veterans’ hospital and met a soldier evacuated by a drone; the rescue of a nine-year-old boy from the Sumy region. It was considered difficult to destroy, but its end took only minutes. We have repeatedly written in the Ukraine Battlefield update that motorway bridges, including the one linking Russia with occupied Crimea, are difficult to destroy. They are massive reinforced-concrete structures that cannot be brought down even by repeated ballistic-missile strikes, as we are currently seeing in Russian attacks on Kyiv’s bridges. Moreover, the Ukrainian army does not yet possess such weapons. Nevertheless, it managed to destroy a symbol of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s rule over Crimea, to which he attached great personal importance. After all, he opened it himself. Watching the videos that follow, it may appear to have been surprisingly easy. But the entire operation was not only prepared over many months; it was also perfectly timed and executed. This enabled the Ukrainians to destroy a strategic target even without heavy long-range weapons, outpacing the Russians, who have the advantage of far greater resources in this area. How was this possible? Ukrainian, Russian and Western sources have commented on this in great detail. All of them will gradually be given space, along with visual evidence. First, you can watch footage from Wednesday morning. It demonstrates two things: the extent of damage to the railway section is unknown, but trains can still pass over it for now. Second, the road section has indeed been irreparably destroyed. Вперше опубліковані кадри знищеної автомобільної частини Кримського мосту зблизька. На жаль, залізнична частина продовжує функціонувати. Тимчасово. pic.twitter.com/QXrnd4IJMo — Serhii Sternenko (@sternenko) November 18, 2026 The outcome had been known since Tuesday, however. Far more interesting is how it came about. Before watching the videos, it should be noted that some have been edited and that individual clips may not precisely reflect the chronological sequence of events. But it all really happened surprisingly quickly, as even the Russian sources discussed later acknowledge. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: EU opts for voluntary targets to secure key materials used in high-tech industries
noticias.resumen: The blueprint announced on Wednesday is the latest move by the EU executive to make the bloc's industrial base more self-reliant, but lacks a legal base.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission, on Wednesday (18 November), set out three new targets to increase investment in and production of advanced materials by 20 percent, but shied away from proposing a new law that would enshrine them.
The EU executive says that it wants the Advanced Materials for Europe agenda to make the EU a world leader in designing, producing, and using safer and more sustainable advanced materials by 2035.
That will require EU states to work together to increase investment in advanced materials research and innovation by 20 percent, create 20 percent more EU-based startup businesses in the sector, and increase the number of projects reaching higher deployment levels in advanced materials by also 20 percent.
Advanced materials are engineered substances such as carbon fiber-reinforced polymer, silicon, alloys and ceramics which are used in the manufacturing of high-tech goods, primarily in the electronics, energy, construction, mobility, health, and aerospace defence sectors.
The blueprint is the latest move to shore up the EU’s industrial base and reduce its reliance on Chinese industrial inputs.
China also provides almost 100 percent of the EU’s supply of heavy rare earth elements, creating supply chain vulnerabilities and geopolitical risks.

noticias.titulo: Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták
noticias.resumen: Miklós Seszták, a minister under Viktor Orbán, is under investigation by Péter Magyar’s new anti-corruption body — and it took 12 treasury staff, five banknote-counting machines and eight hours to tally the €17m in buried cash linked to him.
noticias.texto: Earlier this week, Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar called for the resignation of parliament members belonging to former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party, as well as its ally, the Christian Democrats (KDNP). Magyar’s demands came after authorities last week found buried cash at the premises of former minister Miklós Seszták, a current KDNP lawmaker who served in Orbán’s cabinet. The money stolen by politicians under the previous government led to the decline of the Hungarian economy, Magyar told parliament in Budapest on Monday (16 November). Seszták was only one small cog in the entire mechanism, Magyar said. “If one person was able to bury so much money, how much money do you think disappeared during your rule over 16 years?” the prime minister asked MPs from Fidesz and KDNP. Péter Magyar addresses the Hungarian parliament (Source: MTI) There was every reason to fear that the revelations were only just beginning, Magyar said, adding that proceedings were under way in another 24 cases in which the government had filed criminal complaints. A total of 64 such complaints have now been filed over the past six months. “After this, does anyone still dare to say that Miklós Seszták was a lone perpetrator?” Magyar asked opposition MPs. “That your community excludes corrupt politicians from its ranks? On the contrary, for you it is a ticket into the party!” The Hungarian prime minister called on MPs from the former governing parties to apologise to Hungarian citizens and surrender their mandates. “After Friday’s footage, there can be no doubt that on 12 April we defeated the Hungarian Cosa Nostra ,” Magyar said. According to him, Fidesz was building an alternative reality “in which I almost buried the six and a half billion myself.” He added that the buried cash case was not only a warning to opposition MPs, but also a reminder to politicians in the current government that nobody is above the law. In his speech, Magyar thanked investigators, prosecutors, the police, the National Investigation Bureau and the National Asset Recovery (NNI) and Protection Office (NVVH) for their work, and called on everyone to cooperate with law enforcement. noticias.titulo: EU Commission ‘confident’ that Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia will join new €45bn Ukraine loan
noticias.resumen: The EU Commission has come up with a new financing plan to fill Ukraine's €70bn funding gap next year, and thinks it has found a way to convince member states who want to opt-out by clearly separating civilian from military spending
noticias.texto: The European Commission on Wednesday (18 November) proposed a new €45bn loan to Ukraine for 2027 — with president Ursula von der Leyen telling reporters she was “very confident” that all 27 member states will join, including hold-outs Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia. The new funding would cover roughly two-thirds of what the commission estimates is a €70bn hole in Kyiv’s budget next year. It comes on top of the €90bn Ukraine Support Loan agreed by EU leaders last December for 2026 and 2027, but which has proved insufficient as the cost of the war keeps rising. Of the new package, €20bn would go to budget support, split between macro-financial assistance and the Ukraine Facility, while €25bn is earmarked for military needs. “For almost five years Ukraine has stood guard against Russian aggression,” said EU economy commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who presented the proposal alongside von der Leyen and defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius. “Supporting Ukraine is not only the right thing to do, but also the smart thing to do,” he added. Dombrovskis also pointed to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, including government buildings and especially the energy grid. The new scheme largely copies the existing €90bn loan. That means that the commission will borrow the money on financial markets. The amount is backed by the so-called headroom in the EU budget, which refers to the margin between the maximum budget and what the EU actually spends. Ukraine will only have to repay the principal amount if Russia pays for the damage it has caused. The proposal consists of two legal texts. The instrument can pass by qualified majority. But whether the EU can borrow the money against the long-term budget requires unanimity. Allies asked to pay one third The commission hopes partners such as Canada and Japan will cover the rest of the gap. Various mechanisms are proposed to make that easier. First, the commission wants new G7 and EU loans to be repaid from the profits on frozen Russian assets, as is already the case for the 2024 G7 loans. “And we will [also] place our own loans under this provision,” the senior official said. So far just €4bn has been collected. The official expected the profits to amount to roughly €5-6bn a year, and said repayment would take “decades.” “I will be long retired, and probably worse than that, before this money comes back,” the official also said. Second, triple-A rated countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Canada could give guarantees to the EU budget, capped at €5bn, which provides a “relatively cost-efficient way to provide support to Ukraine,” another official said. So far no partner has signed up. “I cannot say that there is reassurance, there is no done deal, but there is interest expressed,” the official said. Who pays the interest? Ukraine is responsible for paying the interest, but officials admit Kyiv cannot afford it, so the first interest payments, due in 2028, could be covered by the EU’s next long-term budget for 2028-2034. The commission’s July 2025 budget proposal already includes a €100bn Ukraine reserve, and Dombrovskis said it remains to be negotiated whether the interest costs come on top of that amount or out of it. One official estimated EU borrowing costs for Ukraine over the next budget period at around €42bn, “depending on the pace of disbursement.” Those costs would be shared among member states according to the usual key based on gross national income. The commission will publish its borrowing plan for 2027 in the second half of December, officials told press. Opt-outs Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic did not contribute to the €90bn loan and, together with Bulgaria, want to stay out of the new one as well. “Slovakia will not participate in providing another loan to Ukraine … Period. We’ve done enough,” Slovakia’s prime minister Robert Fico again said ahead of an informal leaders’ summit in Dublin last week. But von der Leyen on Wednesday said she was “very confident that we will agree by 27,” and backed Merz’s call for all member states to take part. “I support the Chancellor in this idea too,” she said. Unlike last time, the loan will now be built within the EU’s long-term budget, meaning “shared budget, shared responsibilities,” von der Leyen said. By separating civilian from military spending in the legal text from the start, the commission hopes to win over the four hold-outs. There is “no problem to indirectly assign their commitments towards the civilian part,” von der Leyen also said. “For some it’s easier to associate it with civilian support than military,” a senior official later explained. EU leaders are expected to discuss the proposal and the next long-term budget at a special summit on 26-27 November.

noticias.titulo: Xi’s protocol choreography at APEC: a message in the greetings
noticias.resumen: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen has delivered the expected diplomatic set pieces: speeches ...
noticias.texto: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen has delivered the expected diplomatic set pieces: speeches on free trade, criticism of sanctions, and the prospect of a rare trilateral meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Yet the most widely circulated images and videos from the opening day have focused less on the statements than on the staging. Xi personally met Trump on the tarmac as Air Force One arrived, an unusual gesture for a Chinese leader. The two shared a brief embrace before walking to their motorcades, accompanied by a red carpet, honour guard elements and a military flyover. Chinese state media framed the reception as reciprocity for Trump’s personal greeting of Xi at Joint Base Andrews in September. It was the first time Xi has extended such a welcome to a foreign leader at an airport since taking office. Videos of Putin’s arrival showed him being greeted on the tarmac by Cai Qi, a senior Chinese official roughly 20 cm taller, a height contrast that was widely noted and commented. Subsequent videos show the Russian president approaching Trump and Xi ahead of the leaders’ group photograph. The two exchanged a handshake and brief words while Xi stood nearby, observing. Not only that, he was met by the tallest Chinese man they could find, making putin look like a child beside him. https://t.co/wxqZPkTbD6 pic.twitter.com/B4F35p1nYY — Ole Stålesen (@night_waker) November 18, 2026 In the sequences before the formal group photograph, Trump was seen gesturing as if to position Putin beside him, but Chinese protocol staff directed Putin instead to a place farther along the front row, next to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, with Xi remaining at the centre and Trump standing immediately beside him. Trump tried to pull Putin right next to him for the family photo, only for Xi to send the Russian dictator further down the line — not even next to Xi, but past China’s First Lady. Watch Putin shuffling off to the sidelines, looking visibly deflated. Global superpower, my ass 😁 pic.twitter.com/liGtJ4qad4 — Kate from Kharkiv (@BohuslavskaKate) November 18, 2026 At the banquet, Xi and Trump arrived together and were seated next to each other, while Putin had been brought into the hall earlier and waited for them; once seated, he was placed at a different table rather than in an equally prominent position alongside the two. 🚨 Xi and Trump arrived at the APEC gala dinner together. Putin wasn’t brought along While the U.S. and Chinese leaders walked side by side, the Kremlin dictator appears to be sitting in the front row waiting: behind one balding guest, the “Russia” sign is clearly visible.… https://t.co/OeGOucVCGX pic.twitter.com/TNQfgHORy3 — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 18, 2026 Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a markedly cooler reception. She arrived to no welcome ceremony and was met only by a retired Chinese diplomat, in contrast to the fanfare and high-level greeters accorded other leaders. At the banquet she exchanged a brief handshake with Xi, who responded with little more than a smile and no substantive exchange, and she received no further attention from the hosts throughout the events. The minimal protocol was widely read as a deliberate signal of Beijing’s continuing displeasure over her remarks on Taiwan. Takaichi did not receive a warm reception when she arrived in China for the APEC summit. The video on the right shows how China welcomed South Korean President Lee (which was similar to the greeting given to President Trump). pic.twitter.com/lvX7Gf33ux — Jeffrey J. Hall 🇯🇵🇺🇸 (@mrjeffu) November 18, 2026 Protocol in Chinese statecraft is rarely incidental. The contrast – a personal airport greeting and embrace for the U.S. president versus a more conventional reception for the Russian leader – has been interpreted by observers as a deliberate political signal. It places the bilateral U.S.-China relationship at the centre of the summit’s optics while treating the Russia relationship as established and less in need of public reinforcement. The three leaders are scheduled to meet together on Thursday on the summit’s sidelines, a first such trilateral gathering. Earlier in the day, Xi had used his APEC address to call for free and open trade and investment. Putin, for his part, criticised Western sanctions and described some Western powers as “former hegemons.” The formal speeches set the policy tone; the carefully arranged greetings and handshakes supplied the visual one. In Chinese diplomatic practice, the distinction between a personal airport welcome and a standard group-photo encounter is understood by both participants and audiences as conveying relative priority. The trilateral meeting on Thursday will determine whether the choreography of arrival and greeting translates into any substantive outcome on trade, Ukraine, or other issues. For now, the images of who was met on the tarmac, who initiated the handshake, and who stood where have already circulated more widely than the prepared remarks. Caption: US President Donald Trump (C, top) disembarks the plane as Chinese President Xi Jinping (C, bottom) waits to greet him upon arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, 18 November 2026. China is hosting the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen from 18 to 19 November. EPA/KEVIN FRAYER / POOL

noticias.titulo: Crosetto calls for a 5,000+ Italian cyber force and a European response to hybrid warfare
